## HIPPOCRATES ON ANCIENT MEDICINE. <note>original: "De Veteri Medicina"</note>

**M**edicine has already existed from ancient times, and both a principle and a path have been discovered, through which many and excellent things have been found over a long period of time; and **THE REST** will likewise **BE DISCOVERED** thereafter, if someone is capable and, being acquainted with what has already been found, proceeds from these to further inquiry. But whoever, having rejected and disapproved of all these, attempts to investigate by another path and in another form, and boasts of having found something: he is deceived and is mistaken, etc. By these words, the Paracelsian <note>The medical doctrines of Paracelsus (1493–1541), which often rejected classical tradition in favor of alchemy and mysticism.</note> school is criticized just as much as the spurious chemistry-hating <term>Misochymica</term> <note>Literally "chemistry-haters," from the Greek 'miso' (hate) and 'chymia' (chemistry); referring to traditional physicians who rejected chemical medicines.</note> Galenism. <note>The traditional medical system based on the works of Galen (129–c. 216 AD).</note>

<summary>Libavius quotes Hippocrates to argue that medical progress must be built upon established ancient knowledge rather than radical new theories. He uses this authority to attack both the followers of Paracelsus and those traditional Galenists who refuse to incorporate chemistry into medicine.</summary>

<keywords>Hippocrates, Ancient Medicine, Paracelsus, Galenism, Misochymists, medical methodology, history of medicine</keywords>

# ANDREAS LIBAVIUS
## To the Reader, Greetings. <note>original: "Lectori S.," an abbreviation for "Lectori Salutem."</note>

**L**EST <note>The original Latin begins with a decorative initial 'N' for 'Ne' (Lest).</note> you be unaware, Reader, of what is happening here, I must briefly advise you. In this way, you will both understand and judge more correctly. Since **Alchemy**, that mystical discipline of the wise Philosophers—a work of great and perfect mastery, as *Geber* <note>An 8th-century figure, often called the father of chemistry, though many works under his name are later medieval additions.</note> and *Mesue* <note>Referring to the influential medieval medical and pharmaceutical writings attributed to Johannes Mesue.</note> say—continually gained greater and more brilliant advancements in both theory and practice within France and Germany through the efforts of industrious men (among whom **JOSEPH** <term>Quercetanus</term> <note>The Latinized name of Joseph Du Chesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent French physician and advocate for chemical medicines.</note>, physician and counselor to the Most Christian King of France, holds a leading place), it happened that on the occasion of a book published by Quercetanus titled: *On the Material of the True Medicine of the Ancient Philosophers, its Method of Preparation, and its Excellence in Curing Diseases*, <note>original: "De priscorum philosophorum verae medicinae materia, praeparationis modo, atque in curandis morbis praestantia"</note> etc., the school of Parisian physicians was provoked. They condemned it with one impulse and, petitioning the magistrate, they demanded that anyone who used other remedies in healing should be punished by death,

->### TO THE READER<-

...besides those things which he calls ordinary—that is, those described by **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and others of that faction, which are available everywhere in pharmacies, both those of old standing and those which are forged anew daily according to their model. In these, there is either nothing of the Chemical, or only certain rudiments, such as infusions, decoctions, and extracts <note>original: "insusa, decocta, expressa." These are traditional pharmaceutical preparations involving soaking, boiling, or squeezing, which Libavius considers primitive compared to advanced chemical distillation.</note>. Added to this was a **censure**, in which not only the chemical works of **Quercetanus** <term>Du Chesne</term> but even the art itself <note>referring to Alchemy or Chemistry</note> is simply condemned. 

The censure was accompanied by the apology of **Jean Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1606), a staunch defender of Galenic medicine against the new chemical practitioners.</note> on behalf of Hippocrates and Galen, as if, with the growing splendor of **Alchemy** and the medicines prepared through the study of this art, Hippocrates and Galen were being accused of some crime, and it were necessary to plead a case on their behalf. 

The other physicians in France did not tolerate this monstrous deed; their learning, experience, and skill have brought far more nobility to **France** than have the scholastic lectures of those who condemn. I do not know if the names of these detractors have been heard anywhere in **Germany**, except for that legalistic **Riolan**, a bold and talkative man, and one prone to every sophistry, as the matter itself will show...

...inclined path. Therefore, they bravely resisted that shameful censure and strenuously defended this most noble, most true, and most useful art <note>The "art" refers to Chemistry or Alchemy as applied to medicine.</note> without any loss to the **Hippocratic** profession—which neither **Quercetanus** <term>Joseph Du Chesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent physician and advocate of Paracelsian chemical medicine</term> nor anyone else had at that time publicly attacked. 

Unless I am mistaken, it was partly the success and glory of the chemical physicians in their practice and the admiration for their science that "stirred up the hornets" and "disturbed that marsh" <note>original: "crabrones & camarinam illam mouit." Libavius uses two classical metaphors: "stirring up hornets" and "moving the Camarina" (a Sicilian marsh that, when drained, caused a plague), both meaning to provoke a dangerous or troublesome situation.</note>. Partly, it was because it was believed that the names of **Hippocrates** and **Galen** were being obscured by the terms **"Hermetic"** or **"Chemical"** being substituted for the common dogmatic medicine. They feared that, once **Galen** and **Hippocrates** were finally cast aside from the hands of students, the entire power of medicine would be limited to chemistry alone. 

But that fear is empty, since for a long time now a common body of knowledge has been formed from both **Arabic** and **Greek** teachings. Thus, medicine is no longer purely **Galenic** or **Hippocratic**, but also **Arabic** <note>Libavius refers to the medieval medical tradition that synthesized Greek authors like Galen with Arabic authors like Avicenna and Rhazes.</note>; several leading authorities are found within it, giving to each what is his due. 

At that same time, I had in my hands a revision of **Alchemy**, along with an explanation through certain commentaries. It immediately struck my mind...

...of that madness of condemnation was known at least by name. But I restrained myself nonetheless, because I thought there was some private dispute with **Quercetanus** <term>Joseph Du Chesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and key figure in the development of Paracelsian chemical medicine</term>, until I received the formal decree of proscription and the apology added to the censure, along with various other writings sent back and forth. Then I understood that it was not a private matter, and that it was not the case of **Quercetanus** being tried, but rather the case of **Alchemy**. 

But which **Alchemy**? Was it Paracelsian medicine? Was it that fraudulent kind that thrusts counterfeit metals forward as gold and devotes itself entirely to deceiving the unwary—the sort of men who wander through public marketplaces and even try to win over the courts of princes with the grandiloquence of their enormous promises? 

No, it was neither of these. It was rather about that alchemy which concerns itself with the **philosophers’ stone** <note>original: "lapidem philosophorum"</note>, although this aspect is only touched upon incidentally and perfunctorily, as if in passing. It concerns the alchemy that teaches how to prepare **magisteries** <term>concentrated chemical essences or "master" preparations</term>, principles, simple essences, extracts, the **fifth nature** <note>The "quintessence," believed to be the purest, most potent element of a substance.</note>, oils, waters, alkaline **elixirs**, **glass of antimony** <term>stibii vitrum; a medicinal preparation made by melting antimony ore into a translucent glass, often used as a potent emetic</term>, **precipitated mercury**, and many other such things, and how to turn them to medical use. If all these things are to be condemned, it is manifest that...

...that no safety remained for my labor; no dignity—let alone favor—could be hoped for. Furthermore, since I had to comment on the work of the **great magistery** <term>The "Grand Magisterium," the highest process of alchemical transformation</term> or the **philosophers’ stone** <note>original: "lapidis philosophorum"</note>, and yet I noticed that the censors wished to act according to the laws and desired that those who use **chemical remedies** <note>original: "chymicorum remediorum"</note> be punished with death, it became openly known that no life remained for either me or my work.

I therefore came to an examination of the **Parisian censure** <note>The 1603 decree by the Paris Faculty of Medicine condemning the use of chemical medicines</note>, and with moderate diligence I investigated the principal arguments and carefully refuted them. And lest such scholastic audacity should go unpunished amidst so much license and such a heinous act, I did not want my examination to be "toothless"—even though it is hard to imagine what severity could overcome the rage and most furious insanity of the **censor Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine who led the attack on chemical physicians</note>.

But do not think, Reader, that I am accusing or criticizing the school of medicine simply and in its entirety. It is well known that when **Fernel**, **Sylvius**, **Houllier** <note>Jean Fernel, Jacques Dubois (Sylvius), and Jacques Houllier: legendary figures of the Paris Medical Faculty from the mid-16th century who represented its "Golden Age"</note>, and other supreme men were teaching there, **alchemy** was by no means condemned, nor were **chemical physicians** <term>chymiagros; doctors who integrated chemical preparations into their practice</term> handed over to death. Instead, the art was held in the highest praise and cultivated in their writings. From this it happened that many Frenchmen were moved to take up the same art...

...to <note>original: "nandam," likely the conclusion of a word like "exornandam," meaning to adorn or honor</note> its reputation, and being roused, they published famous commendations of it. We do not wish that school—which was brought to the height of fame by the most praiseworthy founding of **Charlemagne** <note>Carolus Magnus (742–814), traditionally credited with founding the schools that became the University of Paris</note> and the favor of subsequent kings—to be offended. 

But as for those who now abuse its power and title—the censors of **Alchemy** and the denouncers of **Chymiatrists** <term>Chemical physicians who integrated alchemy into medical practice</term>—they are unworthy of receiving any reputation from that school or being praised by any learned man. We have dragged these men forth to state the cause of such an unjust condemnation. Having found them lacking in just proofs, we have condemned them, and we lead them around like captives in a **triumph** <note>A reference to the Roman "triumphus," a parade for a victorious general where defeated enemies were paraded through the streets</note>, so that they themselves may experience that fate which <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Elder, the leader of the Parisian opposition to chemistry</note>—exultant and already acting as if he were in a victory parade before even winning—had threatened against the **Chymiatrists**.

While this is being done, according to my modest ability and by the right by which I know myself bound to defend the truth, that condemning council seeks various diversions. Through its brawler <term>Riolan</term>, it proclaims that I am not defending **Alchemy** (which the council wishes to seem as if it has not condemned, except for mineral medicines), but that I am merely defending <term>Quercetanus</term> <note>Joseph du Chesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent French physician and chemist</note>, <term>Turquet</term> <note>Theodore de Mayerne (1573–1655), a royal physician who faced professional exile for his chemical views</note>, <term>Harvet</term> <note>Israel Harvet, a physician from Orléans who defended chemical medicine against Riolan</note>, and <term>Bancynet</term>. But in...

<page-num>II</page-num>
->### TO THE READER<-

# TO THE READER

How could I possibly defend these men, who are great in their own praise and splendor, and truly greatest in their innocence and virtue? How can I defend those against whom I read nothing except old wives' tales and reckless insults—devoid of any merit—and insane slanders which collapse under the weight of their own rashness? The cause of **Quercetanus** <term>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent French physician who advocated for the use of chemical remedies alongside traditional ones</term> is not at stake here; why would he even need a protector? Indeed, if there were a need, he is quite capable of defending himself through his own virtue and learning. When I deny that I am speaking for **Quercetanus**, I am called a protector of **Paracelsianism** <term>The medical system of Paracelsus, which often rejected traditional Greek medicine in favor of alchemy and chemistry</term>—and a reckless, inconsistent one at that! They claim that I, who once wrote against the invectives of **Gramanus** <term>Johann Graman, a radical follower of Paracelsus</term> in defense of **Galenic medicine** <term>The traditional medical system based on the teachings of the Greek physician Galen, focusing on the balance of four humors</term>, have now supposedly defected to the opposite side. They say I have criticized and thrown away **Hippocratic** medicine <term>The foundational Greek medical tradition emphasizing clinical observation and natural healing</term> to embrace the **Paracelsian** way. Because of this, **Riolanus** <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a conservative leader of the Paris Medical Faculty and a fierce opponent of alchemy</note> and his associates trust that they can destroy me with my own "anti-Gramanian" weapons.

<margin>
* Note that the term **Chymiatria** <term>Chemical medicine; the application of alchemy to pharmacy</term> or the title of **Hermetic medicine** <term>Medicine derived from the "Hermetic" tradition of secret knowledge and alchemy</term>, when used in a healthy sense, detracts nothing from that general medicine which they call **Hippocratic**, Dogmatic, **Galenic**, Rational, Greek, or Latin.
</margin>

But I want you to know that there is a certain middle way between simple, pure **Paracelsianism** and pure **Galenism**. In this way, [the name]...

<gloss>
...they call it, but it is a name of a subdivision, much like **Arabic medicine** <term>The medical tradition developed in the medieval Islamic world which introduced many new drugs and chemical processes</term>, which differs from **Galenic medicine** only in the style of its explanation and the addition of **Chemical** and other remedies. Some even call it "parabolic" and "symbolic" medicine due to the use of parables and symbols...
</gloss>

But accidental variations do not destroy the essence of the art.

<meta>Catchword: surpass.</meta>

<summary>Libavius defends himself against charges of inconsistency, arguing that one can support chemical medicine (Chymiatria) without entirely abandoning the classical traditions of Galen and Hippocrates. He proposes a "middle way" that integrates chemical innovations into the established medical framework.</summary>

...where **Galen** <term>Claudius Galen (129–c. 216 AD), the Greek physician whose system of the four humors dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</term> acts as the supreme pontiff and dictator. Indeed, they enclose **Galenic medicine** within such narrow limits—as if it stood at the very peak of perfection—that they want nothing added or taken away. They turn Galen’s teachings into a kind of divine commandment and will, from which one must not depart to the right or to the left, not even in his choice of words or his method of teaching. For this very reason, **Lacuna** <note>original: "Lacuna"; likely Andrés Laguna (1510–1559), a Spanish physician who edited Galen but was sometimes criticized by stricter Galenists</note> was scolded, and **Paulus** was called the "ape of Galen" <note>original: "Paulus Galeni simia"; this refers to Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century physician often accused of merely mimicking Galen's work without original thought</note>. These followers demand such total adherence that Galen's pronouncements are treated almost as objects of worship.

The middle path <note>original: "Media vero vita"; literally "the middle life," referring here to a balanced way of practicing and studying medicine</note>, however, is to reject those things that have been handed down inappropriately or falsely by either side, while accepting, expanding, and clarifying those things that are true and useful, thereby making them even better.

But you say, "I see you speaking quite often in the manner of **Paracelsus** <term>The school of Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), known as Paracelsus, who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine</term>, but too little in the manner of **Hippocrates** <term>The ancient Greek physician regarded as the 'Father of Medicine,' whose approach focused on natural causes and clinical observation</term>." 

Look again, I say—look again and again, and do not judge so hastily. Consider that even Paracelsus often says what is true, while Hippocrates says not a few things that are false. You will perhaps even see things that are found in neither Hippocrates nor Paracelsus. Often the words have the same sound, but...

To be sure, it can happen that one person explains a matter more clearly than another, and some disagreement may appear in the explanations of the two. 

But if the opinions are compared more precisely, it is seen that there is little or no difference. Add to this that differing opinions regarding the difficulty of things do not destroy a **total consensus** within the same field of study; nor is someone immediately an enemy who does not speak or feel according to another’s whim. Consensus and friendship do not consist in every single word or short sentence, but in the harmony of minds and the commonality of the whole pursuit. The more hidden a matter is, the more opinions there can be about it. Our **knowledge** in this life is **imperfect**. Therefore, concerning things more remote from the senses and more hidden, our opinions for the most part

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND AC-
# COMPLISHED GENTLEMAN ANDREAS 
## Libavius, most celebrated physician 
## and philosopher, 
### Greetings.

**I** have always considered it the noblest duty of that more noble and hidden philosophy, most learned Libavius, foremost among physicians (as is evident from my writings), to investigate with skillful research those things which lie hidden within the secret and most rich majesty of nature. 

And although the monuments of antiquity, full of wisdom and learning as they are, ought not only to be read by all, but also admired, and so far as we are able, learned and imitated; nevertheless, I have always judged it worthy of a wise philosopher (and by this do not understand the magic of **<term>Paracelsus</term>** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist known for his revolutionary but often controversial medical theories</note>) to look also toward some more divine principle, since I have found from experience that in many of their books, more is understood by the ingenious than is actually read. 

Thus I maintain both that those things which they discovered must be learned, and moreover, that new things must be discovered which posterity may learn from us. Truly, my admiration for antiquity grows with the very discovery of things; the greater the remaining harvest of things yet to be found, the more I am moved to admire the care of the ancients in discovery and their generosity in passing it down. 

However, neither lethargy nor credulous simplicity has ever carried me so far as to regard them as **<term>Pythagorases</term>** <note>The followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras were famous for their absolute devotion to their master's words, never questioning his authority</note> who could never be mistaken in anything; and therefore, with unthinking credulity, to treat their writings just as if they were that famous "**he himself said it**" <note>original Greek: *αὐτὸς ἔφα* (autos epha); a phrase used by the disciples of Pythagoras to indicate that the master's word was the final, unquestionable authority</note> to them...

<summary>A dedicatory letter to Andreas Libavius advocating for a balance between honoring ancient wisdom and pursuing new scientific discoveries. The author argues that while the ancients should be studied, a true philosopher must not follow them blindly as unquestionable authorities.</summary>

-> # TO THE READER. <-

...I would acquiesce to the **Pythagorean** <note>original: "Pythagorico"; likely referring to the Pythagorean practice of *ipse dixit*, where a master's word is accepted as absolute authority without proof</note> way. Instead, I have judged that Nature herself must be consulted, inspected, directed, and imitated by the physician-philosopher and her skillful servant, rather than the approach of anyone who thought they could be constrained everywhere and forever by perpetual dogmas; such a person will be laughed at by **Plato**, expelled by **Aristotle**, and will suffer the lash of **Galen’s** decree.

Therefore, I believe one should rather imitate *Eupompus* the sculptor <note>A Greek artist of the 4th century BC who famously advised the sculptor Lysippos to follow nature itself rather than the style of any particular master</note>, who, when asked which of the preceding artists he followed, replied that Nature itself must be imitated, not an artist. It is not that the discoveries of the ancients are not of a kind that can enrich us, but we must ensure that by our own laziness and credulous persuasion—or rather by prejudiced opinion—the art which is most rich by the testimony of even the great **Hippocrates** is not rendered barren.

Our art is indeed most fertile, no different than nature itself. For just as nature is ennobled not so much by its own work as by the care of a good farmer, so is the art of medicine ennobled by the industry of a wise practitioner. The nobility of this art is not only preserved above all others, but is even increased by the discovery of most-proven remedies. Therefore, let it be work enough for us, and more than enough provided, to have written about many health-giving medicines, and to have brought those subsequently discovered into practical use.

If you ask, most celebrated sir <note>Addressing Andreas Libavius</note>, what cause impels me to the treatment of this argument, know that it is of great interest to both of us. For while we are both occupied in this work for the sake of the public good—and not without the greatest labors—striving to adorn that field of study which we both profess with a wealth of many hidden and most elegant things, and to enrich it more and more daily, we have nonetheless sought to keep the authority and reputation of antiquity "safe and sound" <note>original: *sarta tecta*; a Roman legal formula literally meaning "patched and roofed," used to describe buildings or reputations kept in good repair</note>. Yet, despite this, they have not feared to [attack] us, and first of all me...

# TO THE READER.

**B**

...certain **CENSORS** have arisen who falsely and wrongly boast of antiquity, of which I have been—and still am—just as vigorous a defender as they themselves. Yet such men, possessed by an ill-will and driven by a critical sting to rebuke all the best efforts, have raged not only against me, but also against the most ancient and noble chemical art <note>original: "chymicam artem"; referring here to the early scientific study of matter and medicine, often associated with Paracelsian thought</note>. Have we not seen this same thing happen to the great leader of **Physicians**, **Libavius** <note>Andreas Libavius (1550–1616), a German physician and chemist famous for writing the first systematic chemistry textbook</note>, that distinguished defender and student of antiquity? But who are those adversaries of his? Most ignorant men, and plainly blind, who cannot conceive—much less admire—those hidden and plainly divine matters contained in his writings.

If only one attacks you too harmfully and impudently, **Most Learned Libavius**, there are a thousand others in our **France** (which certainly rings today with both military and civil <note>original: "togata"; literally "toga-wearing," referring to the peaceful achievements of scholars, lawyers, and statesmen as opposed to soldiers</note> glory) who look up to you and admire you; you may be sure this is said without any desire for flattery. For my mind shrinks entirely from the deceptive dye <note>original: "fuco"; a term for cosmetic rouge, used here metaphorically for fake or "painted" praise</note> of such blandishments. 

But so that you may see how much I value you and admire your writings, I have chosen to testify to such things in this short letter, and even to offer a sacrifice to your name with a few grains from my small granary—though only a grain, and a tiny one at that. For you know that of old, the common people were accustomed to supplicate the gods with only milk, and those who lacked incense <note>original: "thura"</note> offered a <term>salted cake|mola salsa; a mixture of toasted flour and salt used in ancient Roman sacrifices by those who could not afford expensive offerings like frankincense</term>. Farewell, most celebrated of physicians, and while you enjoy such great fame among the wise, continue to extend it through your writings and deeds (which is the true work of virtue). Farewell again, and love me always, as I am most fond of you.

->Your most devoted,<-
->**Joseph Quercetanus, Counselor and Royal Physician.**<-

# TO THE READER.

Furthermore, the most distinguished and learned men have written to me in much the same spirit: Lord **Theodore Turquet de Mayerne** <note>Theodore de Mayerne (1573–1655) was a highly influential Swiss-born physician who served kings in both France and England and was a major proponent of chemical remedies.</note>, ordinary physician to the King of France; and Lord **William Baucynet**, and Lord **Israel Harvet**, both most excellent and skilled municipal physicians of Orléans. Indeed, they cultivate <term>chemical medicine</term> <note>original: "Chymiatriam"; the practice of using chemical and mineral preparations as medicine, a controversial bridge between traditional herbalism and alchemy.</note> and, through most successful practice, demonstrate that it is entirely consistent with the teachings of Hippocrates. Let us allow his bones to rest softly, and let us deal only with that Riolan whom he himself depicted in his anti-chemical pamphlets.

Fare you well and live long.

### rious Galenic medicine.

**M**EDICINE, specifically the dogmatic medicine of the <term>Hermeticists</term> <note>Hermeticism refers to a philosophical and medical tradition associated with the legendary Hermes Trismegistus; in this context, it represents "chemical" or alchemical medicine which seeks the hidden "essences" of things.</note>—which is one and the same as the <term>Hippocratic</term> <note>Refers to the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates, the "Father of Medicine."</note> and the genuine <term>Galenic medicine of the Arabs</term> <note>Galen was a 2nd-century Roman physician; Du Chesne argues that the medieval Arabic translations preserved the "true" Galen, unlike the "spurious" versions taught in the universities of his day.</note>—has two primary branches: *Hygiene* and *Therapeutics*. The former encompasses the healthy constitution and preservation of man; the latter concerns the restoration of health from an adverse and unhealthy state.

*Hygiene* is divided into *Physiology* and *Dietetics*, as it considers the principles of generation and essence, and the preservation of those things generated through certain aids. These aids are called <term>non-naturals</term> <note>original: "res non naturales." In Renaissance medicine, these were six external factors that affect health: air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, excretion and retention, and the "passions of the soul" (emotions).</note> by the common schools, though they ought especially to be "according to nature" and, by their own nature, contribute to that affinity which they call "likeness."

*Physiology* discusses the natural constitution and explains the dual origin of the human body, in the *Aristotelian* manner. For it teaches that some things occur and exist by the force of the elements and elementary qualities, such as elementary heat, moisture, cold, dryness, roughness, smoothness, density, rarity, flexibility, rigidity, and so forth. Other things, however, exist by reason of an origin according to the species, coming from the seminal first-principle and the blood in blood-bearing creatures, from which the conception is formed. Hence, the two principles of man (for medicine deals chiefly with man, and with others by analogy) are the seed and

<sup>a</sup> Note that these things are said concerning the properties of mixtures in general, regarding those things which involve the whole substance. ...blood: yet these two are not mixed outside or beyond the elements, but originally contain an essence enfolded and solidified within the elements. From a <term>seminal principle</term> <note>original: "seminario principio." In this context, it refers to the internal "seed" or spiritual blueprint that determines what a living thing becomes.</note> proceed not only individual species, but also the essential or specific properties in all things that are born from a single, varied, or analogous seed. Therefore, for something to become a human, a lion, a dove, a frog, a moray eel, an oyster, a rose, gold, crystal, bitumen, etc., depends on that seminal principle. That something is also a nutriment, a medicine, a purgative, altering the whole nature—such as a strengthener, a poison, an <term>antidote</term> <note>original: "alexipharmacum," a medicine used to ward off poison or infection.</note>, etc. <sup>a</sup>—arises from the same source. For none of these can arise from the mere force of the elements, or from elemental qualities <note>Such as hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note>. Since the <term>Hippocratic</term> and <term>Hermetic</term> philosophers understood this well, and saw that the whole science of successful healing depends on that foundation, they placed <term>essential physiology</term> <note>original: "Phyſiologicam eſſentialem"; the study of the vital, hidden forces of life rather than just the physical elements.</note> far above the elemental. By investigating the hidden aspects of mixtures in the ineffective bodies of separated elements—or "matter," as the <term>Arabs</term> <note>Medieval Arabic scholars who were central to the development of chemistry and medicine.</note> call it—they revealed the "species," that is, the essence equipped with formal properties. They did this through the benefit of that art [alchemy] which manifests what lies hidden in things beneath the elemental husk, and by separating and gathering... and they nourish. They are communicated to the air through exhalations. Hence rain, dew, aerial honey, etc., have the power of nourishing. Moreover, it is washed into the waters or is even present in their mixture of its own accord, since neither simple water nor simple earth can be given, God here from the beginning creating these elements so that they could be the matter of animals and plants by their nature.

-> # WITH SPAGYRIC, GALENIC, AND PARACELSIAN [MEDICINE] # <-

...and it is called <term>Spagyrics</term> <note>original: "Spagiria." A term popularized by Paracelsus for the art of separating and recombining the components of substances to create medicines.</note>, or, because of its essential juice, Alchemy. While **chemists** are busily engaged in this, they have found that every essential power lies in the inner nature of the mixture, which, when it is reduced to its simplest form, appears in three types. These are the **three principles of the chemists**: namely, liquor, oily fatness, and salt, which are symbolically called **mercury**, **sulphur**, and **alkali** or **salt**. These names for mineral principles have been transferred to plants and animals as well.

**Hippocrates** seems to have intended to designate these through the spiritual, the moist, and the solid, which he established as the three constituents of similar parts, and he also taught that they exist in the whole body in another way. **Aristotle** calls them the primordial moisture, the innate heat, and the implanted spirit; from these joined together, he fashions that nature which is far nobler than the elements, as if it were related to the element of the stars. In this nature, every specific power and virtue of the soul dwells, and it is nothing other than the **Hermetic essence** produced from a <term>seminal beginning</term> <note>original: "seminali primordio." The underlying "blueprint" or life-force in a seed that directs its growth.</note> and a conception of ethereal nature. 

These principles are found to exist potentially within the "similar members" <note>An anatomical term for tissues that are uniform in substance, like bone or fat, as opposed to "organic" members like the hand.</note> in a state according to nature. Likewise, they are found in nutrients and remedies, and finally even in an adverse constitution—that is, in diseases, their causes, and poisons. Therefore, from here are sought the first foundations of **Physiological medicine**. Elemental physiology explains the elements of the <term>sublunary world</term> <note>original: "mundi sublunaris." In the ancient worldview, the region below the moon where things are made of the four elements and are subject to change and decay.</note>, and their qualities upon which they depend, concerning which the schools have [written] regarding elemental temperaments...

<margin>
**b**
In elemental simplicity there is no **essential power** for generating, nourishing, or healing; rather, there is only a certain external assistance which contributes to nutrition and generation in a different way than those things which are constitutive of the species itself. Thus, [the elements] are indeed applied to healing, but they do not possess the remedy of a specific property, insofar as they only alter things on an elemental level. In this, there is little power of the medical art; anyone, even without training, can warm frozen limbs in winter, dry out wet things, etc. However, when it is not an elemental moistening that is required, but an **essential** one—as in the case of <term>hectic consumption</term> <note>original: "tabe hectica." A chronic wasting disease, often involving a persistent fever and the "drying up" of the body's healthy moisture.</note>—elements are of no use. </margin>

### A COMPARISON OF HERMETIC AND HIPPOCRATIC MEDICINE

[...manifest truths] which they defend tooth and nail, nor do they want to hear anything regarding the principles or the symbolic or parabolic teachings of the <term>Chemical Physicians</term> <note>original: "Chymiatris." They say that blood, both types of bile <note>Yellow bile and black bile, two of the four "humors" or bodily fluids thought to govern health.</note>, and phlegm (or mucus) are sometimes understood in terms of their elements, and sometimes in terms of their essence. In this way, they are indeed named as such when the body is in a secondary or afflicted state, but they are actually understood as the dominance of hidden essences. To these must also be added the <term>seeds of things</term> <note>original: "semina rerum." An ancient concept revitalized in the Renaissance to describe the spiritual or physical "blueprints" that allow specific things to grow and manifest.</note> and the primary nourishing essences. 

From this, it follows that even if the signs of disease are the same in both systems, they are explained differently. It is clear from what has been said how the method of curing differs from one system to the next. In terms of general principles, the method is certainly the same, but it differs in specific practice and opinions, as the following "conflict" <note>The author likely refers to a formal debate or a comparison of case studies between the different medical schools.</note> will testify.

However, it should be noted that some people prefer simple teachings, while others express many things through parables and symbols. This difference in style does not destroy the underlying agreement on the nature of things. Moreover, it happens that some judge things more correctly than others, just as there is a diversity of studies and opinions in every human science—and no small amount of argument even regarding divine matters. For the knowledge of this world is imperfect.

...having embraced the best things; however, some are illegitimate. Thus, in the Hermetic profession, some are **Spurious**, and others are **Genuine**. We call those "Spurious Paracelsians" who depart from virtue toward one extreme and persecute <term>Galenic medicine</term> <note>The traditional medical system following the 2nd-century Greek physician Galen, which focused on balancing the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> excessively. Certainly, they act foolishly; while they wish to correct errors, they slide prone into the opposite extreme of vices. They criticize the elements, qualities, humors, and many other things, but in an irregular way. Later, they even mix in magical madnesses and devise far more monstrous theories than any Galenist ever could. Therefore, just as the <term>Hermeticists</term> <note>Chemical physicians who followed the "Hermetic" tradition, believing that medicine should focus on the spiritual and chemical "essences" of substances rather than just their physical qualities.</note> separate themselves from the spurious Galenists, so too do they separate themselves from these Paracelsians, so that they may follow the best path in the middle. These things are confirmed by the following "battle" of Alchemy triumphing over the Parisians. <note>This refers to the "antimony war" and other intense legal and academic conflicts in 17th-century Paris between the conservative Faculty of Medicine and the new chemical physicians.</note>

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM #

...the all-powerful healer <note>original: "pancratem e medicatrix." This refers to the concept of "Natura Medicatrix," the idea that Nature itself is the primary physician.</note>, whose servants (of preparation and application) are called physicians. It is their duty to use vital and potent remedies to uproot "radical" diseases <note>Diseases that have taken root deeply in the body's constitution.</note> born in the body from their "seeds." This is achieved through the help of a certain vital balsam <note>In alchemy, "Balsam" is the internal preservative principle that maintains health and resists decay.</note>, which is the firm foundation of true medicine and the genuine cure for all diseases. Even <term>Fernelius</term> <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician who attempted to bridge the gap between traditional medicine and "hidden" or occult causes.</note> sensed this in his <term>book on Hidden Causes</term>, calling it an "occult property." He took this lead from many passages in <term>Hippocrates</term> and <term>Galen</term>, on which occasion the book *On Ancient Medicine* is cited.

<margin>Names of Medicine</margin>
He adds that this medicine is called by the more "secret" philosophers <note>Refers to alchemists or Hermetic philosophers.</note> the **fifth essence** of things, the **Elixir**, **potable gold**, the **stone**, and the **heaven of the philosophers**; these are different names for one and the same thing.

<margin>The Fifth Essence</margin>
It is called the **fifth essence** <note>Also known as "quintessence." In ancient physics, there were four elements (earth, air, fire, water); the fifth was the celestial or spiritual substance of the stars.</note> because it is something beyond the four elements and does not arise from their mixture, being divine both in its source and its effects.

<margin>The Elixir</margin>
It is called the <term>Elixir</term> because it is an incomparable medicine for preserving life and driving away diseases.

<margin>Potable Gold</margin>
It is called **potable gold** <note>Liquid gold. In alchemy, gold was considered the most "perfect" and incorruptible metal, and thus its essence was thought to provide the most perfect health.</note> because of its excellence; for although it can be made from all things under heaven, it is most excellent when found in gold.

<margin>Concerning the Stone</margin>
It is also called **the Stone**, beyond the version found by the <term>gold-makers</term> <note>original: "Chrysopoeorum." Specifically refers to alchemists focused solely on transmuting base metals into gold.</note>. It is named as a medical essence of "hardness" or because it shares the nature of the "salt of life" <note>The preservative principle in things.</note> found in all things, which serves as the hardest and firmest foundation of bodies, in which the rest [of the medicines]...

<margin>Truly, all the dignity and praiseworthy effect of medicines lies in purgatives, restoratives, antidotes, and nutrients.</margin>
The rationale for all these medicines is found not in the mixture of elementary qualities <note>The traditional Galenic "hot, cold, wet, dry" qualities.</note>, but in their **internal essence** and the entire nature and "form" of each substance. This is true of "specific" remedies, even if they are sometimes discussed in very elementary terms. But as I have said, there is more in the hidden center than in the outer shell, and <term>Galen</term> himself could hardly extricate himself from this marvelous mixture.

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALEN #
<page-num>39</page-num>

He scattered his follies among the common people without consulting the physicians. Among sixty doctors, there is not even one who has not renounced and condemned the principles of that <term>vain art</term> <note>Original: *mataeotechniae*. A Greek-derived term for a useless or fraudulent craft.</note> (for so he calls **Alchemy**). The task of punishing them was entrusted to the censor (Riolan, who names himself as the sole authority; in my view, the voice of the college) in this introduction. The matter itself:

1. Regarding **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the origins of alchemy and Hermetic philosophy were attributed.</note>, whose writings breathe something deep and sublime, since he was held by the Platonists to be Moses; yet he was no "chemical blower" <note>Original: *sufflo*. A derogatory term for alchemists who spent their time blowing on furnace coals.</note>.

2. According to **Paracelsus** <note>The radical Swiss physician who pioneered chemical medicine; here, the author ironically uses Paracelsus's own controversial reputation against the alchemists.</note>, the Devil invented Alchemy; therefore, it should be called "Diabolical."

3. A fourth sect <note>Traditionally, ancient medicine was divided into three schools: the Dogmatic, the Empirical, and the Methodic. Riolan argues against allowing "Spagyrists" to form a fourth.</note> should not be introduced as distinct from the Empirical, because <term>spagyric</term> <note>Chemical medicine based on the separation and recombination of substances.</note> remedies were not discovered by reason, but by experience. From this it follows that they are unscientific and empirical.

4. Chemistry is neither an art nor a science: for just as the bedside doctor and the surgeon serve the physician, so the pharmacist is served by the distiller. Thus, Chemistry, the self-proclaimed "queen of arts," is merely a lowly handmaid to pharmacy. Even there, the <term>quintessence</term> <note>Original: *quinta essentia*. The "fifth element," believed to be the purest and most potent part of a substance.</note> is not prepared, but only waters and oils; indeed, there is no quintessence in this sublunary world <note>The Earthly realm below the moon, which was believed to be subject to decay, unlike the perfect celestial spheres.</note>.

5. Chemistry can expand pharmacy through many formulas of distillation; it cannot constitute a new art, unless every other individual preparation were also considered a unique art.

<margin>*Note that nothing is written here against anything except chemical preparations.*</margin>

6. The physician and the pharmacist should be distinct; the former should prescribe, the latter should work, so that the patient is not deceived by the material, the price, etc. Therefore, spagyrists should not prepare remedies at home.

7. The state can do without chemical preparation, as it once did in the time of **Galen** and **Hippocrates** <note>The two most famous physicians of antiquity, whose herb-based medicine was the standard for centuries.</note>, because the perfection of healing does not consist [in...]

8. Common remedies are safer than chemical ones—such as antimony and precipitate—which are extremely dangerous. The chemists prescribe these to others while they themselves prefer <term>dogmatic</term> <note>The traditional Galenic medicine based on established principles rather than trial-and-error chemistry.</note> remedies. 
9. The Galenists are friends of nature, using gentle means, and never using violent ones unless preceded by infinite <term>distinctions</term> <note>Original: *diorismis*. These are specific medical conditions or qualifications defined before a treatment is applied.</note>.

<margin>Galenic medicine is a common public good in Paris.</margin>
Medicine is a most common art which both the learned and the unlearned use; Chemists are not permitted to use it in this way. These remedies were invented by the Devil, mixed into oils and waters so that deadly substances might be more pleasing. 
10. The art of the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>The "quintessence" or the purest, most medicinal part of a substance.</note> and the philosopher’s stone is not a single art, because they have different goals. <term>Gold-making</term> <note>Original: *chrysopoeia*.</note> is condemned; it is judged that its promoters should be restrained through their published books.

<margin>Democritus.</margin>
11. Democritus is denied to be a chemist, because he was blind and held principles different from the chemists, such as <term>vapors</term> <note>Original: *aroma*. There is, however, within every metal a certain "gold" <note>Referring to the idea that a "pure" or "noble" portion exists within base metals that can be separated, rather than created.</note> that could be separated from the mixture.

...natural things. To the Chemists, all things are in all things <note>original: *Chymicis omnia sunt in omnibus*. See the arguments in the examination. 

<margin>Diseases. Regarding these, there is only one question: Whether healing is performed by likes.</margin> 28. Diseases are to be driven out by **contraries**, not by "likes," according to the argument of the **Hippocratic doctrine**, which has been proven. Health is preserved by likes; therefore, disease is expelled by contraries, etc. Finally, a passage is cited from **Paracelsus** in which it is said that he attributed his art to the Devil. Such is the summary of the defense.

He indicates on page 7 that the Spagyric art <term>Spagyricam</term> is an ornament and a part of dogmatic medicine.

-> # THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS # <-

<margin>Riolan, by attacking chemical essences, imprudently makes art equal to God and nature.</margin>

**Chapter 12.** He examines the reasonings of God alongside common and particular nature; he claims a generative power flows daily from the sun, which he conveys by the "vehicle of light" in ***Chapter 14***, and by this means he produces all sublunary <note>Referring to the "sublunary sphere," the region of the cosmos below the moon—the Earth—which in Aristotelian physics was the only place subject to change and decay.</note> things; and he mocks the Platonists. **Chapter 13** treats the nature and mind of man, and concerning sensation and understanding. In **Chapter 14**, he distinguishes a "principle" <term>principium</term> <note>In this context, a fundamental constituent or source of a substance, such as the starting point of a physical body.</note> by its physical reality and by reason: he recounts the principles of Aristotle <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> and repudiates those of the Chemists; he recites the Aristotelian fable concerning the fire and heat of the sun. He banishes "essences" from both heaven and earth, and pronounces chemical science to be vain because it seeks "essences" which are nothing. He attacks the "elements" of Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician who sought to reconcile Paracelsian chemistry with traditional medicine.</note> along with the "three principles" <note>The Paracelsian "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which Quercetanus argued were the true building blocks of matter.</note> which he believes are not inherent in things, but are created from a universal matter that can be changed into anything through art (which is certainly the highest praise of Alchemy, though Alchemy itself hardly dares to claim it. For it is plainly a divine act to draw such a wonderful oil from **Indian cloves** <note>cloves (*Syzygium aromaticum*), a precious spice from the East Indies used in chemical extractions to produce aromatic oils.</note> if there were no power in them other than a matter that can be changed into any appearance. Indeed, no chemist can make **rose water** from anything if nature has not first created it. If he could, he would possess the power of God and nature, which is impossible). In **Chapter 15**, the principles are driven out of chaos and cast down from heaven. In **Chapter 16**, they are expelled from the center of the world, and the names of the planets are stripped from the metals <note>Alchemists traditionally linked the seven known metals to the seven planets (e.g., Gold to the Sun, Iron to Mars, Lead to Saturn).</note>. **Elixirs, tinctures, oils, essences, magisteries**, and other things shown by the Chemists are said to be nothing more than elementary matter thinned out by heat and changed into those forms, etc. He casts **Water of Life** <term>Aqua vitae</term> <note>Literally "water of life," referring to distilled alcohol or concentrated medicinal spirits.</note> "off the bridge" <note>A metaphorical expression meaning he utterly rejects or discards the concept.</note> and denies that it is a spirit separated from wine.

...and in every way he rages wildly against chemical principles. The same argument against these principles continues in **Chapter 17**, where he deals especially with animals. In **Chapter 18**, the composition of man is examined, and the parabolic adaptation of chemical principles to the structure of nature is mocked; the certainty of its goal is stripped from the chemical art; it is attributed to chance occurrence and the changing of a being into a non-being—mostly slanderously. Much is added concerning the humors <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Galenic medicine held were the keys to health and personality.</note> in man, arterial blood, and urine. It is denied that anyone possesses wisdom who finds Galen <margin>Galen.</margin> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the Greek physician whose teachings formed the backbone of Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> displeasing; the Paracelsian <note>Referring to the followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who rejected traditional medicine in favor of using minerals and chemicals.</note> opinion regarding chemical principles intruded into medicine is criticized. 

A false doctrine concerning opium is proposed in **Chapter 19**. Galen’s doctrine regarding the temperaments <term>temperaments</term> <note>The specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—unique to an individual.</note> and flavors is defended, which is also the subject of **Chapter 20**. Salt is excluded from the list of temperaments, and it is ordered to be exiled from the causes of smells, tastes, colors, and nutrition. The power of opium is examined anew. In **Chapter 21**, it is denied that salts are separated <note>i.e., naturally existing as distinct entities within a body.</note> but are instead created by the art [of chemistry]. Distillates <term>distillates</term> <note>Substances produced by boiling and condensation; Riolan argues here that these "pure" extracts are less effective than traditional herbal preparations.</note> are not indeed rejected, but are nevertheless attacked because they do not purge, and because distilled oils are less effective than decoctions <note>original: "coctis" — medicinal preparations made by boiling herbs or plants in water.</note>. 

In **Chapter 22**, it is denied that salt made through combustion <note>The process of burning organic material to ash to extract its "essential" salt, a common alchemical practice.</note> contributes to the fundamental thesis. In **Chapter 23**, he calls the stories about salt "tricks" and denies that the "primordial moisture" <note>The innate fluid believed to be the source of life and vitality in a living being.</note> can remain in substances that have been roasted. He accuses alchemy of fraud on the authority of a certain [François] de la Noue <note>François de la Noue (1531–1591), a famous Huguenot captain and writer known for his moral and political discourses.</note>. In **Chapter 24**, he denies that metals can be safely ingested, except those which more closely resemble food; the rest are harmful, even if they may appear beneficial for a time. Thus, the response to the first treatise is completed. The second treatise, because of these same repeated arguments, is resolved in a few—

# THE ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN SPURIOUSNESS

...that he carried perpetually with glass of antimony <note>original: "vitro antimonii"; a glassy substance made by roasting antimony ore, used as a powerful emetic</note> in his pocket, <margin>Pills of spirit of vitriol.</margin> although its legitimate use was unknown to him. He recounts the story of one who ridiculously requested some "pills of spirit of vitriol" <note>This is a joke at the expense of the physician's ignorance: spirit of vitriol (sulfuric acid) is a liquid and cannot be made into a pill</note> from a pharmacist.

<margin>Note on the censors of the Parisian College of Medicine.</margin>
He assigns to those judges the ears of Midas <note>original: "Mydæ auriculas"; a reference to King Midas, whom Apollo gave donkey ears as a mark of his foolish judgment in a music contest</note>, and describes them according to his wit as men whose character and doctrine are poorly spoken of by all physicians who practice medicine in any nation or place. These are men who impudently dare to prescribe laws of healing to others, when they themselves are in the greatest need of instruction. For besides six of them at most, one would be loath to expect a response from the rest in a matter of great importance—and such a response would not be worth even a penny <note>original: "asse"; a small Roman coin of little value</note>. Whence it follows that it is a mark of praise to be excluded from such a college, rather than to be counted among its numbers.

For the Hippocratic chemist <note>A physician who combined traditional Hippocratic observations with the new chemical preparations of Paracelsus</note>, when called to heal, is equipped with a double defense, while those men have scarcely one. The chemist can send away a student more learned than himself, but not the Parisian doctor, who will feel the loss of this exclusion most keenly. He also points out that the exclusion of learned doctors is absurd, since traveling quacks <note>original: "circumforanei"; literally "market-stalkers," referring to unlicensed wandering healers who sold remedies in town squares</note> cannot be prohibited from practicing. Finally, he calls upon the physicians of Europe against the Parisians to restrain the petulance and arrogance of that condemnation. This is essentially the summary of the defense by Turquet <note>Theodore Turquet de Mayerne (1573–1655), a pioneering physician who eventually became the chief doctor to four kings of England</note>, Doctor of Medicine and Royal Physician, as well as a most skilled chemist.

...is practiced nowhere more than in **Paris**. These are the prefaces to the battle. The contest itself begins with the definition of the art. It is demonstrated against the censor that Alchemy selects its material and prepares it studiously. It utilizes not only distillation, but also infusion, boiling <note>original: "excoctione"</note>, and pressing. 

<margin>
Chemistry is an art.
</margin>

Chemistry is an art consisting of an essential method, subject matter, and dignity, so much so that its industry not only surpasses the common workshop <note>original: "officinam," referring to the standard apothecary's shop of the time</note>, but indeed leaves nothing of excellence to it. If the common **pharmacopoeia** <note>A book containing directions for the identification of samples and the preparation of compound medicines.</note> of the people is considered an art, then chemistry is even more so, as it crafts remedies more skillfully and wisely. It operates not merely by natural chance or by accident, but scientifically according to just precepts established by both reason and experience. 

The argument that medicine can do without chemistry is rejected as a **begging of the question** <term>petitio principii: a logical fallacy where the conclusion of an argument is already assumed in its premises</term> found in their reasoning, based on the claim that medicine lacked it in the past; for in that way...

Through proper preparation, these chemicals become milder. <page-num>64</page-num>

->### ON THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS<-
<note>original: "ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS." This title likely refers to the "spurious" or false arguments of the Paris Medical Faculty against chemical medicine.</note>

<meta>catchword: of vinegar.</meta>

For the sake of this [flavor or scent], it is added (just as cinnamon water is). It is false that "no acute disease exists without fever." Nor, even if chemical remedies were not effective in acute diseases, should they be discarded for that reason, since they would still be of help in "cold" conditions. <note>In Galenic medicine, diseases were classified by "temperaments." "Cold" diseases were often chronic conditions believed to require "hot" or chemically active remedies.</note> The comparison of juices, decoctions, and infusions with distilled waters is a deceptive one; however, such waters are found more abundantly in the [apothecary] shops than in the laboratories of the **chemists**, who prefer to delight in other forms of medicine.

The argument regarding the "burnt smell" <term>empyreuma: a scorched or burnt odor and taste resulting from heating organic matter in a still</term> is flawed. It occurs either through lack of care or because of the nature of the process, where it can be corrected by "improvement" <note>the addition of substances to mask the odor</note>; alternatively, the remaining heat actually promotes the use of the medicine rather than hindering it. The same charge could be leveled against decoctions [herbal teas]. It is false to say that medicines act materially and not "formally," <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "form" is the essential nature or active power of a thing, whereas the "matter" is just the physical substance.</note> because action comes from the "form"; yet distilled medicines are not entirely without matter. 

More regard should be paid to the potency <note>original: "virtutis"</note> of a remedy than to the integrity of the "mixture" <term>crasis: the specific balance of humors or qualities in a substance</term>, lest the censor repeatedly object that this balance is destroyed during the labor of preparation. One sweats better from a small amount of the acidic liquor of **Guaiacum** <term>Guaiacum: a medicinal wood from the Americas, famously used to treat syphilis by inducing sweating</term> than from whole jugs of a decoction. The **chemist**, by removing useless parts, makes a medicine more effective than the [apothecary] shop does by adding to it. 

The censor is refuted by [citing] **Riolan** <note>likely Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a titan of the Paris Faculty who, despite his conservatism, was a necessary reference for any medical debate</note> regarding softening and hardening agents, showing that these effects are due to primary rather than secondary qualities. In clearing obstructions, chemical remedies are swifter than the decoctions of **Riolan**, although the chemist does not lack his own methods of boiling. The refined "thinness" of chemical preparations is a recommendation in this case, not a disgrace. This "thin" substance does not evaporate as quickly as the censor thinks. 

Regarding **water of life** <term>aqua vitae: concentrated alcohol or brandy</term>, **Riolan** is in error concerning the demonstration where a linen cloth is not destroyed by its flame. The cause is different [than he claims]. The heat of burning **spirit of wine** <term>spiritus vini: ethanol</term> is strong, as the senses testify. It is a lie that chemistry lacks astringent [binding] agents, as the example of **vinegar** <note>original: "aceti"</note> proves.

of vinegar, tincture of corals, water of scammony <note>a plant resin used as a strong purgative</note>, of rose, etc. But even the "terrestrial substance" <note>the solid matter remaining after distillation</note> is extracted by the **chemists** most excellently. Chemical salts are also defended on the grounds that they are useful for healing, and not all of them are caustic <note>corrosive or burning</note>. The argument regarding the **burnt smell** <term>empyreuma: the scorched odor produced by heat</term> is futile, since no such smell exists in the remnants of the ashes; nor is salt a "fiery effect" produced by fire. For if it were, it ought eventually to vanish entirely into fire—but it does not. Rather, it is converted into glass and stone, which are as far removed from fire as the earth is. Chemical salts are so far from being caustic that they can even be "cold" in temperament. Likewise, fire dissipates the excess of heat in sharp substances, leaving them less hot. Fire dissipates the **fiery volatile salt**, leaving behind the **fixed earthy salt**. 

The controversy over whether **likes are cured by likes** or **contraries by contraries** <note>the debate between using remedies similar to the disease versus those with opposite qualities</note> is said to be misunderstood by *Riolan*. For the **chemists** hold the same view as *Hippocrates*: that the disease must be opposed, but the nature of the body's parts must be preserved. The latter is achieved by "likes," and the former by "contrary operation." Diseases are not properly "healed" or "cured" in themselves; rather, the parts of the body are cured, and from them the diseases are driven away. 

This is the summary of the defense by *Harvetus* <note>Israel Harvet, a French physician and champion of chemical medicine</note>. He was opposed by *Riolan* under the pseudonym *Joannes Antaruetus* <note>a pun meaning "Anti-Harvet"</note>, a "candidate of medicine," whom in his madness Riolan calls his "son," and later identifies as himself. Let us recount the summary of his argument as well. 

The beginning is quite ridiculous. For the old man, with one foot in the grave <note>original: "capularis," literally "belonging to a coffin"</note>, leaps forward with youthful energy, <margin>*Riolan falsely proclaims Quercetanus and Turquet defeated.*</margin> boasting first of having defeated *Quercetanus* <note>Joseph Duchesne, a famous Paracelsian physician</note> and *Mayernius* <note>Turquet de Mayerne, another renowned chemical physician</note>—which is a foul lie. Then, as is his habit, he reviles and despises both *Harvet* and *Baucyne*—

### ON THE ALCHEMY OF THE FALSE PARISIANS

He denies that essences produce better actions, because mixtures [once separated] are deprived of heat, form, <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "crasi." In Galenic medicine, this is the specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—that gives a substance its unique medicinal character.</note>, and matter; he claims they are no longer natural because their parts have been divided by fire. He asserts that while a more intense and violent action and heat can be produced by these methods, it is not a "better" action or heat.

<margin>Note: The extraction of essences is attributed to the Devil as its author.</margin>
He claims that anyone who thinks otherwise does an injustice to God and **NATURE**. On this false foundation, he argues that the Devil taught the chemists how to corrupt mixtures, which occurs through their dissolution into elements and principles, whereby the <term>temperament</term> is destroyed. He concedes that <term>distilled</term> and <term>extracted</term> substances possess matter, but not in a way that is properly tempered for their specific functions, because the genuine balance of qualities does not remain within these "secret" essences and principles. Following the authority of Heurnius <note>Johannes Heurnius (1543–1601), an influential Dutch physician who sought to reconcile traditional Greek medicine with practical observation.</note>, he prefers a <term>decoction</term> <note>A medicinal liquid produced by boiling down herbs.</note> of anise over anise oil for treating colic. He argues that heat in a thick substance provides more warmth than heat in a thin one, using the example of iron. He further argues that solid things act more powerfully than a few thin essences, because the essences evaporate before they can even reach the affected area. He believes that astringency <note>The quality that causes body tissues to contract or "tighten."</note> is owed to the physical matter itself, citing the example of Rhubarb. 

Regarding the objection about salts, he denies it is relevant to the matter; he denies that salts are the principles of bodily constitution or nutrition, and denies that they exist in a finished state or can be separated naturally. He claims they are mostly caustic. He argues that ashes are hot in potential but cold in actuality, using the argument of lye <note>A liquid obtained by leaching ashes, used for cleaning or in medicine.</note>: he claims its biting coldness is harmful to ulcers, not in an absolute sense, but that it "burns" by accident. He attributes the power to erode to heat alone, noting that lemon juice dissolves pearls <note>original: "uniones." Large, high-quality pearls often used in expensive medicinal cordials.</note> without eroding them, just as it is said the blood of a goat or a hare dissolves a diamond, or <term>posca</term> <note>A common ancient and medieval drink made of vinegar, water, and sometimes herbs.</note> dissolves ivory. He concludes that acrid things lose their heat when burned, because the "third or fourth degree" of heat <note>Galenic medicine categorized the intensity of a substance's qualities into four degrees.</note> perishes during the burning of acrid substances, just as it does in others.

<header>### ON THE SPURIOUS PARTS OF ALCHEMY ###</header>

...this question arises. It is shown that the [Galenic] pharmacy is implicated in the same "sin"—if indeed it is a sin—by its use of so many compositions, extracts, decoctions, and so on. The essential power of chemical remedies is innate, not acquired <note>The author argues that the medicinal power is already inside the substance; the chemist's fire just reveals it rather than creating an artificial "unnatural" power.</note>; this is proven by the example of whey, the spirit of Guaiac <note>term: spirit of Guaiac; a distilled oil from the Guaiacum tree, often called "Holy Wood," used extensively to treat syphilis</note>, the extract of colocynth <note>a powerful and bitter purgative made from a type of desert cucumber</note>, and others. In these processes, only the impurities are cast aside. 

If burning and the chemist's art were said to add a "foreign" power to medicines, then the Galenic pharmacies and even common kitchens should be sent into exile. Some things are purely artificial, some are purely natural, and some are mixed. Art <note>original: "Ars"; here meaning the skill or science of the chemist</note> governs fires to achieve certain effects; it mixes, separates, and performs other tasks. If nothing should be discarded from natural things because "God made them best" (and nothing better can be provided), then chickens ought to be eaten with their feathers still on! 

<margin>Note that God is called the author of the mixture.</margin>

Different things are given for different ends. Even if nothing in nature is "useless" to nature itself, it does not follow that nothing is useless to the chemist's art. By this same argument, the Paris pharmacy <note>The medical establishment of the University of Paris, which fiercely opposed chemical medicine</note> is overturned, because it also separates things that were joined by God. Just because things were made good by God does not mean they remained in that state (otherwise, man would have no need for medicine). God also gave man the faculty of discernment—indeed, He even gave it to the beasts, who distinguish things by taste and smell—even though the Author of the mixture <note>God</note> alone knows the nature of things first and perfectly. 

It is in this discernment that physicians ought to excel. It is shown once again that **Libavius**, **Zwinger**, and **Gesner** <note>Andreas Libavius, Theodor Zwinger, and Conrad Gesner: three major 16th-century scholars and physicians often cited as authorities in medical debates</note> are being cited in a slandering and deceptive way. (This is how the matter stands: that fool does not understand the business **Libavius** had with **Gramanus** <note>Johann Graman, a radical follower of Paracelsus; Libavius often criticized radical Paracelsians while still supporting chemistry</note>). 

God, and not the devil, demonstrated the solutions <note>the process of dissolving substances</note> and operations of things necessary for the uses of life. If the chemist "corrupts" a substance <note>meaning to break it down into its parts</note>, he also generates something new. He does not make the "forms" of things worse; rather, unlike the traditional physician, he makes them nobler, because with these chemical remedies he helps the patient more safely, easily, and quickly.

<header>->THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM. 75<-</header>

Chemical substances <note>original: "Chymica"; refers to remedies prepared through distillation, sublimation, or other chemical arts</note> possess their own true form, by which they exist. They also possess a temperament <note>term: temperament; in pre-modern medicine, the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a substance's nature</note>. And although they are extracted from whole plants or minerals, they do not cast off their native disposition. It is ridiculous to deny the power of heat to these refined essences, and then, in turn, to accuse them of possessing a "violent heat" which they supposedly receive from the chemist's art. They are more essential and effective—as witnessed by Riolan—acting like a lightning bolt, a flash of light, and so on.

Refined chemical essences are administered in such a way that they achieve their effect, specifically by being mixed with appropriate liquids. There is also a place in the [human] body where they are received and which they alter to transmit their power. It is false to claim that everything is given "drop by drop" by the chemists. According to the authority of Galen <note>term: Galen; the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated European medicine for over 1,500 years</note>, certain small things create great changes by touch alone (such as the sting of a scorpion). The same is true of colocynth <note>a powerful purgative made from a bitter cucumber-like fruit</note>, Diagridium <note>term: Diagridium; a preparation of scammony resin, often roasted or mixed with quince to make it less harsh on the gut</note>, and others.

In every medicine, there are parts with different faculties. These separated parts must be judged according to the nature of each individual component. Chemists cannot be said to lack astringent <note>substances that cause body tissues to contract, used to stop bleeding or secretions</note> remedies. The logic regarding salts is examined, and many of Riolan's logical, medical, and physical "crimes" <note>meaning: intellectual errors or fallacies</note> are demonstrated. They can form caustics <note>substances that burn or corrode organic tissue</note>, just like Aristotle's fire. Ashes and salts are cold in their inherent quality, insofar as the element of Earth predominates in them. They are named after whichever element predominates. To erode is not a property of heat itself, a fact confirmed by the authority of Galen. Riolan's sophistry <note>false or misleading reasoning</note> regarding the changing of the question about "acrid" substances is criticized. For Harvet wrote that acrid things become *less* acrid when burned, but Riolan changed the wording to "losing their acrimony" <note>Harvet is accusing his opponent of misrepresenting his argument to make it easier to attack.</note>.

Action comes not from the "dead head" <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>original: "caput mortuum"; the useless, inert residue left over after a chemical distillation or sublimation</note>, but from the principles, which are compared to forms, just as the "dead head" is compared to matter.

->### ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN SPIRITS<-

It is clear that the chemists cannot be defeated using the principles of Aristotle. Riolan is pitted against Riolan in his judgment of Aristotle, whose principles he explains in one way and then another. He mocks the ignorance concerning **masteries** <term>preparations where a substance is purified to its most potent form</term>, **oils**, etc., which Riolan calls "parts of matter." He also ridicules the crude understanding of principles and essences, by which Riolan claims the **crasis** <note>original: "crasin"; the healthy or balanced mixture of qualities/humors in a body</note> is destroyed. In truth, the essences lose nothing, but are merely separated from the **caput mortuum** <note>original: "capite mortuo"; the "dead head" or worthless, charred residue remaining after distillation</note>. That there is some latitude in temperament—and that the whole does not perish immediately—is taught by the example of infusions of Rhubarb, senna, etc.,

<margin>Riolan is slain with his own sword. Chapter 3, on spirits and innate heat.</margin> 

which preserve their **specific powers**. To call chemical products "fictions" contributes nothing to the argument. Riolan is struck with his own weapons, since he has confessed that besides the oily humor, two others are present, and that the oily one is drawn out by chemists. It is obvious that this is not created by art, but merely separated. If chemistry produces oils by art, then it is an art, and not a fiction. The argument is refuted that chemistry cannot separate metals and stones because they are entirely homogeneous. It is said that they appear so to the senses, but not in their inner recesses, as experience testifies through **resolution** <note>The process of breaking a substance down into its component parts</note>:

<margin>Antimony and precipitates.</margin> 

**Antimony**, **precipitates**, etc., when rightly separated from impurity, act more nobly than Rhubarb, which is nevertheless used in its own place instead of them. In Chapter 4, Riolan’s **artificial fire** is exploded <note>In this context, "exploded" means to be rejected or driven out with contempt</note>, because all fire is natural; although some fire, due to the compositions of the material, its gradations, etc., might be called 

<margin>Whether fire is artificial.</margin> 

**artificial**. Natural and artificial differ, etc. Fire applied by art retains the properties of its own nature. The subtleties argued in favor of artificial fire are refuted, which are surely ridiculous and like old wives’ tales, not to say foolish; for example, the claim that it is artificial because "it has need of fuel" or "it is struck out by art."
