# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM #

...from flint; the caution is produced by art, therefore the fire is artificial. In chapter 5, a proof is established that salt, sulfur, and mercury are the constitutive principles of perfectly mixed substances.

<margin>On the principles</margin>
Principles are sometimes elements, sometimes similar parts <note>original: "similares partes"; in the Galenic tradition, these are homogeneous tissues like bone or nerve, but here applied to chemical constituents</note>, and sometimes that logical matter and form: some are closer, some more remote, some intermediate, some more general, and others more specific.

<margin>The three principles are inherent in matter and are not created by fire.</margin>
The three chemical principles <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, the "Tria Prima" of Paracelsus</note> are present within matter; they are not created by art, just as the elements are not created when a craftsman burns wood. If they were artificial products, they would have existed in the mind of the craftsman before they were extracted. But they are extracted even when we are thinking of no such thing. They are not created by the fire, because a natural agent does not always generate the same thing from different materials, which is what happens here; nor does it generate opposites from a single thing through a single action. If fire made the principles, it would generate opposites (since these principles are opposites). Therefore, fire does not create them, but separates them. The specific property of fire is to separate heterogeneous <term>consisting of different parts</term> things and to gather homogeneous <term>consisting of similar parts</term> things. It is not the case that if all things are made from elements, they cannot also be made from principles. The elements are remote components, while these principles are the near ones. In this way, several of **Riolan's** <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent conservative physician and critic of alchemy</note> minor questions are resolved.

<margin>Mercury.</margin>
The foolishness regarding mercury is mocked, as if the word signified quicksilver <note>liquid metallic mercury</note>, whereas a liquid substance is actually intended. The denial that quicksilver is the fundamental matter of metals is rejected in chapter 6. The reasoning of **chemical anatomy** is explained, showing it is not medical anatomy <note>dissection of a corpse</note>, but chemical anatomy, which dissolves mixtures into essences, essential parts, and the **caput mortuum** <note>original: "caput mortuum"; literally "dead head," the worthless charred residue remaining after distillation</note>.

<margin>Here medical matters are treated, with reference to the censures of scholastic terminology.</margin>
This is the subject of the first section. In the first chapter of the second section, it is denied that the semiotics <term>the branch of medicine concerned with the study of signs and symptoms</term> of the chemists differ from the **Galenic** system. For diseases are investigated through symptoms, and so on. However, it is one thing to consider simple substances...

It also clarifies that "chemical anatomy" refers to the distillation of substances into their essential parts rather than biological dissection.</summary>

->### ON THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS ###<-

...to recognize [substances] by their signs, and another to recognize diseases, as discussed in chapter 2.
The <term>etiology</term> <note>the study of the causes or origins of diseases</note> of Paracelsus is reconciled with the Galenic theory of humors, and it is said that the principles must be considered as existing within the humors. If it is correctly stated that the human body is composed of salt, sulfur, and mercury, it is also correct that these can be the causes of diseases when they depart from their natural state. <margin>A defense of Paracelsus</margin> Paracelsus opposed the primary qualities <note>the four Aristotelian qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, and consequently the humors as well, because he saw that in them nothing was considered except these qualities, which even Hippocrates rejected in his book *On Ancient Medicine*. Riolan <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), a conservative French physician and fierce opponent of Paracelsian "chemical" medicine</note> is refuted here, as he argues that the primary qualities are more powerful in producing disease or health than any other factors. It is written that the Chemists, following the authority of Hippocrates, discovered other causes of diseases. <margin>Remedies similar to nature</margin> To coagulate and to congeal are the same thing.

Thus ends the second section. In chapter 1 of the third section, the author argues that remedies must be sought that are similar to nature, because nature itself is the healer of diseases, whether acting alone or with assistance. If remedies similar to nature were not to be sought, then the medicine alone would cure the disease, which contradicts the teachings of Hippocrates and Galen. Medicine must be guided by nature. It is not guided except by what is similar, because only similar things can be joined together. Nature attracts similar things and expels foreign ones.

**Objection:** But medicines are harmful to those who are healthy. 
**Response:** This is because the proper <note>original: "proprium"; referring here to the specific ailment or "familiarity" the medicine is meant to address</note> is then absent. Therefore they do harm, just as food harms when taken immoderately; likewise, they harm through untimely use, excess, or poor preparation. Riolan is even cited against Riolan, where he teaches that appropriate substances are attracted by the parts of the body because of their kinship, and thus nutrients become beneficial; that purgatives perform their purging through an "attractive familiarity"; and that even small amounts of very potent things can do harm. <margin>Antidotes</margin> <term>Alexipharmics</term> <note>medicines intended to ward off poison or infection, often called "alexipharmaca"</note> counter poisons either through a sympathy with the heart,

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENIC MEDICINE #

...to the heart, or an <term>antipathy</term> <note>a natural repulsion or opposition between substances</note> toward poisons. Moderate substances have an affinity [with the body] because they can be transformed into its very substance. Even violent substances are made gentle through <term>re-purification</term>: just as an <term>alexipharmic</term> <note>an antidote or preservative against poison; original: "alexipharmacum"</note> that is sympathetic to the heart is created from the venomous viper. If these substances harm one person, it does not mean they are all harmful, unless one were to say the same of food. Foreign things should not be given to foreign things, but rather "their own to their own" <note>original: "sua suis," referring to the principle of using substances compatible with the body’s nature</note>. This is why so many different medicines were created, so that there might be a specific one for every person. What is mild for a robust person is violent for one who is weak. Nature is the adversary of disease. Therefore, that which is friendly to nature is likewise an adversary to disease.

<margin>*A remedy similar to nature.*</margin>

A remedy, therefore, ought to follow the law of nature. It is said that Paracelsus also held this view. Even Riolan <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), a conservative leader of the Paris Medical Faculty and a critic of chemical medicine</note> himself declared in chapter 2 that the better remedies are those more familiar to nature. It is demonstrated there that those remedies are superior and should be preferred over others which are better suited to driving out diseases. No remedy should be rejected outright: even children are purged with <term>scammony</term> <note>a harsh purgative resin derived from a Mediterranean plant</note>. The "sin" lies in the neglect of <term>correction</term> <note>the chemical process of removing toxic or unwanted qualities from a drug</note> and in excessive dosage—errors which are also committed with food and in the <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>bloodletting</note> practiced in Paris.

<margin>*Emetics.*</margin>

Emetics <note>substances that induce vomiting; original: "vomitoria"</note> are commended because they cure many diseases without danger, such as well-prepared <term>antimony</term> <note>a controversial mineral remedy that was the subject of intense legal and medical battles in 17th-century France</note>.

<margin>*Minerals.*</margin>

Minerals are defended on the grounds that animal and vegetable substances can be even more harmful than they are. The same argument is made in chapter 3, where it is shown that substances do not become hotter or more acrid simply by the "fire of the chemists." In the same place, there is a discussion regarding those things that are burned and corrected by washing. Thus, Riolan ought not to accuse the chemists, since Galen himself established the same principle. Riolan’s misrepresentation in his citation of Aristotle is noted in chapter 4. The method of preparing chemical extracts through <term>infusion</term> is described, which refutes Riolan’s scorn. He is also shown to have abused the authority of Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a chemist who sought to bridge the gap between traditional Galenism and new chemical methods</note>.

<page-num>84</page-num>

...salt <note>The text continues from the previous page's "salem" (salt)</note> is returned to urine, dung, and blood, in which there is a tempered salt; for this reason, it is not always perceptible on the tongue (as if hidden within the balanced mixture), but it emerges when it becomes predominant. If it is changed from them, why is it not also drawn in? To this is added the testimony of *Lobelius* <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> and *Pena* <note>Pierre Pena, a French botanist and collaborator of L'Obel</note> in their commentaries on butterbur.

Nutrition is not located in the tongue. Therefore, what is sweet for nourishment is not to be judged by the tongue.
</margin>

Goats feed on willows. "Sweet" is not defined as what is sweet to a human, but is judged relatively. *Hippocrates* <note>The famous Greek physician, here called "Hippo"</note> is cited regarding nourishment and principles. <margin>
Whether chemical salt is artificial.
</margin>

If the Chemists made it by fire, it would also have to be produced from the <term>dead head</term> <note>original: "capite mortuo," the useless solid residue remaining after distillation or sublimation</note> after being heated in a reverberatory furnace for a long time, which does not happen. (Add the observation of *Bauhin* <note>Gaspard Bauhin, a Swiss botanist</note>: when the entire earth of the ashes is exhausted in the production of salt, <term>halonitrum</term> <note>a mineral salt, likely saltpeter or a similar nitrate</note>, alum, and <term>chalcanthum</term> <note>vitriol or copper sulfate</note>. So also says *Scaliger* <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a polymath who wrote extensively on physics and medicine</note>. If art <note>human skill or chemistry</note> made salts, it would be making bodies and substances. It is false to claim that things which are separated must be present in actuality: for example, the parts of milk are not present in actuality before separation. If things that are merely placed together and confused, but not truly mixed, are separated, then milk was not a true mixture.

...judged the dogmatic <note>referring to the traditional Galenic school of medicine</note> teachings to be safer and kinder; that some prefer the dung <note>original: "mucerdam," literally mouse-droppings; a common insult directed at the foul-smelling chemical preparations of the Paracelsians</note> of *Paracelsus* over cassia <note>a mild, sweet herbal laxative used in traditional medicine</note>; that *Scaliger* <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned scholar who defended traditional learning</note> was the mortal enemy of the Chemists (the forgers of gold, not the others); and that he wrote against *Cardano* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a polymath whose mystical views often clashed with Scaliger’s rationalism</note> for the sake of victory rather than for the truth.

<margin>According to Riolan, nourishment must be unsalted.</margin> 

To the question of "sweet nourishment," he responds that sweet water is sucked out from salt water by fish; if salt is taken in along with it, that salt is either made sweet through multiple coctions <term>coction: the "cooking" or ripening of fluids in the body, essentially the process of digestion and metabolism</term> or it is driven away. It does not pass into the substance of the body because the primordial humor <note>the fundamental fluid that sustains life in Galenic theory</note> is unsalted, and the nature of nourishment must be of the same kind. He argues that urine is made from whey, and by the mixing of this whey, the urine would turn salty if it were not already so by its own nature. Salt in living things is like an excrement, or it is not present in actuality. 

<margin>To make salt from water.</margin> 

The Umbrians are said to have made salt from water (how ridiculous!), just as the chemists claim to make it from urine, rather than simply separating what was already there. Yet, disease comes from salty waters. Salt benefits fertile earth only as a seasoning. In the same way, nature seasoned the blood with salt. (Therefore, is it not by nature?) It is done so that the blood is more greedily desired. If flesh were salty, the broths into which it deposits its nourishing juice (and at last it deposits juice, not "power") would be seasoned with salt in vain. (And yet **NATURE** seasoned the blood with salt. Why not also the flesh, and the fat, and the milk, etc.?) 

A concession: although a few things might be nourished by salty and bitter things, <margin>Look at the bastard Galenists of the Parisian school.</margin> it is nonetheless true: every living thing is nourished by the sweet. (But that is irrational <note>original: ἄλογον (alogon)</note>; because the genus is diminished by the specific case). Why is it true? Because rare things are not part of the medical art <note>i.e., medicine deals with general rules, not exceptions</note>. (Namely, they are accidental; but perpetual species have their essence in their genera even if they are rare, such as the *Unicorn*, *Asbestos*, the *Phoenix*, etc.) The idiosyncrasies <note>the unique physical constitution of an individual</note> of plants and animals do not over[turn]...

<margin>The vision of the Parisians is dull.</margin>
He thinks sight should be consulted, as to whether anyone has seen this in cemeteries <note>likely referring to the observation of salts or "bloom" appearing on decaying matter or bones</note>. If anyone wishes to call ash "salt," he does not wish to argue over the name, provided it is denied that this is a chemical salt, separated by artificial fire. Elements exist in mixtures potentially, not actually: (and yet they are separated. So too are the principles.) Much less are the principles present in actuality. He asserts they are created by the force of fire, and not merely separated. He calls it nonsense if anyone asserts otherwise. Art and nature differ. Art is outside the work; nature is within. Art composes, while nature generates (and yet nature also composes mixtures, if the scholastics <note>medieval university philosophers</note> speak truly concerning the mixture of elements).

<margin>The fire of Riolan.</margin>
Nature generates out of potentiality and actuality. Fire is either natural or artificial. The former is celestial <note>solar heat</note> or elementary. Artificial fire is intense, gentle, or moderate.

<margin>Chemical works.</margin>
In chemical works, natural fire is not the efficient cause. Therefore, chemical works are artificial. The chemists transmute physical matter into artificial, mathematical forms once the natural form is corrupted. Chemical works are physical by reason of their matter, but mathematical by reason of their form, in the same way as a silver triangle <note>meaning the "triangle" is a geometric concept imposed on the natural silver</note>. Chemical matter is natural; the form cannot be so, since it is not innate but acquired by art: for that matter is stripped of its natural form, its temperament, its configuration, and its vital and moderate heat by artificial fire. In response to the argument that if art <note>referring to alchemy or chemistry</note> resolves a substance into three parts, they must be present in actuality: He responds that the matter is transmuted into them. For example, wine 
<margin>The resolution of wine.</margin>
is resolved into **water of life** <term>aqua vitae: a concentrated alcoholic spirit produced by distillation; the "water of life"</term> through rarefaction into vapors, which then become liquid through condensation. Wine consists of matter suited to be changed into this substance, just as the elements are transmuted. Just as air exists potentially in water, so "water of life" exists in wine. Regarding nutrients: a living being is nourished 
<margin>Nutrients.</margin>
only by those things that have lived. Stones and metals have never lived. Therefore, a living being is not nourished by them; and consequently, not by **potable gold** <term>potable gold: a medicinal liquid supposed to contain gold, highly prized by alchemists as a universal cure</term>. 
<margin>Water.</margin>
Galen and Aristotle deny that water provides nourishment, though watery substances might. Why does water not nourish? Because it is a "simple" <note>original: *simplex*; in ancient science, a simple substance consists of only one element and lacks the complexity required to build body tissue</note>. Water is the vehicle for nourishment, not the nourishment itself, as Hippocrates says. 
<margin>The Parisians would rather err with Galen.</margin>
You might object by citing Scaliger and Rondelet (though Scaliger, in *Exercise 39*, thoroughly denies that water nourishes). As for me, I **WOULD RATHER ERR** with Aristotle, Galen, and Hippocrates, than share the correct opinion with Rondelet and Scaliger. These modern authors are scarcely yet known. Let us act by reason, not by authority. For this is what it means to philosophize.
<margin>Air nourishes.</margin>
The air that is inhaled immediately restores the constant dissipation of ALL spirits. The "natural spirit" <term>natural spirit: in Galenic medicine, the vital force responsible for nutrition and growth, believed to be centered in the liver</term> is restored partly from the healthy vapor of the blood and partly from the air processed in the lungs. Thus, AIR is said to nourish. 
<margin>Riolan argues against Riolan, albeit clumsily.</margin>
Thus, many animals are said to have lived for a long time solely by the inhalation of air; in the same way, odors provide nourishment. Democritus is said to have lived **FOR A LONG TIME** on the scent of bread warming in the oven. 
<margin>Water nourishes.</margin>
Water makes up for the loss of the moist substance, because moisture is restored by moisture. In this way, **WATER NOURISHES**. 
<margin>The most learned School is ignorant of the elements in the books "On the Soul."</margin>
Many have prolonged their lives for a long time by the drinking of water alone. Mixed substances can restore solid matter. That which is to nourish a mixture must itself be a mixture. That which has never lived cannot be assimilated into a living thing.

To nourish is to be assimilated <note>original: "Nutrire est assimilari"; a core principle of Galenic medicine stating that food must be transformed into the likeness of the body's own tissues</note>. That which has never lived, you would not call "potentially living." Only that which has lived retains the seed-bed <note>original: "seminarium"; the vital principle or "seeds" necessary for reproduction or growth</note> of its predecessor. Many things that have lived cannot nourish; much less, therefore, can those things which have never lived. Go now and contradict the school [of thought] which all learned men admire. Water does not have a principle of life; it is one thing to be generated *from* water, and another to be generated *within* water. It is one thing to be generated from water simply, and another from decay: because through decay it acquires heat, and with heat, it acquires a new power. Worms are generated in snow through <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>antiperistasis: a scientific theory where a quality is intensified by its opposite, such as internal heat becoming more concentrated when surrounded by external cold</note>. The heat of a progenitor is mild; the Chemist's heat is immoderate. 3. Born from opposites destroyed by fire...

A man is not to be honored above the truth. *<term>Plato, Republic, Book 10</term>*.

That which has lived has lost the seed-bed <note original: "seminarium">A source or "nursery" of life-force or vital principles.</note> of its preceding life. But if it should have retained it, not...

...however, it follows that something cannot potentially live where no preceding life existed. If water nourishes the moist substance of a living being, *Riolan* must believe that water itself once lived, because according to him, only things that have lived can provide nourishment. The opinion of *Rondeletius* <note>Guillaume Rondelet, a 16th-century physician famous for his work on marine biology.</note> is brought forward regarding the heat, flavors, and mixing of the waters in which animals live; likewise, he argues that the solid parts of those animals are also nourished by those waters. 

In a syllogism: A living thing differs more from a non-living thing than one living thing differs from another living thing; yet many things that once lived do not provide nourishment. Therefore, things that never lived nourish even less. The major premise here is sophistical, being only "relative" <note>original: *secundum quid*. This is a logical fallacy where a general rule is applied to a specific case without considering the circumstances.</note>. The distance is between life and non-life: in other matters, there can be agreement, such that the disagreement among living things themselves might be greater than between living and non-living things (for example, air and living things, or water, etc., agree more with each other than the venom of a scorpion agrees with a man). Whether something is living or non-living is irrelevant when the matter of the substance of nourishment is questioned. That which lives does not provide nourishment by virtue of the fact that it is alive, but by being fit to become like the one being nourished. 

(It is ridiculous if you were to say that plants must also be nourished by living things. But man first lives the life of plants <note>Referring to the "vegetative soul," the most basic level of life in Aristotelian biology responsible for growth and nutrition.</note>; and afterward is nourished naturally through analogy, etc.) Plants are formed and nourished by the elements, according to *Galen*. The reasoning is ridiculous: [it would imply] brute animals ought to be fed on meat and not plants, because a brute animal differs less from another brute animal than from a plant; and so on. A contradiction is rashly objected against *Baucynerus* <note>Likely a reference to a contemporary academic opponent or a misspelling of a scholar like Bausch.</note> when he says: non-living water nourishes, and water has the principle of life, because 
<margin>Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals*, Book 2, Chapter 3.</margin>
worms are created from it and are 
<margin>The heat of the sun.</margin>
nourished by that same water. A contradiction is objected against the candidate *Riolan*, seeing that to him...

Such a substance is called "celestial." The comparison between the generative spirit and the **chymical** spirit is vain. Is it simply not speaking according to your taste? <note>original: *ad saliuam tuam*; literally "to your saliva," an idiom meaning to suit someone's particular palate or expectations.</note> But Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne, the Paracelsian physician being defended here.</note> was not your slave. He dedicated it to you so that you might judge it, not so that you might pursue him with some unheard-of rage. You were free to accept it or reject it. What was the need for a public attack? You are the ones who did an injury to Quercetanus, and you have torn him apart with many insults. It was his right to complain about you. An injury depends on the intent and the purpose; for Quercetanus, there is a legal presumption in his favor based on the evident facts.

12. **But also [you claim he did it] "secretly":** Namely, that he did not show the writing to be seen before it was committed to the printing presses—something which modesty forbade. For he had dedicated it to the physicians themselves; when we wish to do this, we do not usually show it beforehand, lest arrogance spoil the favor. How is it "secret" when it is a public writing? How is it "secret" if he dedicated it to you by name? How is it "secret" when it was already common knowledge throughout all of Europe? You are observing the proper behavior of Madness. <note>original: *Mania*. The author suggests Riolan’s logic is that of a madman.</note>

Rulan- <note>The text cuts off, likely referring to Martin Rulandus, another famous supporter of chemical medicine.</note>

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENIC MEDICINE

<margin>

</margin>
...and so much a follower of Hippocrates that almost no one is more so. He does not cast aside Hippocratic medicine: But in it, he investigates something more hidden than what the eyes of the common people perceive. He is among the number of those who manifest the secrets within things, with a most ancient zeal, as is apparent from Mesue <note>Johannes Mesue, an influential Arabic medical authority whose works were foundational to medieval and Renaissance pharmacy.</note>. He retains, observes, and praises Hippocrates’ humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) believed to govern health.</note>, the similar parts <term>similar parts: In Galenic anatomy, tissues like bone, fat, or fiber that are uniform throughout, as opposed to complex "organic" parts like the hand.</term>, the solid, the moist, and the spiritual; Hellebore, spurge <note>original: "esula"</note>, and all the rest, insofar as they are discovered to be true through use, experience, and the consensus of nature.

<margin>
Note: If the Hermetics differ from the Hippocratics in nothing else than the preparation of remedies, it is false that Hippocratic medicine is destroyed by Quercetanus, unless the Hippocratics have themselves been changed into something else.
</margin>
For what truth is there in Hippocrates, I ask, that he does not accept? But he views these things with Chymical eyes, not Riolanic eyes <note>Referring to Jean Riolan, the staunch conservative leader of the Paris Medical Faculty and chief opponent of chemical medicine.</note>. In the four humors he recognizes essences; he recognizes them in the similar parts; he recognizes them in medicines. You yourself wrote to Turquet <note>Theodore de Mayerne (Turquet de Mayerne), a prominent physician who combined Galenic and chemical medicine and was eventually forced to leave Paris for England.</note> that you Galenists differ from the Chymists in nothing other than the method of preparation. <margin>
Hippocrates, in his book *On Winds* <note>original: "de flatibus"</note>, taught that all diseases arise from spirits; but for that reason, he did not cast aside principles and humors, as the Paracelsians <note>Followers of Paracelsus who advocated for mineral-based chemistry.</note> are accustomed to do.
</margin>
If Hippocrates were to rise again and place the healing faculties not in the simple external elements, but in the flavors, and if he were to separate their subject—which is the juice—from the dregs, and thus apply it to use: in your judgment, he would be a deserter. Likewise, if he were to discuss the limbs as Aristotle sometimes did—who found something more divine in them than the aforementioned elements—and were to set that apart: he would be a deserter. If he were to make and heal all diseases through the spirit, proposing a spiritual essence hidden in mixed bodies, he would, of course, be considered a madman. You yourself know no other spirit...

## ON PARISIAN ALCHEMICAL FALSEHOODS ##

<margin>
Libavius opposes Paracelsian impostures, not Alchemy itself. He praises Paracelsus for his good qualities and rejects him for his bad ones.

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM #

Now you cast me among the common dregs, treating **Libavius** no more honorably, it seems, than **Fernelius**, **Rondeletius**, **Schegk**, **Ruland**, **Curaeus**, **Scaliger**, **Quercetanus**, **Turquet**, **Harvet**, **Baucynet** <note>Libavius lists a "who's who" of prominent 16th-century physicians and scholars, many of whom tried to integrate chemistry with traditional medicine.</note>, and the entire college of chemists—past, recent, present, and future. These men have students to whom you could not even serve as a common servant <note>original: "cacula"</note>, a bellows-boy <note>original: "sufflo"</note>, or a charcoal-burner <note>original: "carbonarius"</note>. Such is your character. We are moved by pity toward you rather than by hatred. If only you would learn to be wise; it is for the sake of the truth that we enter this arena <note>original: "palæstra"</note>. For your own sake, we would not even turn a hand.

26. *“The second book of **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and prominent advocate for chemical medicine.</note>, which defends his first, is again condemned by the school.”*

False. A faction of hostile physicians condemned it, not the "school." And it condemned it based on your report without a just hearing of the case, and without summoning **Quercetanus**, who was undoubtedly in Paris at the time. A fine condemnation indeed! **Riolan** reported it thus: "The report having been heard, it judges," etc.

27. *“Lest anyone like you—that is, someone very ready to contradict, etc.”*

...are sometimes called <note>original: "appellantur"</note> those chemical physicians who handle chemical things and put them to use. which is an art? Behold the judges and condemners who, though they have carefully calculated their reasons, are ignorant of what it is they have undertaken to condemn. <header>A PART OF THE MIRROR OF ALCHEMY</header>
<meta>Catchword: philosophy</meta>

is understood in itself; in this way you have a **hieroglyphical** <note>In the 17th century, "hieroglyphical" referred to symbolic or mystical meanings hidden beneath the surface of words.</note> sense, by which the ailments of the body are exchanged for golden health. This is achieved through the universal condition of bodies, the spirits, the heat, and the innate moisture, which are brought from a poor state to an optimal constitution by the help of a certain medicine called the **elixir of life**.

Riolan, who is most ignorant of the secret wisdom, applies this term only to the tangible and metallic gold of the macrocosm <note>The "greater world" or the universe, as opposed to the "microcosm" of the human body.</note>. For that reason, he separates the other meaning from it and makes it purely medical. Yet even that first meaning touches upon medicine. He denies—foolishly and unskillfully—that the two have anything in common except the name; nor is any other argument needed to prove him wrong than the solemn custom and disciplinary tradition of the philosophers and craftsmen themselves.

What is it to you, you insane man, with what intention the name was given to the thing? Do you understand even a spark of Alchemy? But how was it "rashly" given? He says it is like the name "dog" being given to the star-dog <note>Sirius, the Dog Star.</note>, the domestic dog, and so on. Previously, he had said it was a "homonym by chance" <note>original: *ἀπὸ τῆς τυχῆς* (apo tēs tychēs). This is a technical term in logic for words that sound the same but have unrelated meanings by mere coincidence.</note>. 

You err, you madman! Homonymy arises from some similarity when it is used not by fools, but by wise men who occasionally employ allegories and metaphors; and Alchemy, beyond all other arts, is wonderfully parabolic <note>Full of parables or symbolic stories.</note>. Metaphorical homonymy is guided by a certain reason, not by fortune. Has even Fernelius <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician whose works were standard in medical education.</note> of the fusible and metallic **philosophy**...

## CHAPTER IV.

### *The reason why the Parisian School so often changes its position.*

**I**t is strange that the Medical College comes forward in public with the ambitious title of the **PARISIAN SCHOOL**, the most learned and famous of all schools, as if that entire University <note>The author refers to the University of Paris (the Sorbonne), arguing that the Medical Faculty is only one small part of it and shouldn't claim to represent the whole institution.</note> condemned Chemistry. But in the public notices, only the Medical College with its Dean is mentioned. If this is a "school" by itself, then the college of Theologians will also be a school by itself, as well as the Lawyers and the philosophers. The medical faction does an injustice to all these schools while it places itself before everyone in fame and learning; it does so to all other European schools as well. That pride is shameful and worthy of being sharply restrained by the Rector and the other members of the University.

But it is even more marvelous that, while wishing to seem most learned, it offers no arguments other than those of the foulest ignorance and no small amount of fatuity. The madness of Riolan <note>Jean Riolan (1539–1605), a prominent conservative physician and fierce opponent of chemical medicine.</note> says that the decree was made with well-calculated reasons. That certainly does not appear at the heart of the controversy, which they repeatedly change, providing the greatest proof of a headlong and ill-considered judgment. In the petition to the Paris Parliament <note>original: "Senatum Parisiensem"; the high court of justice in Paris, which had the power to issue legal decrees regulating medical practice.</note>, the college desires that whoever treats the sick with remedies other than the customary and ordinary ones should be punished with **DEATH**; (a crime than which there is hardly any more wicked among physicians, and clearly opposed even to Christian piety. For what if the King himself should heal a cancer with his finger? <note>A reference to the "Royal Touch," the traditional belief that the monarchs of France and England could heal scrofula and other ailments by touch.</note> What if an anointing...

For we read thus: It condemns by unanimous consent not only the Spagyric <note>The "Spagyric" art refers to the branch of alchemy focused on medicine, specifically the process of "separating and recombining" substances to purify them.</note> books of Quercetanus; <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), known as Quercetanus, was a prominent French physician and diplomat who advocated for the use of chemical remedies alongside traditional ones.</note> but even the Spagyric **ART** itself; and it urges all doctors, wherever they are in nations and places, to practice medicine according to the doctrine of Hippocrates and Galen; <note>Hippocrates and Galen were the foundational authorities of traditional Western medicine; the "Galenists" of the Paris Faculty viewed chemical medicine as a dangerous heresy.</note> which the prayer of the petition indicates should be understood most especially regarding remedies. In the spagyric books of Quercetanus, the most essential thing is the chemical preparation of medicines. His consultations do not cast aside the medical precepts of Hippocrates. His book *On the Medicine of the Ancients* treats a chemical medicine made from wine and gold. If he [Quercetanus] was involved in such a superstitious matter, he did not sin more shamefully than Giambattista della Porta; <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615) was a famous Italian polymath who wrote extensively on "natural magic" and physiognomy.</note> nor than Horapollo; <note>The supposed author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphics, often cited in the Renaissance for symbolic wisdom.</note> nor than Solomon, the wisest of the Jews; nor than Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who studied the nature of matter; here cited as an anatomical authority.</note> and other anatomists; indeed...

...not even to Galen. What is madness, if this is not? By condemning the spagyric books of Quercetanus, it is certain that the medicine of preparation has been condemned.

The school ought to have condemned this insanity. We condemn it ourselves. The *Parisians* are not the first authors of this condemnation, but others; indeed, we ourselves were earlier, as our public records testify. Did the school lack the words with which it could explain this opinion of theirs? This is not consistent, if it is the most learned of all. Deceit...

### THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM

<sig>I 2</sig>

There is a certain sophistry underlying this, by which the speech is so framed that Paracelsianism appears condemned, but in truth, Alchemy is rejected and proscribed—the very art whose remedies Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician who championed the use of chemical medicines within a traditional framework</note> prepared with such industry and applied with such skill and expertise that those Galenists <note>Traditionalist physicians who followed the teachings of Galen, focusing on the balance of the four bodily humors</note> were mocked even by the common people. From this come those tears <note>original: "Hinc illæ lacrymæ"; a classical Latin idiom meaning "that is the true source of the grievance"</note>.

Many arguments for this trickery could be brought forward. Whenever the censor is pressed regarding the excellence of chemical works—such as oils, waters, and salts (which, if they are simple, are nothing other than essences made from the three principles <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsus: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> through the exaltation of the art)—as well as Elixirs, balsams, extracts, masteries <term>magisteria: chemical preparations where the raw material is transformed but not entirely broken down</term>, and such things, he denies that these are condemned by his school, and he does so in more than one place. 

But when the argument reaches the matter of temperaments <term>crasios: from the Greek *krasis*, referring to the specific mixing of humors that determines a person's health</term>, he rages most fiercely against them, writing without shame that these things are created by the agency of Satan. On page 19 of the *Apology*: *Destruction is more certain from the use of chemical remedies. I do not doubt that these remedies were invented by the Devil, etc.* 

In the *Response to Turquet* <note>Theodore de Mayerne (1573–1655), a royal physician whose support for chemical medicine led to a famous conflict with the Paris Faculty</note> he says: It is not the cause of Quercetanus, but the cause of Alchemy that is being tried. Which alchemy? That which consists entirely in the preparation of remedies: this is the state of the case. See for yourself! The Censure opposes itself to Paracelsian medicine, which invents and thrusts forward new precepts from chemical resolutions in place of Hippocratic <note>Relating to Hippocrates, the "father of medicine," whose theories emphasized natural balance</note> ones. Yet the explanation and defense of the Censure condemns that Alchemy which consists entirely in the preparation of remedies. Page 45 of the *Apology*: *Your art contains a few good things which we approve; far more evil things which we condemn.* However, a name is given based on the majority; therefore, the spagyric <note>Spagyric refers to the alchemical process of "separating and recombining" to create potent medicines</note> art...

# THE ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN FORGERIES

...rejecting it as depraved and useless. The *Madness* <note>original: "Mania"; likely referring to a specific polemical pamphlet or the perceived "insanity" of the Faculty's decrees</note> of the school neither approves nor disapproves of **Chemical remedies**; a judgment that also extends to the art by which they are prepared. On page 20, when the author names "Alchemy," he does not mean new remedies or a new method of preparation, because he believes these merely illustrate traditional dogma. On page 86, you extol to the heavens those preparations that the school does not condemn, and so on. Likewise, on page 20, only the "fourth sect" is condemned, which is there called **Paracelsian**.

But the school opposed to Turquet <note>Theodore de Mayerne (1573–1655), a royal physician who was famously censured by the Paris Faculty for his chemical practices</note> condemns the preparatory art itself. The "Madness" school directs its censure toward the practice of medicine, while exempting the preparation of the drugs; this is the exact opposite of the anti-Turquet stance. On page 5 of the *Madness*: Bauchinetus <note>Likely referring to a member of the medical community or a specific critic of chemical medicine</note> understood that chemical remedies are not condemned by it. 

Yet Turquet cannot understand the same thing, for in his proscriptions, the heart of the controversy concerns the **preparatory art**. This is defined as being a single part of that branch of pharmacy <term>pharmaceutice: the study and art of preparing and dispensing drugs</term> which teaches how to prepare remedies. If this is true, the Medical School is acting insanely by taking up arms against a branch of pharmaceutical medicine; it is tearing out its own entrails in a civil war. 

Soon, that chemistry is condemned which prepares the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and curing all diseases</note> or medicines; this is once again attributed to the Devil as its author and is called an auxiliary of Magic. In the blink of an eye <note>original: "vix manum verteris"; literally "you have hardly turned your hand"</note>, the opponent of Turquet <note>original: "Antaruetus," a name used to signify an adversary of Turquet de Mayerne</note> appears in the arena, denying that the school completely repudiates chemical preparation. He states the position thus: 

"Medical counsel cannot be entered into with those who differ from the dogmatists <note>The traditional Galenic physicians who adhered to established academic medical doctrines</note> regarding the principles and causes of diseases, and their remedies." 

Yet, where **REMEDIES** are mentioned, chemical ones are clearly understood.

->**THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM**<-

We have noted that in the *Madness* <note>original: "mania"; likely referring to Riolan's polemic *Mania Academica* (1608)</note> chemical remedies are at times not condemned; at other times they are neither approved nor disapproved (which is foolish talk. Riolanus himself allows freedom of choice to those who study new things, so that they may be permitted to "be insane" <note>original: "insanire"; a play on the title of Riolan's work, suggesting that Riolan views any departure from tradition as a form of madness</note>; which is certainly a fine concession! The Chemists, in turn, permit Riolanus his favorite spirits, so that he too may be abnormally insane. Hardly has he exhaled those words on *page 9 of the Madness*, when look, on *page 10* he breathes this: *“In imitation of the Arabs <note>The "Arabs" refers to medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna and Rhazes, who introduced many chemical processes into pharmacy long before Paracelsus</note>, whatever NEW remedies and new forms of remedies can ever be devised should be referred to pharmacy* <term>pharmaceuticen: the art of preparing and dispensing medicines</term>, *I contend again and again; I do not reject them for this or that reason, nor do I think they should be rejected,” etc.*

Here you see by what diverse paroxysms the "Manic" Riolanus is agitated. In the progress of his *Madness*, we shall even hear that the chemists perform miracles. So much has the school changed from its former posture of condemnation. But nonetheless, that "Manic" senate <note>Referring to the formal assembly of the Paris Medical Faculty</note> stubbornly opposes every argument brought forward in favor of chemistry, so that what it grants with words, it soon destroys and takes away again in practice. Such is the state of the controversy, that you still do not know where we ought to find

### CHAPTER V.

->*The School of Paris Defeated and Triumphed Over.*<-

**H**e who is so hard-pressed by the light, the truth, and the strength of arguments that he is forced to write things plainly contrary to his previous judgment—rendered so ambiguous and wavering in his own cause that he flees with no certain footing, turning now here, now there—and stands publicly convicted before all wise men of many insults, blasphemies against God and His creatures, outrages, wrongs, lies, and contradictions: such a man must be pronounced conquered, bound, and led in a public triumph by public decree. The anti-chemical medical school of the Parisians is so pressured in this case against Alchemy; a fact that is notorious to those publicly fighting against it, such as *Quercetanus* <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician who championed Paracelsian chemical medicine</note>, *Haruetus* <note>Israel Harvet, a pro-chemical physician from Orléans who engaged in a famous pamphlet war with the Paris Faculty</note>, *Turquetus* <note>Théodore de Mayerne (1573–1655), a hugely influential chemical physician who later became the doctor to four English kings</note>, and *Baucynetus*; and it will be visible to the eye in our examination of the *Madness* <note>original: "Mania"; referring to Jean Riolan's polemic *Mania Academica* (1608)</note>. Do you want it in a few words? *“Would that they were punished with death, whoever cures the sick with anything other than the customary and ordinary means.”* (Those means, of course, are the *old Galenic ways* <note>Traditional medicine based on the works of Galen, which relied on balancing the four humors using plant-based remedies rather than chemical minerals</note>). But on page 10 of the *Madness*, new remedies are received into medicine; and on page 20, they are said to illustrate dogmatic medicine <term>dogmaticam: the traditional, theoretical medicine based on Hippocrates and Galen</term>, etc. It is not the custom for those using accepted new remedies to be punished with death. Therefore, this school must be declared conquered, bound, and triumphed over by public decree. But it will continue to rave nonetheless. Let it rave, I say. It is bound in chains of darkness: it has been disarmed and can inflict no violence. A brief argument:

From separated mixtures they bring forth and reveal <term>arcana</term> <note>secret, powerful remedies extracted from natural substances</note> just as the ancient wise philosophers and Alchemists did according to *Mesue* <note>Masawaih al-Marindi, a medieval physician whose name was attached to popular pharmaceutical texts</note>. It should state that the School itself decided nothing; rather, a few men of a medical faction rose up against the Chemical physicians by their own private judgment. These men seem to have been punished enough already by the infamy they have brought upon themselves through their own madness and recklessness. ## CHAPTER VII.

->*What weapons the mad Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a conservative physician at the University of Paris and a fierce critic of chemical medicine.</note> wishes to deploy against the examination by Libavius; where at the same time the "Antigramanias" are discussed.*<-

On **p**age 6 of *Madness* <note>original: "Mania"; referring to Riolan's polemical work against Libavius.</note>, *Riolan* is confident that out of ten selected *Parisians*, even the least of them will slit my throat with my own weapons. "Are you not that *Libavius*," he says on *page 9*, "the *Anti-Gramanian*, who wrote that the truest remedy is the one that is safest?" With these and similar remarks, he often insults me. It should be known that I have written nothing for *Quercetanus* <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), the royal physician who championed the use of chemical medicines.</note> by design. If, while I fight for chemical truth, I happen to include him, he may rejoice not in my protection, but in the truth's. He himself has fought enough for his own sake, and **HE HAS CONQUERED**. As for the weapons from my *Antigramania* <note>Libavius had previously attacked the chemist Graman for his lack of medical training, a fact Riolan tries to use to show Libavius is inconsistent.</note>, they can in no way help the school of *Paris*. *Gramanus* is one man; *Quercetanus*, whom the school opposes, is another. The cause of the former is one thing, the cause of the latter quite another. I did not write against *Gramanus* without preserving the praise due to true <term>Alchemy</term>. *Gramanus* was then a <term>pseudo-chemist</term>, having brought himself from the pastorate into chemistry by his own rashness. *Quercetanus* is a true chemist, a *Doctor of Medicine*, and a follower of <term>Hippocrates</term>. <header>THE ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN COUNTERFEITS</header>

...was sending in. Here, to put it briefly, even if I had not only attacked the chemistry of Graman and similar <term>pseudo-chemists</term> <note>original: "pseudochymicorum"; those Libavius considered to be practitioners of "false" or superstitious alchemy.</note> and <term>Paracelsian</term> <note>Followers of Paracelsus who favored chemical remedies, often viewed as radical by traditional physicians.</note> physicians, but had also corrected true chemistry, I would have done nothing foreign to the medical profession. I would not have criticized the art itself, but rather the abuse of the art—feeling quite differently than the Parisian school, which condemns not only the <term>spagyric</term> <note>original: "spagyricos"; a term for chemical medicine involving the separation and recombination of elements.</note> books of <term>Quercetanus</term> <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent French physician and advocate of chemical medicine.</note> (that is, the description of the art), but even the art of **Alchemy** itself, which is the same as spagyria. 

Who does not know that philosophy is worthy of the highest honor if it remains within its own boundaries? But if that same philosophy flies out beyond true Theology, it must be restrained and brought back into order. To what end, then, does that mad school so often throw my *Antigramania* <note>Libavius’s earlier work attacking the "pseudo-chemist" Johann Graman.</note> in my face? Why does it not make distinctions instead, so as to teach well? Why does it refuse to see my distinction? Clearly, malice has occupied its eyes and mind. 

This is the gratitude it shows me for my many labors and late-night studies endured in defense of <term>Hippocratic medicine</term> <note>The traditional system of medicine based on the ancient Greek teachings of Hippocrates.</note>. On the other hand, when I defend true **Chemistry** to the best of my ability, I have not cast off my former spirit, nor have I become a deserter to the camp of the **Paracelsians**. I make use of the words of <term>Crato</term> <note>Johannes Crato von Krafftheim (1519–1585), a distinguished physician to three Holy Roman Emperors.</note> to Zwinger:

<margin>Letter 137, scholia.</margin>
> "I ought not to remain silent," (he says) "that our common friend does me a remarkable injury when he treats me as an enemy and oppo[nent] of chemistry..."

...to demonstrate that these things are by no means simply new, although things can appear new to a particular person or place, just as the art of tailoring <note>original: "sartoria"</note> would appear new to naked Indians. **Riolan’s** madness on page 11 responds: "You recommend Alchemy chiefly on account of its antiquity." I marvel (he adds) that you, who are most fond of novelty, make so much of antiquity. That is a lie; it is he who is most fond <gloss>most fond</gloss> of novelty. As **Horace** says: <note>Libavius is quoting Horace's *Ars Poetica*, lines 70–71, regarding the evolution of language and custom.</note> many things shall be reborn that have already fallen, and those words which are now in honor shall fall. The Gospel seemed to be new after the Law, but it was so only in its manifestation. By it, the ancient law was abolished. Imagine that chemistry were new in its revelation and our knowledge of it, yet in reality it would not be new. Do you hear what we say to that? Let it be the work of the "Arab **Democritus**." We say he was a chemist who knew medical secrets <note>original: *arcana*</note> alongside chemical secrets at the same time. Is there not mention of **SECRETS** in the introduction to the book of antidotes, and in the treatise on oils [extracted] by resolution <note>chemical decomposition or distillation</note>, lest such secrets be so hateful to you? At that time, the healing art of medicine encompassed both **Hippocratic** medicine and <term>chymiatria</term> <note>chemical medicine</note>; it did not outlaw **Alchemy**, nor did it hand over those using chemical methods to the cross <note>i.e., persecute or execute them</note>, as your school foolishly does. **Mesue** recited the common things of **Democritus**, such as **agaric** <note>a type of medicinal mushroom used in ancient pharmacy</note>, etc.; regarding those things which ought not to be made common, he remained silent.

Behold, here are our principles which you wanted shown to you; and to be more generous, I even give you the elements, and furthermore the **fifth nature** <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or quintessence was thought to be a pure, incorruptible substance superior to the four elements</note>. Hence, argue thus for **Democritus** <note>Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher known for his atomic theory, which Libavius here links to chemical theory</note>:

> *He whose doctrine regarding the solidifying and dissolving of bodies agrees with chemical principles—it is probable that he was a chemist.*

> *The doctrine of Democritus regarding the solidifying and dissolving of bodies agrees with chemical principles, as we have already shown from Riolanus. Therefore, it is probable that Democritus was a chemist.*

Aristotle’s doctrine of the elements is raised as an objection. In vain, I say. For elements exist for Democritus too, as has been shown; I was hoping for the best from **Riolanus** <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), a conservative physician and fierce critic of the new chemical medicine</note>. I thought a wise disciple of chemistry would emerge from a madman, according to Aristotle’s decree: *Opposites arise from opposites* <note>original: *Contrarium fit ex contrario*; a fundamental principle in Aristotelian physics and Galenic medicine</note>. But he is a "big bad fish" <note>An idiomatic insult suggesting Riolanus is slippery, cold, or troublesome</note>. He returns to his foolishness, according to the word of the wise man: *Though thou shouldst bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him* <note>A reference to Proverbs 27:22, appropriately using a mortar and pestle metaphor for a chemist’s opponent</note>. This is Riolanus's own "fifth essence," and it is immutable. But how so? Behold:

<margin>Riolanus is a liar.</margin>
This doctrine of Hippocrates and Empedocles, he says—out of your habit of slandering—you call **THE FICTION OF ARISTOTLE** <note>original: *ARISTOTELIS COMMENTVM*</note>. What doctrine, I ask, do I call so? That all things are made from opposites,

He also launches a sharp polemical attack on his rival Riolanus, mocking his stubborn adherence to traditional Aristotelian views.</summary>

<header>ALCHEMY CONCERNING THE SPIRIT OF PARIS</header>

contrary things, which exist together in nature. All elements concur; none is prior. This is your lie, **Riolanus**. I have not spoken even a word about these matters in my examination. **Aristotle**, I say, argues against **Democritus** through logical reasoning, whereas **Democritus** wishes to be convinced not by these, but by arguments that are proper and natural to the subject. I say that you, led astray by these Aristotelian fabrications, judge **Democritus** most unfairly. Indeed, the arguments produced against <term>atoms</term> <note>original: *atoma*; the indivisible, fundamental building blocks of matter proposed by Democritus</note> are not physical, but mathematical; they concern continuities, the length, width, and depth of a mathematical body, and so on, regarding <term>indivisible</term> lines <note>original: *insectilibus*; lines that theoretically cannot be further divided</note>. **Democritus** would laugh at these, not refute them. For because he likewise posits his <term>atoms</term> as bodies, he acknowledges that they possess the mathematical properties of bodies, but held that these do not obstruct the imperceptible atoms nor take away their physical properties. There is no need for logic-chopping to refute **Democritus**; there is a need for a proper demonstration drawn from physics.

Let us hear even more charming things. That leader of the wise (namely **Aristotle**, who nevertheless acts foolishly in many matters, and who is not even accepted by **Riolanus** when it suits him; indeed, to **Riolanus** as judge, it seemed that **Democritus** approached Christian truth more closely than the others) taught against **Democritus** that mixed substances are not born by <term>concretion</term> <note>original: *concretione*; the process of gathering or sticking together</note> and a kind of gluing together of those <term>little bodies</term> <note>original: *corpusculorum*; small particles of matter</note>, but by <term>mixture</term> <note>original: *mistione*; the total philosophical blending of substances into a new, unified essence</note>, that is, by the united essences of the four elements. Oh, what a deed! What if **Democritus** said that his <term>atoms</term> were mixed by God long ago, and did not require <term>concretion</term> from the very beginning <note>original: *ab ovo*; literally "from the egg," meaning from the very start</note>, although they further coalesce with the elements...

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM #

...how might they be able to form a more robust and thicker body? **Aristotle** judges the first principles of nature based on things that come after them <note>original: *ex posterioribus*; a philosophical method of reasoning from effects back to causes</note>. Those things which are born within <term>mixtures</term> <note>original: *mistis*; a technical term for substances created by the combination of elements</note> are not yet perfectly mixed, nor do they receive the logic of their essence from a collision that has already occurred, but they hold it from the movement of the starting principle toward the essence. Meanwhile, as a larger mass is created from a small one <note>referring to the process of biological growth</note>, this also does not happen merely from a framework of elements; rather, that which provides nourishment, or is supplied in an analogous way, is already mixed. 

And this is our **chemical essence** which, while it emerges amidst the crowd of elements, drags many superfluous things along with it; and even from the remains of generation and growth (for nothing is made out of the whole), it carries away superfluities. **Democritus** does not actually disagree with **Aristotle** on this; but the madness of **Riolanus** understands neither of them. It is ridiculous to deny that visible bodies are made from the <term>concretion of atoms</term> <note>the "growing together" or joining of fundamental particles</note>; since, in fact, those things are said to be concretions, and those things are mixed most exactly which come together by their <term>smallest parts</term> <note>original: *minima*; the physical limit of division in a substance</note>, such as watery and smoky things. From this, metals possess the most exact logic of mixture, and their matter is <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury, considered by alchemists to be the base of all metals</note>, an inseparable and uniform substance.

<margin>
It is a wonder why **Democritus** is not judged by his disciple **Hippocrates** <note>the "Father of Medicine," whom tradition often linked to Democritus</note>, rather than by **Aristotelian** quibbles which seem to be nothing other than a fiction falsely attributed to such a great man.
</margin>

Why do you, foolish man, deny what is evident even to the senses of old women curdling milk? Where was the butter in the milk? Which particle did you see? Which particle of cheese did you see? *As cheese, we are curdled by God.* <note>A reference to Job 10:10: "Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?" used here to describe the formation of the human body.</note> In the whey, where was the salt? But if you wish to compose diverse things, the chemists know that this is done best with liquids or spirits, in a completely natural way. Thus, external elements are able to coalesce with essences, and furthermore, many more things can be made through the innumerable mixtures that follow.

# ALCHEMY: ON THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS #
<note>original: *Alchymiæ de Spur. Paris.*; this likely refers to Libavius's response to the Paris medical faculty's 1603 decree against chemical medicines</note>

<margin>Riolan defeated by the authorities.</margin>
Finally, even if Riolan is stupid, he nonetheless feels himself defeated by the argument from the authority of the craftsmen. But what kind of monster is he attempting to create? He calls it an argument of the rhetoricians, not of the philosophers. Yet, philosophers and physicians are cited! Riolan, repeat your own words: "the first proof of ignorance is to contradict the wise." For you, an argument is valid when it suits your taste <note>original: *ad salivam facit*; literally "makes saliva," a Latin idiom for something being to one's liking or "palatable"</note>, and when it does not, you are moved neither by **Galen**, nor **Hippocrates**, **Scaliger**, **Rondelet**, **Fernel**, **Cureus**, or others. Learn that one must believe craftsmen speaking in their own art according to their own principles—not simply because they say so, but because they are craftsmen who possess the <term>form</term> <note>in the Aristotelian sense, the essential nature or internal logic of a discipline</note> established by the art through reason, experience, and the senses. He who rejects the consensus of craftsmen cries out against common experience. 

Learn this as well: when testimony is called a "rhetorical argument," it is understood as the kind used in the forum <note>the law court</note>; such as: "Hey, where is Casca? Where is Ruscio? You speak, Chremes; you speak, Simulus; speak, Corisca; speak, Thestilis; speak, Corydon." <note>Libavius is mocking Riolan by listing stock names of slaves and peasants from Roman comedy and pastoral poetry (like Terence and Virgil) to represent unreliable or unscientific witnesses.</note> But a logical argument is not without reason and a technical foundation; if it lacks these, it is then rejected. The testimony of craftsmen regarding their own subject cannot be cast aside so lightly, because they are fortified by the <term>form of the art</term>. Furthermore, nothing is more valid in this genre than the following:

> *Alchemy is the most ancient: Because chemical craftsmen are the most ancient.*

The art exists before the craftsmen. If the craftsmen are the most ancient, why should the art itself not be? Most ancient is **Tubalcain**, that smelter of bronze and iron <note>A biblical figure from Genesis 4:22, traditionally regarded by alchemists as the first metallurgist</note>. Therefore, the art of smelting, which is chemistry, is older. But...

-> # GALEN’S TRIUMPH # <-
<note>original: *Galenia Triumphus*; Libavius likely uses this title sarcastically to frame his defense of chemistry against the rigid Galenism of the Paris Medical Faculty.</note>

<sig>L 2</sig>

Why is the argument from authority trivial? Speak, you madman:

<margin>*That vice is more ancient than virtue.*</margin>
What is there (you ask) that I cannot demonstrate with examples and authorities? And at the same time, you swear by the immortal God. It would be a wonder indeed if, by the word of some author or craftsman, you could show—much less demonstrate—that two contradictory things are true at the same time; or that a gnat is an Indian Elephant; or that the stars of the highest heaven could be touched by the fingers of a Pygmy standing on the ground, by means of direct physical contact.

But what are you actually capable of? By a similar argument, you can prove that vice ought to be embraced rather than virtue, because there are more people who are vicious than there are those endowed with virtue. A fine thing, I say, if being vicious were a craft and those vicious people were "craftsmen." On the contrary, I can conclude from the multitude of the vicious that virtue is a certain divine thing, which so few attain because it is so excellent—a possession belonging only to the best, who are rare. 

In the same way, it must be that Alchemy is a truly excellent science, precisely because a great multitude of <term>pseudo-alchemists</term> <note>original: *parachymicorum*; Libavius uses this to describe those who pervert the art of chemistry or work "beside" it improperly</note> are found, as well as many who hate it. For "Art has no enemy except the ignorant." <note>original: *Ars autem non habet inimicum nisi ignorantem*; a common medieval and Renaissance proverb defending the liberal and mechanical arts.</note> If chemistry did not exist, how could there be pseudo-chemists? If it were not a noble art, how could the most unrefined Paris School <note>The Medical Faculty of the University of Paris, which issued a famous decree in 1603 condemning chemical medicines.</note> rage against it so fiercely? 

Go on: you can show by the same argument that vices are to be embraced over virtue because vice is "more ancient" than virtue. Back to the schoolmaster's rod of logic, Riolan! <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a prominent Parisian physician and fierce critic of alchemy.</note> That is not an argument from testimony; it is an argument from an <term>adjunct</term> <note>in logic, a property or circumstance associated with a subject but not part of its essence</note> where the comparison is drawn from things that are unequal or from "the greater." Thus, in a prosyllogism—

## ALCHEMY AGAINST THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS ##
<note>original: *Alchymiæ de Spuriis Parisiensibus*; Libavius refers to the members of the Paris Medical Faculty who opposed chemical medicine as "spurious" or "false" philosophers.</note>

...[we] are not led by authority. For you say that vice is older than virtue because human nature is more inclined toward lust; this is an argument from cause. I wonder in vain whether you were drunk or sober when you blurted those things out. Indeed, it is clear that you were possessed by madness. Furthermore, it is a false argument. Is a habit not prior to its privation? Is an affirmation not prior to a negation? God, the principle of good, is prior to those things that arise from good; the innocent Adam is prior to the guilty one. Sin, the wages of which is death, entered only incidentally. In himself, man was a good creature of God. If you say that examples of evil are prior to examples of good, you will be no wiser. For even the Devil was good in the beginning; the angels were good; God is good. Adam was good, Eve was good; all creatures were good.

Therefore, you curse the art that ruins its own craftsman. To be sure, he cites thirty-six authors, among whom are even the most famous: Aristotle, Galen, Hippocrates, Thomas Aquinas, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus, Arnold [of Villanova], Geber, Marsilio [Ficino], and others. > *That art which was approved by those authorities is not ignoble, nor to be condemned.*
> *Alchemy was approved by those authorities. Therefore [it is not ignoble or to be condemned].*

Riolan proves the minor premise, because either <term>chrysopoeia</term> is being considered, or medicinal Alchemy. Each has authority from those men. <margin>A triumphant syllogism.</margin>
> *He who has been forced to deny his own thesis is defeated.*
> *The Parisian school has been forced to deny its own thesis. Therefore, it is defeated.*

Therefore, it does not condemn Alchemy at all: And as a consequence, that censure of the school is false, by which not only are the spagyric <note>original: "spagyrici"; referring to the "spagyric art," or medicinal alchemy, which involves separating and recombining the "pure" parts of substances</note> books of Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne, the chemical physician being defended here</note> condemned, but even the spagyric art itself; all those condemning statements which are read in the pamphlets of Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Younger, a prominent critic of chemical medicine</note>, mentioned above, are false.*

The major premise in this entire dispute has only two parts. For the claim that some wish to call Paracelsian medicine "Alchemy" is a fiction; and it is not even admitted by Paracelsus himself. Alchemy is one thing, medicine is another. Alchemy, besides its manual practice <note>original: "Enchirian"; from the Greek "encheiresis," referring to the physical work or manipulation of substances in a laboratory</note>, has only two parts; one concerning magisteries <note>original: "magisteriis"; high-level alchemical preparations where the whole substance is transformed into a more potent form without necessarily separating its elements</note>, and the other concerning essences. Examples of each are proposed: from the magisteries, the transmutation of metals, principles, elements, etc. From the essences, extracts, oils, waters, alkali <note>original: "alcali"; referring to salts extracted from plant ashes, a key product of chemical laboratory work</note>, etc. Now, the school condemns neither part. The reason is that the censor writes: *It concerns the magistrate ALONE to distinguish harmful arts from useful ones*; (even if this were false, let us grant it to Riolan for now.) Likewise, he claims the censure does not touch gold-making; yet in his "Apology," "Excursion," and "Frenzy," Riolan wants to appear to have refuted it with invincible arguments. By this very act, he either accuses himself of bad faith—because he judged what he was not commanded to judge—or of a meddling impudence by which he wandered into foreign matters, even though it is a crime to exceed the limits of one's mandate. Regarding healing alchemy <note>original: "medicatrice Alchymia"</note>, we have the defendant confessing in his own words.

## CHAPTER IX.

->*Concerning the argument of whether Alchemy is an art and science, or nothing at all.*<-

**P**age 10 of the *Apologia* <note>The "Apologia" was Riolan’s 1603 attack on the use of chemical medicines</note> is written as follows: "You commit two sins at once: first, that you distinguish Spagyric <note>chemical/alchemical</note> remedies from empirical ones <note>treatments based purely on experience or trial-and-error without a theoretical framework</note>, and you introduce a fourth sect of medicine <note>Traditionally, there were three sects: Dogmatic, Methodic, and Empirical; Riolan accuses the chemists of trying to create a fourth</note>. Second, that you call chemistry a true art and a perfect science of healing, when it is neither an art nor a science." These are his words there, quoted exactly. He then proceeds to a demonstration that it is neither an art nor a science, using those arguments which I have set forth in my examination. He turns Alchemy into a little handmaid <note>original: "ancillulam"</note> of pharmacy; if we wished to establish a new art from it, we would also have to call all other modes of preparation "new arts." The force of this argument is that a part of an art is not an art in itself. Chemistry, he claims, is truly a part of the art of medicine, because it is merely a certain mode of preparing remedies in that part of medicine which...

A handmaid to a mistress is not the mistress; the service of an art is not the art itself. That which is a hollow name and a title without substance is not an art. These were the arguments of **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan (1539–1605), a conservative French physician who led the opposition against chemical medicine.</note> which are now exploded. Nothing prevents a part or member of an art from being an art even when considered by itself; just as **pharmaceutics** is a certain art in itself, and yet it is a member of medicine. **Arithmetic** is an art in itself, and yet it is a part of philosophy. Therefore, **Alchemy** is also called an art by every wise man, not by some recent or private judgment, but by ancient estimation and public authority. You wretched man, you do not know what you are babbling. Ramus, in one tiny drop of himself and a single syllable of his logic, has more wisdom than all your stools and academic Chairs. Attack his logic, if you have the strength. As for your belief that the followers of Ramus are ignorant of Aristotelian matters, you are mistaken, nor is there any need for words. So that you may see your madness, I shall use your own foundation:

> *Those arts which differ in subject and end are distinct from one another.*
> *Chemistry and medicine differ in subject and end.*
> *Therefore, chemistry and medicine are arts distinct from one another.*

The major premise <note>The first part of a logical argument (syllogism).</note> is your own principle from the Aristotelian school. I shall prove the minor premise <note>The second part of the argument.</note>, because (to speak only of the preparation of medicines, in which you sometimes contend all of chemistry is occupied) Alchemy has minerals and fossils <note>original: *fossilia*. I was not concerned with the degree of honesty with which the argument was presented. I examined the matter itself and stated that by the very fact they are called **artificial**, they are proven to be products of art. To which logician, I ask, is it not clear that **art** and **artificial** are related terms <note>original: *coniugata*; in Aristotelian logic, these are "conjugates," or words derived from the same root that share a logical connection</note>, and that art is the symbol of the cause, while the artificial is the symbol of the effect? That which is artificial comes from art, just as that which is natural comes from nature. If chemical preparations are artificial, it is necessary that their cause is art. If, therefore, <term>Harvet</term> <note>Israel Harvet, a physician and champion of chemical medicine against the conservative Paris Faculty.</note> had argued in this way, he would have knocked down <term>Riolan’s</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Elder, a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine.</note> negation with a powerful battering ram, and would have demonstrated that chemistry is an art, contrary to what the censor had written. Why then this madness? He raves in his own fashion, so as not to lose his sense of propriety. He attributes such an argument to me:

> ->*The preparations of the chemists are artificial. Therefore, they are arts.*<-

The poor wretch lies. None of that trivial reasoning is mine. This is how I speak: If all the preparations of the <term>pharmacists</term> <note>original: *pharmacopœi*</note> are skillful, they will all have originated from art—and indeed, all together from a common art. Yet individual preparations come from their own specific type, etc., which can be explained logically. There is an art of dividing, an art of defining, an art of <term>syllogizing</term> <note>The process of forming a syllogism, a three-part logical argument.</note>, etc.; each of these is a distinct art with its own goal; yet they unite into the single art of <term>Dialectic</term>, and they all cohere in the common goal of reasoning well. First, therefore, <term>Riolan</term> commits the crime of forgery <note>original: *crimen falsi*, a legal term for falsifying a document or statement</note>, and then he judges the reasoning with malice. For what error would there have been, even if I had written: "individual preparations are individual arts, because all are skillful," that is, arts produced by art...

# THE ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN FORGERIES #

Riolanus was ashamed to openly confess his own folly, so he hides it with verbal evasions as the <term>sophists</term> <note>Sophists were ancient Greek teachers often accused of using clever but fallacious arguments; Libavius uses the term to suggest Riolanus is being intentionally deceptive.</note> are wont to do. From this, he claims I am **strangled by my own sword** <note>original: *iugulatus sim meo gladio*; a proverbial expression for being defeated by one's own logic or arguments</note>. But what does this have to do with the point? <note>original: *quid & hoc ad rhombum?*; literally "what is this to the spinning top?", a Latin idiom meaning "beside the point."</note> Answer the question you were asked: Is chemistry an art?
