# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM #
<note>original: "Galenia Triumphus." This title ironically refers to the perceived victory of traditional Galenic medicine—which relied on balancing the four humors—over the newer chemical or "spagyric" medicine.</note>

<margin>In the *Anticurio*, page 74: "We recoil from the violence of your remedies and nearly classify them as poisons. For even your <term>magisteries</term> <note>concentrated medicinal extracts or "master" preparations</note> are excessively hot." Page 89: "If one person is saved by your remedies, ten others perish," etc.</margin>

...prepared with <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>literally "water of life"; highly concentrated alcohol or spirits used as a solvent.</note>, etc. An infusion is superior to an extract. Your chemical preparation is longer, more laborious, and more expensive, yet less effective than ours. Therefore, it is useless. Novelties please only for a time, etc. Our traditional preparations have already been accepted for many centuries; if these methods of yours were known to the **Arabs** <note>referring to the medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna and Geber, who were early pioneers of chemistry</note>, why did they lie forgotten until today, unless time itself demonstrated that this invention was useless, etc?

On *Page 44*: "We prefer to use juices or <term>decoctions</term> <note>medicinal liquors made by boiling plant material</note> rather than distilled waters, in all of which some 'little spark of fire' remains; we do not use them unless fresh herbs are unavailable," etc. On *page 45*, he says that the <term>temperament</term> <note>the "complexion" or balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in a substance</note> is either destroyed or at least diminished by distillation. "Your art contains a few good things, which we approve of, but far more evil things, which we condemn. A thing is named for its greater part. Therefore, we repudiate the <term>spagyric art</term> <note>the alchemical process of separating and recombining the components of a substance</note> as wicked and useless."

On *page 46*, he continues with a comparison of secondary qualities and writes that the temperament perishes when the <term>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</term> <note>known as the "Tria Prima," these were the three fundamental chemical principles according to Paracelsus</note> are separated from the mixture. On *page 48*, regarding the treatment of obstructions, he compares chemical oil with decoctions; and on *page 49*, he brings forward "burning water" <note>concentrated alcohol</note>. On *page 50*, he says: "You commend your remedies chiefly on the grounds that they are purified of dregs and freed from the bulk of matter by distillation or extraction." And he concludes: "Your art is maimed in the most important part of medicine" (because he thinks it possesses no remedies that are cold, austere, or bitter). He says that <term>crocus martis</term> <note>literally "Saffron of Mars"; a term for iron oxide (rust) used for its astringent properties</note> was an invention of the **Hippocratics** <note>followers of Hippocrates; Riolan is trying to claim chemical discoveries for traditional medicine</note>. Finally, he attacks **Heurnius** <note>Johannes Heurnius (1543–1601), a Dutch physician and professor at Leiden</note>, whom he goads for being too addicted to Alchemy, and compares oil of anise with a decoction of the same. This is the summary of that chapter, from which it appears that the debate is not about any medical precept or any Paracelsian invention, but about that form of Alchemy to which Heurnius was devoted.

### THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS ###
<note>original: "Alchymiæ de Spur. Paris." This refers to the "Spurious Parisians"—likely a jab at the Parisian medical faculty who Libavius believes are being dishonest about their use of chemical medicine.</note>

<margin>These remedies on page 115 from the summary are called elixirs, tinctures, magisteries, essences, oils, etc.</margin>

...devoted; concerning that art which produces waters, oils, salts, extracts, principles, <term>antimony</term> <note>a metallic element used in chemical medicine as a powerful—and controversial—purgative</note>, precipitates, <term>crocus of Mars</term> <note>literally "Saffron of Mars"; a name for iron oxide (rust) used as a medicinal tonic</note>, and so forth. This art is condemned in express words, although it contains certain good things, because it is placed alongside many evils. When this furious condemnation was brought before the school, <term>Riolan’s</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Elder, a staunch defender of traditional Greek medicine against the new chemistry</note> madness was revealed, and he denies the act. For he writes on page 27: *“The School was able to condemn the entire medicine of <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>the famous and controversial Swiss physician who championed chemical medicine</note> for this reason alone: that it confesses itself to have proceeded from the Devil”* (a foul lie which <term>Riolan</term> is not ashamed to repeat). Does he deny that the <term>Spagyria</term> <note>the art of separating and recombining natural substances, synonymous with medicinal chemistry</note> to which these medicines belong was condemned? Yet that which was treated in that entire condemnatory chapter was indeed condemned. That was not the medicine of Paracelsus, but the **Alchemy of Heurnius** <note>Johannes Heurnius, a Dutch physician who attempted to integrate chemical medicines into traditional practice</note>. Therefore, the school stands convicted of an unjust condemnation, because what it once condemned it now practices without penalty; and thus, it renders its own prior condemnation void, and condemns itself. Let a triumphal arch be erected for the truth on this account as well!

As for the question of whether a book should be condemned because it has good things mixed with bad, or bad with good, whether many or few (for <term>Riolan</term> argues both ways—that an art should be condemned even for a few evils of great significance), one must see whether the causes are equal in every case, and ensure that apparent evils are not mistaken for true ones. The works of **Ovid**, **Martial**, and other poets have not been condemned—especially **Homer** and those who wrote many false things about the gods that are contrary to Christian piety; rather, they are ordered to be selected <note>original: "eligi," referring to the practice of "expurgation," where offensive parts are removed but the useful or beautiful parts are kept for students</note>. There is also evil of great significance in **Pliny** and **Galen**...

# CHAPTER XII.
## *On Rulandine Antimony.*

**G**lass of antimony <note>original: "Vitrum antimonii," a glassy substance made by roasting antimony ore, used as a potent emetic and purgative</note> is sometimes rejected by the wise so that they might wrest it from the hands of the wicked, who wander about everywhere and thrust it into every disease without any knowledge or prudence in its use. But for those who know how to correctly prepare and employ it, it is not an ignoble medicine in their judgment. Ruland the elder <note>Martin Ruland the Elder (1532–1602), a German physician and advocate of chemical remedies</note>, under the names of "Holy Earth" <note>original: "terrae Sanctae"</note> and "Crocus of Metals" <note>original: "croci metallorum," a reddish-yellow powder made from antimony</note>, understood nothing other than that which Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist whose commentaries on Dioscorides were standard medical texts</note> teaches how to prepare, as he [Ruland] wrote to me while he was still alive. Furthermore, his *Centuries* <note>original: "centuriae," referring to Ruland's *Curationum empiricarum et historicarum centuriae*, a collection of hundreds of medical case studies</note> show how successfully he used it. God willing, when I reach the section on the glass of antimony in the third part of my commentaries, I will note more. 

The authority of Riolanus <note>Jean Riolan, likely the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine and a fierce critic of chemical remedies</note>, as well as that of the Parisian College, is of no consequence, because they chatter recklessly about a matter unknown to them both in its art and its use. The maniacal Riolanus attributes these words to me: *of Ruland, who affirms that he saw many liberated from great diseases by the use of antimony.* But these were my only words: *Concerning the glass of antimony, it is proven by the Centuries of Martin Ruland the elder.* He did not only see it; but since he was a systematic doctor, a practitioner of <term>chemical medicine</term> <note>original: "chymiatriae," the synthesis of chemistry and medicine</note>, and an illustrious chemist, he both prepared it and, according to his experience, employed it in medicine with praise. Riolanus will not strip that praise from him—Riolanus, who foolishly boasts that he has liberated more than a thousand patients from great diseases by the use of only senna and agaric <note>original: "senna & agarico," traditional botanical purgatives; Libavius is mocking Riolanus for relying on simple herbs while criticizing complex chemical preparations</note>.

# ON THE PARISIAN FALSEHOODS REGARDING ALCHEMY
<note>original: "ALCHYMIAE DE SPVR. PARIS."</note>
## CHAPTER

[Jean Riolan] attacks Ruland as if he were a useless witness, because he believes that those who have pledged themselves to a particular sect <note>original: "sectae," referring here to a specific school of medical thought, such as Paracelsianism</note> are not to be trusted. A rabid dog spares not even the well-deserving and the dead. If we should not trust those who have given their name to a sect, why should we trust the Parisian doctors who defend their own sect tooth and nail? Was Ruland truly a Paracelsian <note>A follower of the radical Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who championed chemical medicine over traditional herbalism</note> doctor? Not at all, as his various writings demonstrate. To embrace, prepare, and healthfully employ chemical remedies does not make one a Paracelsian, even though Paracelsus also used them. 

Next, he [Riolan] hurls a reproach at Ruland, hinting that he killed many patients who, being deceased, are unable to complain; he claims that ten must perish by antimony <note>A metallic element used as a powerful, often toxic, medicine in the early modern period</note> if one is to be saved. No doubt his surviving son <note>Martin Ruland the Younger (1569–1611), who continued his father's work and would have been Libavius's contemporary</note> will respond to this. Meanwhile, the same accusation can be turned back against Galenic medicine <note>The traditional medical system based on the teachings of the Greek physician Galen (2nd century AD), relying on the four humors</note>: namely, that the earth covers its errors <note>A common satirical saying suggesting that when a doctor's treatment kills a patient, the evidence is buried in the grave</note>. Truly, it is easy for anyone to level accusations. 

But concerning me, he writes as follows: "On the advice of Libavius, flee mineral essences, the use of which is extremely dangerous." If he means that the unskilled should be warned by me, he speaks correctly. For in their hands, a noble essence is like a sword, or fire in the lap of fools. But if he simply attributes this warning to me—which is mostly his own opinion, as he condemns antimony in both its proper use and its abuse—he does me an injustice, as will be seen in my commentaries. He calls me a Paracelsian, though he himself is a writer of madness. We must forgive one with an errant mind. He brings up the "Anti-Gramanicus Libavius" <note>original: "Antigramanicum Libauium," referring to Libavius's polemical work against Johann Graman, a defender of radical Paracelsianism</note> in vain. For he understands nothing of it. The judge is a fool. No one who is wise will follow him.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## Riolan's Proofs that the Parisian Methods are Superior to Chemical Ones.

<margin>Note this cold detour regarding which methods are to be preferred, since the argument about the Devil being the author of chemistry <note>A common accusation by conservative doctors that chemical medicine was "diabolical" or "black magic."</note> is not yet finished. The matter of precedence is discussed on page 29 of the examination. But Riolan, so that he could fly through pages 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14, substituted it with that "Diabolical" argument.</margin>

**I**t must be deplored how wretchedly insane that Parisian college <note>The Faculty of Medicine at the University of Paris, which was famously conservative and opposed to chemical remedies.</note> is; though refuted so many times, it nevertheless puts forward the same delusions. What need is there, Riolan, to undergo the judgment of the sane and insane so often? I had refuted all your reasons, as others have also done excellently. You answer nothing firmly to anyone. What you answered to previous critics, you answer also to me. But I have demonstrated that all of it is weak, frivolous, false, and mad. You ought to oppose yourself to my demonstrations. In vain you take refuge in your trifles and the responses you gave to others. But let us see your arguments for the sake of the students:

> *By infusion <note>The process of soaking a substance in a liquid to extract its properties.</note> and decoction <note>The process of boiling a substance to extract its essence.</note> we retain the constitution, form, strengths, and natural properties, both hidden and manifest. Chemists, in order to extract essences, violate the temperament, form, and faculties by corrupting the matter.*

->Therefore, the Parisian methods are superior to the chemical ones.<-

The latter part of this premise is a stinking lie. It needs no refutation. Regarding the skill of infusion and cooking, we accept Riolan's judgment, and thus we argue on behalf of the chemists as follows:

> *Those things prepared through infusion and cooking retain their temperament, form, and faculties, both manifest and hidden.*

<header>ALCHEMY [DEFENSE] AGAINST THE SPURIOUS [DOCTORS] OF PARIS.</header>

*Most chemical extracts are prepared through infusion and decoction.*

*Therefore, most chemical extracts retain their temperament, form, and both their faculties <note>original: "facultatesque utrasque." Likely referring to both the physical properties and the spiritual or medicinal "virtues" of the substance.</note>.*

The major premise is Riolan’s. The minor premise is evident through the very constitution of the [chemical] art. From Mesue <note>Johannes Mesue, an influential medieval authority on pharmacy whose work was respected even by the conservative Galenists.</note>, I have cited above the example of the extract of myrobalans <note>A dried fruit used in medieval medicine as a digestive and purgative.</note> which is made by infusion and boiling, and is called a "work of great mastery" <term>magisterium: a high-level chemical process where a substance is purified or transformed without losing its essential medicinal nature</term>, by which the essence is separated from the raw matter. Anyone who judges otherwise simply because they have decided to stand against the principles of the art should not be listened to. Let us also add something regarding the other essences.

*If preparations made by infusion and decoction retain their constitution <term>crasis: the healthy balance or "mixing" of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a substance</term> along with their form and faculties, then those prepared by analogous methods also retain them—and all the more so the more skillfully they are handled.*

*The first part is true. Therefore, the second part follows.*

The connection is clear, because similar things should be judged similarly. Furthermore, what is done more skillfully is also done more prudently and wisely. Therefore, the same must be pronounced even more strongly regarding this. Now let us take up the conclusion:

*Many chemical essences are prepared in ways analogous to infusion and boiling (indeed, the preparation of the highest medicine is nothing other than boiling, ripening, and perfection).*

*Many chemical essences, therefore, retain their constitution along with their form and faculties.*

Since, however, we must strive not only to ensure that the good already present remains, but also that the evil <note>Referring to the "impurities" or toxic elements of raw plants and minerals.</note> departs; and if something is less than good, it should be exchanged for something greater, as the matter itself carries with it, by the gift of nature, the potential for a more noble medicine...

### CHEMISTRY AGAINST THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS

...rhubarb. Yet it purges, by Riolan’s own testimony, although he says it does so to a lesser degree—perhaps knowing something of his own laziness rather than of the art of chemistry. From this, we argue thus:

> *That which has retained its power and action, which depend on its <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "crasi," from the Greek krasis, referring to the specific mixture of qualities or humors that gives a substance its medicinal power.</note> and form, could not have lost its temperament.*
> *The extract of rhubarb has retained the power and action that depend on its temperament.*
> *Therefore, the extract of rhubarb could not have lost its temperament.*

The minor and major premises are taken from <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a prominent conservative physician of the Paris Faculty of Medicine who opposed chemical medicine.</note> himself. Consequently, he writes nonsensically against himself when he claims that the essences of the chemists lose their temperament through preparation (if indeed he understands temperament to be the internal and essential foundation of a mixture). 

But listen to his "ingenious" argument: Why is the purging power less in an extract than in an infusion? Because, he says, a <term>double cooking</term> <note>original: "duplex coctio." Riolan argues that excessive heat destroys the medicinal "spirit" of the plant.</note> is added to the infusion, from which something of the purging power must necessarily perish. This is a marvelous "extraction" indeed, in which there is first an infusion, then a first cooking, and thirdly a second cooking! 

Certainly, let an infusion be made. But where is this first cooking? Where is the second? The chemist, when performing an infusion, does not always cook it; but when the structure of the substance is firmer, as in <term>myrobalans</term> <note>A type of dried plum-like fruit used in medieval and early modern medicine as a purgative.</note>, he adds a very light boiling, and that in a closed vessel and a <term>double boiler</term> <note>original: "diplomate," referring to the *balneum Mariae* or bain-marie, which provides gentle, indirect heat.</note>. Nothing can perish here. When the essence has passed into the <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent used to extract medicinal properties from a solid substance.</note>, filtration and <term>expression</term> <note>The process of squeezing or pressing the plant matter to extract the remaining liquid.</note> take place, exactly as in the infusions of the Parisian pharmacies. If anything perishes, it perishes for the Parisians as well. Furthermore, the solvent is separated with great industry without any boiling. Perhaps Riolan’s maid-servant cooks the infusion until it reaches a thick...

# GALEN’S TRIUMPH

...infusion, just as syrups, jellies, and the thickened juices of pharmacists are usually made, and so on. Let it be so. Tell us, Riolan, why does your purging power perish in an infusion to which cooking is added? Because, you say, it consists in the "spirit," or the finest portion of the substance. Well then! But who was that Riolan who used to rage so vehemently against chemical "spirits"? Behold, you are cut by your own sword:

> *That which consists in a spirit, or a most subtle portion, can be raised into an <term>alembic</term>.*
> *The purging power of <term>rhubarb</term> <note>rhabarbarum</note> consists in a spirit, or a most subtle portion. Therefore [it can be distilled].*

Consequently, Riolan wrote falsely in his *Apology* (page 42) that the purging power perishes through distillation, or is at least diminished (as he says on page 45). By this very fact, his fabrication about the <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "crasi," from the Greek krasis, referring to the specific internal "mixture" or balance of a substance that gives it its identity.</note> perishing through distillation is proven false. 

2. Consequently, it is not necessary for chemists to destroy the <term>balance</term> <note>original: "temperie," the specific ratio of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> of a substance through their processes of separation.

3. On page 72 of the *Anti-Turquetus* <note>A polemical work by Riolan attacking the chemical physicians, specifically targeting Joseph Duchesne or Theodore de Mayerne (Turquet), who served as physicians to the French king.</note>, he mocks the axiom that remedies should be "spiritual" rather than "material." He treats it as if it were absurd to use spiritual things to treat diseases—suggesting that such things are for the enjoyment of demons rather than humans.

### ON THE ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN IMPOSTORS

By a <term>Riolanian preparation</term> <note>Methods of preparing medicine favored by Jean Riolan, typically involving gentle heating or infusion rather than harsh chemical distillation.</note> the <term>temperament</term> <note>In ancient medicine, the "temperament" was the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that gave a substance its medicinal nature.</note> is not removed, but the natural powers and qualities are preserved; yet by a <term>chemical</term> <note>In this context, "chemical" refers to spagyric or alchemical methods like distillation or calcination which use stronger fire.</note> one, it is removed. and gathers <term>homogeneous</term> <note>Things of the same kind; the "pure" parts of a substance.</note> things. But tell me, were those parts of the substance of the <term>mixture</term>, or not? You cannot deny they were. But once a part of its composition is lost, it is impossible for the <term>mixture</term> to remain the same mixture it was before. It follows, therefore, that they too corrupt the <term>mixture</term>. If this is not a crime for them, why should it be for the <term>chemists</term>, who arrange these <term>separations</term> with far greater skill? From this, I argue against you thus:

> *The <term>pharmacists</term> <note>In the original Latin, *pharmacopœi*, meaning those who prepare and dispense drugs according to traditional recipes.</note> of Riolan imitate good cooks.*
> *Therefore, they corrupt the <term>mixture</term> for the sake of the internal juice,*
> *and consequently, they do not preserve it.*

The logic of the consequence is because cooks do the same thing. Thus, Riolan has confounded himself with his own example. Let the Baker also step forward. He makes <term>loaves</term> from <term>barley</term> <note>original: *hordeo*</note>. Correct. From this, against Riolan:

> *He who makes <term>bread</term> <note>original: *panem*</note> from <term>barley</term> corrupts the <term>barley</term>.*
> *For it no longer remains that which it was.*

*The change of a noble being into something more ignoble is a relative generation.*

-># THE TRIUMPH OF GALEN <-

<page-num>213</page-num>

...[to the] image of God He created man. That form is better than the form of a fly. He who gave man the highest reason also granted that the works of reason should be the best. The <term>Image of God</term> <note>original: "Imago Dei". This is because man has drawn a certain divine power from the image of God, so that he might represent the power of God—who has communicated the rays of His goodness and virtue to us in a certain way—as if in a mirror. Therefore, man also performs extraordinary works. These works must necessarily turn out more excellent than those which nature would have made by itself, specifically because of the correction and assistance which suggest some weakness in nature.

Therefore, these three things left together in one mixture, because of the weakness of their connection and their inability to resist, behave as imperfectly mixed things; they can by no means be long-lasting. Thus, we see that almond oil easily putrefies, deposits dregs, and becomes plainly unfit for use; indeed, it cannot even last as long as the almonds themselves. Other oils, such as those of olives, turnip seed, flax, sesame, etc., as well as oily fish broths, do not only deposit dregs but also contract a heavy odor and an intolerable taste.

The Chemical Apprentice responds to this proposition that it is false. For the second part is false, which is the judgment of the coupled axiom. The reason is that arts can differ in their specific subjects, as well as in their forms and ends—or in their particular matter and form—but meanwhile agree in something common. <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a conservative Parisian physician who opposed the use of chemical medicines.</note> brings forward nature, which craftsmen should model themselves after; and nature which constitutes its own things by the joining of matter and form. I shall convince you by the three souls of <term>Plato</term> <note>Plato’s division of the soul into the rational, spirited, and appetitive faculties.</note>, or the faculties of <term>Aristotle</term>: I shall convince you by the <term>similar and dissimilar parts</term> <note>A classic Aristotelian distinction: "similar" parts are homogeneous (like flesh or bone), while "dissimilar" parts are organs made of different tissues (like a hand or eye).</note> of animals; I shall convince you by the heap of similar parts. Bone, flesh, and the rest have their own forms and their own ends; they also have their own final and particular matter, by whose sensible qualities they are perceived. But nonetheless, all these together constitute the one body of a man in number, just as the soul—of celestial or rather divine origin—and the body—made from the earth—are most diverse things [yet one]. ## CHAPTER XV.

### On whether <term>chrysopoeia</term> <note>The alchemical art of making gold from base metals</note> is possible; regarding page 36 of [his] "Madness," and page 15 etc. of his "Examination."

**R**iolan is a poor debater; for he dictates his own dreams when he ought to be responding to objections. The roles of the questioner and the respondent are distinct, yet he has been defeated by arguments. Therefore, he answers nothing; instead, he offers up his old delusions in place of responses. We would be perfectly justified in mocking an athlete who, having been knocked down so many times, nevertheless brandishes his ruined and broken weapons while gasping for breath. But let us be of a calm mind and listen to his arguing once more, to see if by chance he has grasped any wisdom or light that may have been hidden beneath the benches of Paris <note>original: "scabellis Parisiensib."; a disparaging reference to the lecture stools of the conservative University of Paris medical faculty</note>. He wishes to show by four arguments that <term>chrysopoeia</term> is impossible. If Geber <note>The Latin name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century father of alchemy</note>, Paracelsus, Bernard [of Trevisan], the Pharmacist of Treviso, Barnaud, the Hoghelandes, and that Scot, Alexander Sethon <note>original: "Conthonius," a frequent contemporary rendering of Alexander Seton, known as "The Cosmopolite"</note>, and many other countless men who have both seen and produced gold, were to hear this attempt, they would immediately drive out that **metaphysical** "smoke-seller" <note>original: "fumiuendulum"; a common period insult for a charlatan or one who sells empty promises</note> and prick him with their gold-making styluses. Reason is of no value in matters of the senses where we have the testimony of the senses—not those of the common people, but of craftsmen who freely submit their gold to every test, as Arnald [of Villanova] is recorded to have done in the booklet of Robertus Valensis; for in such cases, the evidence is manifest. I present his first argument:

> *Nature cannot, and much less can art, [accomplish] any work*

*...to produce without a proximate and synonymous <term>efficient cause</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being</note>. But the proximate efficient cause of gold is a gold-making force implanted by nature in specific earth, and not in others, which art <note>Here meaning "human skill" or technology</note> cannot produce. Therefore, the production of gold, or the transmutation of other metals into gold, is impossible.*

The meaning of his argument is that to produce gold, a unique and specific "gold-making" agent is required—which craftsmen call *solificum* <note>original: "solificum"; literally "sun-making," as gold was associated with the Sun</note>—just as the agent for silver is called *lunificum* <note>original: "lunificum"; literally "moon-making," as silver was associated with the Moon</note>. He argues that this power is denied to human art because it resides only within the nature of certain soils. The conclusion he draws is that gold cannot be made by art. This same argument was recounted at greater length on pages 7 and 8 of his book *The Madness*, where <term>chrysopoeia</term> <note>The alchemical art of making gold</note> is said to have been condemned with "invincible arguments" by the School of Paris, acting as a censor of vanity and deceptions. This "invincible" reasoning was so pleasing to him that, although 
<margin>Riolan the Tautologist <note>One who repeats the same thing over and over</note></margin> 
Libavius is often accused in the *Examination* of committing tautology, Riolan himself did not hesitate to make himself liable to the very same charge and fault. Why use many words? We will grant Riolan his entire argument, provided he first allows art to take what it does not possess from elsewhere and make it suitable for its intended purpose. Once that is done, it is no longer the craftsman who makes the gold by his own power, but nature herself, assisted by the craftsman and awakened to her task. Thus, we argue to the contrary:

> *He who possesses the gold-making force—bestowed by nature upon a specific earth—once that agent has been prepared and applied to the properly arranged matter, and governed as is fitting, can produce gold as easily as a farmer produces wheat once the seed is cast into the earth. Indeed, he can do so even more easily and quickly, as the agent is more nimble and the subject more ready to receive the change.*

*The gold-making chemist possesses a gold-making power entrusted by nature to a specific earth.*

*Therefore, when the gold-making chemist has prepared that <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The active agent or force that triggers a change</note>, etc., he can produce gold; consequently, <term>chrysopoeia</term> <note>The art of making gold</note> is possible.*

I prove the minor premise <note>The second statement in a logical argument or syllogism</note>. For since that efficient cause is present and powerful in no thing so much as in its own natural body—in which it received from nature the power of acting upon its own matter to produce its like—and since the chemist is able to take that body, or earth, from nature; and not only take it, but even to activate its dormant and enclosed power and to subtly awaken its motion with great skill; it is manifest that he can possess the gold-making power, or that it can be conferred by nature onto another subject and body of offspring. "In gold are the seeds of gold," says Fernelius <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician</note>, the Parisian doctor, following Augurelli <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli (c. 1441–1524), an Italian humanist and author of the alchemical poem "Chrysopoeia"</note>. 

But how that enclosed nature might be brought back—how it might become, as it were, lively from a dormant state, and agile and moving from a state of rest—and how the matters of the <term>agent and the patient</term> <note>In Aristotelian physics, the "agent" is the active force and the "patient" is the material being acted upon</note> are brought together into an actualized union <note>original: "symbolum"</note>—this entire anti-chemical college is too thick-headed to understand. If they wish to learn, however, I command these "good" doctors to shed their old skin along with their wicked anti-chemical minds, and to listen attentively at the knees of Quercetanus <note>Joseph Du Chesne (c. 1544–1609), a famous Paracelsian physician and chemist</note> among the "sons of the discipline." Perhaps they will obtain something. 

**Argument II.**

To procreate its like is a property of living things; gold (even philosophical gold <note>A refined or "living" form of gold that alchemists believed could act as a seed or ferment</note>) is inanimate. Therefore, the spirit of gold cannot procreate gold.

The conclusion changes gold into the **spirit of gold**, which in its own sense is not opposed to us, provided that that <term>sophist</term> <note>Referring to Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch opponent of chemical medicine</note> does not construct some monster for us out of Aristotelian "spirits." For the **minor premise**, an <term>anticipation</term> <note>A rhetorical device where one answers an opponent's objection before they make it</note> is posed.

"It is necessary," he says, "for the patient..."

...to be transmuted into the active agent. Secondly, procreation occurs not only from something similar, but even from the dissimilar and the contrary. For suppose the chief faculty of the soul is the procreation of its like: it does not follow that this belongs only to animate beings.

There is also a "sophistic darkness" in that same <term>prosyllogism</term> <note>A preliminary logical argument whose conclusion serves as the premise for a following argument</note>. This faculty does not belong to the soul in a simple sense, but to that which is called the "nature of living things," which also has the "nutritive faculty" as its companion; this is the third part of the soul according to Plato, or the "concupiscible" <note>The "desiring" part of the soul, associated in classical medicine with physical needs and growth</note>, which some include within the liver in humans. Once the foundation of the <term>syllogism</term> is undermined, the rest of the structure falls and, overcome by a massive breach, it gapes open. These are the "invincible" arguments of the [Parisian] school. From what has been said in favor of <term>chrysopoeia</term> <note>The art of making gold</note>, we argue more correctly and forcefully thus:

> *That which possesses form within matter and touches it when joined to a specific*
> *recipient, can make from that recipient something similar to itself. For the*
> *natural goal of an agent is the similarity of the recipient.*
> *The **soul of gold** (or the spirit, seed, <term>tincture</term>, or whatever*
> *suitable name you wish to call it) is a natural agent, which*
> *possesses form within matter, and touches the specific recipient when joined.*
> *(For the form is not separable [from the matter].)*
> *Therefore, the soul of gold can make something like itself out of a specific*
> *recipient; and consequently, <term>chrysopoeia</term> is not impossible.*

Lest you say that from the "spirit" or "soul" of gold only a spirit ought to be produced, and not physical gold, natural procreation through seed stands in the way, by which both are produced at once. Like to it...

**Argument III.**

> *He who cannot give the <term>crasis</term> <note>From the Greek 'krasis,' meaning a 'mixture' or 'temperament'; in alchemy, it refers to the specific internal balance of elements that defines a substance's true essence</note>, form, and properties of gold, cannot make gold.*

The **minor premise** <note>The second statement in a logical argument</note> is first explained by the power of art, by which the "accidental" qualities of true and natural gold—such as color, hardness, weight, and so on—can be conferred upon <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "hydrargyro," literally 'water-silver'</note>: But not the **constitution** <note>original: "crasis"</note>. To this is added the confession of <term>Libavius</term> <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a famous chemist who was often critical of extreme alchemical claims</note>, who does not wish to be persuaded that the transformed gold is the same as the natural; for although it may be the same in its "accidents" <note>Outward, non-essential characteristics</note>, it is not so in its essence. Such gold is taught to be "sophistical" <note>Fake or deceptive</note> and merely apparent, with **Aristotle** as the judge. Thus says <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a leading conservative physician in Paris</note> from his professor's chair.

But that "black philosopher" <note>Likely a reference to an alchemist, as 'blackness' or *nigredo* is the first stage of the alchemical work</note> breaks forth again, and calls the **major premise** "sophistical." For "to give" is twofold: one is to confer something by one's own power; the other is by the power of an assumed nature. He who can give the constitution in neither way is rightly denied the ability to make gold. (It is not relevant to speak here of divine and miraculous power.) He distinguishes the **minor premise**. For the gold-maker indeed, by his own innate strength and power or his own motion, would not produce the constitution even in common things, just as Pharaoh's magicians could not [produce] lice— <margin>The magicians of Egypt could not produce lice from dust, while the alchemist works with nature's own forces.</margin>

...to create lice <note>original: "pediculos facere." I was defending the opposite view. Gramann, however, argued quite unskillfully, and Riolan did not notice that Libavius wanted reason and experience to be understood together at the same time; and that judgment regarding artificial things <note>lab-made substances</note> ought to be made by craftsmen whose senses are fortified by skill. Antimony was a central focus of alchemical medicine, used to make everything from glass to powerful emetics</note> unless they were a craftsman? To a miner or a metal caster, antimony might be very well known in its raw state, but if you show that same person things made from it through art, he would be the most ignorant of all men concerning them. Works of art are judged by the "eyes of art," while natural things are judged by natural means. As for what pertains to...

Riolan understands nothing of the artificial gold about which <term>Ulstadius</term> <note>Philipp Ulstad (fl. 1500–1543), a Nuremberg physician and alchemist famous for his work on distillation</note>, <term>Albertus</term> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the medieval scholar to whom many alchemical treatises were attributed</note>, and others speak. > *Alchemical gold-makers <note>original: "Chymici chrysopœi"</note> can do this. Therefore, etc.*

**Then, from what Riolan has conceded, we argue thus:**

> *He who, through the mediation of a gold-making nature, can provide the temperament; and furthermore even the weight, color, stability <note>original: "fixitatem," the ability of a metal to resist being consumed by fire</note>, and other properties <note>original: "accidentia"</note> of gold; he clearly can create natural gold. The gold-maker can do this. Therefore.*

**Furthermore:**

> *If the chemist can, through his art, grant to quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo," or mercury</note> the weight of gold, its stability, color, ductility, malleability, and the other hallmarks by which—when they are found—the <term>weighers</term> <note>original: "Zygostatae," officials who checked weights</note>, <term>assayers</term> <note>original: "docimastae," those who test the purity of metals</note>, <term>gold-beaters</term> <note>original: "bractearii"</note>, and goldsmiths pronounce it pure, refined, and true gold, never doubting that the internal nature and temperament—without which these traits could not exist—lie beneath these detected external traits; then he can turn it into gold. The first part is possible according to Riolan’s own testimony; therefore, the second part follows.*

There is also an argument from the method of mixture known to nature. For if the chemist has grasped this through the favor of God, he will, by its power, bring about a true mixture; although it would be ridiculous to imagine that the chemist can do nothing unless he mixes separated things. Yet he also perfects what nature has left imperfect in a certain respect. **Argument IV.**

### ON THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS

*Even if we grant that pure, refined gold can be made by art: nevertheless, out of a hundred (read: a hundred thousand) times a thousand people who have applied themselves to this study, you mention scarcely two or three who have completed the work; whom I believe were deceived by an accident.*

*Therefore, the art is harmful and to be shunned.*

In this argument, Riolan has forgotten his own theme. He wanted to prove that <term>gold-making</term> <note>original: "chrysopœian," the alchemical process of transmuting base metals into gold</note> was impossible; yet he concludes that it should be avoided. He should have demonstrated that gold cannot be made by art; instead, he concedes that it can be made. Thus, he is clearly entangled in maniacal fits. Riolan’s opinion is cheaper than seaweed. It proves less than the buzzing of a gnat. 

For what weight does a man, more ignorant than ignorance itself in chemical matters, carry against the most experienced practitioners? That number—a hundred thousand times a million—is ridiculous. Who has ever counted so many gold-making philosophers? Many carry the wand, but few are Bacchus <note>original: "Multi Thyrſigeri; pauci Bachi." A Greek proverb suggesting that many people participate in a ritual or study, but very few are truly inspired or attain the actual essence of the mystery.</note>. Countless people have attempted the art, but that does not mean they were gold-makers. # ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS

...it does not argue against the thesis. For the fact that a thing is whole, finite, and **perfect** does not prevent it from aspiring toward something **more perfect**. A thing may be "simply" such [in an absolute sense], or "relatively" such [in a certain respect]. Sometimes it is so in itself by its own **actual state**; sometimes it is so only in relation to something else. And a thing that is perfect in itself can nonetheless possess a **potentiality** <note>original: "potentiam." In Aristotelian philosophy, this is the capacity of a thing to become something else, like a seed having the "potential" to become a tree.</note> by whose force matter aspires to a nobler state—just as the matter of water has a potentiality for fire, even though water is nonetheless in itself a finite, perfect, and whole element.

Every one of these things which are generated is said to be "most perfect" specifically when it has attained the excellence of its **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; in biology, the parent is the efficient cause of the child.</note> and is able to generate something just like itself. A boy cannot yet do this; and yet a boy is whole, finite, and perfect. The difference lies in the **succession of forms**. Each form is a perfection in itself and is already an "end" <note>original: "finis." The goal or final state of a process.</note> at which the motion—as far as it leads to this state—ceases. 

But in the meantime, nothing prevents that preceding state from being an **imperfection** when compared to the state that follows it. From this imperfection, motion proceeds further toward a more distant end; once that end is present, the motion that tended toward it also ceases. Yet even from here, through continued motion, progress can be made toward something further still. 

Just as a continuum is divisible and can be distinguished by its parts, so too is there **motion in matter** through various forms until the ultimate form in a certain species is reached. In the meantime, it can happen that due to some intervening hindrance, the motion is intercepted—either in the matter as a whole, whereby the process ends in some subordinate form (which was an imperfection relative to the final form), such as when an apple is plucked while it is still raw; or when the <term>chyle</term> <note>original: "chylus." In the medical theories of the time, this was the milky juice produced from digested food in the stomach, which then had to be "cooked" or refined further by the liver into blood.</note> is not fully cooked in the stomach but remains in a state of impurity, etc., or in some...

But they do not have the same definition. <note>The Censor in a brief excursion on page 120.</note> says: "What else is the whole than its parts?" Are "finite" and "perfect" also nothing more than their parts? Certainly not. Rather, a **whole** is, as was answered <note>page 68 of the examination, from text 31 of the fifth book of Aristotle's Metaphysics</note>, that which lacks none of the essential parts regarding matter and form; it is not simply the parts alone. For if it were, it would exist only in a material sense. Instead, it consists of the parts joined according to their **species** <note>in this context, the specific nature or "blueprint" of the substance</note> and held together under their own form, which is the form of the whole. In this way, logicians define a "whole" as that which contains its parts—a definition that encompasses both matter and form, and is therefore essential. For example, the "perfect time" of someone is when they have completed it so that they have run through all its parts—just as you might speak of the "perfect age" of an old man who has reached every stage of old age and finished them. 

Next, that is "perfect" which is **according to excellence and the good** <note>original Greek: τὸ καθ' ἀρετὴν καὶ τὸ εὖ</note>, such as a "perfect musician." This term is also transferred to bad things, such as a "perfect sycophant" or a "perfect slanderer." Excellence, too, is a kind of perfection. For each thing is perfect when, according to the form of its own excellence, no part of its natural magnitude is missing. 

Likewise, **those things to which an excellent end belongs are called perfect; for they are perfect by virtue of having an end** <note>original Greek: οἷς ὑπάρχει τὸ τέλος σπουδαῖον, ταῦτα λέγεται τέλεια. κατὰ γὰρ τὸ ἔχειν τέλος τέλεια</note>. These are Aristotle’s words in that passage. He says nothing there about the "whole," the "perfect," and the "finite" being the same thing.

But there is also nothing [new] in the following chapter **concerning the limit** <note>original Greek: περὶ πέρατος (*peri peratos*); this refers to Book 5, Chapter 17 of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>. An "end" is a certain kind of limit. The "finite" is that which is limited. If this is applied to magnitude, it is easily understood: to be finite is to be enclosed within the boundaries of quantity. Regarding motion, however, the "finite" is that which ceases to move further because it has been led to its end. There is also one kind of end which is "perfect," and another which is "imperfect." <margin>Aristotle, *Magna Moralia*, Book 1, Chapter 3</margin> That is "perfect" which, once attained, leaves us with no further need for anything. That is "imperfect" which, upon its arrival, leaves us still desiring something else. 

There are altogether many passages in Aristotle concerning the end, the limit, the whole, the finite, and the perfect; but I find the senile folly of Riolan in none of them. He himself is unable to point out a specific text. Instead, having seized upon the definition of the "perfect," he reasons from a certain description of it—namely, that the "whole," the "perfect," and the "finite" follow one another—such that whatever is a "whole" must necessarily also be "perfect" and "finite." 

But I say, oh you fugitive from logic, it was not for you to prove that those three terms occasionally coincide. You were claiming they were *the same thing*, to the point that one ought to say: **lead** <term>plumbum: the metal lead</term> is a "whole" (because it contains all its own parts); therefore it is "perfect," and cannot aspire to any further perfection. This reasoning of yours is fatuous, nor can it be proven by the authority of Aristotle. In fact, the contrary follows from this very point. Because a "perfect" thing is that which has an "end," and a certain kind of "end" is "imperfect," it follows that in a certain way, a thing can be called "perfect" even if it is "imperfect" with respect to an *ultimate* perfection. Thus, **lead** is indeed "perfect" in its own "end," but that end is "imperfect" in respect to the "perfect metal" <note>likely referring to gold, the "perfect" end-state of metallic evolution in alchemical theory</note> whose form and completion it lacks...

# THE GALENIC TRIUMPH

An imperfect metal can have its own **end** <note>The "end" (*finis*) refers to the Aristotelian "final cause" or the purpose for which a thing exists</note>; and then it can also achieve another, more perfect end through **restored motion**. With the **gold-maker** <note>original: *aurifico*; an alchemist</note> acting as the agent, the metal can be led through to the form of gold, as the highest and most perfect end of the metallic genus. By this distinction, the objection of <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a prominent Parisian physician who opposed the use of chemical medicines</note> is resolved. What does that madness snarl? **It is nothing to do with the matter at hand** <note>original Greek: *οὐδὲν πρὸς Διόνυσον*; literally "nothing to do with Dionysus," a common proverb for something irrelevant</note>. The solution remains. Thus, the examination is sound.

Lest his foolishness remain entirely silent, he denies that I speak of the "end" properly and philosophically. If you ask why? Then we were considering that principle of Riolan’s: *Let us act by reason, not by authority.* For that is what it means to practice philosophy. Moreover, that distinction of Aristotle's is far removed from anything that could apply to the present business. <meta>catchword: and essen-</meta>

See chapter 3 of the first book of the *Magna Moralia* <note>A treatise on ethics traditionally attributed to Aristotle</note>, where the order of ends <term>finis</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" is the purpose or goal for which a thing exists or is made</note> is discussed in relation to the perfect and the imperfect, the ultimate, the penultimate, and so on; it is added there that the "end" is not a simple concept, but a twofold one. For of some things, he says, the end is **action and use**, such as sight; of others, it is the **habit** <term>habitus</term> <note>The state, form, or internal disposition of a thing</note> or form. However, use is more desirable than the habit. For use and action are the true goal, since a habit exists for the sake of its use. If you apply these principles to your **lead**, you will learn that while the form of lead is indeed its natural end, the **better use** of lead is its **transmutation** into gold, or into medicine. Thus, the chemical goal is superior to the natural one.

*In the second book of the Physics, text 23,* it is taught that the study of nature also recognizes the "end" and "that for the sake of which" a thing exists. There, he calls nature the "end," insofar as the process of generation <note>The process of coming into being or growing</note> tends toward a specific form or nature. For in those things where there is a continuous motion, the eventual limit of that motion is the "ultimate" and "that for the sake of which" the motion occurred. Thus, let the form and nature of lead be the end of lead. But when another motion is initiated by a natural agent—tending toward gold—and the motion stops once gold is acquired, then **gold** will be the end and the reason for which the lead existed. 

If, as is written in that same text, not every final stage is an "end," but rather the **optimal** stage, one can easily conclude that since gold is better than lead, gold is the true end in the generation of metals. This is clearly contrary to Riolan’s opinion. Furthermore, this remains true if we relate the metals back to ourselves. For, in a certain way, **we ourselves are the end**. Therefore, when we use all things that exist, and create medicines from mixtures that have been broken down <term>resolutis</term> <note>Referring to the chemical process of "resolution" or "analysis," where a compound is separated into its essential components</note> for this purpose, we are the end of those mixtures, just as...

He concludes that since humans use these substances for healing, humanity itself serves as the ultimate purpose for which these natural mixtures exist.</summary>

...complete; an act <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" or "actuality" is the fulfillment of a "potential."</note> becomes a potential which another act then brings to a close. You would have used a better example if you had produced something from the nature of minerals, and compared living things to living things, minerals to minerals, and those things which possess the principles of art and nature to one another. Elements are transmuted in such a way that fire can be called the "end" and the complete or perfect being; and yet, the other elements are nonetheless bodies that are complete in themselves. From Galena <term>galena</term> <note>The primary ore of lead.</note> comes lead; from lead comes minium <term>minium</term> <note>Red lead, used as a pigment.</note>, litharge <term>lithargyrus</term> <note>A secondary mineral form of lead oxide.</note>, lime <term>calx</term>, and many other things. One thing is "nobler" than another—that is, it has a nobler purpose—whether you look at its state or its use. And yet, each thing by itself enjoys its own nobility, form, and purpose. Having thus proven these points regarding the "final end" <note>original: "de fine"</note>, let us declare the truth for the chemists with this syllogism:

> *If lead is lead by its own end, and yet is also destined for another—being what it is for the sake of another, as if subordinated to another as a "final end" toward which it can be led when motion is applied; then, assuming the transmutation of lead into gold (for which it has the potential in its matter), gold-making <term>chrysopoeia</term> <note>The alchemical term for the creation of gold.</note> posits nothing absurd.*

*The first part is true.*
*And therefore, so is the latter.*

(whatever causes our philosophers have chosen) it is governed by the light and motion of heaven, and not by an "influx" <note>original: influxu; the idea that celestial bodies "flowed" a physical substance into the lower world</note>—as if some severed substance were carried down from there, or as if some fifth fire generated a likeness of itself in the prepared elementary (or rather, the mundane) spirit. This spirit cannot remain stable in the depths outside of a mixture, but as we see in radiant light, it is born and passes away immediately; this can also be ascribed to human spirits.

This is one hypothesis. The second is that heaven is not a material part of mixtures, but concurs in the generation and conservation of mixtures (which are composed of the elements) as a universal cause, not as a particular one.

The third: celestial heat, in which the principle of life resides, likewise descends from there. But because it cannot travel by itself, it is said to use a vehicle called "light." Elementary fire <note>The common fire of the kitchen or forge</note> is rejected here. For it does not generate life, but rather burns and corrupts, as it seems to Riolan. The <term>formative heat</term> <note>original: calor opifex; the "workman-like" heat that shapes developing embryos or plants</note> ought to be gentle and moderate, not excessive and intemperate.

If you ask whether that which descends is a quality or a substance, the answer is that it is a quality and an accident. You ask again: in what primary subject does that vital heat reside? It is said to be in the spirit, beneath which nature has spread an "airy moisture," so that life might be more permanent—since the substance of spirit is fleeting and vanishing.

Let us stop here. What, I ask, has the madness of Riolan said or left unsaid here that could be relevant to the matter? I hear talk of the generation of living things. ### ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS
<meta>catchword: this</meta>

But Riolan's madness <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657) was a prominent French physician and a fierce defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories.</note> tastes quite deeply of this error. Let us dive into the abyss of "Parisian wisdom" and fish for pearls from its depths. He begins his web of argument against the <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: quintam essentiam; the "fifth essence," a highly purified substance thought to be distinct from the four elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note> of the <term>chymists</term> <note>original: chymicorum; in this era, "chymistry" referred to a blend of what we now call chemistry and alchemy.</note>. It can be summarized by the following syllogism:

->*Nothing essential flows down from heaven.*<-
->*Therefore, the quintessence in mixtures is nothing.*<-

The first part of his argument <note>original: antecedens; the premise that nothing "essential" descends from the stars.</note> is proven, he claims, because whatever flows down is merely "accidental"—such as heat traveling in the vehicle of light. However, even beginner <term>chymists</term> can overthrow this whole idea with a short breath. They deny that his conclusion follows. Their reasoning is that for a "fifth nature" to exist within mixtures, there is no need for a continuous flowing down or a cutting off of celestial essence. From where, then, does it come? It arises from a twofold cause.

The first cause is that the Creator of all things originally mixed the whole; He placed the <term>seminal principle</term> <note>original: principium seminale; the internal "blueprint" or spark that allows a plant, mineral, or animal to grow and reproduce its own kind.</note> as the foundation of generation, through which every creature capable of birth is propagated. Therefore, what comes into the hands of the <term>chymist</term> was either created as a mixture by God from the beginning, or was generated according to its substance through that seminal principle in its own likeness. In either case, it possesses a <term>fifth nature</term>.

The second cause is itself twofold. From the very start of nature and the first "separation," a certain <note>original: fex quaedam coeli; literally "dregs of heaven."</note> sediment of heaven, or a thicker part, remained in the body of the middle world; this part is related to the elements. While the power of heaven acts upon this, it is led toward a starry purity—at least as much as can be achieved given the "elemental contagion" from which it is never entirely freed, so that the continuity of the world remains intact on all sides. If you prefer a simpler explanation <note>original: crassa & pingui minerua; an idiom meaning "with a thick and fat Minerva," or a plain, common-sense approach.</note>, consider wine separated from its dregs. In wine, there is a <term>fifth nature</term> in regard to its...

### ON THE ALCHEMICAL ERRORS OF THE PARISIANS

...and that the **form** <note>original: forma; in Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> be separable. This must be either **fire** or **air**. Yet it can be neither. For how could the "highest fire"—whose perfection exists in the very place of its own form—descend to earth without **coagulation** <note>The process of a liquid or gas becoming solid or semi-solid.</note> or **transmutation**? 

In truth, **air** cannot be so "informed" by light that it receives a new **substantial act** <note>original: actum substantialem; the process by which a thing's potential becomes a reality. The author is arguing that light doesn't physically turn air into a brand-new type of matter.</note> and becomes a new body composed of the matter and form of celestial light. Insofar as air is a transparent body, it can be acted upon by light; but not simply because it is air. Indeed, there seems to be no kinship between air and light, since air is often agitated by the most violent winds, while light remains constant as long as the sun or stars are present. For example, the air outside is freezing in winter, yet the air inside a room, protected by windows, is warmed by the sun's rays. Therefore, another **subject** <note>original: subiectum; the underlying material or "substrate" that receives an action or property.</note> is required.

Those who explain **Aristotle’s** theory of "friction" <note>original: affrictum; Aristotle suggested that objects moving quickly, like arrows, catch fire because of friction with the air.</note> as a kind of thinning of the air bring nothing new to the debate besides a certain cleverness. Aristotle was speaking of **local motion**—using the example of an arrow burning in the air—not of a fundamental change in the substance itself. If "thinning" occurs, it is necessary for the thinning agent to possess a form within matter and to physically touch it. But let this dispute remain before its own judges <note>A polite way of saying "let the experts keep arguing over this point."</note>.

In the second hypothesis, we accept that the **heaven** above us is a "universal cause," but not the same as the air that is here with us. Indeed, even the universal heaven can be directed by its own power. For every natural **agent** <note>Something that acts or produces an effect.</note> is limited by the unique nature of the **subject** and the **patient matter** <note>original: materiæ patientis; the passive material that is being acted upon by an external force.</note> it works upon, because the action of the agent happens within the "patient." Thus, in a certain way, the heaven can become a "particular cause" for specific earthly effects. 

The <term>chymists</term> <note>original: chymici; early chemists or alchemists.</note> do not need the third hypothesis. For they are not concerned with **vital heat** <note>original: calore vitali; the innate heat believed to sustain life in living organisms.</note> simply because it is "vital," unless you understand "life" as...

> *A **spiritual substance**, whether it be made of air, or fire, or both together, is **elemental**.*
> *Therefore, the spirit which is extracted by the Chymists will be elemental.*

Regarding the greater context: It is not unknown in the schools that there is a homonymy <note>A term used when one word has multiple, distinct meanings.</note> in the word **spirit**. The **Platonists** <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato, who often emphasized the role of a "world soul."</note> posit a certain **spirit of the world** that travels through all things, which cannot be of an elementary <note>Made of the four physical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> nature. In the **lesser world** <note>The human body, viewed as a "microcosm" or small-scale version of the universe.</note> there are **animal, vital, and natural spirits**. Of these, the **animal spirits** especially—which the mind also employs—are said to be celestial, serving as the vehicle or, as I might call it, the **primary bond** that ties the soul (which is the breath of life inspired into man by God the creator) to the body; this bond consists mostly of the **primigenial moisture** <note>original: humido primigenio; the fundamental fluid present from the start of a creature's life</note> and heat. Likewise, spirits of an **ethereal nature** are ascribed to the sense of sight; although these are animal spirits, they are determined by the organ of sight so that they are prepared for the act of seeing. **Aristotle** sometimes calls air "spirit," and of this kind is that which is inhaled and exhaled, even if it is sometimes more like a breath and sometimes more like a vapor. *In Book 2 of On the Generation of Animals, Chapter 3,* he describes the **generating spirit** in this way:

> Every virtue or power of the soul seems to participate in another body, and that more divine than those which are called elements. However, just as souls differ among themselves in nobility and ignobility, so too the nature of that body differs. For there is in the **seed** of all things that which makes the seeds fertile: namely, that which is called **heat**. This is not fire, nor is it any such faculty, but rather the **spirit** which is contained in the seed and the foamy body, and the nature which is in that spirit, corresponding in proportion to the **element of the stars**. **Celestial heat** is placed within the spirit. Heat excited in the air through alteration <note>A change in quality rather than essence</note> can reside within it, but since it cannot endure in a foreign subject, it will achieve nothing noteworthy unless the generation is continued and multiplied. 

Yet even so, that heat only represents the nature of that from which it proceeded; it is not celestial by its own essence. Furthermore, if it were celestial in this way, it would be necessary for the heavens themselves to be actually hot. He saw an <term>anticipation</term> <note>original: prolepsis; a rhetorical device where one anticipates and answers a potential objection before it is made</note> concerning heat.

-> ### GALEN’S TRIUMPH ### <-
<note>original: GALENIA TRIVMPHVS; refers to the victory of traditional Galenic medicine—based on the four humors—over the "new" chemical medicine.</note>

*Fiery and immoderate heat is not celestial. The spiritual fifth essence <note>original: quinta essentia; the "quintessence," or the purest, most potent medicinal core extracted by alchemists</note> of the chemists possesses a fiery and immoderate—indeed, a scorching and feverish—heat.*

*Therefore, it cannot be called "celestial" or "analogous to the heavens" simply because of celestial heat.*

For the sake of brevity, I have condensed the preliminary arguments into a single <term>syllogism</term> <note>a formal logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion</note>. The <term>minor premise</term> <note>the second statement in a syllogism</note> is proven by the same argument as the major. The essence of gold, which serves as the <term>idea</term> <note>original: idea; here used in the Platonic sense of a perfect archetype or "blueprint" for all other metals</note> for all others, possesses such a scorching heat that its frequent use induces <term>elephantiasis</term> <note>a term used in antiquity to describe severe skin diseases, including forms of leprosy, believed to be caused by "burnt" or overheated black bile</note> by drying out the blood and the liver. Therefore, this is even more true for the other essences.

To this proposition, let some commoner from the Ethiopian or Arabian nations respond. If celestial heat—which <term>Riolanus</term> <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), a highly influential and conservative French physician who defended Galenic medicine against chemical innovations</note> says is carried by the "vehicle of light"—scorches so intensely that it is cursed by some, and even in Europe occasionally sets forests ablaze, or when collected by burning mirrors <note>original: speculis igniariis; parabolic mirrors used to concentrate sunlight to start fires</note> and concave vessels, inflames and burns ships and other combustible things, it might not be absurd to call a certain "celestial" quality fiery and immoderate.

Furthermore, perhaps no one has ever been in heaven, or in the "place of fire," who could bring back a sensible demonstration of it such as the study of physics requires. In the sacred scriptures, we read that celestial fire often descended and devoured sacrifices, soldiers, and other things. This same fire had to be maintained by elemental fuel. Likewise, at the proclamation of the Law, it set the mountains of Sinai on fire; it is also believed to be present in thunderbolts. By this same fire, the entire world will one day be consumed. Even the angels are sometimes made into a "burning fire" <note>a reference to Psalm 104:4, "Who maketh his angels spirits; his ministers a flaming fire."</note>. For this reason, the most ancient wise men believed no other...

Did they even possess the true essence? Or if they did, did they use it skillfully? Chemists view the judgment of Riolan’s "better reputation" with suspicion, as he cannot even distinguish a good reputation from a bad one. But in truth, since these things are to be laughed at...

Riolan may propose it, but he does not recognize his own failing <note>original: morbum; literally "disease," but used here to mean a flaw in logic or an error</note>; instead, he attributes it to me. For he says that I write absurdly when I claim that life must reside in a more active <term>subject</term> <note>original: subiectum; in traditional philosophy, the underlying substance or "matter" that supports qualities or properties</note> than the elements. Why do I ask this, my dear "Ridiculan" <note>original: Ridiculane; a mocking pun on Riolan's name and the word "ridiculous"</note>? Because, he argues, if natural heat were more active, it would destroy rather than create. Page 21 of the *Examination*. Here is my response:

<margin>Whether heat is in a subject more powerful than the elements.</margin>

> *If the critic could deny that living things are nourished by those things which have never lived, why can he not conclude that life exists in a more divine body—one that approaches life more closely than the elements <note>the four basic building blocks: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note> do? Life is the "act" of the soul, and the soul itself is the principle and **first act** <note>original: actus primus; a technical Aristotelian term referring to the fundamental state of being alive or the soul's presence in a body</note>. It must, of necessity, exist in something more active than the elements. Such is the nature and substance of the heavens.*

<margin>Riolan’s foolishness regarding heat.</margin>

These are my words. Riolan imagines a heat that acts as the "subject" of life, forgetting that heat is merely the instrument of some higher principle. On its own, heat can do nothing but warm things up. However, by the power of that primary agent <note>the soul or vital principle</note>, it creates **chyle** <note>original: chylum; a milky fluid produced from digested food</note> in the stomach; it forms blood in the veins, the liver, and the heart; it produces semen in the testes and milk in the breasts; it enables sight in the eyes; and so it continues through the other organs according to their specific **faculties** <note>the innate powers or functions of specific body parts</note>. Heat is not even the "subject," let alone a "more active subject." Furthermore, even if I had written that heat was the subject, would I have meant a simple, solitary heat? Life does not exist in the simple elements. Therefore, it does not exist in the heat of those simple elements. One must instead understand the heat of **mixed bodies** <note>original: mistorum; substances composed of a combination of elements</note>. But which of these is more active for life: the dry or the moist? In your own judgment, is it the moist, or perhaps the air? To this—

Even more, **lapis lazuli**, **glass of antimony**, and **mercury** <note>original: hydrargyrus</note>—those very "cold" things—purge, and although these are denied to be "living," they nevertheless exceed the power of the elements. 

But the ridiculous folly of **Ridiculanus** <note>The author’s mocking nickname for Jean Riolan</note> is manifest enough. Otherwise, we could also point to other acts of life in plants, beasts, and man, and ask what simplicity or "mixture" of elements could possibly be a suitable subject for each individual life if a nature analogous to the **ether** <note>The "fifth element" or celestial substance, thought to be the source of life and movement</note> were absent. However, the chemists demonstrate that "subject" in their mixtures: namely, a certain **spiritual essence** lurking within the mixing and the hidden recesses of elemental matter. From where then will you produce "corpulence" <note>original: corpulentiam; here meaning physical mass or three-dimensional substance.</note>? Out of the air is fashioned a sort of rainbow, or Venus, or another image <note>original: simulacrum</note>, in which it might descend.

It is received in the air as if in its own and appropriate subject, says **Riolan**. Is it in the same way he taught that images are received in a mirror, and that the power of purgatives migrates into spring water without the spirit or the juice? That would be consistent. Does he also recognize a mode of irradiation there? Provide another "proper" subject. 

The **Chemists** <term>Chymici</term> <note>Refers to the followers of Paracelsus or other laboratory-based philosophers who sought chemical rather than purely logical explanations for nature.</note> say that a form can never exist in another if it cannot have its being in itself; and therefore, if it descends, it must descend through the **influx of celestial spirit**, or, having been sent down long ago, it must cling near the middle. It is also a marvelous thing that this heat is celestial by its nature, moist and hot, and packed with a "carrying light"; and yet, in **Riolan’s** <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent French physician and a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories.</note> judgment, it is tempered by aerial moisture. But how can heat that is moist by its nature be tempered by the moisture of the air? Adding like to like only makes it more of that quality; it does not "temper" it, for tempering only occurs through the application of opposites.

Therefore, it was not moist before when it leaped forth from heaven, but dry. And indeed, this is necessary. For if something moist is tempered by moisture, and later it must be mixed with the humors from which humans and beasts originate, it will be suffocated and entirely overwhelmed, unable to define its own boundaries.

However, even though **Riolan** is as dry as a pumice stone, we have nonetheless squeezed this "oil" out of him: he is forced to admit that that heat—which he himself calls "vital" and sent down from heaven—is a spiritual body that possesses a certain **crasis**.

He objects to me regarding human spirits, which I have elsewhere called **aerial**—not because I think they are composed of air, but because they correspond in similarity. I did not say they *are* air. I called them "aerial" because of their thinness, divisibility, purity, and the similarity of their sensible qualities...

...in them; otherwise, I recognize them as no less mixed and born from a bloody nature, as well as seminal spirits and the chymists' **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: quinta essentia; also known as the "quintessence," this was considered by alchemists to be the purest, most potent extract of a substance, distinct from the four earthly elements.</note>.

<margin>Whether the Fifth Essence belongs to matter or to form.</margin>

On pages 46 and 47, the question is raised whether the **chymical essence** <note>The active medicinal extract produced through chemical distillation or separation.</note> belongs to the matter of mixtures or to their form. This is a tricky question; the terms must be distinguished. The **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy. They viewed the world through "matter" (the physical stuff) and "form" (the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is).</note> understand by the word "matter" the material cause, which in physics is a body that is mobile by nature. By the name of "form," they understand the formal cause which gives a thing its being and, in the case of mixtures, makes them be—and be called—mixtures. Others call this the "inner **crasis**" <term>crasis</term> <note>original: crasin; a Greek-derived term referring to the specific temperament or "blending" of qualities that defines a substance's character.</note>. This form is inseparable from the matter. 

The **chymists** <note>Early modern practitioners of chemistry and alchemy.</note>, in their own discipline, do not care what the Greeks <note>i.e., the ancient authorities like Aristotle or Galen.</note> repeatedly say. They use the terms "form" and "species" to describe the essence enclosed within the mixtures, which is the primary subject of the **faculties** <term>faculties</term> <note>original: facultatum; the inherent medicinal powers or virtues of a substance, such as the ability of a plant to purge or heal.</note>, and it can be separated by art. They call "matter" the useless **dregs** <note>original: crassamentum; the heavy, solid waste left over after an extraction or distillation.</note>. 

Thus, when **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a famous conservative physician in Paris who often clashed with chemical doctors.</note> infuses his **rhubarb** <term>rhubarb</term> <note>original: Rheum; a common medicinal root used as a laxative. Riolan is being described here as making a liquid infusion or tea from it.</note>, he thinks the physical body and the matter are the waste products to be rejected; but the virtue <note>original: vim; the medicinal power or "kick" of the drug.</note> is that which has migrated into the liquid. In this process, the form must necessarily perish, unless he wants it to remain in the leftovers. 

But virtue is not form. According to his own judgment, only the virtue is transferred. Therefore, to answer the question **clearly** <note>original: diserte.</note>: speaking "chymically," the fifth essence is the formal part; speaking "Peripatetically," it is material. In the latter view, the previous form has been destroyed, and what was "potential" in the mixture has been brought into "actuality." Thus, this matter—which we call essence—does not have its original form, but rather the form that emerged from potentiality through the motion of a natural agent directed by art. This happens in two ways...
