But the question at hand is not about magisteries. Thinness is indeed joined with the most "formal" essences <note>Essences that represent the "form" or organizing principle of a thing.</note>; but to exist as a certain quantity is not the same as being "thin" or "thinned out"—it is something else entirely. Therefore, we do not always thin things out or make them **volatile** <note>Easily evaporated.</note>; on the contrary, we also **fix** them <note>Make them solid and heat-resistant.</note>. If they are composed of elements and emerge from them, certainly they were at some point made from them. In another sense, however, the heavens do concur—namely, by universal and particular **time**. At that time, the heat excited in the air awakens the **seminal power** <term>vis seminalis</term> of those things exposed to the air, and impels them toward the motion appropriate to them, provided other supports are not lacking. In yet another sense, the heavens do not concur [directly], but a **celestial nature** is already inherent within **univocal seeds** <term>univocal</term> <note>In traditional biology, "univocal generation" refers to offspring that are the same species as their parents (e.g., a cow producing a cow).</note>. Look, you fool. I deny no principle, but I declare the true sense of the principle. Indeed, what you tell of the benignity of your heat, you will soon destroy yourself when... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, leading into the next page's discussion of heat.</note>

...Parisians <note>referring to the conservative medical faculty at the University of Paris</note>, since Aristotle has decreed it, why do you depart from him regarding the generation of man, in which female seed is denied? <note>Aristotle famously argued that only the male provides "seed" (form/motion), while the female provides only "matter" (menstrual blood). Hippocrates and Galen argued both parents provide seed.</note> Aristotle’s opinion in Book 3 of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 10, is excellent: "Generation," he says, "seems to be thus both by reason and by what is seen to happen in the case of bees. However, we do not yet have sufficiently explored facts of what happens. But if ever these things are sufficiently known, then **SENSORY PERCEPTION** <note>original: "sensui"</note> must be trusted more than reason. Faith must also be given to reason, provided that what is demonstrated agrees with those things perceived by the senses." A logical demonstration (he says in Book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 6) is more remote from its own principles the more universal it is. These points, applied to our present purpose, persuade us that we should rather agree with the <term>chymists</term> <term>chymists: early chemists or alchemists who emphasized laboratory work and observation over abstract philosophy</term> because they use divine oracles greater than any faith; they use sense, they use reason, and Experience—the bridge between the two.

*Another argument:*

> *Nothing under heaven is eternal except the mind; celestial substance is immortal and incapable of suffering.*
> *Therefore, in the elemental world, there is no celestial substance.*

The force of this <term>paralogism</term> <term>paralogism: a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning</term> is this: if a <term>quinta essentia</term> <term>quinta essentia: the "fifth essence" or quintessence, a pure celestial substance sought by alchemists to cure diseases</term> were in the sublunary world <note>the Earthly realm below the moon</note>, something would have to be eternal, immortal, and incapable of suffering. This is not the case, except for the mind—which is nonetheless ridiculously excluded here since the discussion is not about incorporeal things. The <term>chymist</term> could respond jokingly that not even the heavens are eternal, and if the heaven exists in any way, nothing prevents the quintessence of mixed bodies from existing in that same way. Indeed, the Earth is older than the heaven, and as the heaven grows old...

The **Aristotelian** demonstrations concerning heaven are useless because they clash with the very principle of its nature. At one point, he says heaven was created (*On the Parts of Animals*, Book 1, ch. 1); at another, he says it was not (*On the Heavens*, Book 1, ch. 10). He wavers concerning it in *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 1, ch. 5, and *On the Heavens*, Book 2, text 17, 6, 3. If he had known that heaven was created, he would have simultaneously recognized the cause of corruption within it.

**Aristotle** says <note>original: "inquit Arist."</note> that to do this is nothing else than to build up something that is indeed eternal, yet changing in form (*On the Heavens, Book 1, Text 107*). In this way, species are perpetuated by the succession of individuals (*On Generation and Corruption, Book 2, Chapter 1*). Since the nature of that kind cannot be eternal [individually], in what way can it be that that which is born is eternal? It cannot be so in **number** <note>Meaning numerical identity; the specific individual does not live forever.</note>. For the substance of things exists in individuals, which, if they were such [eternal], would be everlasting. But in **species**, it is possible. And so the race of men, and of beasts, and of plants is forever. Thus far he speaks.

We add that nothing is changed in the whole. Thus the **middle world** <note>Likely the terrestrial realm between the heavens and the center of the Earth.</note> will remain until the end, with no total part failing. The parts of the elements are changed, but the wholes never, although the same <term>potency</term> <note>The inherent power or capacity for change and existence within matter.</note> is present in them. Thus the integral parts behave as species. **Riolanus** <note>Jean Riolan, a conservative physician of the Paris Faculty and a staunch opponent of "chymical" medicine.</note>, since he excepted nothing [from destruction] except the mind, seems to have **dreamed between the knees of Saturn** <note>original: "inter Saturni genua somniasse"; a Latin idiom suggesting someone is being foolishly old-fashioned or out of touch with reality, as Saturn was an ancient, superseded deity.</note>. 

Otherwise, he could have known the eternity of sublunary things by this reasoning: that the **corruption** of one is always the **generation** of another, and corruption makes either matter or another thing. At least he might call this "akin to the celestial," which remains always, and which becomes another essence after it has been separated from the heap of mixed elements. **Job** constantly asserted that he would see God in his own flesh <note>A reference to Job 19:26, "And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God."</note>. Tell me, censor, where did the **essence of the flesh** hide after <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The biological decay of the body, which alchemists viewed as a necessary stage of transformation and purification.</note>? What God has composed, you might be able to dissolve to a certain extent according to the senses, but you cannot do so entirely. It is clear that that school babbles from the chair whatever clings to the surface; they do not look into the interior. 

Another [point].

*Gravity and levity are the reasons why some things move downward,*

*The Heavens are neither heavy nor light.*
*Therefore, it is not precipitated by weight to the generation of a mixture,*

Who would not laugh at the foolishness of that school? An argument is taken that clearly does not prove the point in question. For as for a "celestial nature" being present in mixtures <note>Physical compounds or bodies</note>, it does not originate from there <note>i.e., from moving up or down physically</note>, but because it was placed by the Creator from the beginning in the <term>matrix</term> <note>A "womb" or source-medium, in this context the fundamental elements that give birth to physical things</note> of the earth and the water which is mixed with the earth. Certain Chemists <note>original: "Chymici," referring to alchemists or practitioners of iatrochemistry</note> say it was entrusted to the elements as if to Platonic "receptacles" <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where matter acts as a "receptacle" for eternal forms</note>. From there, in its own time, it produces fruits similar to itself. We add that it does not only have roots in the earth—rising from there and expanding itself in every direction—but it is even present in the seeds of things. But we have spoken of this before.

But let us now suppose that this nature must be sought from the heavens; is there then a need for "the heavy" and "the light"? <note>Aristotelian physics argued that objects move toward their "natural place" based on weight (gravity) or lightness (levity)</note> Not at all. For by whatever vehicle **Riolanus** <note>Jean Riolan, a leading conservative physician who opposed the use of chemical medicines</note> drew out "moist heat," perhaps by that same vehicle the celestial offspring flows down, especially since it is said to be so closely related to the "aerial spirit." This is one explanation. Another is that it is sent down by the "whirling" <note>The rotational movement of the celestial spheres</note>. A third is by "influence." A fourth is by "friendship" <note>A translation of "sympathy," the idea that like-things in the universe are naturally drawn to one another</note>. For perhaps it should be said that there is a certain innate appetite in matter by which it is carried toward the celestial form; or that a particle of the celestial aura is drawn just as a magnet draws iron. The "constellated signs" of the magi <note>Astrological talismans or symbols believed to capture planetary power</note> and the "art of eliciting Jupiter" <note>An ancient Roman ritual, *Elicius*, used to draw down lightning or divine favor from the sky</note> tend toward this idea. **Riolanus** even proposed a certain necessity, according to which when matter reaches its final disposition...

<header>THE ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN SPURIOUS WORKS</header>

You see here a <term>paralogism</term> <note>A piece of false reasoning or a logical fallacy that appears valid on the surface</note> and not a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A formal logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>. To detect the <term>elenchus</term> <note>A logical refutation, specifically one that proves the opposite of an opponent's conclusion</note> within it, and to understand by what force the argument is applied to the question, one will need singular wit. Why does heaven send down a quality and not a substance? Because after the death of the animal, not even the <term>vital heat</term> <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the "innate heat" believed to be the primary engine of life and digestion</note> remains as it was before; so far is it from being the case that a celestial substance remains. 

By this argument—which we find laughable, since the question does not trouble us as <term>chymists</term> <note>Early modern scientists or alchemists who sought to understand the composition of matter</note> do not require the sending down of a celestial substance—the contrary can be concluded: 

1. To argue that it does not remain implies a departure. That which was previously present departs. Therefore, the celestial substance *was* present. 
2. Beasts are formed by a small spark of vital heat, by its power and presence. Moreover, that vital heat is celestial, which in a <term>perfected</term> <note>Meaning a "higher" animal, such as a mammal, as opposed to "lower" creatures like insects</note> organism was in a more perfect degree. But it cannot exist consistently, nor can it cling to <term>putrilage</term> <note>Decaying or rotting matter</note> without its own <term>subject</term> <note>The underlying material or substance in which a quality, like heat, must reside</note> that possesses a celestial nature. It follows that some celestial substance was present in the living as much as in the corpses. If that substance had to be sent down from heaven, why should heaven not influence by substance? 
3. If that heat by which beasts are generated from <term>putrefaction</term> <note>Decay; it was a common scientific belief until the 17th century that small creatures like maggots or flies were "spontaneously generated" from rotting matter by the heat of the sun</note> is celestial, it can be seen to have flowed in anew, rather than being a fragment cut off from the remains of the rotting thing. If the matter is to be disputed according to the judgment of Aristotle <margin>Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals*, Book 3, last chapter</margin>, then it must be established that all things consisting in an <term>equivocal manner</term> <note>Spontaneous generation, where the offspring is not of the same species as a parent (e.g., worms from mud)</note> seem to be born either in earth or water with putrefaction, and with rain...

->[having been] admitted. For when the sweet part is separated to serve as the foundation, what remains takes on a form by which it is <term>concocted</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, "concoction" is the process by which the body's heat matures or "cooks" nutrients into useful substances like blood</note>, not by which it putrefies. For putrefaction is the rotten waste of a concocted thing. Moreover, animals and plants are generated in the earth and in moisture, because there is moisture in the earth, spirit in the moisture, and <term>animal heat</term> <note>Also called "innate heat," the vital force that distinguishes living things from inanimate matter</note> in the universe, and so on. Elsewhere, he <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, whom Riolan is following here</note> attributes a kinship between that heat and spirit and the element of the stars; once this is grasped, they quickly take shape.

Therefore, when corpses putrefy and turn into <term>beasts</term> <note>Referring to the theory of "spontaneous generation," where small creatures like maggots or beetles were thought to arise naturally from decaying matter</note>, this can be said to happen not only by the efficacy of the residual vital heat, but also by a new influx, which **Riolan** previously maintained was continued by means of the light of the sky and the air. From this it is gathered that there is a celestial nature in spontaneously generated beasts in a twofold way: one through a new influx, the other through the departure of the previous nature and a new grasping within the concocted matter.

Perhaps **Riolan** wanted to conclude that a substance is not sent down from heaven because it would have to remain after death—which does not happen. For when scarcely a trace of heat remains, how could there be a substance? In the second way, if heaven touched only "virtually" <note>By means of an inherent power or "virtue" rather than physical touch.</note> or by quality, as **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan, a prominent conservative physician in Paris who opposed many chemical and innovative medical theories.</note> wishes, it would likewise strive toward a likeness. This reasoning of mine—provided for the sake of argument, not as a concession of fact—**Riolan** calls a "gross ignorance of physics." You err, I say, **Riolan**. I have not spoken without physical principles. How then can I [lack] physics...

### How plants are generated among the Parisians, and what "quintessence" <term>Quintessence|The "fifth element" or the purest, most essential part of a substance, often sought by alchemists.</term> their lettuces have, according to the madness of Riolan.

**A**ristotle raises a question in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter one <note>Aristotle's *De Generatione Animalium* was the standard text for understanding reproduction and biology in the 17th century.</note>, as to the way in which a plant or an animal is generated from a seed. It is indeed certain that they are born from some matter, of which some things have with them the first matter received from the female—such as those things born in the form of an egg or a little worm—while other things take from the female for a long time, such as those which are produced not only in the form of animals on the outside, but also on the inside. 

But it is the efficient causes <term>Efficient cause|In philosophy, the agent or force that actually brings something into being, like a carpenter making a chair.</term> that are the most disputed. For either an implanted principle acts, or an external one does. If it is an external one that granted movement to the seed, then there is nothing absurd about placing the generator outside as well. But that generator no longer touches [the seed]. Truly, it is necessary for the efficient cause to touch [the thing it creates]. 

Therefore, the philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" refers to Aristotle.</note> solves the question by saying that that first cause touched it when it conferred movement to the seed, which movement afterwards brings about the effect. He establishes that all things produced either by nature or by art are made by that which is already in "actuality" <term>Actuality and Potentiality|The Aristotelian concept that a seed is a tree "in potential" (potentiality), but only becomes a tree when that potential is realized (actuality) by a life-force.</term> out of that which is such in potentiality. He says that external conditions indeed proceed from the primary qualities <note>The four qualities of hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, but the "reason" <note>original: "rationem"; here meaning the internal blueprint or structural logic of a living thing.</note> by which it is already flesh or bone cannot come from those qualities, but rather from the movement proceeding from that which generated it—and which is in actuality that which the matter from which it is born is in potentiality. Therefore, this foolishness is nonetheless exploded, because it is one thing to be concocted, perfected, and generated; it is quite another to rot. It is one thing to be dissolved by rot; it is another to stand firm and be born.

The soul and the form do not operate by themselves; instead, they employ this very heat, which, by acting upon suitable matter, has multiplied its own form within that matter through the process of alteration. Its goal was only the [attainment of the] form. Therefore, once that is acquired, does the heat recede? It does not follow that the nature received from the parent recedes, or if it remains, that it becomes idle. For its duties are many. From the opposition, it might often appear to one who fixes his mind on its harmful nature that it does not **exist** <term>to be; original Greek: εἶναι</term> at all. For since there is something divine, good, and desirable, we say there is a contrary to it. He makes **matter** <note>original: *materiam*</note> a co-cause of **form**; he opposes **privation** <note>original: *priuationem*; the lack of a specific quality or form.</note> to form. He considers form as something divine, good, and desirable. Privation, being the opposite of this—because the consequences of opposites are themselves opposite—must necessarily be something ignoble, evil, and worthy of hatred. Therefore, if anyone should wish to look upon its **maleficence** <note>original: *maleficium*; the quality of doing harm or evil.</note> and turn their mind toward it, it will seem not to exist at all.

And indeed, privation is "non-being" in itself, while matter is "non-being" by accident <note>i.e., matter is not "nothing," it just happens to lack a specific form at a specific time.</note>. Thus, it cannot be a constitutive principle of things. Nay, as noted in text 68 <note>A reference to a specific section in Aristotle’s *Physics*.</note>, it is not necessary to propose three principles when two suffice: namely **matter** and **form**, which through absence and presence, or through **potency** <term>potential; the capacity to become</term> and **act** <term>actualization; the state of being</term>, create change.

**Privation** is truly an **equivocal** <note>original: *æquiuocum*; a term that can be used in different senses.</note> word, as is clear from the *Metaphysics*; whatever is used to argue its state is entirely a matter of logic. But in truth, since "generations" <note>The process of things coming into being.</note>—which are movements toward form—are said to happen because of this privation, when we speak of these very things, it should be counted as **beneficent**, not maleficent. 

Aristotle himself also does not say that privation is maleficent in itself, but only in a certain respect. In natural generation, it cannot be a cause of evil in itself, but only by accident, insofar as it is necessary for another form to succeed the prior form which has been cast off...

This is just as when a physician removes the "form" of an ulcer and rouses nature toward healing; in this way, he becomes the cause of health and should be called a benefactor, not a malefactor. Let Riolan, that Aristotelian dreamer, remain convinced of the "maleficence of privation" <note>original Greek: τὸ κακοποιὸν στερήσεως; the idea that the absence of form is an active evil force.</note> if it so pleases him. 

If privation is nothing in actuality, but only a certain condition of matter by which form is understood to depart or be absent, then it cannot actually *effect* anything at all—since every effect comes from a "form"—much less can it do anything good or evil. This "itch" and these scholastic scraps <note>original: *quisquilias*; literally dregs or waste, referring to trivial academic arguments.</note> ought not to have been brought back into the arena where, by Riolan's own judgment, to philosophize is to act by reasons and not by authorities.

Aristotle established that the **equivocal generation** <term>spontaneous generation; the ancient belief that living creatures like insects could arise from non-living matter like rotting meat</term> of animals and plants is produced by a twofold heat: the heat of the season, and the heat of the waste products in the states of decay <note>original: *putredinibus*; refers to the heat generated by fermentation or rot.</note> from which animals are born.

He claims that this heat sifts, boils, and organizes <note>original: *concernere, concoquere, & constituere*; "concoction" was the process by which heat matured or "cooked" raw matter into life.</note> materials from the sea or the earth. 

He teaches that this process is understood to be received into the **animal spirit** <term>spiritus animalis; a refined "breath" or fluid thought to reside in the nerves and drive movement and sensation</term> and to effect conception and impose motion. Furthermore, he teaches that nothing else is understood here than this seasonal heat, which he also calls "animal heat" and the "animal principle." He maintains that it exists throughout the universe, with the spirit being in the moisture, and the moisture in the earth. Truly, these things are not of great importance. The virulence and malice of the censors, who slander even well-spoken things, is well enough known.

# GALEN’S TRIUMPH.

Aristotle taught that <term>conception|original: "conceptus." Here referring to the initial spark of life or the formation of an embryo.</term> arises in earth and moisture. If any boy in our basic grammar schools defined a bubble as "excrement," he would be soundly whipped. What, then, is owed to Riolan and the Parisian scholastics who teach so authoritatively from their chairs? Insofar as they try to prove such a thing, they deserve the lash. If a bubble contains heat, spirit, and foam, as Riolan says; and if that heat comes from heaven along with air and light, by what right is it called "excrement"? Yet it is not only called "excrement," but is also said to be ineffective by itself. From this, I argue:

> *That which is entirely ineffective by itself cannot be effective through the parts of which it consists.*
> *The genital seminal bubble is ineffective by itself.*
> *Therefore, it is not effective through its parts—which are the primigenial humor, spirit, and heat. A "fine" sort of generation that would be!* <note>Libavius uses "bella generatio" (a fine/beautiful generation) sarcastically to mock Riolan’s logic that something "ineffective" could produce life.</note>

This is a foolish pronouncement. For if the seed—whose body is like a foamy bubble—is that which by its own nature contributes to the whole, and through whose motion a being similar to the parent is procreated, then generation does not happen by accident. Instead, the seed—by its own nature and by an implanted principle, not an external agent—strives toward a form that is the same species as the parent. It is therefore plainly necessary that the seed be effective by its own power. From this, the opposite conclusion follows: If the seed is effective both as a whole and in its parts, then the <term>quintessence|The "fifth essence," a term used by alchemists to describe the purest, most medicinal, and life-giving part of a substance, separate from the four heavy elements.</term> contained and propagated within the seed-stuff must also be effective. You will note, moreover, the stupidity of the man who divides the bubble into foam (which he calls "excrement," though it was the bubble itself), spirit, and heat. Here, not without merit...

<margin>Note the absurdity of Riolan's division.</margin>

## CHAPTER XXVII.

->Concerning Riolan's dual spirit, fixed and volatile, from page 55 of his *Mania*, and pages 23–24 of his *Examination*.<-

**R**iolan the Censor denied that the spirit was a <term>fifth essence|original: "quinta essentia." In alchemy, the purest, most potent substance extracted from a body, distinct from the four elements.</term>, because it would have to be either "natural," "animal," or "vital" <note>These are the three Galenic spirits: natural (produced in the liver), vital (in the heart), and animal (in the brain).</note>. Yet it is none of these. We laughed at the absurdity of the argument, and we still judge such a "censor" to belong among the ranks of fools. For the spiritual <term>fifth essence</term> of the <term>chemists|original: "chymicorum." Here referring to those who practice the art of chemical extraction and transformation.</term> is not made of those organic spirits that are carried forcefully through the passages of animal bodies—which Hippocrates calls the "third part of the limbs." Instead, the essence is drawn out from solids; it consists of the <term>primigenial moisture|original: "humido primigenio." The fundamental life-fluid believed to be present in an organism from its inception.</term>, innate heat, and the <term>implanted spirit|original: "spiritu insito." An internal, stabilizing spirit found within the structure of a substance rather than circulating freely.</term>. This spirit does not appear entirely in an airy, volatile form, but is for the most part condensed, coagulated, or fixed. Indeed, it takes on both dispositions. Therefore, nothing can be concluded against the <term>chemists’</term> <term>fifth essence</term> by looking at those organic spirits. Even the "maniac" Riolan, in his own fury, recognizes the weakness of his argument. Having abandoned it, he substitutes a new fabrication about a dual natural spirit: one "influential" and the other "fixed." And...

He also attributes a vanishing essence even to that which is "fixed," so that you may see how falsehood struggles with itself when it stubbornly opposes manifest truth. To make the judgment clearer, let us propose a <term>syllogism|original: "syllogismi." A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</term> to illuminate this "Parisian light" <note>Libavius is sarcastically referring to the Medical Faculty of Paris, of which Riolan was a prominent member.</note>, lest it be suffocated by the darkness of Riolan’s madness.

> *If the generating spirit—which is held to be the most celestial of all spirits—is in its substance elementary <note>Made of the four physical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, and celestial only in its quality and powers: then the "Fixed" spirit will not be of a better condition or nature.*
>
> *The first part is true. Therefore, the latter is also true, and consequently the spiritual <term>fifth essence</term> of the <term>chemists</term> is not celestial.*

The terms must first be clarified. For that "generating" spirit was previously called the "influencing" spirit <note>original: "influens." In early modern medicine, the "inflowing" spirit was thought to travel from the organs to the rest of the body to provide life.</note>. From where does it flow? He says it arises partly from the vapor of the blood, and partly from inspired air—or air and fire tempered together. Here, this spirit comes to the aid of the "fixed" spirit. For otherwise, the fixed spirit would vanish, and the limb would perish from a slow wasting. 2. Both the fixed and the influencing spirits are of the same nature. For in order to repair the nature of the fixed, the influencer must be of the same kind <note>original: "congener." A principle in Aristotelian physics that like nourishes like.</note>. This serves as the proof of the <term>major premise</term>. The <term>minor premise</term> is left to be disproved.

Behold here an example of the Philosophy found in the medical college of the Parisian school—which, in the judgment of Riolan, is the most learned of all schools, and for that reason to be revered and admired. It is truly a wondrous collection of unheard-of portents! If that "fixed" spirit is a vanishing essence, by what logic can it be called "fixed"?

### -> ON THE BASTARD ALCHEMY OF PARIS <-

That which is fixed is not volatile. But if such a thing is to be brought about, there is need for great ingenuity in the art, and for powerful agents in nature, which must necessarily cast it down from its own nature and lead it into a contrary state—just as the <term>Peripatetics|original: "Peripatus." The school of philosophy following Aristotle, who taught that elements could transform into one another.</term> say that water or fire is made from earth, or air from water. 

But if the "fixed" spirit within us is so windy and easily scattered, that "inflowing" volatile spirit <note>The *spiritus influens* was thought to be a life-force traveling through the body.</note> will be much more windy and unstable. It will eventually happen that all spirits depart from <term>Riolan|Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent and conservative physician of the Paris Medical Faculty.</term>, and his body itself would be useless for the <term>fifth essence|original: "quinta essentia." In alchemy, the purest, most refined substance; here used to mean the vital principle of life.</term>—and not without reason. For he possesses none, but is entirely composed of air flowing in and out; according to the saying: **"Full of cracks: it flows through here and there."** <note>original: "Plenus rimarum: Hac atque illac perfluit." A quote from Terence's *Eunuchus*, often used to describe someone who cannot keep a secret or, in this case, someone whose theories (or body) cannot hold substance.</note> 

By what agent, then, O **Parisians**, can it be brought about that this inflowing volatile spirit made from air and vapor becomes fixed? Who is that <term>Vulcan|The Roman god of fire, used as a metaphor for the alchemical fire or the transformative power that "fixes" volatile substances.</term> among you who performs the fixation? It is a grand assumption to claim that elementary air is mixed with the vapor of blood, and thus "cooked" in the natural vessels by heat so that a **fixed spirit** is produced from it—especially a spirit whose fixity is so very slight. But delusions are fitting for a madman.

The spiritual essence of the **chemists**, if we are to speak of living things, is the <term>radical moisture|original: "humor radicalis." The fundamental life-sustaining fluid of the body, thought to be the fuel for the body's innate heat.</term> so united with heat and spirit that you may extract parts differently affected by rarity, density, color, and so forth, yet you cannot separate the whole. Salt, in relation to liquid and oil, is indeed called "fixed"; yet it too is spiritual, partaking of both conditions. Secondly, it is said that the "generating spirit" is the same as the "inflowing" spirit. Therefore, the matter of both will also be the same;

Doubtless **Riolan** is a dictator in his academic chair. How "shrewd" indeed! Such is the nature of those marvelous hypotheses.

It must certainly be admitted that if the "volatile spirit" is made of the same dregs as the "fixed spirit," both are closer to flat, spoiled wine <note>original: "vappæ." Therefore, it is foolish.

Against Riolan, however, many defenses for the quintessence <term>quinta essentia: Literally the "fifth essence," a refined, incorruptible substance distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, water, air, fire), often associated by alchemists with the vital force of life.</term> can be constructed from that very same discourse. This is also the case in nutrition. If that which is similar in its potential provides nourishment, it follows that an ethereal, nutritive essence must exist within mixed bodies, which can then pass into the celestial substance of the "similar parts" <note>In Galenic anatomy, "similar parts" (partes similares) refer to uniform tissues like bone, fat, or fiber, as opposed to "organic parts" like the hand or liver.</note>. That generative nature within seeds cannot be changed in a moment, for nothing is completed suddenly. To endure until the end, it must be restored and increased by its like. In this way, our quintessence is also amplified. 

Furthermore, the "fixed spirit" will be of the same nature as the essence extracted from the limbs. But it is impossible for this essence to consist of air and the vapor of blood. Therefore, the spirit cannot consist of them either. The minor premise is evident from their specific properties. For if it did consist of them, we would be able to increase these essences simply with air and blood-vapor. 

Moreover, if that generative spirit is "natural," it cannot be sought from the heavens, the air, or fire, only to flow in and then vanish again—as if the foundation of life were nothing more than a perpetually burning breath <note>original: "deflagrans semper halitus"; Libavius is mocking the idea that the vital spirit is just a transient, smoky vapor.</note>. > *That which, once extracted, loses its own power—even if it were granted to be a celestial essence—would nevertheless be ineffective.*
>
> *The essence of the fixed spirit, once extracted, loses its own power.*
>
> *Therefore [it is ineffective].*

<margin>,,</margin> The minor premise is proved because the spirit loses the heat by which <margin>,,</margin> alone it is effective. That it loses this heat is obvious. For death has <margin>,,</margin> taken it away, and death is the deprivation of innate heat.

The reason is that even if the spirit were to lose its "own" power—namely, that specific power it possessed within the living body by which it lives—it would not necessarily be ineffective. [Let us grant] for a short while (to return the favor to Riolan) that [the spirit] would nonetheless not lose its proper power through extraction from a limb that has died. For it possesses a twofold power: one that administers life, which must nonetheless be driven and governed by common organs—and when these fail, the actions of individual parts are not stirred; the other power is proper to the mixture <term>mistio: In natural philosophy, this refers to the specific elemental blending that gives a substance its unique chemical and medicinal properties.</term>. The same applies to heat. Its organic power, which presides over life, indeed fades away in death, but the other, the radical heat, remains, which it received specifically from its generation and mixture. This heat then begins most truly to be its own and to exercise its own action when the common form <note>The "common form" is the soul or organizing principle of the living creature; Libavius argues that once the soul leaves, the material's internal chemical properties (the "mixture") actually become more prominent.</note> has been removed and the act of life rests. 

Unless malice and madness were wrestling within Riolan, do you think he could have written such nonsense? He is a man who trusts in his own decoctions, infusions, and pressings to be able to transfer the specific virtues of things into a foreign subject even after death, and to keep them almost entirely intact even after a third or fourth stage of decay! Death is the deprivation of life, and in those things which lived by the benefit of heat, it often occurs when the heat is extinguished; it also often occurs from other causes, which are nonetheless eventually followed by the dissipation of that heat. But that no other heat can be understood except the functional heat prepared for performing the duties of life—at the level at which it can provide that—rather than the innate and implanted heat, you should learn from your own Aristotle, Riolan. For Aristotle does not take away innate heat <term>calor innatus: The "internal fire" believed to be the source of life and digestion in ancient and Renaissance medicine.</term> by the death of the animal or plant, but by putrefaction <note>original: "putredine". Libavius is citing the Aristotelian idea that the material "heat" of a substance remains after the death of the organism until the substance itself rots away.</note>.

# CHAPTER XXVIII.

## Whether the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quinta essentia." In traditional philosophy, this is the "ether" that makes up the heavens; in alchemy, it refers to the most purified, potent extract of a substance.</note> is analogous to the celestial nature; regarding page 56 of the manuscript.

### Examination 24.

<margin>
Note from this dispute that Riolan rushed into the contest with blind impulse, or perhaps listened more to his own malice than to well-considered reason. Otherwise, he would have seen that the term "fifth essence" has one meaning in Physics and another in Chemistry.
</margin>

**T**he critic <note>Referring to Jean Riolan the Elder.</note> denied that chemical extracts were "celestial," arguing instead that they are merely "elementary" <note>Made of the four earthly elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. The response is that they are elementary <term>in a certain respect</term> <note>original: "secundum quid." A logical term meaning something is true only in a specific context or under certain conditions.</note>; however, they are also truly celestial according to <term>analogy</term> <note>original: "analogian." Libavius argues that chemical essences "function" like the heavens because of their power, even if they aren't literally made of heavenly matter.</note>. This is true first because, from the dawn of the world, the root and seed of the celestial nature was implanted into mixed bodies, and second because these extracts are the innermost part of those mixtures in which their virtues lie hidden. When these extracts are separated and compared with the common elements of the world, they cannot be called "elementary" in a simple sense.

Indeed, this naming by analogy is taken from **Aristotle**, who calls the nature of heat, spirit, and the <term>primordial moisture</term> <note>original: "humidi primigenii." The fundamental fluid thought to sustain life in an organism.</note> found in seeds "analogous to the element of the stars," insofar as it is more divine than the elements, which on their own can produce no living thing. Truly, the "celestial" is of two kinds: that which is celestial in a simple sense, and that which is celestial according to analogy. Let no one think that when we extract the most noble part from mixtures—in which the medicinal virtues and powers reside—we wish it to appear that we have extracted that most simple body of the <term>ether</term> <note>original: "ætheris." The "fifth element" that fills the space of the universe above the terrestrial sphere.</note>. Yet, we draw out the "celestial by analogy" so evidently that we can demonstrate with all our might that there is something more excellent, noble, and superior to the elements. Within the order of worldly bodies that possess a simple nature, this must be considered an entirely celestial substance. Nevertheless, since this is not simply—

-> ### ON THE FALSEHOODS OF THE PARISIAN ALCHEMY ### <-

Not long ago, in "page 51 of his madness" <note>original: *pag. maniæ 51*; Libavius is mockingly citing a specific page in his opponent's book as a work of insanity.</note>, he denied that the generating spirit remains in the things generated, because it would be idle. Now he even kindles fevers with its immoderate heat. Furthermore, if that spirit—analogous to the celestial—has the power to exceed its own heat (by which it is judged entirely preternatural), yet is not different in substance but only altered in the degree of its quality, what prevents the celestial body itself from suffering in the same way? In this way, the syllogistic principle is overturned, so that the opposite may be said: It does not follow that if <term>chemical</term> <note>original: *chymicæ*</note> essences are analogous to heaven, they must be moderate.

Thirdly, it must be noted that <term>to be moderate</term> <note>original: *τὸ moderatum*</note> is not always referenced to our touch and judgment; but often simply to the nature of any given mixture. Therefore, even **Euphorbium** <note>A caustic plant resin used in medicine, but dangerous in high doses.</note> has its own temperament, and so does **hemlock** <note>original: *cicuta*</note>, although both are immoderate toward us, or possess an immoderation <note>In Galenic medicine, "immoderation" or "intemperies" refers to a state where one of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, or dry—is out of balance.</note>. Now we come to the minor premise. We say that it is false. The prosyllogism is sophisticated <note>In this context, "sophisticated" means fallacious or deceptively argued.</note>. For what purpose does it serve to select only one or two minerals from an infinite number, by which—because they are immoderate toward us—all essences are simply said to be excessively hot? We do not deny that the **oil of the Philosophers**, **petroleum**, and **oil of sulf-**

<header>GALENISM’S TRIUMPH <note>original: *Galenia Triumphus*. Likely a sarcastic title for this section or a reference to a specific debate title, as the author is currently defending chemical medicine against traditional Galenic views.</note></header>

...cine <note>Completing the word "medicine" from the previous page.</note> has nothing more divine than the elements. For it strips the celestial nature away from mixtures, as well as their analogy with the heavens. How suitable, I ask, is such a medicine? On the other hand, **chemical medicine** <term>chymiatria: the use of chemical and mineral substances in medicine, as opposed to purely herbal Galenic remedies</term> holds itself quite differently, and for this reason alone it should be called the "true medicine." Take away the **chemical essences** <note>The concentrated, "pure" part of a substance</note> lurking in the depths of the workshop's mixtures, and it will be filled with nothing but **elemental corpses** <note>The "dead" or useless matter left over after the potent essence has been extracted</note>. Whatever is achieved that is praiseworthy in **Galenic practice**, it is done not by the power of the elements, but by the essences lurking within them. Since Nature herself separates these by chewing and digesting so that she may enjoy their nourishing quality, is it not wrong to prevent Art <note>Here meaning "alchemy" or "chemistry," which was often called "the art" that imitates nature</note> from imitating nature? But let another proof of this madness be brought forward.

->*A fiery nature extracted from elemental things cannot*<-
->*be celestial.*<-
->*Chemical essences are fiery natures extracted*<-

Are the **quintessences** <term>Quintessence: Literally the "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated medicinal core of a substance, separated from its raw "elemental" bulk</term> of the chemists of an elementary, fiery nature? In your view, certainly not all nor even most are—unless, perhaps, the quintessence of water-lilies, roses, violets, and similar plants are also considered fiery. When craftsmen attribute the name "fire" or "fiery" to this "fifth nature," they are referring to **celestial fires** <note>The "fire" of the stars and heavens, thought to be life-giving and non-consuming, unlike a kitchen fire</note>. If they are not discussing quintessences properly so-called, but rather **masteries** <term>Mastery: A high-grade medicinal preparation achieved through specific alchemical skill (magisterium)</term> and other extracts, they either use the term in a modified sense—as when they call something "fiery" because it is hot, spirited, penetrating, and **formal** <note>In the philosophy of the time, the "form" was the active, life-giving power of a substance, as opposed to its passive "matter"</note>—or they mean a separated element.

In the same way, the **Dogmatic physicians** <note>The traditional medical establishment that followed the established theories of Galen and Hippocrates</note> have their own "fires," which are by no means the element of fire or that "meteoric" heat, but are something else entirely. These include the heat found in living beings, hot spirits, **potential fires** <note>Substances like lye or acids that burn the skin like fire despite not being actual flames</note>, and various mixtures that are predominantly hot and dry, etc. 

Thus, we prepare **caustic waters** and **stygian fires** <note>original: *ignes stygii*; likely strong acids like nitric acid, named for the underworld river Styx due to their corrosive power</note>, whose force far exceeds elementary fire. Because these are mixed essences and thus participate in something elementary, they can in some way be compared to the element of fire; however, since they must be judged by their whole nature and their effects (which exceed the nature of the elements), they approach the class of celestial substances more closely the more they are refined. This phrasing is also absurd: *to have produced blood from chyle by the change of potentiality into actuality;* where one should have said *out of chyle*, and not *by the change of potentiality into actuality*. For a **privation** never becomes a **state of being** <note>original: "Privatio enim nunquam fit habitus." In scholastic logic, "privation" is the absence of a quality; it does not "turn into" the quality, rather the matter acquires the quality.</note>; but matter is changed or moved out of potentiality, etc.

I shall prove the minor premise <note>In a formal logical argument (a syllogism), the "minor premise" is the second statement that connects a specific case to a general rule.</note>: Because it is impossible to separate the **temperament** <term>Temperament: In ancient medicine, the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that defines a substance's nature.</term> and the specific quality from a mixture. There is also another impossibility in their promise. For it is impossible for the *crasis* to be separated from a mixture by the process of cooking. Are you unaware, when your own kitchens present you with cooked meats, that the meats remain essentially what they were?

...were it to be perceived in the infusion, only an alteration or migration of form and qualities from one subject to another would occur. Flee, therefore, from that shop of imposters, and do not entrust the health of your body to such lying windbags. Turn instead to **chemistry**. This can successfully provide you with true essences for every medical purpose. To understand this more rightly, pay attention. Riolan denies that **chemical essences** <term>Chemical essences: The pure, active "soul" or medicine extracted from a raw substance through alchemical processes.</term> exist "in act" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "in act" (actu) means something is currently and fully real, whereas "in potential" (potentia) means it has the capacity to become real.</note> within mixtures. From what has been said, we construct this syllogism:

*That medical workshop is to be approached for the sake of health which does not use deception, but displays the naked essences of things, and exhibits them as efficacious and convenient for use, having drawn them forth from the hiding places of elemental impurities and filth.*

Now, who would not prefer the divine and wonderful works of a divine and admirable art over the tasteless and loathsome scraps of the apothecary shops? Chemists thus produce their essences, as Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical ideas.</note> testifies.

->**Therefore.**<-

And consequently, they are the **perfectors** of things to which, along with the **form** <note>In the philosophy of the time, "form" was the internal principle that gave a substance its specific identity and powers.</note>, they give specific and formal powers. Since perfection relates to imperfection as it does to the deprivation of form, why shouldn't they be called the makers of forms? But since ignorance and impudence can observe no moderation, it happens that Riolan even here attributes too much to the chemists. For they do not always generate from potentiality; rather, they more often merely **separate** that which has already been generated by nature from its elementary dross, and they adorn it with accidental gifts, just as they also do in their Great Works. They make use of alterations, augmentations, separations, conjunctions, and other techniques. Hence it is commonly said that they **separate the pure from the impure**.

<margin>On the essence of gold.</margin>
Riolan attempts to prove by the specific example of gold that chemists *create* essences out of matter rather than *extracting* them; he denies that its essence possesses the same temperament and form as whole gold. Did they then create that temperament by art? Either it was already there in actuality, or it existed in the potentiality of nature. In either case, they did not make it themselves, but rather they brought forth what nature held either manifest or hidden, which accords with the word "extracting." They manifested the most noble <term>medical entity</term> <note>original: "ens medicum"; the vital, active healing principle within a substance</note> which was confined within the tightest enclosures of nature, drawing the internal nature out into the open, and as they say, **turning the interior of nature outward.** Have they not performed a distinguished work? Whether you think that should be compared with the transformation of blood into the heart is up to you. <term>Chemists</term> <note>original: "Chymici"</note> do not care about that. Nevertheless, lest you wander in uncertainty, you should have stated which essence of gold you were speaking about, so that we could answer you specifically. For to you, <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; a term for a concentrated medicinal preparation or the highest achievement of the chemical art</note>, essence, and the rest...

We respond that in gold there is one interior form and action, and another exterior one. This [exterior] one serves worldly business and ornaments more than medicine. But that [interior] one is wonderfully and almost exclusively required for proper healing. If chemists have removed the external splendor of its appearance, they have not removed the entire form and temperament, since they have brought forth the interior form, which is what is most sought after. Nature acts in this way too in nutrition and generation, lest you think chemists lack nature's own reasoning. Here is a <term>prolepsis</term> <note>original: "prolepsis." A rhetorical device where the author anticipates an opponent's objection and answers it in advance.</note>, as if I were arguing thus:

->*A change for the better is not to be blamed;*<-
->*when an essence is made from whole gold, the change is for the better.*<-
->*Therefore, this is not to be blamed.*<-

# GALENIC TRIUMPH
<page-num>385</page-num>
<header>GALENIC TRIUMPH</header>

You deny the minor premise of the argument because you claim the transformation has declined into something worse, with the force of fire bestowing a far more vehement heat and power upon the gold. Then you say nature is offended by every excess, rejoicing only in moderation. Do you hurl such spineless and frivolous trifles at the chemists and expect to deserve a public monument? Surely it would be a monument to your own misfortune and madness. The bellows-blowers <note>original: "sufflones." A derogatory nickname for chemists and alchemists, referring to their constant stoking of furnace fires with bellows.</note> of the chemists reply that you chatter most ignorantly about the essence of gold. There is a certain way of preparing it through specific "waters" of their own, which they call Stygian fires <note>original: "ignes stygios." Named after the River Styx in the underworld; in alchemy, this refers to powerful mineral acids or corrosive solvents (like *aqua regia*) that "burn" or dissolve metals through chemical action rather than physical heat.</note>, not because of their heat-qualities but because of their effects. 

But no fire, even the most vehement—such as is certainly used in the smelting and testing of gold, even with the addition of sulfur, antimony, and other most biting and sharp medicines—can strip gold of its outward appearance and its external temperament; far be it from heat being made more violent by those means. Indeed, those "waters" of ours, even when applied cold, unlock and dissolve the structure and framework of gold. We see the basic principle of this in the workshops of common goldsmiths, who reduce a fairly solid piece of gold into a paste using quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo." Mercury.</note>. Far different instruments are needed for gold to become essential <term>essentiale</term> <note>Refers to the alchemical process of reducing a substance to its "essence" or "tincture," which was believed to be its pure medicinal soul, free from the "gross" or "dead" metallic body.</note> than your simple fire. Therefore, do not tell tall tales about the power of fire to the uninitiated.

->*If gold cannot acquire excessive heat even by the most savage fires of the hottest furnaces, much less does it acquire it by the far more modest fires of the chemists.*<-

->*But it cannot acquire it from those savage fires, as experience witnesses. Therefore, much less will it be possible by these chemical fires.*<-

<margin>If that which is according to nature for each thing is moderate, then even excesses of fire are moderate to fire.</margin>
Our essence, when it has been brought forth from the hidden by God, does not turn away from the excess of fire, so that like a fixed <term>salamander</term> <note>original: "salamandra fixa." The salamander was a mythical lizard believed to live in fire; in alchemy, it represents a substance that is "fire-proof" or "fixed," meaning it does not evaporate or degrade when heated.</note>, it rests friendlily within it. Indeed, gold is even made purer and more noble by the fires of the metallurgists. Just as fire delights in fire, so gold seems to be charmed by it, as if it were a certain natural fire of its own. Every thing rests within its own form. The chemists have brought the interior form of gold into the manifest. Why should it not rest in this state as well? And experience also teaches this. If the state in which a mixture rests and is preserved is considered moderate, then the form and temperament of the chemical essence will be moderate. Therefore, I conclude against you thus:

> Whatever is preserved, is preserved by moderation alone.
> 
> The chemical essence of gold is preserved. Therefore [it is moderate].

Consequently, the chemical essence of gold possesses its own temperament and moderation, and no true excess—except when Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine and a fierce critic of chemical remedies.</note> raves by practicing medicine poorly.

*Wisdom of Solomon 16:20:*

What if we were to say, I ask, that this Manna—produced miraculously in nature by God—was nothing other than a <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: *quintam essentiam*; the "fifth essence," or the most purified and potent core of a substance</note> extracted from the Sun by God’s singular providence? By divine arrangement, this substance was extracted from matter in the air, formed in a specific way, and endowed with great powers. No one can deny that God used nature for this purpose, though it was uniquely governed and miraculously directed. 

From this, an argument might be made: The Sun is able to extract an essence from <term>mixed bodies</term> <note>original: *mistis*; substances composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water)</note>; therefore, a <term>chemist</term> <note>original: *chymicus*; in this period, the terms for chemist and alchemist were often used interchangeably</note>—using the Sun or a similar heat or instrument—is also able to do so. This premise is made clear by the celestial Manna. 

We are not searching too scrupulously into the Manna of the Israelites to see whether it was fashioned from ethereal or aerial substance, whether it was created anew, or whether it was condensed from vapors with such miraculous abundance, power, and other miraculous gifts. Nevertheless, it clearly appears to have been a "mixed body" <note>original: *mistum*</note> of some kind, because it was able to provide nourishment, it had a flavor, it could rot and generate worms, and it was liquefied and dissolved by heat. Even today, they tell of something similar being produced in those regions, and what the common manna is like.

The location, the time of collection, the use, and the <term>properties</term> <note>original: *passiones*; the physical characteristics or behaviors of the substance</note> all agree. These resolved vapors were undoubtedly carried upward, and there, by the omnipotence of God, they were reconstituted with other things into a new...

**Author.** Indeed, I have never doubted that it was done by a miracle <note>original: *miraculo*; an event that exceeds the known laws of nature, attributed to divine agency</note>. Who, indeed, among those who care for divine matters, would deny this? 

But since some miracles are purely divine, while others use nature as a servant, I assign the generation of **Manna** <note>the "bread from heaven" provided to the Israelites in the desert</note>—which was miraculously provided—to this latter kind. It is just as when God also produced perfectly natural waters from a rock, but in a non-natural way. Do you see the foolishness of your criticism? You say it could have happened "naturally" from condensed dew in dense forests. Imagine that! Even though we have no record of forests in **Stony and Desert Arabia** <term>Arabia Petraea</term> <note>a Roman provincial name for the Sinai Peninsula and surrounding regions, known for its harsh, rocky terrain</note>; yet, there is nothing absurd in divine power seeking matter from remote places. 

But I say that a more sublime power must have been added to that natural mode, so that such Manna would be collected in that place in such great quantity and strength, where it never appeared at any other time, and where it also ceased afterward, so that it was found only around the military camp. 

If it was natural dew, miraculously gathered, shaped, sent down, and made effective, then my argument holds firm: it is likely its matter was previously extracted by the **Sun**, and that this matter is analogous to a heavenly nature, which is why it is called **heavenly bread** <note>original: *panis cœlestis*; a common biblical term for Manna</note>. 

But you deny the service of nature. By what argument? "If ordinary power could do it," you say, "then an absolute and extraordinary power—to which miracles belong—was not necessary." But where did I say that this miracle consisted of ordinary power? Insofar as it was a miracle, it had extraordinary causes. But nothing prevents us from attributing its matter and its extraction to the service of nature...

The common sort speak of "temperament" as if it were a certain blending of the **primary qualities** <note>The four basic building blocks: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> in which, by cooling what is hot and heating what is cold, a certain middle point is reached. This temperament is cited by reason of these contraries, and is categorized into its various types by "justice," "weight," "excesses," and so on <note>The author refers to the Galenic classification of temperaments: *ad pondus* (by equal weight) and *ad iustitiam* (according to the functional requirements of the body part)</note>.

Others, looking toward the matter, call the form of mixtures a "union of altered things." This is the "mixing" itself, which bestows upon the thing both its name and its "form of mixture," which is then followed by the power of the **primary and secondary qualities** <note>Secondary qualities include things like taste, smell, or hardness, which result from the primary mix of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>. 

A third class of powers, which are called **formal**, **occult**, or **astral** <note>These are "hidden" powers that cannot be explained by simple heat or moisture, often attributed by Paracelsians to influences from the stars</note>, plainly refute the former opinion which constructs the form of a mixture out of **tactile qualities** <note>Qualities that can be felt, like temperature or texture</note>. For they show that there is something entirely internal within a mixture to which those powers must be referred as an **essential principle**. It is impossible for these powers to arise merely from the hot, the cold, the moist, the dry, and their various blendings.

The common doctors, who establish their art by the method of primary and secondary qualities, therefore exclude those "third powers" from their method, ascribing them instead to "experience"—that which simply notes the effects. But they ought to attend to almost the whole...

...which is truly medical, scientific, and skillful, depends on a principle of **specific powers** <note>original: *poteſtatum ſpecificatū*; powers unique to a particular substance rather than general qualities like heat or cold</note>. Therefore, in our medical method, we must give primary consideration to the **interior temperament** <note>original: *interioris temperiei*; the hidden, essential balance of a substance that governs its medical effects</note>, by whose power the exterior harmony of the **elementary qualities** <note>The four basic qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> is governed. 

If, therefore, **Riolanus** <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), an influential French physician and fierce defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories</note> understands "temperament" as the harmony of tactile qualities <note>Qualities that can be perceived by touch, such as heat or moisture</note>, he speaks falsely when he says the **form of a mixture** <term>form of a mixture</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the internal principle that makes a thing what it is; the "form of a mixture" describes the unique nature created when elements combine</note> is merely temperament. Furthermore, his distinction contains a childish error. It is certain that the "form" of a mixture cannot be an **essence** that immediately follows the temperament, if the temperament is merely the instrument and power through which the form becomes effective. **Accidents** <note>original: *accidentia*; in Aristotelian logic, these are properties like color, size, or temperature that can change without changing the essential nature of the thing</note> are posterior to **substances**. He indeed invents marvelous "preparations of matter," claiming that the final stage draws its "form" from the **Sun** or the heavens through light and heat. But it is necessary for form to be generated internally, if it is a "nature" produced from another nature of the same species. Nature is an **innate principle** <note>original: *inſitum principium*</note>, not an external one. 

Therefore, this fiction is empty. But even if you suppose that the form is drawn from a "final disposition" <note>The state of matter just before it receives a new form</note> of matter, it cannot be the "form of the mixture" insofar as it is a mixture; rather, it would be the form of a plant, or an animal, or other things which are what they are, and not merely as they are "mixed." Nor, if it were the form of a mixture, could the temperament precede it, since that final disposition and preparation must also be the cause...

## CHAPTER XXII.

### *Whether chemical essences should be referred to form or matter.*

**I**n the argument of the censor <note>Referring to Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of Galenic medicine who acted as a critic or "censor" of new chemical ideas</note>, it had to be assumed that the chemical quintessence <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: *quintam essentiam*; literally the "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated medicinal part of a substance, separated from the four elements</note> is a physical form, and therefore inseparable from matter. I denied that it was a "physical form" in the way that physicists—following the advanced lectures <term>acroamaticis</term> <note>original: *acroamaticis*; referring to Aristotle’s "acroamatic" works, which were intended for his advanced students rather than the general public</note> of Aristotle—are accustomed to speak and think about form. That madman Riolan thinks I am denying that it is a form at all, or at least that there is no other form besides that principle which is metaphysical <note>abstract or spiritual</note> rather than physical. Therefore, he argues as follows:

> Your essences are the most effective principles and the most active substances.
> Therefore, the name of "form" must not be denied to them.

If you were speaking skillfully in your premise, I could grant you the argument. For quintessences are indeed "forms," but they are not your imaginary and "physical" forms, since they are things composed of matter. They are called "forms" and "species" <note>the specific nature or appearance of a thing</note> only in relation to the dregs from which they are separated. In the same way, you, in your workshops, want the temperaments <term>crases</term> <note>original: *crases*; the specific "mixture" or "temperament" of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) that define a body's health or nature</note> and forms to be separated from their own matter and infused into a foreign subject. Truly, because of the wretched and unfortunate logical errors <term>solecisms</term> <note>original: *soloecismos*; a term for grammatical mistakes or, in this context, errors in logical reasoning</note> of your premise, you should be driven out by our camp-followers. For us, "principles" are certain magisteries <term>magisteries</term> <note>original: *magisteria*; in early chemistry, these were "master-preparations" where a substance was refined or concentrated without losing its essential nature</note> which, although they are worked upon through skillful refinements <note>original: *exaltationibus*; chemical processes like distillation intended to "exalt" or raise a substance to a higher state of purity</note> and change...

### CHAPTER XXIII.

->*Whether the mind of man is a physical or metaphysical form; referring to my page 59 and Examination 25.*<-

In the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 1, Aristotle maintains that the physicist should not treat of the soul in its entirety, because not every soul is "nature," but only some part of it, one or more. Furthermore, because a "final cause" <note>The purpose or "end goal" for which something exists</note> does not apply to abstract things, he designates a discrepancy of reason rather than of the thing itself; in this way, in physical matters, he referred the consideration of forms in their general sense to **metaphysics**. Stated simply, the logic goes like this: A physical form is a temperament; the mind is a physical form; therefore the mind is a temperament. Again: A temperament perishes when it is dissolved. The mind is a temperament. Therefore, the mind perishes when dissolved. But this was discussed above; Riolan delights in **sophistries** <note>Arguments that seem clever but are actually false or intended to deceive</note>. ...to act, the end of which is the work itself. Whether you achieve this through your own hands or through the service of others—provided that you are, as it were, the guiding spirit and director toward the best result—sometimes matters very little, but at other times it proves to be quite important. The kings of the East and the South, along with philosophers and priests, once administered alchemy themselves; nor are there lacking today both noblemen and wise men who are neither shamed nor wearied by small furnaces, casting, distilling, and similar tasks. Should some common physician—whose very function ought to be the ability to prepare medicines well—so highly prize his own "majesty," even though such dignity cannot truly exist apart from his medical skill? 

When a king performs a kingly deed, he adorns his dignity; he does not diminish it. So it is when a physician handles medical things, or a craftsman handles the tools of his craft. When <term>Riolanus|Jean Riolan (1539–1605), a prominent French physician and critic of chemical medicine</term>, along with other <note>original: *Aristarchis*; referring to Aristarchus of Samothrace, a famous ancient critic, used here to mean harsh or pedantic critics</note> critics, ought to respond to arguments of this kind, he strikes out with many words concerning the "distinct offices" of the physician, the surgeon, and the pharmacist. Yet all of these are contained within the single character and scope of medicine. All are prepared for the purpose of healing well: in their general category they are doctors, but in their specific types they are anatomists, <term>Rhizotomi|literally "root-cutters," the ancient term for herbalists who gathered and prepared medicinal plants</term>, lecturers, practitioners, surgeons, clinicians, and pharmacists. 

Within any one of these divisions, the duties can be further divided into more specialized offices—or rather, into stations of labor and service. There might be a boy to wash the pots, knead the <term>lute|original: *lutum*; a clay or paste used to seal laboratory vessels airtight</term>, and grind the powders; and an assistant to prepare the <term>still|original: *destillatorium*; an apparatus used for distillation</term>. But it is the Master at whose nod and by whose choice the entire work proceeds. It is he who must be able to judge both the art of preparation and the finished medicine, to note errors, to correct them, and, when the work requires it, to apply his own hand as well.

...and to learn of defects, as in the <term>art of weighing and assaying</term> <note>original: "docimastice Zygostatica"; the technical science of testing the purity of metals using balances and scales.</note>; yet it is an illiberal thing to cast spells or to debase the currency.

Indeed, I say: but knowing such things does not mean one holds these instructions for the sake of using them; rather, it is a more general knowledge for the purpose of identification and judgment—just as Physicians know about poisons, yet they do not use them to poison people. <term>Chemical Medicine</term> <note>original: "Chymiatrica"; the application of chemistry to medical treatment.</note> is understood and studied for the sake of medical practice; <term>Alchemy</term>, as a preparatory art, is studied in itself so that medicine may be prepared for the Physician, and consequently so that the sick person may be properly restored to health. 

Neither the possession of knowledge, nor working according to a science for the sake of its result, is illiberal. To soil one's hands, to scour pots, and so forth—that is indeed servile. Perhaps, I might say, so is sweeping rooms, hauling wood, or fetching the raw materials for medicines by ship and carriage. Such menial services do not make the art itself servile, just as they do not degrade the <term>art of modeling</term> <note>original: "Plasticem"; referring to the plastic arts like sculpture or pottery-making.</note> or other arts that perform some tasks through the labor of servants and beasts. An artisan is permitted to use tools which, though they may be dirty in themselves, nevertheless touch upon nobility because they serve a liberal work. Let us therefore conclude with this <term>syllogism</term> <note>A formal logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two premises.</note>:

> *Chemical Medicine and Alchemy, as sciences existing for the sake of the work, and in the work itself, are liberal.*
> *Therefore, they are liberal both in their exercise and in their own proper modes of operation.*

Consequently, the censor did an injustice to both arts when he condemned them and cast them down into the filth of servile tasks. # ->GALENISM TRIUMPHANT<-
<note>original: "GALENIA TRIVMPHVS." This refers to the traditional medical system based on the teachings of Galen, which Riolan is defending against the innovators.</note>

In the past, during the times of Hippocrates and Galen <note>Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BCE) and Galen (129–c. 216 CE) were the two pillars of traditional Western medicine.</note>, medicine was practiced no less effectively—and I would even dare to say it was practiced better then. For the perfection of healing does not consist in the various ways of preparing remedies, but in the diagnosis of the disease. He who is able to diagnose the disease is able to heal it.

On the following page 16, the theme is stated as follows: *Medicine can do without that mode of preparation, just as it did in the past.* We understand that this is not a question regarding the Commonwealth or the State <note>original: "Republica seu Politia"</note>—namely, whether it could function without <term>chemical Pharmacy</term> <note>The art of preparing medicines using chemical techniques like distillation and sublimation.</note>, which is in no way essential to it. In a State where there is no disease and no sick person, that state would easily do without both the physician and medicine. To Plato <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BCE) famously argued in his "Republic" that a reliance on many doctors was a sign of a corrupt and intemperate society.</note>, such a state seemed to be one in which life is lived temperately. Where there are many physicians, there is much intemperance.

Furthermore, when the question is asked whether medicine can do without [chemistry], and it is not specifically explained whether that medicine is Galenic, Hippocratic, Methodic, or Empirical <note>These were the traditional competing "sects" or schools of ancient medical thought.</note>, we must assume the question is asked in an absolute and simple sense. Likewise, the question is general: not whether it occasionally happens that one heals well without chemical preparations, but whether it can be done entirely. This means we must consider everything within the universal scope of medicine and its entire essential perfection. We are not merely taking up Arabic, Greek, or Hippocratic medicine—to whose era Riolan does not even wish to be recalled—and much less the surgical practices used during the Trojan or Persian Wars. Those ancient systems lacked remedies against the plague and seem to have been mostly concerned with the management of diet and other matters leading up to a natural crisis <note>In ancient medicine, a "crisis" was the decisive moment in a disease when the body either overcame the illness or succumbed to it.</note>, as Paetus wrote to Artaxerxes <note>Referring to an apocryphal letter from the physician Paetus to the Persian King Artaxerxes regarding the health of his army.</note>, stating that...

# ->THE ALCHEMY OF THE FALSE PARISIAN<-
<note>original: "ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS." This title likely refers to a polemical response to Jean Riolan the Elder, a prominent Parisian physician who opposed the widespread use of chemical medicines.</note>

...natural aids do not resolve the widespread raging of a pestilential disease <note>The author is arguing that simple, "natural" remedies are often insufficient for major epidemics.</note>, since nature itself heals those diseases that arise from nature by showing the way, while the rest are handled by the art which was then seen to flourish under Hippocrates. However, the true theme of our controversy is this: whether Medicine, simply in its highest perfection, can do without chemically prepared remedies. Riolan, since he states the question differently, stumbles at the very threshold and reveals the rotten foundation of his cause.

It is possible that for good healing no pharmacy is needed at all, and a patient may recover simply through a proper <term>Crisis</term> <note>original: "Crisin." In Galenic medicine, this was the turning point of a disease when the "corrupt" humors were expelled by the body.</note>. If hunger is a disease, as Hippocrates claims, it can be driven away with unmixed wine and, according to Horace <note>The Roman poet Horace (65–8 BCE), who often praised the virtues of a simple, rustic life.</note>, bread with salt. But it is manifest that this is not the question at hand, unless we wish to argue that we can sometimes do without surgery, or sometimes without the Pharmaceutical art. It is a ridiculous question whether the state can do without medicine without the loss of health, since it is certain that medicine does not force health upon us; where health is present, there is no need for a Physician.

But what is stated in the problem? It is proposed that medicine can do without chemical preparations on the grounds that it did without them in the age of Galen and Hippocrates. But it is immediately answered: first, the argument is false, because if it lacked <term>Alchemy</term> <note>In this context, alchemy refers to the "art of separation"—extracting the pure essence of a drug from its raw, "impure" source.</note>, it lacked the work of the **great mastery** by which things hidden in matter are made manifest. Yet, medicine did not lack this. For the times of Hippocrates and Galen possessed that "manifesting" art, as is evident from their decoctions, infusions, pressings, and other ways of drawing out the inner nature of things. We do indeed deny that "Chemistry," by that specific name, was known to them...
