...in its entirety; we deny even that its absolute and perfect operations were known to those same men. This is one response. The other is that the argument fails due to a **Fallacy of Misconception** <note>original: "Elencho ignorationis," referring to *ignoratio elenchi*, a logical fallacy where an argument misses the point of the issue at hand.</note> and **Particularity**. If the critic himself does not wish to be called back to the times of <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, because people lived more healthily then, why does he drive us there? The question of medicine as it was then is one thing; as it is today is another. Add to this that it has received great growth and has been rendered most highly refined by cultivation up to our own age. Indeed, the medicine of **Hippocrates** was imperfect. He writes indeed in the book *On Places in Man*: IT SEEMS TO HIM that medicine has now been entirely discovered because it possesses knowledge of medicaments (crude and imperfect, of course) and teaches individual customs (but not German ones, nor such as they are today) and circumstances (Greek rather than foreign ones) although he denies it can be learned quickly, because it is impossible for a fixed and certain doctrine to be established in it (how then does it have scientific and universal principles which are perpetually and necessarily true?) as long as the same effect is not always observed in all things. **Alchemy** signifies either a fourth sect of medicine, or new ways of preparing medicine. The former is so unnecessary that it should even be rejected. The latter substitutes stronger **minerals** <term>mineralia</term> for the effective **Hippocratic** <note>Refers to the traditional herbal medicines of Hippocrates</note> remedies; this is not at all necessary—indeed, it is harmful—since the discoveries of the **Arabs** <note>Medieval Arabic physicians like Avicenna and Rhazes, who introduced many chemical substances into pharmacy</note> sufficiently compensated for any Hippocratic deficiency. Furthermore, the common people at least take refuge in the malicious extracts of **Paracelsus** <note>The controversial 16th-century Swiss physician who championed chemical medicine</note> only because of the small dosage and the pleasant taste, by which poisons are made attractive. Likewise, they are not useful because from one pound of raw material, barely one **drachma** <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce</note> of "spirit" is drawn out; this spirit cannot have more power than the whole substance from which it came—yet it would have to be more powerful if the invention were to be considered useful. 

Additionally, the Arabs were themselves chemists, yet they never mentioned these mineral extractions. The discoveries of the Arabs are more powerful. Therefore, we can easily do without these extracts. Lest any utility be left to Alchemy, even **gold-making** <term>chrysopœia</term> <note>original: "chrysopœia"</note> is condemned. <note>original: "canis & porcis"</note> ...dogs and pigs, they did not wish to throw their pearls. There was no need to record every extraction individually, since they are sufficiently commanded by a general rule and a few examples. Thus, by the mention of **Armenian stone** <term>lapis armenus</term> <note>A blue copper carbonate mineral used in antiquity as a vigorous purgative.</note> and **Lapis Lazuli**, consider that a similar rule was given concerning their essences. The remaining secrets <term>arcana</term> were not to be made common.

I wonder more that even when **Aegineta** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician whose works bridged ancient and medieval medicine.</note> proposed a powder or "lime" of **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury. "Lime" or "calx" refers to the powder produced by heating a metal (an oxide).</note>, you neither understand what it is, nor pay attention to its power. Yet the chemist does not linger only on minerals, although in these he finds the highest secrets, most highly commended to the **Italians**, **French**, and **Germans**. With these secrets, men like **Quercetanus**, **Renealmus**, **Turquetus**, **Haruetus**, **Baucynetus**, and many others <note>This list identifies prominent 16th and 17th-century iatrochemists (chemical physicians) such as Joseph Duchesne (Quercetanus) and Turquet de Mayerne.</note> sting and torment you, abounding as they do in a wealthy abundance of successful examples; and this is what causes you grief.

Finally, you conclude: *We could easily do without your extracts.*

Go without them then, in good peace, O men of Paris; and it will soon be apparent how long you shall continue to practice medicine with any praise. Meanwhile, **chemical medicine** <term>chymiatrice</term> shall emerge to the very peak of admiration, and it will leave you to be trampled, laughed at, and consumed as the dregs of the common people. We cannot do without alchemy, because it is a certain essential part of medical perfection, and the "Medical Pearl" of the Arabs. We do not wish to cast away such a great good from the immortal God; we would sooner surrender the names of **Hippocrates** and **Galen** than fall away from the path of perfection.

#### *In what matter the perfection of Medicine consists.*

### THE PARISIAN DISPUTE ON ALCHEMY
<meta>catchword: which [quæ]</meta>

Let the Parisian censors destroy **Alchemy**, for they are so insane even against their own medical practice that they do not blush to disparage it. It belongs to the Physician's knowledge first to have an understanding of **health**, which is the state and form of the constitution according to nature, and the ultimate end and highest goal in practice through preservation and restoration from its opposite. 

The deprivation of health is **disease**; form, state, and affirmation come before negation. A negative state cannot be exactly known if the positive state <note>The author uses "habitu" here to mean the baseline "state" or "habit" of a healthy body.</note> is hidden. If, therefore, the question concerns the duties of a Physician, or which knowledge is more necessary for the purpose of practicing medicine well, one must answer in favor of health—both because it is the state and the superior ultimate goal, and because it provides the two highest indications for action. 

To practice medicine well is to preserve present health through Medicine, and to repair health when it is injured or cast down from its proper state. From this understanding of health, disease becomes better known as its positive opposite. Without the standard of health, we often do not even know that a disease exists. By the standard of health, the patient knows before the Physician does that he is afflicted by a disease—such as a wound, an ulcer, an abscess, abdominal pain, a stitch in the side, and other things which hardly reveal themselves by any outward sign. 

Thus the foolishness of <term>Riolan</term> <note>Referring to Jean Riolan (1539–1605), a dominant figure in the Paris Medical Faculty who was a fierce opponent of chemical medicine and a strict defender of Galenic orthodoxy.</note> is apparent, as he judges that the highest perfection of medicine consists in the knowledge of diseases. This is most strongly refuted by the argument of health, and then also by the proper action of the Physician. No one heals simply by the knowledge of a disease, although without this, the indications for acting well in the other part...

...which are concerned with the healing of those afflicted by disease, are not sufficient. To treat diseases is to **heal** that which is sick. To heal is to lead the body from a state of disease back to health. To this end, a knowledge of both constitutions—the healthy and the diseased—will be of great use. 

However, healing consists of other precepts, namely practical principles arranged for treating well, which are contained within the **therapeutic method** <note>The "Method of Healing" (Therapeutica) was the title of one of Galen's most famous works, though here the author uses the term to describe the practical, hands-on side of medicine.</note>, or that part of medicine called **Therapeutics**. Since, therefore, medicine is a certain art whose purpose is to act effectively toward health—which is to treat well—it can be shown by this very argument that it is more fitting for a Physician to treat well than merely to know well. 

The most noble Physician is he who is best able, once adversities are driven away, to preserve present health and to restore that which has been weakened. He who is occupied only with the speculation of diseases attains almost the lowest part of this art. Indeed, often a perfect knowledge of a disease cannot be reached, and yet the patient can still be helped; hence the Physician is compelled to act indefinitely <note>Meaning acting based on general principles rather than a specific, certain diagnosis.</note> rather than definitely. 

From this arise those disputes among practitioners, who nevertheless believe they can treat well. In diseases there is often "something divine" <note>original: "aliquid diuini". This is a reference to the Hippocratic concept of *ti theion*, suggesting that some aspects of illness or recovery are beyond human understanding or have causes that transcend the physical.</note> which the human intellect does not reach; which would have to be understood if there were to be total perfection in the knowledge of diseases. It is this part that makes medicine a highly **conjectural** <term>conjectural: an art based on interpretation and "best guesses" rather than absolute certainties</term> science. For while to "know" is to understand a thing through its first and proper causes, these causes usually escape us; thus it happens that we most often fail in our knowledge. The primary praise, however...

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM
<note>original: "GALENIA TRIVMPHVS." While the title suggests a victory for Galen, the text actually argues for the integration of chemistry into medical practice.</note>

If <term>chemical preparation</term> <note>original: "chymica præparatio"</note> has added something more excellent to the experiments of the ancients, why should it not be preferred? But is chemical preparation actually so new? In one sense it is new, insofar as it became known later to the **Hippocratic physicians** of Europe—and that varies according to different regions—but in itself, it is by no means new. 

It is also strange for this to be called "new" when it can trace its knowledge back to **Avicenna**, **Mesue**, **Bulcasis**, <note>A trio of foundational medieval medical authorities: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), Mesue the Younger (a likely pseudonymous author of pharmacy texts), and Bulcasis (the surgeon Al-Zahrawi).</note> the most ancient kings of **India**, the early sages of **Egypt**, and others. These chemical things are old. If something is to be preferred because it depends on antiquity and has the weight of experience from it, then chemical medicine should not be pushed aside. 

Yet, some object that experiments with <term>mineral extracts</term> are new, and if you wish to employ them in healing, you are gambling with human health. But this, I say, is once again to change the terms of the debate. Our inquiry was not established to look into new inventions that have not yet been explored through wise use and confirmed by skilled physicians; rather, it was about preparations made chemically versus those made non-chemically. 

When I was disputing against **Gramanus’s** <note>Likely Johannes Gramann, a proponent of Paracelsian medicine.</note> **"Venereal salt"** <note>original: "salem venereum." In alchemy, Venus represents copper; this refers to a medicinal salt derived from copper.</note> and other things entirely "fresh from the anvil"—things brought forth not by the invention and risk of true craftsmen, but by cobblers, charlatans, fugitives, and others who have rushed into medicine out of desperation for their own professions—I rightly denied that things proposed by such people should be put to use where human health might be endangered. We judge that **Celsus** <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, the Roman medical encyclopedist.</note> also pronounced this same judgment against bold <term>Empirics</term> <note>A sect of ancient physicians who relied solely on experience/observation rather than theoretical reasoning; here used pejoratively for unlearned quacks.</note>.

Where knowledge, prudence, and experience—which should be far removed from rashness—concur and confirm the truth of the matter even by the judgment of the senses, the argument of antiquity is brought forward in vain. For the present invention is not "new" in substance, but was made along with the world, or born from such a root <note>The author argues that chemical principles are "natural" and have existed since creation, even if humans only recently discovered how to extract them.</note>, and it can rest upon the same foundations as the ancient remedies; finally, through its wise and praised use, it may be joined to the works of the ancients. 

There is, however, a difference between those who prepare these remedies and those who use new things. In both cases, lack of skill, laziness, or rashness can occur. Therefore, since we cannot deny that there are certain substances of powerful activity <note>original: "vehementis actiuitatis"</note> which cannot be entrusted to just anyone or exposed to common use, it must be advised that such things remain among the **secrets of the skilled** <note>original: "arcanis peritorum"</note>. This is something that **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), a prominent French physician and critic of chemical medicine, though the author here claims Riolan admitted some "secrets" could be kept by doctors.</note> himself acknowledged when he wrote that "secrets" could be prepared by physicians at home. 

Therefore, those special things elicited from <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento viuo," or mercury</note>—though this has become so commonplace that there is no bathhouse attendant <note>The author mocks the low status of those claiming medical knowledge; bathhouse attendants often performed minor surgeries or applied mercurial treatments for skin diseases and syphilis.</note> who does not boast of his knowledge of <term>mercurial ointments</term>, <term>precipitate</term> <note>a solid substance separated from a solution during a chemical reaction</note>, <term>sublimate</term> <note>a solid deposit produced by heating a substance to vapor and then cooling it</note>, <term>cinnabar pills</term> <note>pills made from mercury sulfide</note>, and the like—from <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "stibio," a brittle metalloid often used in emetics</note>, <term>metals</term>, <term>semimetals</term> <note>substances like bismuth or arsenic that share properties with metals</note>, and other <term>minerals</term> ought to remain in the possession of skilled physicians. 

But if to the common people and younger practitioners, who make their first experiments not at their own [risk], but at the [risk]... <meta>The sentence continues on the next page; the catchword "pe:" suggests "periculo" (risk/danger).</meta>

...of the discoveries of experts, certain things must be forbidden; why not those mysteries? But what of preference? Whether something is established by experiment—be it new or old—if the Physician is not reckless or a raw beginner, that which helps better is to be preferred. **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a famous defender of traditional Galenic medicine and a fierce opponent of chemical remedies.</note> says: *Those things are always judged better which have been proven by the authority of infinite ages.* First, that word **ALWAYS** must be exploded here. For if it has already been judged otherwise—as the inventions of the **Arabs** <note>Refers to medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna and Rhazes, whose works introduced new substances and methods not found in Greek texts.</note> teach us, and those things brought from **new lands** <note>A reference to medicinal plants like guaiacum or cinchona bark brought from the Americas.</note> in recent memory—then that "always" fails. 

Furthermore, if "infinite ages" are required for such authority, then let the **Galenic** remedies <note>Medicines based on the teachings of Galen (2nd century AD), typically involving herbal mixtures aimed at balancing the four humors.</note> also be cast aside, for they are defined by only a few finite centuries. Indeed, in many matters, a long duration of time is nothing other than the **antiquity of error**. To judge what is better, arguments weightier than mere antiquity must be brought forward. Therefore, reason fails in this regard as well. It is not always judged better because it was proven of old—just as it is not better to speak like **Evander’s mother** <note>original: "loqui cum matre Euandri." A Roman proverb referring to someone using obsolete, archaic language that no one understands anymore.</note>, or to follow pagan faith <note>original: "gentilitiam fidem"</note>, and so on. 

In medicine also, if it was permitted to **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and others to establish new laws which the ancients were ignorant of, why should it not be permitted to us? We have observed so many new diseases in even a single century, and we possess a pharmacy <note>original: "officinam" (literally a workshop or laboratory)</note> far better equipped with medicines. You write that I respond that **chemical purgatives** are not new, but have already been proven for many centuries. But in your delirium, you did not see it then. I wrote that chemical methods existed both before and after Galen;

-> # ON ALCHEMY AND THE SPURIOUS DISPUTES OF PARIS <-
<note>original: "ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS." This likely refers to the ongoing conflict between the Faculty of Medicine in Paris and the practitioners of chemical medicine, which the author deems "spurious" or false arguments.</note>

And if ancient things are to be preferred according to this argument, then the privilege belongs to the chemists. However, to refute my opinion, you demand that I produce an example of a chemical purgative from **Rhazes**, **Mesue**, or **Avicenna** <note>Rhazes (865–925), Mesue (the Elder or Younger, influential in pharmacology), and Avicenna (980–1037) were central figures in Islamic medicine whose works were standard texts in Europe.</note>. The matter did not require a specific description, which is easy in itself, provided you learn the <term>manipulations</term> <note>original: "enchiremata"; the physical techniques or "handiwork" required in a laboratory.</note> from the Alchemists to whom Mesue directs you.

Do you know that Avicenna mentions sublimate <note>Mercuric chloride, a toxic but medicinal chemical compound.</note>, quicksilver, arsenic, cinnabar, and similar things? Refer these back to the work of perfection. You will have what you seek. That Avicenna did not explicitly set down those chemical skills is not a sign of ignorance, but of prudence and wisdom, which forbids revealing secrets to the common people. Judge the same regarding the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing the Elixir of Life.</note>, which it is likely Avicenna’s *Alchemy* treated.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.

->*Whether chemists, by their own example, diminish the authority of Spagyric medicines.*<-

**Turquet** <note>Theodore de Mayerne (1573–1655), also known as Turquet, was a royal physician who championed chemical medicine and was famously censured by the Paris Faculty.</note> is said at times, when he was ill, to have preferred <term>dogmatic remedies</term> <gloss>traditional medicines based on Galenic theory</gloss> over chemical ones. From this, **Riolanus** <note>Jean Riolan, a staunch defender of traditional Galenism and a bitter rival of the chemical physicians.</note> concludes regarding everyone: that the sick praise dogmatic remedies while the healthy revile them; and therefore, those who are sick in body are sound in mind, while those who are healthy in body are sick in mind. If we wished to follow a similar example of logic, the answer would be: because Riolanus raves like a maniac, then everyone who professes to be a Galenist is also insane. But far be it from us to impute the madness of one man to all. Rather, let the malice of that "bad sheep" <note>original: "mali pecoris"</note> be known to everyone. It is possible that some common remedy might be preferred over a chemically prepared one, not absolutely, but due to some specific circumstance. Is the authority of chemists taken away because of this? Sometimes that which we would prefer to use is unavailable. But words are wasted on such obvious delirium.

...lily. When we use chemical medicines, we are using dogmatic ones, and we seek the evidence for our usage from the principles of medicine. 

As for what concerns the sanity and insanity of the chemists, we say that **Riolan** is most lacking in his right mind at the very moment he thinks himself most sane. The proof of this is his own frantic writing on "mania," than which hardly any more demented work has ever been published. Therefore, when the chemists seem insane to **Riolan**, one must conclude the exact opposite: we must declare them to be most wise. Since they are affected in a way contrary to madmen—because they differ most from the ravings of such people—they only *appear* to be insane to him. 

If he were able to accept advice, we would order him to expel his disease with <term>Hellebore</term> <gloss>a plant traditionally used to treat madness</gloss> and his "black bile" <note>In the theory of the four humors, "black bile" was thought to cause melancholy and madness.</note> with **antimony**, with both being chemically prepared. Medicine was not written for the healthy, according to his own judgment, but for the sick; although (so that you may more fully recognize the man's insanity) a certain part of medicine is devoted to the preservation of health. For this reason, **Mithridates** <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus, famous for creating a universal antidote by taking small doses of poison.</note> and the **Roman Emperors** used **Theriac** <note>A famous ancient "wonder-drug" or universal antidote containing dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh.</note> daily. **Marinellus** <note>Giovanni Marinello, a 16th-century Italian physician.</note>, as reported by **Dotzelinus**, even used it like bread. And **Galen** says: *He who enjoys good health, if he takes Theriac continuously, will be greatly helped.* It is also taken to treat an insane mind, so that **Riolan** would not lack a good remedy—especially a chemical extract—if he could only be cured.

## CHAPTER XL.

->Concerning the words *more active* and *activity* in relation to page<-
->71 of [his] *Mania*.<-

**T**he Pythagoreans and Socratics pleasantly imagined that souls enter into other bodies after death. One might think that **Valla** <note>Lorenzo Valla (1407–1457), a famous humanist and philologist who famously critiqued the quality of medieval Latin.</note> or **Aristarchus** <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace (c. 220–143 BC), a Greek scholar known for his rigorous and often harsh literary criticism.</note> had crept into **Riolan**. He has become such a censor that he assumes authority not only over opinions, but even over languages—something **Galen** <note>The primary authority on ancient medicine whose style was usually the gold standard for Riolan’s faction.</note> was not accustomed to doing. Yet Riolan does both in a manner as un-Galenic as it is his own: that is, foolishly and deliriously.

I use the terms <term>more active</term> <note>original: "actiuius"</note> and <term>activity</term> <note>original: "actiuitas"</note> because the Greeks speak this way—<gloss>more productive, more energetic, energy</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ποιητικώτερον, ἐνεργητικώτερον, ἐνέργεια"</note>—and so do the Latins. For instance, when **Aristotle** writes in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "de ortu," referring to Aristotle's "De Generatione et Corruptione," book 2, text 8.</note> through the pen of a Latin translator, he says that elements are "active" and "passive," and that one is "more active" than another. There is no need for further authority. The word "more active," derived from "active," is known to every schoolmaster <term>paedotribes</term> <gloss>literally 'trainers of boys,' used here mockingly for basic grammar teachers</gloss>. In the same way, "activity," derived from "active," has been granted to common usage.

**Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a foundational text.</note>—who, as **Capivaccio** <note>Girolamo Capivaccio (1523–1589), a respected Italian medical professor.</note> says, was a thousand times more learned than Riolan—prescribes mead after <term>colocynth</term> <gloss>the "bitter apple," a powerful and harsh purgative plant</gloss>. He prescribes this colocynth sometimes in a greater quantity and sometimes in a lesser, according to how great the **ACTIVITY** of the phlegm <term>pituitae</term> <gloss>one of the four bodily humors, thought to cause sluggishness or disease if out of balance</gloss> is. If we can customarily attribute "activity" to phlegm in the medical schools, why not to things that are "more active"? 

But what, then, of Riolan’s *Mania*? <note>Libavius is mocking the title of Riolan’s attack on him, "Against the Madness (Mania) of Libavius."</note> He warns Libavius—that "furious sow"—that it could have been expressed more "Latinly" as *actuosiora* <note>a more classical term for "more vigorous."</note>. This would be relevant, of course, if our dispute were about the elegance of Latin style. Why shouldn't the advisor receive the reward of a donkey? <note>A proverbial expression meaning a fool deserves a fool's payment.</note>

...to whom should we give it? According to **Calepinus** <note>Ambrogio Calepino (c. 1435–1511), an Italian lexicographer whose Latin dictionary was the standard reference of the era.</note>: *Active is* <gloss>energetic, effective, vigorous</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ἐνεργητικὸν, δραστικὸν, δραστήριον"</note>, *that is, that which acts. "Actuose" [busy], however, is laborious or full of acts. From this comes the "actuose life," which to the Greeks is* <gloss>practical, subjective</gloss> <note>original Greek: "πρακτικὸν, ὑποκειτικὸν"</note>. Thus says Calepinus. He easily persuades us to say that the Dogmatic principles of **Riolan** are *actuose*, that is, laborious; but chemical medicines are *more active*, and therefore to be preferred to those others in the restoring of health. But why all these rotten arguments? It is so that all Greeks and Latins—Italians, Germans, English, French, and Spanish—might understand that the medical censors of the Parisian school could not have found a stupider censor than Riolan, nor could they have erected a more insane monument to themselves. Thus beautifully does he dispute against <term>chymiatria</term> <note>Chemical medicine or iatrochemistry, which sought to use distilled essences rather than raw herbs.</note>. O, the whips! O, the rods! <note>An invocation of schoolroom discipline, suggesting Riolan needs to be sent back to primary school.</note> Why do you not diligently examine that so malignant "actuosity"?

### CHAPTER XLI.

->*Whether that which is more active is better.*<-

**I**n the fourth argument, among other things, the discussion concerned the tempering of substances, and it was said that chemical essences are more suited for mixing on account of their greater <gloss>fitness</gloss> <note>original Greek: "εὐθεσίαν"</note> and activity, by which they act and are acted upon mutually without the long fermentation that is required in common compositions. An example is <term>Theriac</term> <note>A complex, ancient poly-pharmaceutical "wonder drug" and antidote that often required months of aging before use.</note>, for which a six-month period is allotted, whereas if the essences had been premixed, a few hours would have sufficed. Riolan cannot deny that chemical medicines are more active. He denies they are better;

He further argues that chemical essences allow for faster and more efficient compounding of medicines like Theriac compared to traditional methods.</summary>

Libavius is arguing that refined, distilled substances are "more active" and thus more medically effective than raw, bulky herbal mixtures, using Aristotelian physics to support his claims.</meta>

<page-num>470</page-num>
<header>PART OF THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY</header>

Truly ridiculous. If things are more active for the sake of well-proportioned mixtures—because the actions of those who act are found within those who are acted upon <note>A fundamental principle in Aristotelian physics: the agent's action occurs in the patient (the subject receiving the action).</note>—and if those subjects are not properly disposed or are immobile, there can be no action from the agent. It is therefore necessary to grant them a "power of suffering" <note>Potentiality or receptivity.</note> and a susceptibility to impression, along with divisibility. Otherwise, no internal mixing could occur. Why should that which is more active and more divisible in mixtures not be better than a sluggish and thick body? 

Let a trial be made by mixing theriacal water with that of cinnamon, oil of cloves, mace, and citron. (For things that are mixed ought to be of a similar nature). Do the same with a whole Theriaca <note>A famous, ancient polypharmaceutical "cure-all" containing dozens of ingredients, often thick and syrupy.</note> and with cinnamon, cloves, mace, citron seed, and rind; I will convince you by your own senses. Thus, if one thing is divisible in act and another in potential—as when salts are dissolved in water, or when <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "stibium," a metallic element often used in chemical medicine as a purgative or emetic.</note>, iron, and similar things are dissolved in <term>strong waters</term> <note>original: "aquas fortes," usually referring to nitric acid or other mineral acids used to dissolve metals.</note>—even if a true mixture does not occur here, it is nonetheless more exact than if you were simply to compose the raw materials of those things. 

Truly, the blindness of fury stood in the way of **Riolan**, who is rushing headlong into insanity, so that he was less attentive to the matter at hand. Let us take the statement simply, and ask whether it is more effective and more excellent. **Aristotle** will answer that the "formal" is better than the "material" <note>Referring to the Four Causes: the "Form" of a thing is its essence and activity, while "Matter" is its passive potentiality.</note>. Furthermore, that which is more active is more "formal," such as fire or the heavens. For these are forms in the highest degree, while other things are rather privations <note>In this context, "privation" refers to a lack of the active qualities found in the higher elements.</note>. And so, by motion, a part of common matter is said to be made more noble, having escaped as air or fire; whereas by immobility and privation it is made more ignoble, which is the origin of water and earth, the two cold elements. Thus, the absolutely active is better. Let us also inquire about that which acts in a determinate...

...for example, in healing apoplexy <note>a sudden loss of consciousness, similar to a stroke</note>, paralysis, epilepsy, lethargy, and similar conditions. Offer an aged Theriac <note>a famous ancient herbal "cure-all" containing dozens of ingredients</note> that is still potent; offer the essence, and then the whole substance with its dregs. You will be convinced by the outcome itself: that which is more active is better. 

So too in nutrition: that which is more easily assimilated, restores the spirits, and is distributed through the body is better than that which is otherwise. What kills more quickly than an airborne poison? What brings relief faster than Bezoardic spirits <note>medicines derived from or mimicking the properties of bezoar stones, believed to be powerful antidotes</note>?

But I say, "O good man," they are certainly better at killing than other sluggish things! Why do you depart from the category of healthy things to the unhealthy? If those were <term>alexiterics</term> <note>original: "alexiteria," medicines used to ward off poison or contagion</note>, would they be worse for health because they are more active? Certainly not. 

For "spiritual" <note>in the sense of vaporous or relating to the body's vital spirits</note> poisons, <term>alexipharmic</term> <note>original: "alexipharmaci," substances used to neutralize toxins</note> spirits are required. Your "Parisian" remedies, the less "spirited" <note>meaning less refined or volatile</note> they are, the less they can resist a raging evil. Betel <note>a stimulant leaf</note>, Durians <note>a pungent fruit</note>, Pharicum <note>a potent medicine or poison mentioned by ancient authors</note>, and Quince <note>original: "Cydonium"</note> also accomplish their work through vapors; by this example, it is clear that there is no power in useless matter, and that which is better...

## CHAPTER XLII.

*On the argument of calumny regarding the formal nature of chemical essences, in response to page 71 of The Mania.* <note>Libavius mockingly refers to Riolan’s published attack as "Mania"</note>

**H**e rages horribly in his cage, this madman, because of what I wrote: "If, as the censor babbles, our essences are formal <note>pertaining to the 'form' or the essential, life-giving principle of a substance in Aristotelian philosophy</note>: and specific virtue follows from these forms, then they cannot be destitute of occult powers." Likewise, if the form is the temperament <term>crasis|the specific "mixture" or balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—that defines a substance</term> of mixed things: and we extract that form, what madness is it to accuse us of corrupting the temperament? 

He calls this a manifest calumny; because he claims he did not write that we extract the form, but rather that we corrupt it—that we are "enemies of nature," "despoiling nature of nature itself," and "stripping mixed things of their own form so that we may clothe them in foreign ones." He belches out many similar things so that it is clear he is a sworn enemy of Alchemy and an incurable adversary. 

But rage more gently, Riolan! I have written nothing slanderous. Unless you wished to go mad with the argument of calumny, you might have recognized your own sickness when it was pointed out to you. Nowhere did I say that you attributed those exact words to the chemists; but I drew them partly from their own assertions—which you know well and often object to as a crime and a folly—and partly from the necessity of the...

<margin>Gg 5</margin>

...by a necessary consequence I attribute this to you, and for that reason I write that you are babbling. So that you may see this, rest for a moment, and turn your mind along with your eyes to the following. <margin>page 39 of the Apology</margin> You begin that long-winded argument about why your medicines are to be preferred, claiming they are more suitable for healing because of both their occult and manifest powers, and their primary and secondary qualities. In that proof, after you reached <margin>page 46 of the Apology</margin> the secondary qualities, you reason as follows:

*A part of the body that has hardened must be softened by some medicament; for example, by ammoniacum <note>original: "ammoniaco"; a medicinal gum resin used since antiquity to soften tumors or swellings</note>. This must be done with the substance whole and pure, not purified of its base matter and dregs, because it softens materially, not just formally. Matter affected in a certain way is the basis of the temperament from which all action proceeds. For physical forms (so you call the temperament <term>crasis|the Greek term for the specific "mixture" of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</term>) do not act unless they are aided by matter tempered in a certain way. Matter is not the "principle which" acts—for all action comes from the form—but it is the "principle without which" action cannot happen; because unless that matter is affected and shaped in a certain way, the form remains idle.*

These are your words there. If they are intended to lead a campaign against the chemists, the argument must be arranged like this:

> *A medicament that lacks its own matter cannot be effective in helping through its secondary qualities; but that which is whole and pure <note>i.e., in its raw, natural state</note> holds its form within its matter.*
>
> *Chemical medicines lack their original matter; but Galenic medicines have that same matter joined with their form.*
>
> *Therefore, chemical medicines cannot be effective, etc. Galenic medicines can, etc. And consequently, Galenic medicines are to be preferred over chemical ones.*

<summary>Libavius deconstructs Jean Riolan’s Aristotelian argument that chemical medicines are ineffective because they separate a substance's "form" (active essence) from its "matter" (physical bulk). Riolan claims that without this physical matter, the medicinal form has no base through which to act on the body.</summary>

### ON THE DECEPTIVE PARTS OF ALCHEMY
<meta>Catchword: which</meta>

The major premise is proven concerning the material action of the form. You cannot prove the minor premise unless you concede that these substances are forms, or formal essences purged of their matter and dregs—which are your very own words. Therefore, whether you said this in earnest or as a hypothesis, I have done you no injury; I have merely produced an argument against you from your own words and, at the same time, considered the logical necessity of the conclusion. Choose whichever you prefer. Be a fool in this instance or in that one. 

It is necessary that the chemists' ammoniacum <note>original: "ammoniacum"; a medicinal gum resin used to soften swellings</note> be a "formal essence" if yours still contains its dregs and matter, and yet this is the very thing being argued against: it must be a physical form or a <term>crasis|the specific "mixture" or temperament of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a substance</term> if it is denied to be useful for that reason. Yet you claim yours is useful because it is not merely a physical form, but matter given shape. 

But you say that we [chemists] destroy the *crasis*. Why should I care about that? You are forced by the evidence of the argument to posit it. Or is it unusual for you to say whatever you like just for the sake of victory? <margin>page 50</margin> You attribute "quintessence" <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; the "fifth element" or the most purified, potent extract of a substance</note> to us, and you even commend remedies for this very reason: because they have been purified of dregs and freed from the thickness of matter through distillation or extraction, by which means they acquire heat. Such things must indeed be considered "formal" in respect to what they were before; this is why they are also called "species separated from matter" by Mesue <note>John Mesue (Yuhanna ibn Masawayh), a historical medical authority whose name was used for popular pharmaceutical manuals</note>. 

Do I still seem to you to have slandered you? But imagine that you were not speaking of a "secret form" (even though your logic demands it, unless it be a case of hopeless stupidity), but of that other form which you oppose to the natural one on <margin>page 71 of the *Frenzies*</margin>; and in the <margin>Apology, page 29</margin> you call "accidental"; and in the <margin>Against Arvetus, page 69</margin> "artificial and mathematical"; and in the <margin>Against Turner, page 65</margin> "accidental," which comes into the place of the natural form.

...which is nevertheless inseparable from its subject: [referring to] pages 12 and 81 of your *Apology*. You call the subject "natural matter," although you deny that its form is natural once it has been prepared by art <note>here meaning "alchemy" or "chemistry"</note>. Let that form, I say, be the one which we introduce into the matter; since it is impossible for natural matter to exist without a natural form; <margin>(1) See page 69 of Antarvetus [Riolan]. Where art and nature are confused. Nature can provide the primary matter for art; but the final result, because it is what it is through the form given by art, cannot be called natural in its primary sense.</margin> (1) for it is from the natural form that it is natural. You must necessarily grant it its own <term>crasis|the specific "mixture" or temperament of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a substance</term>, because a natural form is a *crasis*, and where there is a *crasis*, there is also a <term>temperament|the balance of primary qualities that determines a substance's medicinal effect</term> and power. It follows, then, that you are forced to attribute temperament and *crasis* to chemical preparations.

Now, however, it is impossible for just anything to turn into just anything, because everything changes from one specific state into another specific state. Secondly, it follows that the *crasis* and form of chemical preparations are clearly related to the form of a <term>natural mixture|a compound substance as it exists in nature, before chemical processing</term>. If we demonstrate that in things which are separated (for we will not linger on transmuted substances) the same power remains—both in kind and in number—will it not simultaneously be proven that the same *crasis* remains? This fact we witness with our own eyes in the examples of extracts.

The same follows from the method of extraction by infusion and chemical decoction found in <note>original: "Mesue"; likely referring to Mesue the Younger, a legendary figure in medieval pharmacy whose writings were central to Galenic medicine</note> **Mesue**. By these and similar examples, you are forced to grant chemical extracts their own proper form and temperament. Indeed, when I seemed to be referring chemical essences to matter, you—in your *Mania* <note>original: "Mania"; a pun on the title of Riolan’s work or a jab at his state of mind</note>, pages 58 and 59—resisted me with arguments, contending that they ought to be reckoned among "forms" and "formal things." But nevertheless...

## ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS

Against such manifest light of truth, you strive with everything you have, tooth and nail <note>original: *manibus pedibusque*—literally "with hands and feet," an idiom for exerting every possible effort</note>. Who ever heard anything more foolish? Either chemical extracts are <term>material|relating to the physical substance or "dregs" of a plant</term>, or they are <term>formal|relating to the "form" or essence that gives a substance its specific identity and power</term>, or they are both at once. For you, they cannot be material, because they have been purified and freed from their raw matter; nor can they be both, because then they would be effective due to their material qualities, which you deny. It remains, then, that they must be formal, unless they are simply nothing at all. If they are formal, they must be so either by nature or by art. They cannot be created by art alone. For it is impossible by any human art for an extract of <term>scammony|a plant resin used as a powerful purgative</term> to be made to purge in the same way as the whole, native plant; or, if it is indeed done by art, it would be necessary for that art to possess a divine and more-than-human power. Yet even this is impossible, especially if you look closely at the method of extraction. What must be decided now, Riolan? Are chemists Gods, or men? Indeed, they are men, and not even tricksters or evil magi. They cannot give the power of <term>cinnamon|used here as an example of a specific natural virtue or flavor</term> to matter if nature did not provide it first. It follows, then, that the essences produced by chemists are certain forms first produced by nature. Forms, in mixed bodies, are <term>crases|the specific "mixture" or temperament of qualities that defines a substance</term> according to Riolan’s own judgment. Where there are *crases*, there are virtues and powers. Have I argued poorly? But you must have drunk <term>nightshade|original: *Strychnum*; a plant known to cause madness or delirium</term>. For so you say on page 72 regarding madness: 

*Your extracts have some form and some temperament because they are mixed. But it is a form far different from the natural one, far different from that which nature had given to the mixture. They have powers and actions far different from those which the mixture had when its nature remained whole, etc.*

By these words, you clearly declare yourself a fool. If our essences are mixed, they are so either by nature or by art.

<page-num>477</page-num>

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENIC MEDICINE

<meta>catchword: is</meta>

It is not by art, as is evident in the case of simple medicines. It is, therefore, by nature. From this, both the form and the powers arise. Furthermore, if a form is different, it is because the actions are different; conversely, where the action is the same, the form is the same. In extracts, the action is identical to the action of the whole substances. Therefore, the form is also the same. Let diligent students refer here to what is read on page 27 of *Antarvetus* <note>The pseudonym of Jean Riolan the Elder, Libavius's rival</note>, where he concedes that distilled and extracted things are "materialized" <note>meaning they still possess the physical matter of the plant</note>. But he ridiculously denies the manner of it, since it is necessary for a materialized substance to possess a form within its matter that is suitable to its nature. For example, an extract of <term>fennel|Foeniculum vulgare, a plant used to aid digestion and balance "windy" humors</term>—which contains the power and temperament of fennel—cannot exist without the "form of mixture" <note>original: *forma mistionis*—the specific way elements are combined to create a unique substance</note> proper to it.

In the *Short Excursion* <note>Referring to one of Riolan’s published attacks</note>, page 115, <term>elixirs|potent liquid medicinal preparations</term>, tinctures, <term>magisteries|refined chemical precipitates containing the "essence" of a substance</term>, and essences are presented as forms; yet it is foolishly claimed that the raw materials are transmuted into these forms. So, on page 101 of the same work, he says: *What you show as a form is a visible material.* Yet he himself, through his own "infusions," deposits the form of the mixture into the liquid, as seen on page 56 of *Antarvetus* and pages 37 and 55 of the *Short Excursion*, where the same point is debated. Riolan separates the forms foolishly; he cannot agree with those who distinguish things wisely.

From these statements, his insults can be judged. He writes that I am lying impudently. But it has been shown that I have brought forth the very truth itself. If the form of a mixture is its <term>crasis|the specific "blend" or temperament of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that defines a substance's nature</term>, as is written on page 81 of the *Apology*; and if our extracts are indeed mixtures, as stated on page 72 of the *Mania*; and if they are mixed not by art, but by nature—because we leave simple extracts in the same state as <term>Mesue|Johannes Mesue, an influential medieval Persian physician</term> left the extract of Rhubarb, of <term>myrobalans|dried, plum-like fruits used as laxatives</term>, and so on—then it follows that our extracts have the same powers and actions as the whole plants, and the same as the Parisian infusions, provided they are correctly prepared.

-># ON THE BRANCHES OF ALCHEMY<-

It is certain, therefore, that our extracts possess the <term>crasis|the specific "mixture" or constitutional balance of qualities</term> of natural mixtures. If they have this, then they also possess the temperament which follows the form immediately. As for the fact that Riolan lies most absurdly and petulantly, I can demonstrate this from all his writings against chemistry. But lest we wander too far, let us dwell upon this same page, 71 and 72.

**Lie 1.** *In more than twenty places,* he says, *I have demonstrated that you are enemies of nature.* <note>original: "Plusquam viginti locis demonstravi, inquit, vos esse naturæ hostes."</note> This is a lie. He has uttered insults; he has demonstrated nothing. And if you had demonstrated that chemists are enemies of nature because of the separation of the pure from the impure, you would have made the entire medicine of Hippocrates infamous.

**Lie 2.** *You have despoiled nature of its nature.* <note>original: "Naturam natura spoliastis."</note> This is a lie. That we leave the nature of the substance within the extract of <term>colocynth|bitter apple, a potent purgative</term>, <term>Theriac|a famous ancient "cure-all" compound</term>, <term>tamarinds|a fruit used as a mild laxative</term>, <term>aloes|bitter plant resin used for purging</term>, etc., is a fact that speaks for itself through experience.

**Lie 3.** *You strip mixtures of their natural form.* <note>original: "Exuitis mixta sua naturali forma."</note> This is a lie. That the form remains is shown by the fact that the medicinal action is numerically the same as it was before.

**Lie 4.** *So that you may clothe them in foreign forms.* <note>original: "Ut vestiatis aliena."</note> This is a lie. For we leave to those things that purge by their specific property that same property, as in the extract of <term>lapis lazuli|a blue stone used to purge "black bile" or melancholy</term>, <term>senna leaves|a common herbal laxative</term>, <term>turbith|purgative root of a plant in the morning glory family</term>, and so on. Likewise, the extract of <term>quinces|cydoniorum; fruit used for its astringent and digestive properties</term>, <term>sweet flag|calamus aromaticus; a fragrant plant used for stomach ailments</term>, cinnamon, etc., possesses its original natural power. Only the matter is separated from the <term>species|here meaning the specific essential character or outward form</term>, which was the pursuit of the most ancient wise men according to <term>Mesue|an influential authority on pharmacy whose identity is debated by historians</term>. However, in things where a transmutation occurs, a form that is foreign to the whole category is not introduced, but rather one determined by the power of nature, and this happens commonly in both medicine and the kitchen.

**Lie 5.** *How often is the temperament snatched away along with the matter from your extracts.* <note>original: "Quoties de cui extractis vestris cum materia diripi temperiem."</note> This is a double lie...

->## THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM <-
<note>original: "GALENIA TRIVMPHVS." This is likely the title of the section or a satirical reference to Riolan’s rigid Galenism.</note>

...dacity. <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "Mendacium" (lie/mendacity) from the previous page.</note> For you have not taught, but rather railed against us; nor do we tear away the temperament along with the matter.

6. *The form along with the temperament*: A lie. 
7. *The properties along with the form*: A lie. 
8. *The matter which you corrupt, etc.* A lie. We do not corrupt the matter; rather, we separate the coarse from the subtle and essential, just as occurs in infusions, decoctions, pressings, and the like. 

9. *Your extracts have some form.* A contradiction. You used to deny that you had written that we "extract the form." Now you assert in your response to Harvetus <note>Israel Harvet was a French physician and defender of chemical medicine whom Riolan attacked.</note> that they do have it. But to extract is also to bring the form out from potentiality. 

10. *Because they are active.* But when you were prating about the <term>quintessence|the "fifth essence," considered by alchemists to be the purest, most potent medicinal core of a substance</term>, you said our essences were nothing. If that were so, the name of <term>Spagyrist|a chemist who practices the "spagyric" art of separating and recombining substances</term> would be a hollow title. Furthermore, if our extracts are active—and produced through "corruption" as you claim—then we have earned praise, not blame. If you wish to claim they act for evil, that is merely your own slander. For they do not act in such a way unless they are misused. 

11. *They have a temperament;* Why then do you claim we take away their <term>crasis|the unique constitutional balance or "mixture" of qualities in a substance</term>? Or is it we who create it? We would be gods indeed if that were so. 

12. *Because they are mixtures:* Why do you contend that the mixture is destroyed? Do we "mix" the extract of <term>rhubarb|a root widely used as a medicinal purgative</term>? Not at all. If we could mix things so as to create the nature of rhubarb from scratch, we would again be gods. 

13. *A temperament far different from the natural one.* A lie. 

14. *The powers and actions of your essences are far different from those which the mixture possessed when standing in its whole nature.* A lie. They possess the same powers, and are homogeneous with the essence that was in the whole plants. At the very least, the impure and useless parts have been removed. If you wish to estimate the nobility of the art and its professors, the dignity of its inventors and practitioners, and compare with this whatever curses Riolan with his associates has heaped upon everyone, you will say that we have resisted with too little spirit.

Oils, waters, salts, and elemental dregs—the nut is destroyed, seed and all, because the oil of a nut is not the nut itself. This is what happens when you create <term>elixirs</term> <note>concentrated medicinal preparations</note> and <term>magisteries</term> <note>original: "magisteria"; a chemical precipitate or refined extract</note> through your compositions; when you dissolve metals into "waters" <note>acids or solvents</note> and quicksilver <term>mercury</term>; or when you reduce them into glass and calxes <note>powders produced by heating/oxidation</note>, and so on. We should recognize that in our response, we have addressed both the attacker's insults and his most shameful sophistry <note>deceptive or fallacious reasoning</note>, by which he states as an absolute truth something that should only be said in a limited sense, and attributes to all what was only applicable to a few.

If Riolan had judged our "destructions" <note>the chemical breakdown of raw materials</note> as they truly are, and looked at the goal toward which they strive—namely, human health and a most noble artistic purpose—he would not have called us enemies of nature and of God. He would not have claimed that we destroy "mixtures" to the insult of God, or that this work is an invention of the Devil. He writes that we strip nature of its nature and destroy the <term>crases</term> <note>original: "crases"; the specific balance or "temperament" of elements in a substance</note>, its temperament, and so on, with such a spirit that nothing but the highest venom shines through his words. In that same spirit, a lie is told—or if that word is too harsh, call it a calumny. Our "destructions" are not what Riolan’s faction falsely claims.

For these processes are directed toward an end that contains the essence of the beautiful, the best, and the perfect. Therefore, the operations of the art strive toward the "essence"—whether we are drawing out an actual being from potentiality or non-existence, or whether we are gathering good things from bad through separation <note>the alchemical process of "spagyria" or separating the pure from the impure</note>. Since we are moving toward perfection, we do not "destroy," except in a qualified sense <note>original: "secundum quid"; a philosophical term meaning in a specific respect, rather than in total</note>, but rather we gene- <insert>generate</insert> <note>The text breaks here at the catchword "ramus," completing the word "generamus" or "we generate" on the following page.</note>

...we generate. Let Riolan write an indictment against the farmer who, for the sake of the fruit, "corrupts" the seeds. Let him write against his own ancestors, who did the same so that such a "pretty offspring" <note>Libavius is sarcastically referring to Riolan himself; the argument is that human reproduction also involves a "corruption" of biological material to create a new form</note> might be born. Let him write against cooks, architects, and indeed even against the sun itself and the whole of creation. Therefore, when we look upon this most stupid pretense and <term>sophistry</term> <note>deceptive or fallacious reasoning</note>, we cannot judge Riolan’s malice otherwise, even if his words do not seem entirely insane.

...chemical essences, by the experiment of **Heurnius** <note>Jan Heurnius (1543–1601), a celebrated Dutch physician and professor at Leiden</note>, who nevertheless did not defect from chemistry for that reason, even though you yourself admit he was too devoted to that art. Likewise, an accidental outcome does not strip away the nature and substance of a thing, or that which exists in its own right. 

The nature of Heurnius’s colic was such that it required not oil of anise, but rather a diluted form, a decoction, an infusion, or similar preparations. In these forms, there would be a simultaneous power of cleansing and of soothing pains, along with <term>carminative</term> <note>medicines used to relieve gas and flatulence</note> and <term>discussive</term> <note>substances that disperse or "discuss" morbid humors or swellings</note> properties, heat, and so on. We call that the "extracted juice"; then comes the oil, likewise the water, and the salt. However, not all forms are suitable for every ailment; and there is a marvelous variety even among the individual constitutions of patients. Because of this, it can happen that different people suffering from the same disease at different times cannot be cured by the exact same medicine. 

It is possible that—because the physician, in his specific practice and in the application of the principles of his art, relies on conjectures—he may be forced to pronounce a judgment based on a hypothesis (such as, "if the condition is like this, then this treatment should help"). In doing so, he may err; he may judge a condition to be one way when it is actually another. Thus, he might use oil of anise when he ought to have prescribed a dilution of the extract, or...

However, this oil is separated by expression, and if it is purified, it passes by chemical art into a work of great mastery...

### CHAPTER XLIV.

#### *Concerning the argument of genuine virtue remaining, according to*
#### *manuscript page 73, Examination 32.*

**R**iolanus picks at the responses in the examination; he dilutes or overturns none of them. He acts in the same way in the sixth argument regarding which medicines are to be preferred. The **censor** <note>Referring to Jean Riolan the Younger, who acted as a medical critic and gatekeeper in Paris</note> wanted those medicines to be prioritized whose power remains intact during preparation; he assumed and concluded this regarding his own infusions and decoctions. I responded that by the same logical principle, it is proved that the simple **extracts** of the chemists are superior to the **Parisian broths** <note>original: "iusculis"; a mocking term for the liquid medicines favored by the Medical Faculty of Paris</note> and compositions. 

The reason is that chemical extractions are performed far more skillfully and cautiously than infusions and decoctions; indeed, pure essences are collected through them. Who does not see that what is unmixed, pure, and entirely its own is more genuine than that to which a foreign body—such as water, wine, or the like—has been joined? Mixing destroys the simplicity of the essence. Galenic infusions and decoctions, often increased to an immense degree (for compounds are frequently exaggerated with more compounds and simples)...

...everything is mixed together. Therefore, the simplicity of essence—and consequently a truly genuine nature—cannot remain in those traditional preparations. Now, if a work of genuine virtue is to be preferred over one that no longer possesses its genuine and solitary character (which is the very argument our **censor** <note>Referring to Jean Riolan the Younger</note> uses), it necessarily follows that the chemical **simples** <term>original: "simplicia"; in pharmacy, these are medicines made of only one constituent, as opposed to compounds</term> are superior to the **Galenic** <note>Followers of the ancient physician Galen, who favored herbal mixtures and "humoral" balance over chemical extractions</note> ones. To this argument, Riolan cannot respond with even a single syllable without overturning his own principles. Therefore, to avoid falling completely silent, he proposes a new invention; let us weigh its merits.

> *Only moderate heat is capable of separating the pure from the impure.*
> 
> *Therefore, our Parisian Alchemy is to be preferred over yours.*

He provides the reason for this conclusion by claiming that **Parisian Alchemy** <note>A mocking reference to the traditional pharmaceutical methods of the Paris Medical Faculty, which Riolan tries to rebrand as "true" alchemy</note> separates the powers of mixtures through a gentle heat, similar to **boiling** <term>original: "elixationi"; a slow stewing or boiling process</term>. He attempts to prove his premise by the authority of the **ignoramuses** <note>original: "antigramaniorum"; literally "those against grammar," here implying those who are unlearned or who misuse technical terms</note>. Furthermore, he cites the opposite effect of immoderate heat, which he claims destroys through excess. He attributes this destructive heat to our **Spagyric art** <term>Spagyria: a synonym for alchemy, specifically the process of "separating and recombining" substances to purify them</term>, which he says does not merely "cook" but scorches, burns, and ruins the materials. 

First, one should observe the "decorum of his madness." For it belongs to no other power than madness to argue against Alchemy using the logic of common **decoctions** <term>coctionum: preparations made by boiling organic substances</term> and **infusions** <term>infusionum: soaking a substance in a liquid to extract its virtues</term> such as the Galenists prescribe and administer in their shops—and yet to label these very things as "works of Alchemy." But let that madness pass; let it indeed be a part of Alchemy to cook and infuse, provided it is not done in the manner of Riolan—that is to say, foolishly. Next, we accept his premise only if "moderate heat" is understood...

...with respect to a specific material, which nevertheless would be considered immoderate if applied to another. For example, the heat by which gold is tested or smelted is indeed moderate for that gold, for it is not destructive to it; but if that same heat were applied to lead or straw, it would be immoderate. But we also admit this when the question concerns extraction by heat, which cannot prejudice other instruments and methods. Furthermore, this cannot be accepted regarding chemical works **universally** <note>original: "καθόλου"</note>; because Riolan speaks only of extractions by infusion without transmutation and without the separation of the extracts—that is, only of simple extracts, examples of which are the extract of rhubarb, myrobalans <note>A plum-like fruit used in medieval and early modern medicine as a laxative</note>, and similar things found in **Mesuë** <note>Referring to the works attributed to Masawaih al-Mardini, an influential Arabic medical authority whose texts were standard in European pharmacy</note>. We concede the logical premise regarding excessive heat. For a heat that is simply corruptive is not perfective; and indeed, where the pure is simply separated from the impure, nothing ought to be corrupted by any destructive excess.

However, to call this separation "the corruption of the whole" is irrelevant, since it is not destructive of the medicinal entity being sought. The argument drawn from the *Anti-Gramanius* <note>A reference to polemical works attacking the followers of the chemist Gramanus</note> is ridiculous. In those writings, the primary question is whether that alchemy in which **Gramanus** <note>Ulrich Graman, a radical follower of Paracelsus who emphasized fire above all else</note> proposed only **Vulcan** <note>A common alchemical metaphor for fire or the heat of the furnace</note>—without sense or reason—could be overthrown by the Galenic school. **Libavius** <note>The author refers to himself in the third person here</note> denies that this can be done, and he opposes Gramanus not with simple Galenic discipline, but with **Galenic chymiatry** <term>original: "chymiatricam"; the branch of medicine that combines chemical preparations with traditional Galenic medical theory</term>, which has united into a single body with true alchemy. What vice then, you ask, is finally in the argument? It is the fallacy of *after this* <note>original: "ἐκ τούτου" (ek toutou). From the same principle, the plain opposite is concluded:

> *That art which separates the pure from the impure by gentle heat*
> *is to be preferred over that which does not.*
> *Our Chemistry separates the pure from the impure by*
> *gentle heat; the Parisian infusion and boiling do*
> *not separate.*
> *Therefore, our Chemistry is to be preferred to the*
> *Parisian boiling and infusion.*

I prove the minor premise <note>The second statement in the syllogism above</note> by scientific axioms regarding the extraction of simple essences; for these, one may look at the precepts of Alchemy where we extract through infusions and diplomatic decoctions <note>A "diplomatic" decoction refers to the use of a *balneum Mariae* or double boiler (a *diploma*), which ensures the substance is never directly exposed to the flame</note>. And indeed, if the opinion of <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a powerful member of the Paris Medical Faculty and a staunch defender of traditional Galenism against new chemical remedies</note> is true, the medicinal virtue migrates alone without any part of the physical body passing through. Behold, the beautiful "Parisian Alchemy"; or rather, a prodigious monster.

It is false to say that our alchemy burns and scorches extracted juices during the separation of the impure from the pure; indeed, it does not scorch or burn in the distillations of oils and waters, nor in most chemical masteries <note>In early chemistry, a "mastery" (magistery) was a process that prepared a substance without changing its essential nature, but improving its purity or form</note>. In some places, however, it is ne- <note>The text cuts off here, leading to the next page's "cessary"</note>

...necessary, as in calcinations <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or oxidize it</note>, cementations, ashes, etc. However, it then occurs in the body of the compound until this is dissolved—not in its essence, if indeed that is what is sought. This is what **Aristotle** long ago taught was the function of heat: it gathers things of the same kind <note>original: "homogenea"</note> and separates things of different kinds <note>original: "heterogenea"</note>, as occurs in the workshops of the metalworkers.

# THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS

From this it would not follow that Galenic remedies are to be preferred to chemical ones; since "one swallow does not make a spring." <note>A proverb meaning one instance does not prove a general rule.</note> But both the major and minor premises fail by the logical fallacy of *secundum quid et simpliciter* <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ πῇ καὶ ἁπλῶς"; a Greek logical term for the fallacy of arguing from a qualified or specific case to a general rule.</note>. For it is sometimes the case that a more unpleasant thing is to be preferred to a pleasant one, just as wormwood wine <note>original: "vinum absinthiacum"; wine infused with the bitter herb wormwood, highly valued for its medicinal properties despite its harsh taste.</note> is preferred over plain wine. In my judgment, **Riolan** wishes to prove the minor premise. But **Libavius** would be too simple-minded if he allowed himself to be caught by such a lazy and stupid sophist. I have said that the extract of the common dregs of the **Paracelsians** <term>Paracelsici</term> <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541) who promoted the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine, often criticized by traditionalists for their radical theories.</note> is either equally or more unpleasant than a decoction. Thus even a simple extract of the art might be more unpleasant than some decoction made with honey-water <term>melicratum</term> <note>A classical mixture of honey and water used to dilute or sweeten medicines.</note>, but not a **quintessence** <term>quinta essentia</term> <note>The most purified and potent essence of a substance, believed in alchemy to be the "fifth element" beyond the four physical elements.</note>. So in practice, when an extraction from wormwood wine is given, it is more pleasing than when it is from a decoction in spring water. You please me more, **Riolan**, when you argue than when you bring accusations and lie. Therefore, proceed:

> *Something of the medicinal strength is lost in chemical extractions;*
> *it is not lost in Parisian infusions.*
> *Therefore, these infusions are to be preferred to those extractions.*

The antecedent is proved by the example of **rhubarb** <note>original: "rhabarbarum"; a root used extensively in the early modern period as a potent purgative and digestive aid.</note>, which [the Galenist] teaches should first be 1. infused; 2. the infusion is cooked until the liquid is consumed; 3. it is expressed; 4. the expression is cooked again to the thickness of honey with sugar added. However, this double cooking loses some of the strength. The reason is: because rhubarb has its purging power in its "spirit" <note>In early modern medicine, the "spirit" referred to the volatile, active essence of a substance that could easily be evaporated by heat.</note>. Therefore, we prefer the infusion to the extract.

I respond to the antecedent regarding chemical things that he is playing with a fallacy of accident <term>elencho ab accidente</term> and *secundum quid* <note>A logical fallacy where a general rule is applied to an exceptional case, or a specific instance is generalized improperly.</note>. It can happen that if the craftsman is not attentive, something <meta>Catchword: "pereat" (may perish/is lost)</meta>...

If nothing is lost by the pharmacy when infusing, then nothing is lost by chemistry either; for an infusion is a chemical work whose function is to extract or take up the essence hidden within the whole. For it is an extraction whether the liquid remains or does not remain. They do not overthrow chemistry, but rather establish it, if they act with industry. One thing cannot be preferred to itself in its own kind, if all other things are equal.

You play wittily, Riolan. Go on, display your shame to the world. Why are chemical medicines more expensive?

Chemical medicines can last for many years, and before the fruit of one work is consumed, it can be restored with much leisure. Truly, what folly is it to compare a boiled decoction to distilled medicines? **The twelfth argument** debates mineral medicines and those derived from living things, from which the censor <note>Referring to Jean Riolan the Elder.</note> wishes the latter to be preferred over chemical ones because of their "affinity" <note>original: "symbolum." **The first flaw** is in the very question itself. Formerly, it was disputed whether those things taken from what once lived were to be preferred, or chemical minerals; now, the proposal is only about plants, to which minerals are opposed. ### Argument I.

->*A medicine must be CONQUERED by our nature so that it may be brought into action.*<-

->*Plants, all other things being equal, are more easily brought into action by our heat than metallic things are.*<-

->*Therefore, plants are better medicines.*<-

The minor premise is proved by the unconquerable hardness of metallic things, which cannot be overcome by a kind and moderate heat; and secondly, because metallic things are poisonous.

<margin>Riolan cannot speak in the Galenic manner.</margin>
This argument immediately stumbles at the very threshold and establishes a false principle, if indeed what the <term>Galenic</term> <note>Followers of the 2nd-century physician Galen, who emphasized herbal remedies and the four humors.</note> and Arabic schools teach regarding the distinction between medicines and foods is true. For that which is conquered does not move nature, but is instead moved by it. It is a disgrace for a Parisian professor—and indeed an elderly champion who has spent his life in the books of Galen—not to be able to speak in the Galenic manner. Thus, there is a <term>solecism</term> <note>A grammatical or logical error.</note> in the phrase "to be brought into action." That which was previously in a state and is now at rest is what is "brought into action." The minor premise contains a ridiculous exception: **ALL OTHER THINGS BEING EQUAL**. Therefore, if things are unequal, it will not be so. You argue beautifully, my philosopher! *II. Our remedies that are more similar to nature are to be preferred.*

*There is a greater similarity between plants and human nature than between minerals and human nature.*

<margin>The Parisians, in their zeal for opposing the chemists, overturn the very foundations of their own medicine.</margin>

The minor premise <note>In a logical syllogism, the "minor" is the second statement (in this case, that plants are more like humans than minerals are).</note> is "proven" by many points, which tend toward persuading us that things agree more when they share the same category of "animate and living" and an "identity of form." It is explained by the opposite: just as specific and essential differences (which are considered "forms") differ most greatly from one another. Is not an animate thing more akin to an animate thing, and a vegetable thing more akin to a sentient thing, than an inanimate thing is to an animate one? Is this not a strong argument? Why not just surrender to the chemists? But here is a word in your ear: while Riolan’s own syllogistic principle stands, you can argue in this way:

*Our remedies that are more similar to nature are to be preferred.*

*Opposites are not similar to our nature.*

<note>original: "ALCHYMIA DE SPUR. PARIS." This heading likely refers to a specific section or title within the larger work, possibly critiquing Parisian medical authorities.</note>

"Live, not live, nature, life, soul?" For these have **nothing to do with the point** <note>original: "Nihil enim hæc ad rhombum." A Latin idiom meaning the argument is irrelevant to the matter at hand.</note>. The censor <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine and a fierce opponent of chemical remedies.</note> was confronted with the fact that very potent poisons exist among living plants and animals, which clearly detracts from his statement that remedies are "better" simply because they share a "living" nature with the patient. "What then?" asks the foolish Riolan. This is what follows, I say: your principle collapses. For if the category of living things contains substances entirely adverse to our own natures, it follows that a better remedy is not necessarily available from them just because they possess life; for life can be contrary to life, and one **temperament** <note>original: "crasis." The specific balance of humors or qualities in a body.</note> can be contrary to another. 

He claims that man has received a discerning wisdom to distinguish between useful and harmful things. But not even a crumb of such wisdom appears in Riolan. For when he should have used other arguments to distinguish a better remedy from a worse one, he chooses the one least capable of doing so: life, the soul, and the **specific form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is what makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "vipershape" of a viper).</note> do not provide this distinction. Indeed, within the very same viper there are diverse parts; yet you cannot distinguish them by life or by the form of the species. 

"The juice is the soul of the plant," the censor used to say. If so, then by the juice of the leek, the yucca, and the **monkshood** <note>original: "napelli." A highly poisonous flowering plant, also known as wolfsbane or aconite.</note>, we ought to be able to be nourished because "soul is more similar to soul"; and these would also be "better" remedies, from which we might be healed.
