-> # THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM <-
<note>original: "GALENIA TRIVMPHVS." While the title suggests a victory for Galen, the text itself often uses Galenic logic to defend chemical (Paracelsian) medicine.</note>

<margin>Kk 3</margin>
<meta>catchword: decre-</meta>

...in this very decision <note>The text continues a sentence from the previous page regarding the "disputation" or "decision" of the Paris faculty.</note>, in which, so that they may condemn minerals, they lay down the most general foundation of their art.

*IV. Minerals are most distant from us, and therefore they are removed from us not only by a logical difference, but also by a physical difference further than plants are. Therefore, they are to be secondary to plants.*

The antecedent <note>In logic, the "antecedent" is the first part of a conditional statement—here, the claim that minerals are too "distant" from human nature.</note> is illustrated by both logicians and physicists; the former are said to take their distinction from specific differences, the latter from the greatest physical distance. This argument is expanded thus:

> *If so many plants and animals are available, one should not go into the bowels of the earth. But they are available. Therefore [one should not go].*

This antecedent is false. For minerals are not so far distant from us, since she who is the mother of minerals is also our own mother <note>The author refers to the Earth or Nature as the common mother of both humans and minerals.</note>; our body comes from the same origin as the minerals, and to that same origin we shall return. Furthermore, those things which happen in the belly of the earth are clearly similar to those which happen in us, as is shown by the spirits, the veins, the origins of springs, the movement of vapors <note>original: "flatuum." Often referring to gasses or "winds" within the body or the earth.</note>, vitriolic humors <note>original: "humores vitriolati." Vitriol refers to sulfate minerals; the author compares the acidic fluids of the earth to the fluids of the human body.</note>, salts, sulfurous breaths, and indeed so many things that the **Paracelsians** <term>Paracelsici: followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who championed "iatrochemistry," the use of chemical and mineral substances in medicine rather than just herbs.</term> have made the entire human anatomy analogous to the minerals of the earth. But even so, nothing follows from their argument. Imagine that the distance is indeed the greatest; it does not follow that better remedies are not provided from them.

Indeed, from that very same foundation, the opposite arises. For if remedies ought to be contraries <note>original: "contraria." A core principle of Galenic medicine was *Contraria contrariis curantur*—opposites are cured by opposites (e.g., a "hot" fever is cured by a "cold" herb).</note>, then they should come from the most distant things. For those things which are most distant are contraries. And yet, this is the highest and most universal principle of the **Galenists**... <term>Galenici: followers of the traditional system of Galen, which dominated European medicine for over a millennium.</term>

<summary>The author argues against the Galenic idea that minerals are "too different" from humans to be used as medicine, suggesting instead that the Earth's "anatomy" mirrors human anatomy. He further asserts that if Galenists believe in curing through opposites, the "distant" nature of minerals should actually make them superior remedies.</summary>

# ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN DISPUTE
<note>original: "ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS." This refers to the ongoing debates between the conservative Paris medical faculty and the proponents of chemical (Paracelsian) medicine.</note>

<meta>catchword: Long.</meta>

...the decree, that remedies ought to be contraries <note>The Galenic principle of *contraria contrariis curantur* (contraries are cured by contraries). If a disease is "hot," the remedy must be "cold."</note>. Therefore, they must be at the furthest distance from one another. According to the judgment of Riolanus <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1606), a staunch defender of traditional Galenism against new chemical medicines.</note>, these are minerals. Therefore, remedies are to be taken from this source.

However, since he <note>Riolanus</note> brings forward physicists and logicians rather than physicians in this argument, let us also make use of their help. Things that are the same in <term>genus<gloss>A broad logical category, such as "body" or "substance."</gloss></term> are the same in matter and subject. The human body and minerals are the same in genus. For both are "elementary mixed bodies," corruptible, and so forth. They are, therefore, the same in subject and matter. Furthermore, things that are the same in matter are mutually active and passive toward one another; and such things ought to serve as remedies for our body. Likewise, by reason of subject and matter, they do not stand at the greatest distance: indeed, not even in species. For disparate things <note>In logic, "disparate" things are simply different (like a cat and a stone) rather than being direct opposites (like hot and cold).</note> do not stand at the greatest distance. A mineral and the human body are disparate. If you consult the physicists, you would hear them classifying things in this way:

"The furthest distance," says the critic <note>The "critic" or "censor" refers to Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1606), a leading figure of the Paris Medical Faculty who opposed chemical medicine.</note>, "is that by which forms and specific differences differ; that is, between contrary species under the same nearest <term>genus<gloss>In logic, the immediate category under which a species falls, such as "animal" for a human.</gloss></term>." An animal body and a human body differ by contrary forms under the same nearest genus, as the physical diagram indicates. However, the human and the inanimate are not opposed as contraries, but as <term>disparate things<gloss>In traditional logic, "disparate" things are simply different from one another (like a book and a mountain) rather than being direct opposites (like hot and cold).</gloss></term>. If Riolan’s opinion is true, it is proven that animal-based remedies ought to be shunned, while mineral remedies should be sought. The attached hypothesis can easily be turned around: for if suitable remedies for chronic diseases are not supplied from those sources <note>Referring to plant or animal sources.</note>, nor any that are so <term>polychresta<gloss>From the Greek for "many uses"; medicines that are highly versatile and effective against various ailments.</gloss></term>, it follows that one must have recourse to minerals. No more is needed. It is evident that the elements are most familiar to us, as are the heat and light of the sun; by this, the <term>maniographus<gloss>original: "maniographus." A Greek-derived insult meaning "one who writes madness." The author is mocking Riolan's writing as incoherent.</gloss></term> is more easily refuted. Physicians say that those things are at the greatest distance from us which are most hostile in their <term>temperaments<gloss>original: "craſibus" (crases). The specific balance of the four humors or qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry—within a body.</gloss></term>, such as are found in every kind of mixed body. From such things—insofar as they are such—a remedy should not be sought. But for those which are not such—whether by nature or by art—it is not forbidden to seek them; just as when the heart, liver, or flesh of serpents is used against their own poison, or a scorpion is applied to its own wound, and so forth.

# ->ON THE FALSE ALCHEMY OF PARIS<-

<margin>To him who has gone mad beautifully for the sake of Galenic medicine.</margin> <note>original Greek: καλῶς παραφρονήσαντι ὑπὲρ τῆς γαληνικῆς.</note>
The chemists—according to Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1606), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against the new chemical medicine.</note> (though I did not add those specific words myself)—produce quintessences <note>The "fifth essence" or ether, a substance alchemists sought to extract that was supposedly purer and more potent than the four earthly elements.</note> which do not exist in the center of the world. Since I brought these words forward as a <term>prosyllogism<gloss>A logical step where the conclusion of one argument serves as the premise for the next.</gloss></term>, he claims it is my nature to lie, to deceive, and to hurl insults. This is a jocular sort of insanity! If it is the nature of Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a German physician and chemist. Though a chemist, he was often cited by conservatives when his views aligned with theirs.</note> to lie, with what confidence does Riolan transcribe so many things from his "opposing writings" to defend his own cause? This affliction becomes even more amusing because what he accuses me of doing, he does himself, following the habit of those who are wandering in their minds.

Is it not true that chemists produce—or at least profess to produce—quintessences? But is it not also true that Riolan denies they exist in the center of the world? On page 76 of his *Apology for Hippocrates*, the question of whether a quintessence exists in the sublunary <note>The earthly realm below the moon, composed of the four changing elements, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note> world is treated explicitly, and he seeks to defend the negative view at length. With no less effort, he did the same in his work *Mania* on page 45, where the question is proposed: whether there is a certain "fifth essence" distinct from the four elemental ones. There, he cannot even grant the chemists an essence analogous to the <term>ether<gloss>The celestial substance that makes up the stars and planets in Aristotelian physics.</gloss></term>.

What, then, is the meaning of his current denial? Does Riolan regret his disgrace? The poor man is raving. You scholastic censors, who have erected a monument to this <term>maniographus<gloss>A "writer of madness"; a derogatory term the author uses to describe Riolan's polemical style.</gloss></term>, see to it that this title is inscribed: *To the one raving for Galenism*. For it seems to make no difference to you which way you defend your discipline—through delusions or through wisdom.

<page-num>521</page-num>

## ->THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM<-

Riolan persists in his denial, contrary to the common opinion of natural philosophers and physicians, who—along with Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), whose physics and biology formed the basis of medieval and early modern science.</note> in *On Generation and Corruption*, Book 2, text 50—conclude that mixed bodies, even those of living creatures, consist of the four elements <note>The traditional elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>, because they are nourished by those same elements; just as plants are nourished by water mixed with earth. Hippocrates, in the book *On the Nature of Man*, wrote that plants draw a moisture familiar to themselves from the earth, and he posited that within that moisture were the sour, the bitter, the sweet, the salty, and every other kind, so that all might be able to be nourished. In the book *On Breaths* <note>A treatise in the Hippocratic Corpus discussing the role of "pneuma" or air in the body.</note>, he assigns a threefold nourishment: food, drink, and the spirits—which, when outside the body, is called air.

Now, that water pertains to moist nourishment is clear enough from Hippocrates' book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*; and even if there were never anyone to write it down, experience in plants and animals nevertheless bears witness to it abundantly. This same water also becomes a part of food in <term>elixations<gloss>The process of boiling or decocting substances to extract their virtues or make them digestible.</gloss></term>; just as the earthy parts upon which plants live afterwards become the food of animals. He who denies this is altogether insane. The Paris School, through its <term>maniograph<gloss>A mocking term coined by the author, combining "mania" (madness) and "graph" (writer); essentially "the scribe of madness."</gloss></term>, raves all the more because he so stubbornly denies that things which have never lived can provide nourishment.

However, it is superfluous to say much against such follies. At least let us run through whether any point of importance is brought forward. Riolan says on "page of madness" 78 <note>original: "pag. mania 78"—a pun on Riolan's actual page 78.</note> that only the solid parts are truly and properly nourished. Yet he often assigns to us parts that are solid, fleshy or moist, and spiritual. Who would not marvel at these most inept ravings? The whole composite <note>The body as a whole, made of various substances.</note> is nourished truly and properly. It is necessary that all parts be nourished.

# ON THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS IN ALCHEMY

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the previous page was "test", likely for "testatur" (it bears witness), leading into this discussion of natural faculties.</meta>

If not, then two of our parts will neither be preserved nor grow through natural faculties. No change or assimilation will occur through the **native heat** <note>Also called "innate heat," this was believed to be the vital warmth that drove digestion and life processes.</note> regarding them. The growth of these parts would only be the addition of raw water and raw air to our own water and spirits—and what has ever been heard of that is more monstrous than this? Galen, in Book 1 of *On the Natural Faculties*, calls **nutrition** the "assimilation of that which nourishes to that which is nourished." He says that this must necessarily always be preceded by **agglutination** <note>The stage where food "sticks" to the tissue before being fully absorbed.</note>, just as this is preceded by **apposition** <note>The initial placement of nutrients onto the tissue.</note>. But he teaches that "proper nourishment" is that which is assimilated and nourishes; to call what is merely "glued" or "placed" nourishment is equivocal and improper.

According to Riolan’s teaching, one must imagine that a man is two parts "raw" and one part "cooked"; and that these parts are not mixed into one homogeneous substance, but exist separately. Thus, while that which is solid is truly nourished, that which is liquid and spiritual is merely restored by the addition of flowing liquid and air, and is not truly nourished.

However, all **similar parts** <note>In Galenic anatomy, "similar parts" or "simple parts" are tissues like bone, fiber, or flesh that are uniform throughout, as opposed to "organic parts" like the hand or liver.</note> consist of that triple nature, since in all of them there is **radical moisture** <note>The vital fluid thought to be the "fuel" of life, which slowly consumes itself over a lifetime.</note>, fibers which are the foundation and matter of the solid body, and finally heat with spirit.

Think now what a "wonderful" nutrition those monstrous physicians of the Paris school—who oppose the chemists—fabricate for us. But why does water not nourish? Because it is like whey. The quote refers to Book III of the *Georgics*.</note>, who "feeds the fierce Molossian dog with fatty whey" <note>original: "acrem molossum pascit sero pingui." # THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM <note>Original: *Galenia Triumphus*</note>

<meta>Catchword: con-</meta>

What about the remedy? You insist it must be contrary to the disease, on the grounds that "like" does not act upon "like." I ought to mock you rather than strike you harshly for this. You say that nourishment is "like" the body, do you not? Yet nourishment allows itself to be digested and assimilated into the body. To achieve this, a natural agent is required. If this agent is like the nourishment, then in some way "like" does act upon "like." But if all action occurs only between contraries, your entire argument falls apart. For food is also a contrary in its own way. But go on: you say a contrary remedy must be sought. For what thing? For the disease. 

What if the disease is merely a **privation** <term>privation|In the philosophy of the time, this refers to the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like darkness being the absence of light rather than a "thing" in itself</term>? Must your material remedy still oppose the disease and struggle against it? In the study of physics, contrariety exists between opposing forms. However, **privation and habit** <note>Original: *privatio & habitus*. In logic, "habit" refers to the possession of a quality or state, while "privation" is its absence</note> are logical contradictions, not physical opponents. If a disease is a deficiency, you seek a "contrary" remedy in vain; instead, you ought to help nature with something "like" itself, so that by providing a restorative supplement, the deficiency might cease. 

It appears that you, despite being such a veteran, have not yet learned the first principles of medicine. You discuss disease and remedy as if you were physicists debating heat and cold struggling among the clouds. To be sure, there are times when one must use cooling, heating, moistening, or drying; but this applies to a healthy constitution as much as to an adverse one, and at least where there is a simple **imbalance of temperaments** <term>intemperies|A medical condition where the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—are out of proportion</term>. If the actual substance of the organ falls into decay, or if a mass of excess fluid is the only thing causing trouble, your principle of contrariety is of little importance. We must look for another kind of contrariety—one where the reasoning is focused more on helping nature so that she herself may drive out her enemy. You say the remedy is brought to the disease as if to its own...

He suggests that true medicine supports the body's nature to expel illness rather than just balancing heat and cold.</summary>

## ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS <note>Original: *ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS.* This likely refers to a specific academic debate or a critique of the medical faculty in Paris.</note>

...contrary. Why do you forget the cause? But suppose that cause is grasped together with the symptoms and cast into that single word "disease"; I tell you that a remedy is not only that *by which* we act, but also *for whom* we act. Thus, it also refers to nature, to which we bring aid when it is weakened—that is, we heal it. You call a remedy an instrument for driving away disease. To be sure, if you speak of a **saw** <note>Original: *ferra*, likely a transcription of *serra*</note>, forceps, a **lancet** <term>lancet|original: *phebotomo*, a tool used for bloodletting</term>, a purgative, an altering lettuce, and so on, not all of these are contrary to the disease in themselves.

Rather, all things are ultimately referred back to nature for the purpose of restoring health. Everywhere the logic of **similarity** is greater than that of **opposition** between the disease and the remedy. Indeed, the remedy should not be ultimately opposed to the disease; rather, it should serve health, of which disease is the privation. 

If we strive toward the contrary, and the goal of this life is health, then a remedy must first be prepared to suit health. And because it is "for health"—and health itself is the work of nature—who does not understand that the primary, internal, and final goal is to provide nature with a remedy that is not contrary, but **congruent**? 

One and the same thing (you say) can be used for preserving health and for restoring it. Very well. Therefore, the highest goal is health, which is that primary work of nature. What else? It will preserve health like nourishment while its substance restores the body's strength. Does this mean that the thousand people you restored with **rhubarb** <note>original: *Rheo*</note> and **senna** <note>original: *Senna*; both were common plant-based laxatives used to purge "bad humors"</note> used those medicines as food? We are not speaking of nourishment now, but of the remedy for disease.

**Hyacinth** <note>likely referring to the gemstone zircon or a specific preparation of the flower, both used as "cordials" to strengthen the heart</note>, **Jasper**, and even fragrant things applied externally give strength; those things that unite what has been scattered also give strength. But I say, following the authority of **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), an influential French physician who defended traditional Galenic medicine against new discoveries like the circulation of the blood</note>, the restoration of the solid, moist, and **spiritual parts** <term>spiritual parts|original: *spirituoſarum partium*, referring to the "vital spirits" believed to circulate through the body and sustain life</term>—which is followed by an increase of lost strength, as in those exhausted by labor—is most properly achieved through food.

How is it that this is now ascribed to medicine *as* medicine? On the contrary, the **Galenists** <term>Galenists|original: *Galenici*, followers of the medical system established by the ancient Greek physician Galen</term> say this is an unconquerable quality of nature as such. If it restores strength, it does not restore it through its own primary action, but by **accident** <term>accident|original: *ex accidente*, a philosophical term meaning a secondary or incidental effect rather than an essential one</term>, and thus not as a primary medicine, but as something else. 

If disease is a defect of power or strength, then that which repairs strength heals it. Such a thing is similar to nature. That which is **adverse** <note>referring to the Galenic principle of treating diseases with "contraries," like treating a fever with cold</note> does not repair, but destroys, unless something happens by accident. But what is the logic behind a medicine that restores strength? You say it is by some quality; for example, through coldness, it restores balance and health to the whole or to a part that is too hot. Indeed, one should not cling only to these **elementary qualities** <note>the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, but the logic should be transferred to entire natures and the whole art of healing; but let that be a specific example. I say...

# ALCHEMY: ON THE SPURIOUS PARTS

...restoration depends more on similarity than on contrariety. For that **Medicine** ought to act in favor of the body's temperament and health. Therefore, it must be taken in such a way that it is accommodated to this state. Whether you achieve this through a manifest quality, or through **bloodletting** <note>original: *phlebotomia*</note>, purging, or drawing out humors through **fomentations** <note>warm, moist medicinal applications</note> (the common people cool hot **swellings** <note>original: *oedemata*</note> with warm wine; and **St. Anthony’s Fire** <note>original: *Erysepelata*; a bacterial skin infection</note> is successfully cured with mineral waters, decoctions of soaps, and similar things; likewise, those suffering from **frenzy** <note>original: *Phrenetici*</note> are treated with pigeons <note>A common practice involved applying a freshly killed pigeon to the patient's head or feet to "draw out" the vapors of fever or madness.</note> and spirit of wine, and sometimes even with **blistering agents** <note>original: *Vesicatoriis*; substances applied to the skin to produce blisters, intended to draw out harmful humors</note>), all things must be established according to nature for the sake of health. In this way, a "contrary" is indeed brought against the disease—namely, health itself; but the instrument used is more closely accommodated to nature, which is the primary cause of health.

These considerations regarding **Diet** also pleased **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE)</note>. For a medical diet has in some respects the character of a medicine, and in others that of food; but it is manifest that the latter is more powerful than the former. Therefore, you fight in vain against the "similarity" of the **chemical physicians** <term>chemical physicians|original: *chymiatrorum*; followers of Paracelsus who believed that "like cures like," as opposed to the Galenic "contraries cure contraries"</term>, which, whether you wish to or not, you are forced to admit by the reasoning of nature. It is nature's work alone that produces health, and health is not rarely procured without any medicine at all, nature being aided by physical work alone, as in **dislocations** <note>original: *luxationibus*</note>. In such cases, once the dislocated parts are reset, nature alone perfects the cure. And if an influx of humors is feared, it is warded off by protective measures, or drawn away by **blistering agents**, **skin-reddening agents** <term>skin-reddening agents|original: *Phoenigmis*; substances that cause redness of the skin by stimulating blood flow to the surface</term>, **bloodletting** <note>original: *Vena secta*</note>, or other means.

You say: "The theorem of Hippocrates is not childish: *Contraries should be the remedies for contraries.*" I believe it. But who calls it childish? I said that it is childish to contend with the chemical physicians about "the similar" and "the contrary." Sum...

-> # GALEN’S TRIUMPH <-

<meta>catchword: Whereby.</meta>

...to me, illness and health are contraries. In the end, both are present. That which first contributes to health is the primary agent that heals. Now, it is **nature** that performs this action. She is assisted either by manual work <note>likely referring to surgery or external treatments</note> or by **medicinal substances** <note>original: *materia medicamentaria*; the raw materials used to create medicines</note>. Neither of these holds a relationship of contrariety toward nature itself. Rather, they are opposed to the disease secondarily, not primarily. Are these merely childish points? Yet they explain the <term>Hippocratic Theorem</term> <note>The principle usually summarized as *similia similibus curantur* (likes are cured by likes), though Hippocrates acknowledged both similarity and contrariety in healing.</note>, and thus they unite into one principle. You say it is "childish" in the art of healing to think it matters little whether a similar or a contrary remedy is chosen. On the contrary, I say it matters a great deal. Both principles coincide. At the very least, it matters little which way you state it: If you say that the cure is performed by nature, assisted by things suited to itself (for this is what "similars" are called in this context), it is well; if you say that for the sake of health, the disease is routed by contraries, it is also well. 

If you wish to establish a comparison between these two ways of speaking, the <term>chemical physicians</term> <note>original: *chymiatri*; doctors who utilized alchemy and chemistry to create medicines, often following Paracelsus</note> say it is more correctly stated that one is cured by things "similar to nature," seeing as it is nature that first effects health according to **Hippocrates**. And therefore, remedies should be chosen not so much for being "opposed to the disease" in their manifest qualities, but for "assisting nature." Once this is established, that which is contrary to the disease is also established. For nature is opposed to the disease; therefore, whatever is similar to nature is also opposed to the disease. If you wish to posit only the principle of contrariety, it can happen that you harm nature. For the contrary to a disease can be an extreme just as easily as it can be a mean <note>The "mean" refers to the Aristotelian idea of balance; an "extreme" remedy might be as violent as the disease itself</note>. Through an extreme remedy, nature is forced into a struggle—yet it is nature that is the primary healer.

<summary>This page explores the reconciliation of Hippocratic and Galenic medicine, arguing that "similars" and "contraries" both function by supporting nature, which is the true source of healing.</summary>

<header>ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS</header>

Therefore, since **similarity** encompasses both goals and simultaneously suggests a skillful prudence, the declaration regarding the goal of "similars" is more powerful. In the case of a <term>burning fever</term> <note>original: *causus*; an acute, high fever characterized by intense thirst and heat</note>, you bicker childishly about the prescription of air. It is certain that cold contributes in two ways: both for the sake of assisting nature, and for mitigating preternatural <note>meaning "outside the natural order," often used to describe the heat of a disease</note> heat. Which goal is more worthy? Cold assists nature twice over: through preservation and through the driving away of the enemy. Yet, in both instances, there is also a logic of contrariety. Whichever you choose to declare, if you wish to contend it, I would say you are bickering not like an old woman, but like a fool. For if that air were only contrary to the disease and not also suited to nature—such as air that is freezing cold and ice-like being opposed to the highest heat—you would certainly be waging a medical war by employing it. The same logic applies to drink and food; that which helps more does so through its similarity with nature rather than through its battle with the hot disease, since it is easy for even those things to become warm. But enough of this for now. You seem to yourself to have disputed most robustly against **Libavius** <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), the author, a German doctor and chemist</note>.

<margin>The ridiculous exultation of **Riolan**. You rejoice with the joy of a <term>moth in the flame</term> <note>original: *Pyrausta*; a mythical insect that lives in fire; here used to mock someone delighting in their own destruction</note>.</margin>

And so you are carried away by an old woman's dementia. "I do not wish," you say, "to have anything further to do with **Quercetanus**" <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a famous Paracelsian physician and chemist</note>. "I have found," he says, "the stronger athlete I was seeking." Ha ha he! What says our Virgil?

[...] memory, and a long-lasting madness. You call your Galenic remedies "ordinary," and the chemical ones "new"; you call the former "mixed and whole," and the latter "destroyed and torn apart into essences, principles, etc." You have preferred the former by many leagues <note>original: *parasangis*; an ancient Persian unit of distance, here used metaphorically to mean a great degree or distance.</note>. But let us hear your own words. *Antarvetus, page 26:* "An evil spirit taught you to corrupt mixed things upon this false foundation, etc." [You claim] those mixed things are "whole" compared to the things corrupted by us. Chemical essences are said to be made from the destruction of mixtures, and are therefore to be rejected. *On page 21*, the same man infuses and boils mixtures in their total and **WHOLE** state so that they may yield their power; thus, he prefers them to extracts. Those things which are called "whole" there are placed, in his madness, into this very argument under the name of **TOTAL SUBSTANCE**; *Thus, on page 57 of Antarvetus:* "We infuse and boil things that are whole. You [chemists] present them divided into their principles." *And on page 56:* "We use plants not only infused or boiled, but **WHOLE**, whether taken internally or applied externally." Here the word **WHOLE** has another meaning. *Page 86:* "In nothing does the majesty of God shine forth more than in that harmony of the elements, which draws out a balance <term>temperiem</term> <note>the specific proportion of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) that determines a substance's nature</note> or an admirable concord of mixture from contrary natures. But you [chemists] destroy that concord with fire—whose invention is this, if not the Devil’s?" 

Riolan’s "whole" is twofold: one is true, the other is fantastical and plainly delusional. And yet he prefers both to chemical essences. The "true whole" is that which is received from nature and comes into use without separation, as when **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes the Cynic (c. 412–323 BCE), a philosopher famous for living in a tub and advocating for a life according to nature without the "corruptions" of civilization.</note> dines on raw greens, or geese and donkeys feast on grass; [just as] powders are stored in the apothecaries' shops...

-> # GALENIC TRIUMPHS <note>original: *Galenia Triumphs*; likely a sarcastic reference to the supposed "victory" of Galenic medicine over Alchemy.</note> <-

<sig>Mm 2</sig>

...of gems, corals, and many simple medicines, which are combined into various compositions in which the bulk <note>original: *corpus*; literally "body," referring to the physical mass or volume of the drug.</note> likewise remains; although even insects and the nature of donkeys more wisely distinguish the appearance from the matter—a process which is written in the *Art of Mesue* <note>Johannes Mesue the Younger, a pseudo-epigraphical author whose works were central to medieval and Renaissance pharmacy.</note> to be the proper work of Alchemical philosophers who reveal the hidden aspects of things. This "wholeness" of the apothecary shops is so preferred by the censor <note>Jean Riolan, the Parisian doctor Libavius is criticizing.</note> that he attributes the invention of separating things to the Devil. This "imaginary whole" is so delusional that I have never heard or read anything more insane in this genre.

That fool takes whole herbs, roots, and other things—which do not remain whole anyway, as he crushes them with a knife, a pestle, a mill, and other methods—and then boils or infuses them. This done, he strains and presses them. He throws the rest away; if you ask what happened, he responds that the **WHOLE** substance has passed into the liquid, even though he contends that the liquid has received nothing but a naked power <note>original: *vim*; the medicinal "virtue" or potency of a substance.</note> without spirit or juice. Why would you not reject this "whole," in which nothing of the prior substance remains? In such things, there is neither the matter nor the form of the original; furthermore, it is impossible for power to pass into another subject without its own vessel.

But when the chemists extract the essential parts of the whole by casting away the dregs <note>original: *fecib.*; literally "feces," the term for the useless waste material or "dead head" left after a chemical distillation or extraction.</note>, they truly possess the **essential whole** within those parts. This is because they hold the "form" within its own proper and interior matter (we are speaking of the essential and medical <term>form</term> <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "form" is the internal principle that gives a substance its specific properties and medicinal power.</note> of the mixture); these parts, when joined according to the ratio of the whole, are nothing other than the whole itself, which is complete in respect to its integrating members. Hence, here is our triumphant syllogism:

> A true whole is to be preferred to that which is nothing but a figment.

<header>ON THE DEFILEMENTS OF PARISIAN ALCHEMY</header>

> *A chemical extract is a true whole;*
> *because it possesses all parts of the inner essence at once:*
> *However, Riolan’s "whole" is a foolish fiction.*
>
> *Therefore, the chemical extract is to be preferred*
> *over Riolan’s "whole."*

The minor premise <note>In a formal logical argument (syllogism), the minor premise is the second statement that connects a specific case to a general rule.</note> has already been proven. As for whether the "whole" comes first, we reason in this way:

> *An essence that has been purified <note>original: *defecata*; literally "cleansed of dregs," referring to the removal of non-medicinal matter.</note>, whether unified in its parts—as in reunited extracts and elixirs—or divided into its constituent parts (each of which possesses the matter and form of the whole in its own way), is to be preferred to an impure body packed with elementary dregs <note>original: *fecibus*; the waste, sediment, or "gross" material that carries no healing power.</note>.*
>
> *A chemical preparation is such a purified essence, etc. The "wholes" of the [apothecary] shops, left in their natural state, are impure bodies, etc.*
>
> *Therefore, the chemical essence is to be preferred to the bodies found in the apothecary shops.*

The major premise <note>The general rule or universal truth starting the logical argument.</note> is of such manifest truth that it is proven by common dietetics as well as medical dietetics, and moreover by the entire category of the Pharmacopoeia <note>The official collection of medicinal recipes and standards.</note>: decoctions, infusions, pressed oils, juices, linctuses <note>original: *lohot*; a thick, syrupy medicine intended to be licked from a spoon, a term of Arabic origin.</note>, syrups, juleps <note>sweet medicinal drinks.</note>, and others. For all things of this kind possess the appearance and the basic principle <note>original: *rudimentum*; the elementary beginning or seed of a process.</note> of extraction, but the matter must be judged far differently than Riolan has done. Mesue <note>Johannes Mesue, a legendary medical authority whose writings were foundational to pharmacy.</note> proves the minor premise along with the wisest Philosophers of antiquity who are called Alchemists: and indeed the whole assembly of right-thinking people agrees, to such an extent that even Nature herself bears witness to them; for she separates many such pure things by her own motion, just as...

2. *He cooks and infuses the whole substance.* What is the meaning of this? If it were whole, he would cook the whole thing. Yet he denies having written about this. Perhaps it is that Galenic <term>crasis</term> <note>The Galenic concept of *crasis* refers to the specific mixture or "temperament" of the four primary qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—that defines a body's nature.</note>; so that now we do not have cooks of <term>coctile</term> <note>original: *coctilium*; refers to things prepared by cooking or boiling.</note> bodies, but of temperaments. Now, a temperament consists of the hot, cold, moist, and dry, all compounded together, with two additional factors according to "justice and weight" <note>Galen taught that health was a balance of qualities in "justice" (proportion) and "weight" (quantity).</note>. He will, therefore, cook these. 

Or if the "whole substance" is the *form*, he will infuse and cook that. But forms cannot be cooked. Does he cook whole sheep from the flock, or whole plants and trees? Let him by all means boil down the entire apothecary shop. We have no wish to bicker with foolish dreamers. What is the goal of this cooking? Is it that perfection by which what is raw becomes cooked? Not at all; it is so that it may <term>transume</term> <note>original: *transumat*; to take across or transfer qualities from one thing to another without the physical matter.</note>. A marvelous goal! Transume what? The form, the temperament, and the faculties—both manifest and hidden. Into what? Into a liquid. Oh, by the faith of men! 

Is Riolan a magus, that he can "draw down the moon from the sky" <note>A classical literary trope for performing impossible or forbidden magic.</note>, and transfer forms and the rest from their own subject into another? And can he indeed transfer the form and temperament of a mixture into the simple element of water? It is not likely. For Hippocrates, *in his book On the Sacred Disease*, rejects magic. Is he also a transmuter of things, so that he can make a "mixed body" out of simple water without transferring any physical matter, but only the form, power, temperament, and properties—both manifest and hidden? This is the mark of a madman. For it is certain that this cannot be done. The entire nature of mixture...

## ON THE FALSE ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIANS <note>original: *ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS.*; Libavius is critiquing a group of Parisian physicians, specifically Jean Riolan, who opposed the use of chemical medicines.</note>

What is a mixture, insofar as it is a mixture, is mixed as a whole; but under that whole are particular mixtures. You mix whole qualities with wholes; but not bodies. Since the foundation of the qualities is distributed unevenly, there arises that diversity which appears in the magnet in one part...

But when an <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property or quality (like color, heat, or weight) that exists in a substance but is not essential to what that substance is.</note> migrates, that from which it migrates is deprived of the very thing that migrates. You say: "That is true regarding the same number <note>meaning a specific, individual instance of a quality</note>, but not regarding the species and genus." "Very fine," I say. But Riolan wants it to migrate in such a way that nothing remains in the prior <term>subject</term> <note>The "subject" is the physical matter or body that "hosts" a quality.</note>, following the example of infusions of rhubarb and similar things, whose entire potency is poured out so that nothing remains but a "corpse" <note>original: *cadaver*; here referring to the spent or exhausted plant matter left behind after its medicinal virtues have been extracted.</note>. Those things which are shared by species do not pass by any other movement unless by alteration, generation, or local movement—whether individually or combined. Transfer through local motion carries its subject along, either in whole or in part—as when the spirit, in which the purging power existed in the form of a coagulation or other suitable state, is transferred; or the juice or another internal part; or even the whole, as happens in Galenic powders and <term>electuaries</term> <note>Medicinal pastes made by mixing powders with honey or syrup, which are then dissolved in liquid to be swallowed.</note> which, once mixed into a liquid, are drunk as one. By the transmigration of the spirit and juice in which the quality resided, the former subject is emptied out. In alteration and generation, this is not necessary, unless it perishes for some other reason—as when someone expires during the venereal act <note>sexual intercourse</note> because their spirit and heat are exhausted, or when apoplexy <note>a stroke</note> and so on supervenes. There is a subtle reasoning concerning sensory objects and images propagated to a mirror, and reflected from there, as Aristotle maintains regarding the Rainbow <note>A reference to Aristotle's *Meteorology*, where he explains the rainbow as a reflection of sight or light.</note>. <meta>This page continues Libavius’s critique of Jean Riolan’s theories on the "migration" of qualities. ## THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM

...Not even the image of Riolan’s face in a mirror, and from there into a thousand others (for this can happen, especially if he is viewed from on high by an infinite army of men, just as a single star presents itself to the eyes of everyone in the entire hemisphere), fails to remain in his own face. But it *does* remain. Therefore, it does not migrate. Yet it is seen in the mirror. I say it is seen, but it is not the same thing in number as that which is in his face; rather, it is its propagated <term>species</term> <note>In the physics of this period, a "species" was an image or likeness that an object "sent out" through the air so it could be perceived by the eye.</note>. And indeed, that which stays fixed on the face should not be called an image, but the original form, of which the image is that which appears in the mirror.

Aristotle thought this happened through refraction in the third book of his *Meteorology* <note>original: *3. meteor:*</note>: as if the image were reflected once received in a smooth body. He says the cause of all these things—the Rainbow <note>original: *Iris*</note>, Sun-dogs <note>original: *Parelia*</note>, and so on—is the same. For all these are the result of refraction, which he explains by way of mirrors, some of which reflect only heat, and some also the figure. Thus, Riolan should have been all the less inclined to assert that an <term>accident</term> <note>A property or quality (like color or heat) that exists in a substance but is not part of its essential nature.</note> transmigrates. 

The censorious medical school of the Parisians can find a similar reasoning in the lecture halls <note>original: *subsellis*</note> of Germany. For when the light of a transparent act is diffused in every direction, it is terminated upon a solid, opaque body according to the nature of the thing that bounds it. Thus, a union and a certain common form are created in which color exists together with the likeness of the figure. Light, however, is active and dispersive; air and water are divisible elements. Therefore, the light, having been shaped and colored at its boundary, multiplies its likeness through the divisibility of the medium. From this it happens that, once propagated to a proper distance, it shines back in receptive surfaces, some of which catch only the heat, while others also catch the figure.

<summary>Libavius uses the physics of mirrors and light to argue against Riolan, explaining that qualities (like an image or medicinal power) do not physically "migrate" from one body to another, but rather propagate as "species" through a medium.</summary>

# OF THE SPURIOUS PARTS OF ALCHEMY

For not every material is capable of receiving a shape. Furthermore, both the heat and the shape are modified in the meantime by the nature of the medium through which they pass, and by the nature of the recipient. This is why our face in mirrors appears pale or flushed, more or less distorted, round, long, spread out, or compressed, and so on. If the form itself were to transmigrate <note>In this context, to "transmigrate" means for a quality to literally leave one object and move into another, like a soul moving between bodies.</note> from within us, we would meanwhile be unable to be seen by others, because we would lack a visible form. Learn these things from the "German man," Riolanus <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a French physician who defended traditional Galenic medicine against the new chemical medicine of the Paracelsians.</note>, although I do not think that lights are lacking in France or other studious nations from whom you might hear the same or better things, if you wish.

### III.

->The heat of a glowing coal, without any physical outflow, is seen to be carried to a distant object through the intervening air.<-
->The heat of a coal is an <term>accident</term> <note>A property that exists in a subject but is not essential to its nature, such as color, weight, or temperature.</note>.<-
->Therefore, certain accidents migrate from one subject to another.<-

The major premise is declared; because without the spirit <note>original: *spiritu*—here meaning a subtle physical vapor or essence</note> of the coal, the neighboring air grows hot, and then by succession is carried all the way to the object. To this major premise, we respond with our: **IT DOES NOT SEEM SO**. For that propagation happens partly by alteration <note>The process by which a quality, like heat, changes a substance without changing its essence.</note>, and partly by a warm breath <note>original: *halitu*</note> being communicated. A plentiful and evident proof of this is found in the German **steam-rooms** <note>original: *vaporaria*—these could refer to public baths or the heated rooms common in German houses.</note>, which are sometimes heated by veterinarians using scraps of leather and other things, the exhalation of which is perceived immediately. Indeed, the nostrils sometimes sense the "breath" of the heat more quickly than the skin feels the warmth. Here, a transformation also takes place. For the air nearest the flame becomes fiery and accommodates itself to the natural agent. Thus, it sometimes glows so fiercely around cooking pots that kindling <note>original: *cremia*</note> moved near it will burst into flame...

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM <note>original: *Galenia Triumphus*. Galen was the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories of humors dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note>

...I pass over the fact that such a migration cannot occur here, since a flame does not remain numerically the same for even a moment. There is an old axiom: Two <term>accidents</term> <note>Properties that exist in a subject but are not essential to its nature, such as color or heat.</note> of the same species which are numerically distinct cannot exist at the same time in one subject. For example, the heat that communicates and the heat that is communicated cannot be in the same air at the same time. In the winter hours, iron tools, waters, and similar things become so cold from the touching air that they exceed every degree of moderation. Yet the air itself is cold nonetheless. It retains the quality by which it is affected; it does not send it into exile.

### IV.

*Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a German physician and chemist who sought to bridge traditional medicine and new chemical discoveries.</note> writes in his "Antigramania" that the purging power is deposited from antimony <note>A metallic element often used in early modern medicine as an emetic to induce vomiting or as a laxative.</note> into a liquid through boiling or soaking.*

->*Therefore, an accident passes from one subject to another.*<-

But you cite Libavius unfortunately, and you show by your own example that knowledge does not migrate from the teacher into the student. Instead, if the subject is suitable and his mind is capable of that discipline, it is birthed through "Socratic love" as described in Plato's *Symposium*; if not, he remains a fool or degenerates. Libavius writes that "glass of antimony" loses nothing of its weight, and yet it yields a purging liquid. How, in his own judgment, could the quality have passed? Furthermore, he says that the thing altered follows the nature of the thing altering it, which does not cease to be the alterer, but remains so, unless it fades away by another means, such as evaporation, etc. Alteration propagates the same quality in *kind* <note>original: *specie*</note>, not in *number* <note>original: *numero*. Philosophically, this means the "type" of heat is shared, but the "individual instance" of heat stays with the source.</note>. He adds thirdly that some wish for the <term>spirit</term> <note>In alchemy/early medicine, a "spirit" was a subtle, volatile substance or vapor that carried the active powers of a drug.</note> to be communicated at the same time, in the way...

> *If posterity approved the doctrine of the Arabs and their additions to the medicine of Hippocrates and Galen, it is necessary that it also approved the chemical art, by which the species is separated from matter and that which is hidden in things becomes known.*

And that first part is true, even by Riolan’s <note>Jean Riolan the Elder or Younger, prominent Parisian physicians and staunch defenders of traditional Galenism against the new "chemical" medicine.</note> admission.
Therefore, this second part is also true.

**T**he foundation of this connection is this: Alchemy is a branch of the teachings of the Arabs, which Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose works dominated medieval European medicine.</note> explained, and whose <term>magisteries</term> <note>from *magisteriis*; refers to the master-preparations or refined chemical essences of a substance.</note> and essences he himself employed; it is an art that Mesue <note>Masawaih al-Mardini, a prominent 11th-century pharmacologist.</note> recommended to Physicians, which Albucasis <note>Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936–1013), an influential surgeon and chemist.</note> celebrated, and which none of their followers despises. Thus far, the response to the examination of the seventeen arguments regarding the common preference has been thoroughly scrutinized. It has been discovered that the censorious School of Paris has brought forth nothing but the foulest errors and intolerable insanity; they have nitpicked at words here and there, but have resolved no objection, or have only attempted a solution recklessly. Therefore, we lead these defeated censors, bound and shut up in the cage of ignorance like certain rabid beasts; if they can grow tame therein, so that henceforth they neither bark nor bite, then all is well. ### 8. The Condemnation of the Fourth Sect
He condemns the fourth sect. But you have barely touched upon it with even a few words. What indeed was that school, which at the conclusion of its "Censorial Apology" condemned not only the <term>Spagyric</term> <note>Spagyric: A term coined by Paracelsus, referring to the production of medicines through the alchemical process of separation and recombination.</note> books of Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent physician and alchemist who advocated for chemical remedies.</note>, but even <term>Spagyria</term> itself? For this reason, it pleaded in the vestibule of the Senate that it should prohibit the <term>Spagyrists</term>, even wishing for those using chemical medicines to be put to death!

Posterity will marvel that the SCHOOL—which ought to consist of many wise and honorable men—could lie so shamelessly and boldly to those currently living. I speak of those Physicians who, by common counsel and consent (as Riolanus <note>Jean Riolan the elder or younger, staunch defenders of traditional medicine and enemies of alchemy.</note>, their Dictator and Champion, writes), opposed themselves to <term>Alchemy</term>. If it is a college and council of lies and voices of madness, is it unjust to name them so? From a good tree comes good fruit; from a bad tree, bad fruit. **"From the claw, the lion; from the ears, the donkey,"** <note>original: ex vngue leo: ex auribus asinus. Proverbial expressions meaning a creature is known by its parts; here, the school is recognized as foolish by the "ears" of its arguments.</note> and by its braying.

<meta>image quality: excellent; catchword: effen- (likely continuing "essentiam" or "effectum")</meta>

In that argument <note>Referring to the syllogism on the previous page regarding certain vs. uncertain knowledge.</note> there is so much force that it immediately wore down even the adamantine hardness and shamelessness of the **Sophist's** <note>Libavius uses "Sophist" as a derogatory term for his opponent from the Paris Medical Faculty, implying they use clever but fallacious arguments.</note> brow; it must be illustrated somewhat. I was then looking generally at those things which today are best known to us, both communicated by the **Arabs** <note>Referring to the medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna and Rhazes, who introduced many chemical processes and new drugs to the West.</note> and recently discovered and observed by unerring experts. These are called **new** things in respect to those which **Hippocrates** and **Galen** <note>The two primary authorities of ancient Greek medicine.</note> knew. There is no doubt that they are to be preferred to those things which even today remain in dispute. Therefore, one should not despise something under the title of "new things," as the censor has often done.

If new things are not to be condemned or rejected for this reason, neither are **chemical** things, which are new in terms of specific knowledge and application, but not in reality and general knowledge. Furthermore, if those things which are explored also internally and in their recondite essence—and that plainly, without coverings and impure dregs by which we are often deceived—are to be preferred to things known only crudely and by their external form, then another **prerogative** <term>prerogative</term> <note>original: "prærogatiua." Here meaning a specific advantage or superior claim of one thing over another.</note> arises, which is proper to **chemical essences**; so that in this same argument we may obtain two points, the first of which is in the comparison of wholes with wholes; for the things known to us are to be preferred to the things known to Galen, many of which are unknown to us and cannot be clarified by him. The second point is in the comparison of things known to us in different ways. For without a doubt, that which is known as to what it is, what quality it has, and how effective it is internally according to all its parts...

<header>ON THE CHEMICAL SCURRILITY OF PARIS</header>

...we have known its essences, and its outward form at the same time; rather than what we have known at least by an external gazing upon the coverings of a buried thing, where we have only gained a perspective as far as the "bark" <note>Libavius uses the metaphor of "bark" or "rind" (Latin: *cortex*) to describe the superficial, outward appearance of a plant or medicine compared to its internal chemical "essence."</note> through taste and smell. The former is chemical; the latter is common apothecary-work; indeed, it is mere merchant-trade.

Tell me, French Vintner: Would you prefer your own grape, or that which was born for **Noah**, <note>A reference to the biblical Noah, who was traditionally considered the first to plant a vineyard (Genesis 9:20).</note> or that which comes from **America**? <note>Libavius is comparing familiar, local knowledge with the exotic and unknown drugs then flooding Europe from the New World.</note> You know your own—what it is and of what quality—but are you ignorant of those others? You answer: "Mine," without a doubt. But do you prefer the grape or the **must**; <note>Must is freshly crushed grape juice that contains the skins, seeds, and stems before fermentation.</note> or do you prefer the must or the **wine** when a drink is required? Certainly the wine, and specifically your own, which the wine-merchant has not adulterated. Or rather, you will choose that which you have tested with your own rough chemistry—by which water is separated—to ensure it has no water mixed in, rather than the adulterated version. You will throw away the water extracted from the adulterated wine, and you will drink the wine itself. 

Chemists can even endure the common people passing judgment through these sorts of likenesses. **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (2nd century AD), the primary authority for traditional medicine, whom Libavius argues would have actually supported chemical analysis if he were alive.</note> desired that knowledge through the separation of parts; yet the **Galenists** <note>The followers of Galen, specifically the conservative doctors of the Paris Medical Faculty who opposed chemical medicine.</note> reject and mock it now that it has been found—they are all the more degenerate as disciples! That which Galen himself would prefer, and indeed did prefer in his own wishes, should reasonably be put first. But Galen preferred things known according to all the parts of their essence over things known to him only as a whole. Indeed, that censorious school <note>Meaning the Medical Faculty of Paris.</note> does not hesitate to prefer an infusion to a whole piece of **Rhubarb**. <note>original: "Rheo"</note> But this infusion is chemical in its origin, and if it is made in an essential liquor, it is chemical in its entire operation. Tell me now, Natural Philosophers, Phy-
->sicians,<-

### Chapter 53.

->*The second argument concerning the preference for chemical remedies, regarding page 36 of the Examination of the Mania, page 86.*<-

**T**he force of this argument was: If **chemical remedies** <term>chymica</term> <note>Libavius refers here to medicines prepared through distillation or extraction, rather than raw herbs.</note> in the greatest evils, such as **Stroke** <term>Apoplexia</term>, **Epilepsy** <term>Epilepsia</term>, **Paralysis** <term>Paralysis</term>, etc., provide help more swiftly, more pleasantly, and more safely than the unrefined preparations of the apothecary shops, then they are to be preferred to them. And yet they do provide it, as a comparison by experience shows in those cases, as well as in **fainting** <term>syncope</term>, **fainting fits** <term>Lipothymia</term>, **suffocation of the womb** <term>vteri strangulatu</term> <note>A historical diagnosis often called "hysterical suffocation," believed to be caused by the womb moving within the body.</note>, difficult childbirth, and others. **Riolan’s** <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent French physician and fierce defender of Galenic tradition against chemical medicine.</note> mania contradicts this argument because he claims that in **Epilepsy** or **Stroke** caused by the blood, **bloodletting** <term>venæ sectio</term> <note>The surgical practice of opening a vein to drain blood, a staple of Galenic therapy.</note> helps more quickly. But this is a wretched sophism. **Surgery** <term>Chirurgia</term> is not being compared here with **Pharmacy** <term>Pharmaceutice</term>; rather, remedies prepared in different ways are being compared with one another. **Bloodletting** <term>Phlebotomia</term> is a common aid to **chemical physicians** <term>chymiatris</term> and all others alike. Furthermore, if a **physical medicine** <term>materiale medicamentum</term> is to be set aside simply because **bloodletting** is more effective in some instances, then you might as well reject the entire apothecary's shop in favor of those who come after. All of Riolan’s medicine, insofar as it is separated from **Surgery**, would have to be demoted from its rank whenever a tooth needs to be pulled or the skin needs **scarifying** <term>scarificanda</term> <note>A procedure involving making shallow incisions in the skin.</note>. And so that "Mistress" [Medicine] would no longer pride herself in her majesty, but would be forced to [yield] her throne...

...to yield to a servant of a **Surgeon** <term>Chirurgus</term> <note>In the 16th and 17th centuries, university-trained physicians often looked down on surgeons as mere manual laborers or "servants."</note>. Thus that purple-clad school <note>A reference to the red robes worn by the doctors of the Paris Medical Faculty.</note> becomes a mockery even to bath-house attendants. I see your ignorance.

After **bloodletting** <term>venae sectio</term>, these spirits can stimulate nature to discharge waste; they can clear the remnants of an obstruction. And if by chance Riolan’s conjecture about the blood is false, and the **blasting** <term>syderatio</term> <note>From the Latin "syderatio," originally meaning a "blasting" by the stars; it refers to a sudden loss of sense or motion, such as a stroke or seizure.</note> arises from an astral or hidden cause, they can correct the rashness of a deceived scholastic. Finally, they can also strengthen the body and preserve it so that the **seizure** <term>paroxysmus</term> does not return—and do so far more effectively and swiftly than whole, unrefined substances; indeed, with greater pleasure and more successful skill in their use. 

Dull powders, disgusting decoctions, and massive infusions do not have a place everywhere, especially where nature still languishes and cannot activate a sluggish medicine—indeed, can scarcely take it in. Obstruction is located at the source of the nerves, along with the weakness of nature’s instrument and the laziness of the **animal spirits** <term>spiritus animales</term> <note>In traditional physiology, "animal spirits" were the subtle fluids that flowed through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note>. Because our **Essences** <term>Essentiae</term> are very close to being active—for when only slightly moved they exhale powerful vapors—they can be activated in the mouth, the nostrils, the sutures of the skull, and the arteries. 

Even those who seize upon **burning water** <term>aqua ardens</term> <note>Distilled alcohol, also known as aqua vitae.</note> and apply decoctions, infusions, oils, and similar basics of **chemistry** <term>chymia</term> are forced to admit this. Riolan knows these things too. But a hostile hatred forbids him from admitting it. He places his only hope in **bloodletting** <term>venae sectio</term>—the Parisian style, naturally. If the **chemical physicians** <term>chymiatri</term> <note>Physicians who advocated for the use of chemical and alchemical preparations.</note> agree that the cure lies in that alone, they do not apply essences. But if the cure is in that alone, then what is the purpose of the scraps and messes from your apothecary shops?

<margin>Riolan’s ignorance regarding phlegmatic stroke.</margin>
Now **phlegmatic stroke** <term>Apoplexia pituitosa</term> <note>A "stroke" or loss of consciousness believed by ancient doctors to be caused by an excess of "phlegm," one of the four bodily humors.</note> is brought forward. For this, too, it is said that **bloodletting** <term>Phlebotomia</term> is beneficial by reason of the preceding cause. Let us imagine that is so. Yet the **chemical physician** <term>chymiater</term> can also use that same surgical instrument. Why do you hold back your **medicine boxes** <term>Pyxides</term>? Yet that **sedentary doctor** <term>Sellularius Medicus</term> <note>A derogatory term used by chemists to describe university physicians who "sit in chairs" and theorize rather than working with their hands in a laboratory.</note> denies that an abundance of phlegm can be removed by any such ready remedy: And yet, that disease-causing **phlegm** <term>pituita</term> is neither in the blood nor in the veins, but near the origin of the nerves in the brain, according to the Galenists. To rouse one from a phlegmatic stroke, our **essences** <term>essentiæ</term> are far more penetrating and effective than your little broths, powders, **electuaries** <note>A paste made of medicinal powders mixed with honey or syrup.</note> and similar things. And so, both in well-stocked pharmacies and in the medicine chests of princes, there are chemical balms, **Theriacal waters** <note>Distilled waters containing Theriac, a famous ancient multi-ingredient compound used as a universal antidote.</note>, anti-stroke waters, anti-epileptic waters, and so on—all of them chemical preparations of immediate action. If the patient is not roused by these, you will be as useless as a chattering swallow. What about **fainting** <term>syncope</term> and **choking** <term>strangulatus</term>? The evidence of the truth forces you to grant something to our essences over your unrefined substances. But lest that be without some trickery, you add that the **symptom** is removed, but not the **cause** of the disease. We accept this.
That which more swiftly removes a terrifying and dangerous **symptom** <term>symptoma</term>—one so 
<margin>Riolan defeated by his own confession.</margin>
perilous that it demands the primary care be directed toward itself—is to be preferred over a sluggish remedy. Chemical essences remove symptoms more swiftly than the sluggish substances of the apothecary shops. Therefore, they are to be preferred over them.

# ALCHEMY REGARDING THE SPURIOUS DOCTORS OF PARIS

But what, at last, removes the cause of the disease? Dogmatic medicine, you say? O, you poor fool. Even chemical remedies have their dogmatic <note>In this context, "dogmatic" refers to "Rational" medicine—the traditional academic approach based on logic and ancient theories—as opposed to purely empirical or "folk" medicine.</note> uses. But I say, if there is a need to purge anywhere, the **chemical physicians** <term>chymiatri</term> do not lack effective essences; these are better because they simultaneously inhibit the symptoms. Your little broths often induce **fainting** <term>lipothymia</term> <note>A sudden loss of strength or "sinking feeling," often leading to unconsciousness.</note> rather than preventing it. 

But let us hear how "hysterical" women <note>Referring to *suffocatio intellectus* or "suffocation of the womb," a condition then believed to be caused by the womb wandering or emitting vapors.</note> are treated.

And if they do, **essential** [chemical] preparations are better than **whole** [crude] ones: the very forms of the enemas themselves bear witness to this. For they are made through an extractive decoction. 

*2. Foul-smelling things are applied to the nostrils.* But I say, in this you are no better a doctor than the common women who burn feathers and rubbish; whatever they achieve, they achieve by the power of the vapor. Where are your "whole" substances now? The chemist will more honorably apply his balsam made of **castor** <term>castoreum</term> <note>A potent scent gland secretion from beavers used in medicine to treat nervous ailments.</note>, of **amber** <term>succinum</term>, and similar things; or he will smear on appropriate waters. Since a small amount can do much, and they are very easily distributed and dissipate the suffocating spirit, they can also be successfully dripped into the mouth.

For in its **whole** [crude] state it is quite sluggish. The chemist dissolves it in oil of mace, and does so instantly; if the distilled oil is not at hand, liquid ambergris can take its place. ...[materia]ls extracted, such as **Musk** and **Civet** <note>original: *Moschus* and *Zibetha*. > *Spiritual remedies are more powerful in hysterical cases.*

Therefore.

If spiritual things are to be preferred, then much more so are the **essential spirits**, which the chemists possess in many visible, coagulated forms: for example, as found in Mesue <note>Referring to the works of Mesue the Younger, a standard pharmaceutical authority of the time.</note>, there is oil of **Jet**, of **eggs**, of **bricks** <note>original: *ol. Gagatæ, ouorum, laterum*. Oil of bricks was made by quenching hot bricks in oil and then distilling the result; it was used for joint pain.</note>, and of **juniper**, etc. These are far more effective than the "bodies" from which they come; indeed, they are better than the vapors that normally breathe out of the whole, raw ingredients. The author is likely arguing that chemical "attraction" is more sophisticated than the physical suction of cupping or the cutting of veins.</note>. 

Hear now a **false logic** <term>Paralogiſmus</term> worthy of that most foolish school:

> Let them agree (says Riolan): [chemical essences help] in these few accidents of disease (namely **fainting** <term>ſyncopæ</term>, **suffocation** <term>ſtrangulatui</term>, **loss of consciousness** <term>lipothymiæ</term>, etc.), yet they harm many more. For there are few major diseases without fever, and without some inflammation of a part or the whole, and your essences harm these.

### Regarding the Logical Form

> *That which harms fevers and inflammation helps few major diseases and harms many.*
> *Chemical essences harm fevers and inflammation.*
> *Therefore, chemical essences help few major diseases and harm many.*

# THE ALCHEMY OF SPURIOUS PARIS

<margin>Riolan says that better things come from his adversaries.</margin>

He comes to overturn my syllogism with this false reasoning <note>original: *paralogismo*. A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note>. I have corrected my rash tongue, having learned better from the arguments of **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Du Chesne (1544–1609), a prominent French physician and chemist who championed Paracelsian medicine.</note>, **Harvetus** <note>Israel Harvet, a pro-chemical physician who defended Du Chesne against the conservative Paris Medical Faculty.</note>, and others. For the *Apologia* <note>Likely referring to a specific defensive text in the ongoing "Antimony War" between chemical and traditional doctors in Paris.</note> posited that hardly any acute disease exists without fever. The proof of the **major premise** is that few "great" diseases exist without them. We, however, pronounce that major premise to be deceptive. 

**Fever** and **inflammation** are considered either as a disease in themselves, or as a symptom. If they are symptoms: the <term>proposition</term> <note>A formal statement or premise in an argument.</note> is false. For although a remedy might be unsuitable for the fever itself, it can still be suitable for the underlying disease; once that disease is removed directly, the symptom is removed as a consequence. 

But if they are diseases in themselves, even if the remedies do not match them directly, they still provide help when applied by circumstance—in the same way that <term>Erysipelas</term> <note>A bacterial skin infection, often called "St. Anthony's Fire," characterized by bright red inflammation.</note> is cured by thermal baths, lye-washes, soaps, and the like. **Edemas** <note>original: *œdemata*. Swellings caused by fluid in the tissues.</note> are removed by dissolving and dissipating agents boiled in wine; and so on with other conditions, as was said above. **Horace** <note>The Roman poet (65–8 BCE), here cited for his mention of medical treatments in his Satires or Epistles.</note> expels disease and bile with undiluted <term>Hellebore</term> <note>A plant used as a powerful and potentially toxic purgative in ancient and early modern medicine.</note> during a quartan fever. **Phlegmatic** fevers are driven away by the **essence of pepper**; **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician (980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook for centuries.</note> purges them, etc. 

The **minor premise** is disgraceful because of its specific logical flaw. Not all chemical essences are of the same kind. He is mistaken who pronounces the same judgment on all of them. If the <term>Galenic</term> <note>Refers to the traditional followers of Galen, who used plant-based, "humoral" medicine rather than chemical "essences."</note> pharmacies have remedies against fevers and **phlegmons** <note>original: *phlegmonas*. Acute inflammations or localized abscesses.</note>, then the chemical pharmacies have them too, for they take their essences from the whole of nature and art—no matter how much that unrefined school may babble. Furthermore, if the fevers are merely symptoms, we do not worry about a small and momentary harm from the medicine, because once the primary disease is healed, the symptom will either fade away on its own or be easily removed by appropriate means; this is a common axiom. Unless a symptom is especially urgent, the indication drawn from the essence of the disease is more powerful...

He defends the diversity of chemical remedies against the "unrefined" traditional Galenic school.</summary>

<meta>catchword: Waters</meta>

...[appli]cation, after consideration and consultation concerning the assistance and preservation of nature, which heals the disease first. More wisely than these censors, **Paré** <note>Ambroise Paré (c. 1510–1590), the legendary French royal surgeon who often favored practical experience over rigid theory.</note> recommends spirit of wine <note>distilled alcohol</note> and malmsey wine with **Theriac** <note>original: *Theriaca*. A famous ancient "universal" medicine made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium.</note> for a **quartan fever** <note>a type of malaria where the fever recurs every fourth day</note>. Experience testifies that by these remedies, as if by fires, the matter of the fever is consumed and the fever itself vanishes; we can prove this by many other examples. For there is the same relationship between the cause and the disease as there is between the disease and its symptom.

It must also be noted that **Riolan**, fascinated by the folly of the **primary qualities** <note>The Galenic system relied on the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, thinks of nothing more "divine" regarding diseases, even though—as **Hippocrates** says in *On the Sacred Disease* <note>original: *de morbo sacro*. A famous treatise arguing that epilepsy was a natural, not a supernatural, ailment.</note>—all diseases are divine. The **Chemists** <note>original: *Chymici*. Refers to the Paracelsian or "Spagyric" physicians who used chemical extraction.</note> cannot indeed entirely strip these qualities from essences. However, because it requires little talent to simply temper those qualities, they are more concerned with **essential properties**. These properties cannot be hindered by the primary elements, as is clear in the case of **Philonium** <note>A famous opiate electuary named after Philo of Tarsus.</note>, whose opium—despite being mixed among so many "heating" ingredients—nonetheless acts according to the condition of its own essence <note>i.e., it still induces sleep despite the presence of "hot" spices.</note>.

The greatest physicians study **appropriated remedies** <note>Medicines that target specific organs or diseases through "occult" or hidden powers rather than just temperature.</note>. These do not act by primary or secondary qualities, but by an **astral and occult power**. Nature herself has taught this, having bestowed a purging power upon things that are cold, hot, astringent, or laxative. This is evident in **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyro*.</note>, copper, iron, lead, white and black **antimony** <note>original: *stibii*.</note>, metallic glasses, and similar substances which are usually categorized by some as being "cold" in nature. Riolan himself claims that **Elephantiasis** <note>In this period, a term for severe skin diseases like leprosy.</note> is caused by **adustion** <note>The "burning" or scorching of bodily humors, making them thick and acrid.</note>. Yet **Galen** saw it cured by wine infused with vipers, and **Capivaccius** <note>Girolamo Capivacci (1523–1589), an influential physician at the University of Padua.</note> cures it with viper oil and theriacal salt.

<header>OF ALCHEMY BY THE PSEUDO-PARISIANS</header>

The Theriacal Water <note>original: *Aqua Theriacali*. A distilled medicinal water containing Theriac, a complex ancient remedy made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium.</note> of **Sylvius** <note>Jacques Dubois (1478–1555), a famous French anatomist and teacher of Vesalius.</note> and **Fernel** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician who introduced the term "physiology."</note> provide great help for **quartan fevers** <note>a form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day</note> and mania, as do the even more burning waters of **Riolan** (provided any could truly be so hot); they also find great relief in **Gesner’s** <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss polymath known for his botanical and medical works.</note> Oxymel of Hellebore <note>A syrup of honey and vinegar infused with hellebore, a plant used as a powerful purgative.</note>.
