A similar judgment applies to similar cases. The [Galenic] school is especially hostile toward minerals. Yet these minerals, least of all, exhibit those "wicked" qualities which **Riolan** fears so much in fevers, since they are, as it were, <gloss>qualityless</gloss> <note>original Greek: *ἄποια*. A philosophical term for matter that lacks the four primary qualities of hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note>. But let even these minerals have their "little spark" of heat; for it is easy for **Riolan** to blow hot and cold from the same mouth: whenever he wishes to use them, let him breathe in a little cold, and the heat will evaporate.

### Chapter 54.

->*The third argument for preferring chemical remedies,*<-
->*page 87 of the "Maniographia."*<-

**T**his was declared to them: the more industriously a thing has been prepared, the more suitably it is rendered for medical use; because the industry of art is added to nature, such a thing is superior to those not so prepared. Chemical remedies are of this sort. You are mistaken, Riolan. Your wicked instability commands you to shake with lies that which you cannot conquer with the truth. ## CHAPTER LV.

### Fourth Argument for preferring chemical remedies, regarding page 87 of the manuscript.

The **PREMISE** of this argument is: Chemical remedies are not only easier for restoration and nutrition within <term>Dietetics</term> <note>The branch of medicine concerned with the whole regimen of life, including food, exercise, and environment, rather than just drugs</note>; but they are also like something divine when one’s strength fails; they are admirable in surgery, and so excellent in <term>pharmaceuticals</term> <note>original: *pharmaceutica*—the art of preparing and dispensing medicines</note> that even their enemies are forced to embrace their preparations. Parisian methods cannot be compared to these; therefore, chemical remedies are to be preferred. 

The madness of **Riolan**, having omitted the latter two parts of therapeutics <note>Surgery and pharmacy</note>, only snaps at dietetics, silently implying that the school of censors has lost two out of the three parts of medical practice. Let us follow where he leads. 

Diet belongs either to the healthy or to the sick. The former does not require chemical remedies; the latter consists in the moderation of the <term>six non-natural things</term> <note>A standard medical concept of the time: the six external factors that determine health—air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, evacuation and repletion, and the passions of the mind</note>. 

What is to be concluded from this? Certainly, so that the reasoning might fit his thesis: that chemicals are not excellent <term>analeptics</term> <note>Medicines used to restore or "pick up" a patient's strength</note> and divine restorers of strength in a sudden collapse. But this false reasoning errs by the fallacy of "it does not follow." To the healthy, insofar as they are healthy, not even a Galenic physician would prescribe anything, except perhaps a <term>Hippocratic</term> <note>Referring to the teachings of Hippocrates, the "Father of Medicine"</note> rule 
<margin>*The book on Airs, Waters, and Places.*</margin>
such as this: "Whoever is healthy and strong, he [makes] no distinction..." <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "crimen" on the next page suggests the sentence continues regarding how the healthy need no special regimen.</note>

Rather, water of meat is water **EXTRACTED** by decoction from finely chopped meat, until it flows out from them by sweating <note>original: *refudando*</note>, and in which the meat is fried, the strained liquid of which is served as a drink. 

Thus says Avicenna, who does not recommend those "Riolanian" broths consisting of impure waters and the immature juice of meats, but rather a **chemical extraction** which is performed through a roasting that is simultaneously extracting and maturing; by this method, the masters of the "Great Work" <note>the *magisterium*, or the highest level of alchemical practice</note> also prepare other things. By what method that water is actually extracted so that the meat is fried in it at the same time—and that boiling is joined with roasting, as indicated by the words "sweating" and "frying"—let Riolan ponder; or, if he is unable, let him take our "puffers" <note>original: *sufflones*—a derogatory term for alchemists who worked the bellows, here reclaimed by the author as a title of expertise</note> as his teachers. 

If it pleases you "to fix a star in the heavens," as **Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a philosopher and polymath to whom many later alchemical works were attributed</note> says: the cordial waters are in the vessel on the "earth" <note>the bottom of the distillation apparatus</note>, while the minced meat hangs near the boundaries of the "heaven" <note>the top or "head" of the vessel</note>, enclosed on all sides so that the spirit does not fly away. When heat is applied from below, the dissolved waters rise, and having condensed, they settle around the minced meat, and from there they circulate...

## CHAPTER 57.

### *Argument VI: Concerning the preference for chemical remedies, regarding manuscript page 89.*

**C**HEMICAL matters <note>original: *CHYMICA*; at this time, chemistry and alchemy were part of the same discipline focused on extracting the "active" part of a substance.</note> have been held in greater admiration since ancient times, and were more highly recommended—so much so that they were even kept among the secrets of kings and wise men, removed from the use of the common people. Hippocratic remedies, however, were exposed to everyone, and although they were not looked down upon by the wise, they were nevertheless valued less because of the impurities mixed into their essences. Coarse and bran-filled bread is suitable enough for rustic stomachs; but kings, princes, and philosophers—those educated more liberally and studiously for the performance of great deeds—selected the kernel of the grain. From coarse and filthy food, from murky and stale air, and likewise from impure water, the senses become less sharp and refined. Purer and more essential (or "formal") things have carried every point of privilege <note>A reference to winning unanimous approval, from the Roman custom of "carrying the vote."</note>. What is the point of these follies?

<header>PART OF THE ALCHEMY OF SEVERINUS.</header>

## PART OF THE ALCHEMY OF SEVERINUS. <note>Petrus Severinus (1542–1602) was a Danish physician and an influential proponent of Paracelsian medicine, which emphasized chemistry over traditional herbalism.</note>

...by the study of the more liberal arts <note>Continuing from the word "liberalio-" on the previous page.</note> through which you strive to disparagingly take away from this "flower" <note>Metaphor for the flourishing state of chemical medicine.</note> of ours. That which is fraudulent, an empty promise, or harmful does not flourish among princes; rather, it is crushed by the first or second experiment before it can ever come to bloom. If this branch of medicine flourished among them more than the medicine chests <note>original: *pyxides*; small boxes used by apothecaries to hold pills or ointments.</note> of Hippocrates, it is certain that it possessed greater dignity and preeminence.

You add: "Let the preparatory part flourish." I agree. But your own workshop, which is opposed to the chemists, also falls by this very argument. That which princes and wise men embrace and follow more closely is worthier and more distinguished than that which they omit or cast aside to the common people. You ask: "Is it a fourth sect?" An "old wives' refuge" <note>original: *γραοσφύγετον* (graosphygeton); a derogatory term implying a hiding place for trivialities or superstitions.</note>, that is, something fit for old women. There is nothing about a "fourth sect" in this argument. Move on. 

This praise is common to Hippocratic medicine. Indeed, Apollo and Aesculapius are even held to have been gods. From them, Hippocrates arose. Truly, all medicines are created by the true God, and the wise man does not despise them. But when there is a dispute over whether to prefer these medicines in their pure or impure states, that which princes and philosophers have admired and cultivated more is to be preferred. ...to boil with fever, and thus to suffer against nature. But natural [heat] is active toward natural constitution and operations. Here, that [febrile heat] is not even truly active. For it has no action suited to nature; and yet the actions of agents are disposed toward the patient <note>The author is using a scholastic principle: for an "agent" (like a medicine or heat) to act, the "patient" (the body) must be in a state to receive that action.</note>. But febrile heat heats more: in a feverish way, I say. Natural [heat] also heats more; but naturally. 

But what do these things have to do with medicines? These ought to be so prepared that they are sufficient for providing every moderation. Some may be opposed at the extreme degree to extreme [diseases], and others to those closer to the mean. This is the logic of methodical discovery: that medicines might be held as hot in the **1st, 2nd, 3rd, or 4th degree** <term>degrees — in Galenic medicine, drugs were classified by the intensity of their primary qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) on a scale of 1 to 4</term>, and some at the beginning of a degree, some in the middle, and others at the end. This is the very measurement used by the Galenists concerning primary and secondary elementary qualities. 

Take, for example, something hot in the fourth degree, such as the **spurge plant** <note>original: "euphorbii"; spurge (Euphorbia) was known for its highly caustic and "hot" milky sap.</note>. Let this plant be compared with its "tear" <note>the resinous sap or exudate of the plant</note> or its extracted essence. I say both are hot in the fourth degree; but the **extracted essence is more active**. Let the same assessment apply to the other degrees. Now the **madman-writer** <note>original: "maniographus," a mocking title for Riolan, suggesting his writing is a product of mania.</note> will understand why chemical remedies are praised for their activity, and he will unlearn, if he can, how to rave.

-> # GALENISM’S TRIUMPH # <-

He establishes a dogmatic proof that medicine rests upon truer principles. It would certainly be enough if they were merely "true"; but what is the case? The principles of <term>physics</term> <note>In this context, "physics" refers to natural philosophy—the study of nature and the physical world—rather than the modern mathematical science.</note> are proposed. But, oh good debater, just because the principles of physics are "truer," it does not necessarily follow that your **dogmatic medicine** <note>The "Dogmatic" or Rationalist school of medicine relied on logic and theory to find the underlying causes of disease, as opposed to the "Empiric" school which relied on experience.</note> possesses truer ones, unless you demonstrate that the latter is a subject of the former. This would mean that there are general principles in natural philosophy with which medical matters essentially and uniformly agree, so that medicine begins where natural philosophy leaves off <note>original: "incipiat medicina vbi definit phyfica" — a common Scholastic maxim suggesting that the physician must understand the laws of nature before treating the body.</note>.

But what are those "truer principles"? You say the principles of physics are defined as those which are neither made from other things, nor from each other, but from which all things are made. Truly, principles are described in various ways: as those which do not necessarily follow after other things; as the first causes through which all else exists; as the first inherent things from which something is made, or even the first non-inherent things; or that from which a thing is first known. In every sense, principles are the first things by whose power something exists, is made, or is known—such as nature, art, or an element—so that they pertain to generation, production, and composition. 

In physics, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose theories on matter and change dominated university education in the 17th century.</note> considers **<term>form</term>** <note>The essential identity or "blueprint" of a thing.</note> to be the more important principle, then **<term>matter</term>** <note>The underlying "stuff" that takes on a form.</note>, to which is joined **<term>privation</term>** <note>The absence of a form that ought to be there, which allows for change to occur.</note>. He applies these in the 12th book of his *Metaphysics*, text 22, to sensible things: such as heat as **form**, cold as **privation**, and **matter** as that which is first, by its own nature, potentially heat or cold. 

<margin>Riolan rejects the principles of Aristotle.</margin>

These Aristotelian principles displease you because they are "intelligible" <note>Meaning they are abstract concepts understood by the mind rather than physical things seen by the eye.</note> rather than physical. Indeed, you are affected far differently here than when you were harassing <term>Libavius</term> <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a famous chemist and physician who tried to reconcile traditional medicine with new chemical discoveries.</note> for writing that those principles were merely **logical** and **metaphysical** concepts adapted to physics, since physics...

For the ancient discipline is not to be changed in such a way. Theological power lies first in essentials; it is not removed by parables. # CHAPTER 60.

->*Alchemy and chemical medicine proven. See manuscript page 91.*<-

**H**itherto a comparison has been established between Hippocratic medicine and chemical medicine; the former was preferred, the latter rejected. If you ask what is to be understood by the name "Hippocratic," it can only be answered that it must be taken—according to the opinion of the disputing school <note>This refers to the conservative medical faculty in Paris which followed the ancient Greek traditions</note>—as that which Galen explained and expanded upon from the writings of Hippocrates. The "Short Excursion's Censure" <note>likely a reference to a contemporary academic decree or polemical pamphlet</note> exhorts true students of medicine to remain within this tradition; its remedies are called "ordinary," and anyone who departs from them or adopts others is condemned to death <note>metaphorically or professionally ruined</note> in the "Supplication of the Apology." It is manifest, therefore, that the school deals with a "simple and naked" version of Hippocratism, unless it wishes to be accused of inconsistency and levity. 

This is even more evident in the persecution of **Alchemy**, whose practitioners are called "enemies of nature." Even though alchemy may have a few good points, it is condemned because it is judged to possess far more evils—such as the vain pursuit of <term>chrysopoeia</term> <note>original: "chrysopœian" — the art of making gold from base metals</note>, the fiction of the **quintessence** <note>the "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance</note>, extracts that destroy the <term>crases</term> <note>original: "craſium" — the healthy balance of temperaments or qualities in the body</note> and virtues of substances, poisonous minerals, enormous costs, and so forth. Nor is the case of **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent French physician who sought to reconcile Paracelsian chemistry with Galenic medicine</note> being argued here, who seemed to lean too much toward **Paracelsianism** <note>the medical system of Paracelsus, which favored chemicals over herbs</note>, but rather the case of steadfast Alchemy...

> *Those things which operate most gently, and which have been made mild through preparation from common violent and harmful substances, are safer than their opposites.*

> *Chemical medicines operate most gently, and have emerged mild through preparation from common violent and harmful substances; Galenic medicines, however, are not so.*

> *Therefore, chemical medicines are safer than these, and thus to be preferred.*

I prove the minor premise by the extract of **Rhubarb**, **Senna**, **Tamarinds**, etc. Indeed, <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a famous and conservative professor at the Paris Medical Faculty who was a fierce opponent of chemical medicine.</note> **Riolanus** used to disparage the extract of Rhubarb for this very reason: that it possessed no strength. In some places he prefers his own [preparations] because one **drachm** <note>A unit of apothecary weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> can do more than two of the extract. Likewise, he denies that a purgative can be produced by distillation; he contends that the <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "crasin," the specific "mixture" of humors or qualities that gives a medicine its power.</note> and action of the substance perish during extraction. Thus, these chemical versions can be called "violent" all the less.

Moreover, it was said long ago that **Mesue** corrects **Spurge**, **Colocynth**, and **Hellebore** through chemistry. In the class of minerals, certain preparations add to their strengths, while others take away—as when **arsenic** is prepared, or when there is <term>glass of antimony</term> <note>A glassy substance made from antimony ore; it was a controversial chemical medicine used to induce vomiting.</note>, and so on. But even those things which are violent in one way emerge as most mild in another; thus, for this reason, this art [chemistry] does not deserve to be disparaged so much, that...

## CHAPTER LXII.

*An argument concerning the infusions of Libavius. In response to page 93 of the Madness <note>original: "Mania"; referring to Jean Riolan's polemic "The Madness of the Chemists."</note>, likewise concerning distillations.*

But I pity the childishness of Riolan, which for so many years has not yet **put aside its nuts** <note>original: "posuit nuces"; a Latin idiom meaning to stop playing children's games or to finally grow up.</note>, nor can he yet distinguish between true and false Alchemy. If he does know the difference, he cannot escape the charge of malice. 

Regarding chemical infusion, I have spoken above, and Riolan’s ignorance has been exposed. For when we use the name "extracts" for things made by infusion, or even when we describe the work of infusion itself, we do not mean the simple soakings <note>original: "macerationes"</note> performed in common apothecaries' workshops. Therefore, he speaks ridiculously here as well, claiming I prefer an infusion to all extracts, when by "infusion" I mean nothing other than a chemical extract. On page 269 of the *Antigramania*, I state this: *Infusion is a troublesome thing for a man.* <note>Libavius likely refers to the labor-intensive nature of chemical extraction compared to simple herbal preparation.</note> 

But what is so chemical as that very process? See also the rest of my writings, in which you will find that I attribute many chemical methods to **Galenic medicine**.

[In the same] way that a Galenic powder, infusion, or decoction purges, it is also necessary for a cathartic <term>cathartic</term> <note>A substance used to accelerate defecation; a strong laxative.</note> essence extracted from them to purge in that same manner. Furthermore, regarding minerals: by whatever faculty the **Armenian stone** <note>A blue mineral, likely a grade of azurite, historically used to purge melancholy.</note> and **Lapis Lazuli** purge for the Galenists—both of which are said to be **black-bile-drawers** <note>original: *melanagogi*; medicines believed to specifically target and expel "black bile," one of the four bodily humors.</note> and consequently purge with selectivity—the same applies to the extracts of these minerals. The same judgment holds for copper, iron, salt, the **mercury of Aegina** <note>A reference to the medicinal uses of quicksilver described by the 7th-century physician Paul of Aegina.</note>, mineral waters, and so on. But in truth, since there is scarcely any Galenic medicine that does not purge multiple humors (whether they are drawn out in sequence or all at once), I deny that this "selectivity" is certain; I deny that the result is what the opposition claims; and I deny it can be proven demonstratively that no prioritization of humors occurs there.

I assert that we must often take refuge in that **"asylum of the whole form"** <note>A philosophical concept where the specific effects of a substance are attributed to its total internal essence or "form" rather than its individual elemental components.</note>. This is why **Falloppio** <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), an influential Italian physician and anatomist.</note> wondered at the nature of purgatives rather than explaining them through demonstration. And it is certainly a thing worthy of wonder: that these substances purge not only when swallowed, but even when applied externally; and further, that this "drawing" of humors does not happen at the site where the medicine is applied, but in the stomach, or the bowels, or the mouth (as when **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury.</note> is applied), and in quite varied ways.

For purging sometimes occurs through vomiting, sometimes through the bowels; sometimes through sweat and **diuresis** <term>diuresis</term> <note>The increased production of urine.</note>. Sometimes it happens without any distress, and sometimes it happens violently, according to various circumstances and...

<summary>Libavius argues that chemical extracts retain the same humor-purging properties as raw Galenic medicines and suggests that the specific way purgatives work remains a mystery even to great physicians like Falloppio.</summary>

Sf
<meta>catchword: concerning</meta>

Nature cures diseases, not the Physician. Indeed, the Physician's chief duty is to supply the instruments for nature. Thus far the authorities. We understand, therefore, that a purging medicine makes its own specific influence <note>original: *affectionem*; in this context, the specific quality or "disposition" the drug carries.</note> common to nature, and by altering nature, the medicine defines it; in turn, the medicine acquires strength from nature itself, as if receiving a kind of life or "act." From this it follows that when two things act together in a determined way—nature as the principal agent and the medicament as the instrument—the act of purging follows. If nature is powerfully moved and impelled, the action is powerful; if weakly, the action is weak, and so on for the rest. However, it can happen that nature is affected in a similar way by a medicament of a more general power, which is disposed toward purging several humors at once. From this follows <term>Panchymagogia</term> <note>From the Greek *pan* (all), *chumos* (humor), and *agogos* (leading); a medicine intended to purge all the humors of the body simultaneously.</note> with a degree of choice, and this concept is as agreeable to the <term>Hippocratic physicians</term> <note>Followers of Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE), who emphasized the "healing power of nature" (*vis medicatrix naturae*).</note> as it is to the <term>chemical physicians</term> <note>Also known as iatrochemists; those who used alchemical preparations and minerals for medicine rather than traditional plant-based recipes.</note>. These are properly called "purgatives."

Sometimes, however, an "expulsion" of a bothersome substance occurs rather than a true "purging," such as in vomiting or sneezing, where they say a "provocation" takes place. At other times it is a "washing away," etc. Furthermore, this method of purging is both <term>Hippocratic</term> and is approved by the <term>chemical physicians</term>. The <term>Galenists</term> <note>Followers of Galen (129–c. 216 CE), whose medical system relied on balancing the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note>, citing the same Hippocrates, produce another method, which they say occurs by a **magnetic force** <note>original: *magnetica vi*; the theory that a specific drug acts like a magnet to "pull" a specific humor out of the body's tissues.</note> by which that which is "familiar" <note>i.e., a humor that shares a similar quality with the drug.</note> is drawn out. This force is applied to nature at the same time, so that nature is forced, as it were, to give back that which she wrongly distributed into the limbs, or that which any limb attracted to itself as nourishment, or that which has become corrupted while remaining within a limb. <term>Mesue</term> <note>Referring to "Mesue the Younger," a mysterious but highly influential medical author whose 11th-century texts on purgatives were essential reading for Renaissance doctors.</note> spoke concerning this method.

To make this clearer, let us examine his words: "The <term>Dogmatist</term>," <note>In this context, the "Dogmatist" refers to a physician who follows the established "dogma" or doctrines of the traditional medical schools.</note> he says, "makes a choice of the purging remedy. His meaning is that the <term>chymiater</term> <note>A "chemical physician" or one who uses alchemical preparations in medicine.</note> cannot purge selectively because the minerals he uses are blunt instruments that purge everything; whereas the <term>Dogmatist</term> can target his treatment. From this, he concludes that the Dogmatist's condition and art are superior.

But first, this argument fails because it reasons from a single particular instance. For the chemical physician does not use minerals alone. Secondly, the opposite is actually true—or at least both sides suffer from the same defect, as Riolan’s own words suggest. For since it is often necessary in medicine to use <term>holagogues</term> <note>From the Greek *holos* (all) and *agogos* (leading); medicines intended to purge all the humors of the body at once.</note>, which are called **universal** <note>original: *catholica*</note> because they purge...

...most humors without selection, or without a special affinity. If the Dogmatist <note>The "Dogmatic" or "Rational" school of medicine followed traditional theories, primarily those of Galen.</note> only possesses elective <note>selective</note> medicines, he will be lacking in general ones, just as it is said that the chemist lacks in specific ones. You respond: but that man <note>the Dogmatist</note> compensates for his defect through mixture. First, I say this is reckless, since nature supplies "simples" <note>unmixed, natural ingredients, usually herbs</note> of such virtue; then, by the same token, I say the chemist, through his art—both in preparation and in the blending of mixtures—is able to adapt a general medicine to a specific effect. Since it is established that he purges all humors, it follows that he can also do this or that, especially if the primary cause of the work is nature, which must be led from a general state to perform a determined action. But I demonstrate the contrary thus: That physician is superior who possesses medicines that purge all humors <term>holagoga</term> <note>from the Greek *holos* (all) and *agogos* (leading/drawing out); a medicine that cleanses all humors at once.</note> as effectively as those that purge with selection, and who furthermore possesses such a ready faculty of art that he can turn disadvantages into advantages, and apply them in every way so that nature acts according to his judgment.

To the Chemical Physician <term>Chymiatro</term> <note>A physician who uses chemical or alchemical preparations, often following the school of Paracelsus.</note> belong medicines that are not only general purgers <term>holagoga</term>, but also those that draw blood <term>hemagoga</term>, those that draw water <term>hydragoga</term>, those that draw black bile <term>melanagoga</term>, and those that draw yellow bile <term>cholagoga</term>. He possesses an altogether ready faculty for every wish of healing, the likes of which the pure and simple Hippocratic physician does not have. Why then should the chemical physician not be more excellent? The assumption is manifest. For the chemical Physician possesses all the Galenic medicines and all the power of the Hippocratics; and in addition, he possesses many new discoveries, and the most convenient and ready faculty of art for correcting, adding, or subtracting from his remedies.

# ON THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIAN
<note>original: *ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS*. This refers to a polemic against Jean Riolan the Elder, a Paris physician who criticized Paracelsian chemistry and was often mocked by chemists as the "Spurious Parisian."</note>

Mineral essences (says Madness <note>original: *mania*; the author personifies his opponent's argument as "madness"</note>) purge any humor without selection. Therefore, they harm more than they help. But this argument is also fallacious. They would certainly be harmful in a case where only a bile-purger <term>cholagogue</term> <note>original: *cholagogum*; from the Greek *chole* (bile) and *agogos* (leading/drawing out)</note> should be given, but instead a general-purger <term>holagogue</term> <note>original: *holagogum*; a medicine that draws out all humors simultaneously</note> is administered. Moreover, the principle of that false reasoning <term>paralogism</term> <note>original: *paralogismi*; an illogical or self-contradictory argument</note>—that general-purgers <term>holagoga</term> harm rather than help—is false, since it is possible for them to be of the greatest benefit. In the meantime, he will let those minerals of his rest in their boxes until patients arrive suffering from chronic illnesses, overflowing in every part with impurities, whom no simple Hippocratic physician could heal, even if he moved every one of his medicine jars. ->ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS<-
<note>original: "ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS" likely referring to a treatise titled "De Spuriis Alchymiae" (On the Falsehoods of Alchemy) regarding the medical faculty in Paris.</note>

*Therefore, they <note>referring to chemical medicines as viewed by the opponent</note> cannot purge; and as a consequence, they disturb nature like poisons, irritating the excretory faculty by their bad disposition <term>cacocthia</term> <note>From the Greek *kakochymia*, meaning a "bad state of juices" or ill-health in the body</note>.*

The major premise of this argument is explained by the testimony of Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium</note>, who compared a purging medicine to a magnet attracting iron due to a similarity of substance; from this, it is argued that purges are carried out in the same way. Moreover, that a magnet has a similarity with iron is proven by the theory of "nutrition" held by Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath who famously suggested that magnets were "alive" and fed on iron</note>, who asserted that the magnet feeds on iron, or absorbs it. The minor premise is proven because, just as in an "extract" of a magnet the power of attracting iron perishes, so it also does in chemical minerals. Riolan trusts this false logic <term>paralogism</term> so much that he thinks I am hard-pressed by that comparison. 

But this is a "confidence of fig-wood" <note>original: *ficulna fiducia*; a Latin idiom meaning a weak or worthless trust, as the wood of a fig tree is brittle and unreliable</note>. I say that the major premise begs the question and is based on a contingent falsehood. Galen explained purging by using an example; he did not prove that it happens in exactly the same way. Furthermore, both Galen and Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine"</note> do not always say the same thing regarding the purging faculty. This "similarity of substance" based on Cardano's fiction of nutrition is rejected even by stable-boys <note>original: *caculis*; referring to low-ranking servants or camp-followers, implying even the uneducated know this theory is nonsense</note>. 

But suppose that authority did have some weight. I say: by whatever familiarity a magnet devours and licks up iron, by that same familiarity a purging medicine would "eat" what is to be purged; thus, there would be no need to seek out "familiar seats" <note>original: *sellas familiares*; a euphemism for the toilet or commode</note> to deposit one's burdens. But this is clearly false. For a magnet neither feeds on iron, nor does it attract it for that purpose; but plainly and naturally on account of a consensus of spirits <note>An alchemical and natural-philosophical concept where internal "essences" or "spirits" of materials are in harmony and thus move toward one another</note>, which seek to be united. Iron is consumed by rust, [not by the magnet]...

### THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM
<page-num>647</page-num>

[...iron] is not food for the magnet. This does not benefit *Riolan* <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine in Paris</note> unless he himself also asserts that the stone <margin>(1) Note that the two opinions regarding nature being assisted and overcome can be reduced to one. For that nature which allows itself to be specially disposed and moved by a medicine is said to be "overcome"; that which does not allow it is not conquered. Once "conquered," however, it consents to the movement of the medicine and moves together with it, which is just the same as saying that, having been specifically determined, it expels the things to be purged.</margin> (1) is nourished by iron. Does he therefore think, along with *Cardano* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath who suggested magnets were "alive" and "fed" on iron</note>, that stones are alive? In this way, he will even become a *Paracelsian* <note>A follower of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who used "living" chemical principles in medicine—exactly the group Riolan was trying to debunk</note>, and involve himself in the very sect which he had undertaken to refute. 

But if he himself judges this to be false, what defense can he find in such a futile invention? Let there be a similarity between iron and the magnet. But it is not the same kind that exists between a purging agent <term>purgans</term> and the waste to be purged <term>purganda</term>. For if the primary reasoning of *Hippocrates*, *Avicenna*, and *Mesue* <note>A reference to the foundational Greek and Arabic authorities of medieval medicine</note> regarding "nature healing first" is true, we do not need the invention of a "familiarity" <note>original: "familiaritatis"; here meaning a natural attraction or kinship between substances</note> between the waste to be purged and the purgative (1). It is enough for nature to be determined toward a specific action, and to move together with the remedy by its own faculties, and to prepare the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which traditional medicine sought to balance</note> to be purged so that they may be excreted by the combined force of both; and if this were the case regarding proper purging. Regarding those things that purge differently, one must speak of them according to their own nature. 

To the minor premise <note>A logical term referring to the second part of a formal argument</note>: What then, if they do not have that power? It is uncertain whether that purging actually occurs. *Therefore, the latter follows. I respond to this logical connection that there is an equivocation <note>An ambiguity caused by using one word with two different meanings.</note> regarding matter and form. For either both causes are considered in the whole, or in the homogenous integral parts; and this is also the case with <term>crasis</term> <note>original: "crasis"; in ancient medicine, this refers to the specific "mixture" or "temperament" of qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that defines a substance’s nature.</note>. For the temperaments of individual members can lie hidden under the single temperament of the whole, as with the astringent <note>binding or contracting</note> part in <term>rhubarb</term> <note>original: "Rhabarbaro"</note>, and the purgative <note>laxative</note> part in the same plant. Both can be separated once their inner subjects are divided. By the extraction of the essence—which results in what is specifically called an "extract"—that integral <term>crasis</term> is indeed lost, and if any powers depended on it so as to belong only to the whole, [they are lost]; just as the nutritive power of egg yolks is no longer present in the oil [extracted from them]. In other cases, however, it remains, as in olive oil and in nutritive extracts prepared differently. But the <term>crasis</term> of the specific and homogenous parts does not perish, provided the remedy is prepared according to the art. Experience testifies to this. In that way, the falsehood arises in your logical connection. Let the form of the whole indeed perish, and let it not remain as <term>rhubarb</term> <note>original: "Rheum"</note> as such, but as its juice and essence in which the <term>purgative spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus purgans"; the active medical principle or "life force" of the drug that performs the healing.</note> resides; it does not follow that the irritation [of the bowels] happens without that magnetic likeness, if indeed it must happen in that way. The minor premise must be understood according to this distinction.

## CHAPTER LXV.

*Whether chemists preserve at least the general category of a temperament, but not the specific type. Referring to page 98 of the "Madness."* <note>The author is likely responding to a specific book or chapter titled *Mania* (Madness) written by an opponent—perhaps Lusi—who criticized chemical methods.</note>

**Y**ou define the **genera** <term>genera; the broad categories or "families"</term> of temperaments as the "temperate" (balanced) and the "excesses"—such as hot, cold, moist, and dry—either in their simple forms or in combination. To you, the **species** <term>species; the specific varieties</term> are the differences measured across four degrees, each of which is subdivided into a beginning, a middle, and an end. <note>In traditional Galenic medicine, the potency of a drug's quality (like heat) was measured in four degrees; for example, a "hot in the fourth degree" substance was much more intense than one in the first degree.</note> You claim that we [chemists] preserve the general category—that is, we leave the balanced as balanced, the hot as hot, and so on—but that we change the specific type. Namely, you say we turn the first degree into the degrees that follow, or turn the later degrees back into the earlier ones; and thus, from the "beginning" of the first degree, we produce a "middle" or an "end," and vice versa. 

Suppose this is so. What wrong have we committed? If medical preparation and use require such a change, and we achieve that requirement through our art, do we seem to you so idle and unskilled that we deserve blame? **Jet** <note>a gemstone made of fossilized wood, used in ancient medicine</note> in its manifest <note>outwardly visible</note> state, just like **Amber**, possesses very little heating power—much like olive oil. Yet not only **Mesue** <note>Masawaih al-Mardini, a highly influential 11th-century physician whose texts on pharmacy were standard for centuries</note>, but all chemical philosophers and physicians, draw out from their hidden <note>original: "occulto"</note> depths clearly fiery and burning essences, just as they do from wine. And what kind of essences are these? Divine, sacred, heavenly—the works of the wise and of the **great mastery** <term>magni magisterii; the "Great Work" of alchemy, often referring to the creation of the most powerful and purified medicines</term>. These works have been celebrated with the highest praise until now as miracles of great wonder. To perform this is to perfect a substance, not to destroy it. If even this does not please you, we will retreat, and from the "coldest" we will manufacture the "cold" and "colder." Thus in other matters too we shall be skillful. But you are perhaps unaware that chemists do not care about the "temperaments" of your qualities <note>The Galenic balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>; if they need them, there is no need to break the veins of the art <note>i.e., to strain or over-exert the practice</note>; for they are supplied in abundance from the **greater world** <term>maiore mundo; the macrocosm or the universe at large</term>. As was said above regarding **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian or Assyrian physician whose works were foundational to medieval pharmacy</note>, they segregate the species from the matter, and they manifest what is hidden in things. 

How they would wish to take away your qualities, or take them entirely from the essences, if they could! They would wish to heal **astral diseases**, that is, those which you attribute to the "whole substance" <note>Diseases that affect the very essence of a person rather than just a localized humor</note>, without "Euphorbial" heating <note>original: "calefactione Euphorbiali"; referring to Euphorbium, a plant known in Galenic medicine as being intensely hot in the fourth degree</note> and the rest, just as happens in the "highest medicine" made from gold—of which a certain likeness exists in some minerals, whose essence [no one]...

We might convert the acidic taste of vinegar into something sharp, just as you used to change bitter juice into sweet through the process of nutrition. This is the very inner sanctum—the specific and internal nature—of the chemical art. Nevertheless, in the meantime, we also adapt ourselves to the qualities and temperament <term>crasis</term> familiar to you, and we do not always change the genus or the species.

...firm and indelible connection does not end. Therefore, that which most closely approaches the ether <note>In the cosmology of the time, the ether was the subtle, celestial substance that filled the heavens, superior to the four earthly elements.</note>, as it is commonly defined, is what we call our **fifth nature** <term>quintessence; the purest essence of a substance, extracted through alchemy to act as a potent medicine.</term>.

Next, regarding simple extracts and other distillates, we move back and forth as it suits the nature and use of each specific thing. We take great pride in this mastery of our art. Moreover, in many instances, we preserve the same species and distinguishing characteristics, as seen in juices that are simply extracted or pressed out.

We leave **almond oil** for immediate use exactly as it is; at the very least, we purify it through filters. Waters made from **roses, violets, poppies, water-lilies, sorrel**, and similar plants retain their cooling properties. However, they make a deeper impact because the obstacle of the "thick body" <note>original: "crassi corporis"; referring to the raw, inert physical matter that early chemists believed "imprisoned" the active medicinal spirit.</note>—which previously hindered the manifestation and penetration of their action—has been removed. 

If we wish to make such a substance even colder, so that you have a sufficient means of cooling, we draw away the hot spirit. In this way, your **vinegar** cools you because of the cold spirits contained within it by virtue of the **nitrous salt** <term>niter or saltpeter; early chemists often associated this salt with the "breath of life" and specific cooling or preserving qualities.</term> and the watery phlegm. If you desire heat, we separate the cold parts; if you desire something colder, we draw off the heat and leave you only the cold components. Behold, do you not see how ready and accommodating these **chemists** <note>original: "chymicos"</note> are?

If you seek nothing more than what is found in a whole rose, we simply crush and press it, offering you the purified juice. Yet, we also achieve much through transformations, alterations, and mixtures. What more could you ask for?

You bring forward your own decoctions <note>original: "coctiones"; the traditional method of boiling herbs in water to extract medicine.</note> and infusions as an example. But I ask: what would you actually retain, you who transfer a quality or power into cold water without any of the physical body being present? <term>Fernel</term> <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a legendary French physician whose works formed the basis of medical education for centuries.</note> denied that water was a suitable medium for all things, because its persistent coldness would blunt the powers of the ingredients. How do your decoctions retain the specific temperament of the plant when mixed with water? If you use wine instead of water, the decoction will become hotter.

Whether you act similarly to us or differently, the insult and the blame fall back upon you; for you cannot preserve the general constitution of a substance unless you swallow the ingredients whole <note>The author is mocking the Galenists, arguing that any preparation—boiling or distilling—changes the plant, so their "cooking" is just as "destructive" as alchemy.</note>. Your mixtures and recipes are not of such great value.

The reason for your amazement is this: you believe that he who increases heat does not, by that very act, preserve the specific character of the <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific "recipe" of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—that defines a substance's nature.</note>. Therefore, Riolan cannot help but wonder at what <term>Libavius</term> <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a German physician and chemist who sought to reconcile traditional Galenic medicine with new chemical practices.</note> writes: that if the chemists increase the <term>native heat</term> <note>The innate, vital warmth believed to be the source of life and medicinal power in a substance.</note>, they are unable to dissipate the <term>crasis</term> <note>The vital "mixture" or balance of humors/qualities.</note>. I see that you are returning to your childhood, so that by your own example you confirm the proverb: *old men are twice children* <note>original Greek: "δὶς παῖδες οἱ γέροντες"; a common ancient proverb suggesting that the elderly become child-like in their dotage.</note>. That which is dissipated and destroyed is not increased. Is that not so? For growth is a movement not from "being" to "non-being," but from "not so much" to "so much." So, on the contrary: that which is increased is not destroyed. 

Now, you say that the chemists increase the **NATIVE** heat. Therefore, they retain that very same native heat; they do not destroy it, nor do they dissipate it. Rather, they "exalt" it <note>In alchemy, to "exalt" a substance is to purify it and bring it to a higher state of potency.</note> only in its degree of quantity, and that not through the heat's own essence, but by removing accidental obstacles. For that much heat was already present within the "potential" of nature; but because of the surrounding elemental bodies, it was unable to come into "actual" operation. The chemists simply present it to you, having dragged it out from the dross. Learn better things, Riolan, lest <term>Charon’s boat</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Charon ferries the souls of the dead across the river Styx; the author is telling Riolan to learn the truth before he dies in ignorance.</note> seize you while you are still unrefined. 

However, so that you may learn, I add this also: Native heat is undoubtedly a <term>formal quality</term> <note>A philosophical term meaning a quality that belongs to the "form" or essential soul of a thing, rather than just its material body.</note> (I call it so because it is a "habit" or state of being opposed to "privation") implanted by nature. In a mixture, the hot temperament is, by the power of nature, the first thing produced in the blending...

<margin>A definition of fever more marvelous than a miracle.</margin>
...to arise. You ask: "What is Fever?" You answer that it is innate heat changed into fiery heat. This definition is more marvelous than any miracle of yours. I will imitate your cleverness: What is an old man? He is a boy led through adolescence and manhood into old age. In logic, the <term>genus</term> <note>The general category to which a thing belongs; for example, "animal" is the genus for "man."</note> ought to state "the fire" <note>original: τὸ πῦρ</note> materially and subjectively, or explain the "quiddity" <note>The "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note> of the thing in a general way. 

But a boy is not the "genus" of an old man, nor does he explain the old man's nature. In the same way, since febrile heat is entirely contrary to nature, how can it be **innate**? "It was [innate]," you will say. Therefore, I say, it is not. The question is not what something *was*, but what it *is*. Otherwise, when febrile heat is reduced back to a healthy, innate degree, I could answer someone asking "what is it?" in a similar way: it is febrile or fiery heat changed into innate heat. Are you suffering from such an "itch" <note>A metaphorical "itch" or compulsive habit of mind.</note> that you dare to encrust <note>To foul or sully the surface of something pure.</note> pure chemical vessels? 

But what is the essence of chemistry? 
<margin>A ridiculous definition of chemical essence.</margin>
Like a disciple of <term>Chrysippus</term> <note>A Stoic philosopher famous for his rigid and sometimes absurdly complex logical definitions.</note>, you answer easily: "It is the innate essence of a mixture changed into a fiery essence." 

Aha! That is defining it skillfully indeed! If I were to make an essence from *Euphorbium* <note>A potent, caustic resin from the spurge plant, considered "hot" in the ancient system of qualities.</note>, what would it be? Is it also fire changed into fire? And what if I made it from a rose? Will you say that the rose's coldness has been changed into a fiery state? What coldness is ever fiery? It is a marvel if you call it the **innate** essence of the mixture, for nothing can be innate except by its present, final nature. If it is innate, how can it be contrary to the unique nature of the thing? You play witty games. You do us a favor—we whom you nearly provoked like hornets with so many "drones" <note>original: *fuciis*. A pun meaning both the male drone bees and "deceptions" or "pretenses."</note>.

How then can there be a true destruction of the mixture and form? Moreover, by what judge did you learn that the heats of cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg are "moderate"? To compare their mixture to that of a temperate man...

Who is that temperate judge? <term>Fernel</term> <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a primary authority in Galenic medicine.</note> maintains that nutmeg is hot and dry in the second degree, while cinnamon and cloves are in the third degree. <note>In Galenic medicine, drugs were classified by "degrees" of primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) on a scale of 1 to 4.</note> Is this what it means to be "temperately" or "moderately" hot? For in the still-head there is nothing that "draws" in order to "devour" that oil, which you claimed was the purpose of attraction. On the contrary, in the still-head there is often a cooling mechanism; sometimes there is not even a still-head at all, but rather pipes; often the oil is drawn out merely by soaking <note>original: "maceratione"</note> and is afterwards squeezed out and refined. And what should be said of the press used for nutmeg? What "puffers" <note>original: "sufflones"; a derogatory nickname for alchemists who spent their time blowing on the coals of their furnaces.</note> would not laugh at you for being so foolish?

He wanted to call it "distillation by descent," but because he possesses his ornament and wisdom only on his tongue, he could not stutter it out any other way through the fence of his teeth. 

He denies that these can be extracted except by the "violence of fire." Certainly, whether the process is done by ascent, descent, or inclination, the use of fire is necessary. But that fire is least "violent" in its impression upon the material when the substance is soaked in plenty of <term>solvent</term>, <note>original: "menstruo"; the liquid used to dissolve or extract the essence of a solid substance.</note> which keeps it safe enough from the fire. When the oil is merely squeezed out after soaking in a steam bath, <note>original: "balneo vapido"</note> what "violence" is there here? But even suppose the fire were violent. What follows? The oils extracted by this art would be vehemently hot, if not supremely so. Suppose it were "supremely hot" in the fourth degree. Would...

The response to the **major premise** <note>In logic, the "major premise" is the first part of a syllogism. Riolan’s major premise was that changing a substance's temperature destroys its nature.</note> is made through a distinction between the **elemental constitution** and the **essential** one; between external and internal mixing; and between the whole and its integral parts. To care only for the elemental <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "crasin"; the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—that defines a substance’s nature.</note> is the mark of superficial physicians, who, as it were, cling to the "bark" of things <note>A common metaphor for staying on the surface and failing to reach the core truth.</note> and do not penetrate to the hidden secrets. 

For us, even if the external qualities are changed in genus, species, and individual characteristics, the internal and essential constitutions are nevertheless not changed. In a certain respect, an immoderate thing can be made from a balanced one, yet the hidden essence is preserved in the whole and in the divided parts alike. Since latent constitutions are brought into action—whether a single elemental temperament is created or an imbalance—the action is all the more noble because not only is that which nature established in its "retreat" <note>The "retreat" refers to the deep, internal state of a natural substance before it is acted upon.</note> preserved, but it is also brought to a state of perfection in its way of being. 

The same reasoning applies to the **homogeneous parts**, whose actions before separation were bound in service to another, so that they held the status of potential rather than actual power; but now, having been liberated, they enjoy their own dominion. The **minor premise** <note>The second part of Riolan's argument, which claimed chemists create "immoderate" substances.</note> concerning the superficial qualities of the substance is merely accidental. Thus, the substance is changed in a certain respect; it is so in one way, and the opposite in another. For the path of alteration is reciprocal.

This foundation was also taken up by **Hippocrates** and other **Greeks**, who described the medical art for the general public, and in doing so, provided the **Arabs** with a certain "medical body," though at that time it was less vigorously animated and adorned. ### ON THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS

If a warm <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "crasis"; refers to the specific mixture of the four humors or qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a body's health or a plant's nature.</note> falls into a cold state, a change in the degree of heat must necessarily occur; if it falls into a warm state, it grows hotter still. We see this in the case of lettuce: if it is picked at that stage of growth where it is watery and cold, its pressed juice mixed with water will manifest as something even colder. Yet, through the act of cooking, it will set aside some of its coldness, especially if it is boiled thoroughly with added seasonings. However, if you consider the nature of water itself, element is increased by element; thus, whatever coldness was lost through cooking will be restored more abundantly by the water if warm additives are left out. Much less can a stable <term>constitution</term> remain if the opinion of **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a prominent defender of traditional Galenic medicine against alchemical innovations.</note> is to be upheld. But let us instead employ the transmutative art, and once the impurity has been separated, let us turn a poor argument in our favor to create a powerful <term>antidote</term> <note>original: "alexiterium"; a medicine used to ward off poison or contagion.</note> in this manner:

> *He who makes the tempered from the untempered; a fit remedy from unfit matter; the powerful from the powerless; the essential from the material; and the healthy from the unhealthy; and he who ingeniously procures every degree of virtue, forcing nature to yield up the medical riches lurking in its recesses and oppressed by filth—riches which would otherwise remain hidden and be thrown away along with the impurities, as is commonly done in ordinary pharmacies—he performs something extraordinary in medicine. Indeed, the one who possesses this faculty is to be preferred far above all other modes of healing.*

When the chemist produces [a remedy] with its internal <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "crasis"; the specific balance of qualities that defines a substance's nature.</note> and properties freed from elementary confusion, he does not merely preserve that constitution, but actually ennobles it in its dignity and its fitness for action. It is clear that he preserves the constitution: for he does not create the radical natures and dispositions of the mixtures from scratch; rather, he separates the innate qualities from the dross and reveals powers that are far more vigorous.

We could offer many such arguments against **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a staunch conservative physician at the University of Paris.</note> and show him that he merely "philosophizes about the bark" <note>An idiom meaning to only understand the surface of a matter without reaching the heart or "pith."</note>. It is impossible for something in such a crude state to act as excellently as that which has been separated from all filth and toxicity. It is impossible for a substance that is tightly locked away and trapped within useless matter to produce as healthy an effect as one that has been set free and purified.

Concerning the primary qualities of the elements, which are called "manifest" <note>In the Aristotelian-Galenic physics of the time, the "manifest" qualities were the four basics: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>, there is no need for us to exchange many words with you. If our art labored only in those, there would be no need for the great mastery of the wise, who reveal what is hidden in things. Your qualities are far too well known to every flute-player <note>original: *ambubais*, a reference to Syrian flute-girls, used here to mean common street performers or people of low status.</note>, bleary-eyed man, barber, pharmacist, peasant, and generally to the common people. And if a chemist has need of these, he will take them more correctly from the elements themselves than from your workshop. 

I warn your foolishness, however, not to think that when Galen and other physicians discuss temperaments, they are referring to those simple qualities—since there is either no art, or at least no very valuable art, involved in simple elementary things. Therefore, they do not show so much what is simply hot, or cold and moist; but what is so according to its <term>constitution</term> <note>original: *crasis*, the Greek term for the specific "mixture" or temperament of a substance or body part.</note> and property, such as something cold that is simultaneously suited to the liver; cold suited to the heart, moderate for the heart, or hot but at the same time appropriate for the brain, etc. 

These things are worthy of medicine; and because they simultaneously grasp the inner essence, and it has been observed that in one and the same mixture there are diverse parts—each of which has its own interior <term>constitution</term>, not just your superficial one, differing from the <term>constitution</term> of another part—therefore Galen desired "secretion" <note>In this context, Libavius refers to the chemical process of separation or extraction to isolate the effective part of a medicine.</note>. This is what the chemists have discovered. In this they glory. Consider now, therefore, which of the two are superior in this <term>constitution</term>. Those who are unable to apply pure constitutions to graded diseases and

# ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS #

...to oppose to the astral qualities <note>Libavius is likely referring to the Paracelsian idea that medicines have "astral" or celestial virtues that correspond to parts of the body.</note>, but they offer a confused chaos, as they rudely grind, subdue, and render the whole more confused and impure; they are forced by any means to press it into lumps. They possess remedies of primary qualities <note>The four basic qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> that are less excellent—since these qualities cohere inseparably with the interior constitutions <term>crasibus; the specific "mixture" or temperament of a substance that gives it its unique properties</term>—than those who are able to separate them and apply a remedy to its disease in its own degree. But the chemists are able to do this. 

<margin>
Hollerius <note>Jacques Houllier (1498–1562), a famous French physician.</note>, *Surgery*, book 1, chapter 4. Oils, which through the thinness of their parts penetrate more quickly, are drawn out from softening plasters by the art of the chemists.
</margin>

Whatever the Galenic "simples" <note>Unmixed botanical or mineral drugs.</note> are capable of in that regard, they achieve only through the imitation of the chemists and by their basic principles, as is apparent in juices, mucilages, syrups, electuaries <note>original: *linctibus*, medicinal pastes licked by the patient.</note>, juleps, decoctions, and the like. Therefore, the chemists altogether have more excellent remedies for primary qualities entangled with hidden essences, while the Galenic simples have less excellent ones. 

Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Elder, a staunch defender of traditional Galenism against the "new" chemical medicine.</note> must tell us why in the previous chapter he wasted so many words on the constitutions or temperaments—which he thinks are changed in kind by the chemists—if temperament does not rise beyond the primary qualities which are here opposed to the secondary and tertiary qualities? Was this also a matter worthy of breaking the brains of the Parisians? If we retain the interior constitution which is hidden in the mixture, why do we care about those manifest qualities of the whole substances, which perish through many preparations and mixtures, even while the Galenists themselves fix their gaze on what comes forth from the "inner chamber"? 

But let us move to the secondary qualities. Here Riolan "dances the Cyclops" <note>A Latin idiom, *saltat cyclopem*, meaning to act in a clumsy, ridiculous, or wildly inappropriate manner.</note>. That wretched man is ignorant of chemical essences, and yet he dares to assert that the chemists have nothing similar? "Thus must a limb be softened," he says.

Imagine: although the chemical physicians <note>original: *chymiatri*; doctors who used alchemical extraction to create medicines.</note> may not soften hardened limbs, but rather the hard nodes within them and similar things that are contrary to nature. By what remedy do you soften them? By decoctions, mucilage, thick pastes, etc., which he [Riolanus] thinks are more certain. Excellent. For this, no art is needed. Nevertheless, see what I conclude against you from Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>, the standard-bearer of the dogmatists <note>The "dogmatists" were physicians who followed traditional Galenic theory based on the four humors.</note>. Where something simply must be softened, he who provides a purer medication performs better. 

But the chemist does this, not the simple Galenist. The reason is that in the same mixture, there is not only a softening power, but also a hardening one. For how else would the mixture have hardened and the moisture been bound? He who applies a hardening agent at the same time as a softening one acts wrongly; he acts rightly who separates the former from the latter, and applies the softener alone by opposing opposites to opposites <note>A core medical principle: treating an ailment with its opposite (e.g., treating heat with cold).</note> without any "disturber" present. The simple Galenist, who applies things that have not been separated, uses the hardening agent along with the softening one, and is thus the cause of contrary effects. # THE SEPARATION OF PARTS IN ALCHEMY #

...[similar things] to seek refuge in; the more they are separated from the earthy parts—which dry, bind, and harden—the better these <term>softeners</term> <note>original: *malactica*; remedies used to soften tumors or stiffened tissues.</note> are. Let us enter the chamber of relaxants. Whatever reasoning applies there, applies here too. Wherever something must simply be relaxed, a medication that performs this purely is better than one that hinders the action through a mixture of opposites. # THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM #
<note>The title "Galenia Triumphus" is likely used ironically here, as Libavius spent this section arguing for the superiority of chemistry over traditional Galenic medicine.</note>

...[that your sur]geons were no more skilled than "asses with lyres" <note>A Latin proverb (*asinus ad lyram*) describing someone attempting a task for which they have no talent or understanding.</note> compared to the **chemists**? Let him first be trained in **chemistry**, and then we shall admit him to give testimony. The more material or earthy a substance is, the less it binds together; the **chemists** are most expert in this matter. Or is it that only Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a prominent French physician and staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against alchemical innovations.</note> knows **Galenic** and **surgical** matters? If the **chemical physicians** had found simply better things—for there can be no exact science or demonstrative proof regarding the sheer variety of circumstances—would they have turned away toward **chemistry**? Whatever else **Galenism** possesses, **chemistry** also has, except that the latter prepares substances more sincerely, purely, and correctly in the workshops. Experience has found that the "surgical mass" <note>original: *offam chirurgicam*; likely referring to a crude, unrefined bolus or paste used by traditional surgeons to plug wounds.</note> is a completely common **medicament**; while it performs something in the way of binding, it does almost nothing for the arteries, deeper wounds, and large vessels.

But those things prepared from <term>mummy</term> <note>original: *mumia*; a substance made from bitumen or sometimes ground remains, used to stop bleeding.</note>, <term>virgin's milk</term> <note>original: *lacte virgineo*; a milky lotion made by mixing tinctures (often lead or benzoin) with water.</note>, extract of <term>colcothar</term> <note>original: *colcotaris*; the red oxide of iron remaining after the distillation of vitriol.</note>, tormentil, burnet, pomegranate rind, medlars, dragonwort, <term>dragon's blood</term> <note>A bright red resin obtained from certain plants, used as an astringent.</note>, oak gall, mistletoe, and so on, are far more excellent. Sometimes <term>nitric acid</term> <note>original: *aqua fortis*.</note>, <term>spirit of vitriol</term> <note>A corrosive acid, typically sulfuric acid, used in highly diluted forms or for chemical preparations.</note>, and similar things which penetrate deeply and bind and glue within are most effective. So it is with **oil of Saturn** <note>A preparation of lead (Saturn), often lead acetate.</note> and its sugar, **oil of Mars** <note>A preparation of iron (Mars).</note>, and the solution of astringent minerals—such as amber, mastic, colophony, bitumens, calamine stone, <term>bone-binder</term> <note>original: *osteocollæ*; a mineral (usually carbonate of lime) believed to help fractured bones knit together.</note>, fossil ebony, gems, earths, etc. Also **oil of Venus** <note>A preparation of copper (Venus).</note>, liquor of talc, the **magistery of mica** <note>original: *magisterium lapidis specularis*; a "magistery" is a refined precipitate or essence of a substance.</note>, of alabaster, gypsum, corals, antimony, bones, horns, aloe, the fixed coagulum of rhubarb, lac, etc.

Likewise, there are <term>flowers</term> <note>original: *flores*; in alchemy, this refers to the fine powder produced by sublimation, the process of heating a solid until it turns to vapor and then cools back into a solid.</note> of alum, of vitriol, of metals, and so on. It is very easily apparent that the opposite can be concluded for the **chemists**—not just in appearance, but truly and wisely. For he who has more excellent and successful remedies at the ready in his workshop for every goal of healing—according to all powers: primary, secondary, tertiary, purgative, **alexipharmic** <note>original: *alexipharmacas*; remedies that protect against or neutralize poison.</note>, strengthening, and nourishing for the sick—so that they are available without corruption or decay at the physician's discretion, his medicine, as far as remedies are concerned, is without any doubt to be preferred over those otherwise prepared.

That the **chemical physician** <note>original: *chymiatrum*</note> is so equipped, as has been said, unlike the simple **Hippocratic** <note>A physician who follows the traditional, non-chemical methods of Hippocrates and Galen.</note>, is so plain that nothing could be plainer. Why then should we not award the **palm of victory** to the chemical physician, and accompany him as he triumphs over **Riolan** and the censorious **School of the Parisians**? To this, **Paré** <note>Ambroise Paré (c. 1510–1590), the most famous surgeon of the Renaissance, known for his innovative treatments.</note>, that most noble surgeon of **France**, sings in harmony with us. Here in Book 26 of his *Surgery*, chapter 1, he sings thus:

> *These [chemical medicines] are those which, by some fifth...*

->THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM<- <note>This title likely refers to a work by Albertus Kyper or a similar author defending "Chymical" medicine against the Galenists, or it may be used ironically here as the author dismantles Galenic arguments.</note>

## CHAPTER 70.

> *Whether the purging essences of the chymists evacuate watery humors while leaving the thick ones behind. Referring to the Manual, page 102.*

**I**n order to disparage chemical purges, Riolan gathers arguments from every possible source, even most recklessly (in his *Madness*, page 94) <note>original: *Pag. mania*; the author is mockingly referring to Riolan’s writings as a product of mania.</note>. He claims mineral essences are condemned—and he says these are the only ones rejected by the School [of Paris], page 100—because they purge any humor without selection <note>In Galenic medicine, "selection" is the ability of a drug to target one specific humor (like bile) while leaving others.</note>; page 95. He argues they draw most powerfully from every side, disturb nature, and irritate the excretory power with their <term>malignancy</term> <note>original: *cacoethia*; a term derived from Greek meaning a "bad habit" or a malignant medical condition.</note>, and so on.

Yet now, almost the exact opposite is asserted. Our "fiery spirits" (for so he calls the spiritual essences, or chemical extracts, which the chymists themselves say are spiritual because they are separated from elementary matter, are related to "forms," and approach the nature of spirits in the thinness of their essence) are now said to purge only watery and thin humors while leaving the thick ones behind. 

If this is true, how can he also claim they purge any humor without selection? To evacuate the watery humor while leaving behind thick phlegm and melancholy is, by definition, to *fail* to purge those two humors. Furthermore, if the bile were also thickened, these medicines would not purge that either, being supposedly restricted only to thin fluids and the "waters" of those suffering from dropsy <note>Dropsy, or edema, was characterized by an excess of watery fluid in the body.</note>. 

This contradiction is so typical of Riolan; he is a man accustomed to fighting against himself with opposing weapons. In truth, I did not even touch upon this "sore" in the previous examination; but I wondered why a man who confessed—indeed, even contended against the truth—that chemical essences are thin and fiery...

<margin>original: *precium*</margin>
...and from that, he would dare to write that resolving and attractive powers pass over the thick humors. I taught, likewise, that *chymistry* <note>The early modern term for the combined study of chemistry and alchemy.</note> is equipped with all powers, so that it cannot fail to thin those humors that are thick, and draw out those that have been thinned.

He cannot stomach this. He brings forth *Mesue* <note>likely referring to Mesue the Younger, an influential but semi-legendary Arabic medical authority whose texts were central to European pharmacy.</note> as a witness to argue against me. He says that this author wrote concerning hypochondriac melancholy, stating that in this affliction one must abstain from the more violent <term>cathartics</term> <note>Powerful drugs used to purge the body of excess humors, often through the bowels.</note> because they are fiery. For just as fire—he recounts this as if they were the words of *Mesue*, whom I believe he has not even looked at—burns straw before a log, and exerts its power more quickly upon a subject more ready to be affected, so too do the more violent cathartics. Because they are fiery, they draw out the thin and watery humors first, as they are more ready to follow, leaving the thick ones behind. 

When the madness of *Riolan* <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories.</note> babbled these things, he turned himself to insults. Truly, these things have <note>original: *ad rhombum nihil*; literally "nothing to do with the rhombus," a Latin idiom meaning "beside the point."</note> nothing to do with the point. A debater ought to answer why, when we have extracts of every faculty, he denies that we can purge thick <term>humors</term> <note>The four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that Galenic medicine believed governed health.</note>. For to say they are "fiery"—although this is false regarding all of them, since *chymists* are accustomed to diligently correct these elementary qualities—nevertheless, it proves the opposite instead. For if they are fiery, they are also subtle and thin; they then penetrate and cut into, then thin out [the humors], and can also draw out those things which have been made thin and similar to themselves, because of the heat and the familiarity of nature. What does *Mesue* have to say to this, who does not speak specifically of *chymists*, but of evacuation in general, whether it be done through *Galenic* or *chymical* means? # THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM

It is worth hearing the words of *Mesue* <note>Mesue the Younger, an influential Arabic medical authority whose pharmacological writings were standard in European universities.</note> himself, whom *Riolan* either did not look at (producing his quotes from elsewhere) or did not understand—or perhaps even maliciously distorted. Thus he speaks in *Chapter 7* concerning "Cold Soda" <note>original: *Soda frigida*; a medieval medical term for a headache or migraine believed to be caused by "cold" humors.</note> arising from the melancholic humor; and in *Chapter 24* concerning melancholy and mania in his book on *diseases of the brain*:

The third regimen is the evacuative <note>A treatment plan focused on "evacuating" or purging harmful fluids from the body.</note>, in which three things seem noteworthy. First, that we should not perform a large and sudden evacuation all at once, but rather at intervals, maintaining a proper balance, so that nature regulates the evacuation, and the evacuation does not regulate nature. (*In Chapter 24 he uses the term "evacuative" in place of "evacuation"*). For a sudden and violent evacuation is hardly ever managed by nature in an orderly way. (*In Chapter 24: For this is the precept of Hippocrates. Indeed, sudden and violent evacuation is scarcely regulated by nature.*) It is just like the force of a flame, which acts suddenly upon a subtle substance, but passes over that which is thick.

Truly, it is the work of moderate heat to act equally upon both parts of a thing, whether it is to be boiled or roasted, etc. Here, *Mesue* forbids a violent operation when a thick humor is stuck fast in the limbs. He does not prohibit the use of a medicine that is "fiery," subtle, and thin, which is able to cut into, thin out, and remove obstructions, provided it is applied prudently—lest this action happen so suddenly that we wish to pour out the entire *Camarina* <note>original: *camarinam*; an ancient Greek idiom referring to a marsh that was drained against divine advice, causing a plague. To "move the Camarina" meant to stir up a massive, dangerous mess.</note> at once in a single agitated movement. This is something that the <term>chemical physicians</term> <note>original: *chymiatri*; doctors who utilized alchemical and chemical preparations rather than relying solely on traditional herbal mixtures.</note> guard against far more prudently than is commonly done—unless they feel that the waste <note>original: *colluuiem*; a mass of filth or stagnant humors.</note> in the stomach and neighboring parts has already been loosened...
