-># ON THE PURGING PARTS OF ALCHEMY<-

<margin>Me-</margin>...[the matter] sticks, which nature itself is prepared to drive out through vomiting. Regarding the purgings performed by charlatans <note>original: *agyrtarum*; street-performers or unlicensed healers who sold "miracle" cures</note>, one need not respond with anything other than that they act ignorantly and wickedly, since they ought to abstain from medicine altogether. Both his words and the medicines he recommends prove that this was the intention of *Mesue* <note>A 9th-century Persian physician whose works were central to European pharmacy</note>. Among these are the **Indian Pills**, **Sabor**, and **Heben Girges**, which contain **hiera** <term>hiera: a traditional bitter purgative powder, usually based on aloe</term>, **dodder of thyme** <note>original: *epithymum*</note>, **agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus found on larch trees</note>, **colocynth** <note>the "bitter apple," a powerful laxative</note>, **black hellebore**, **Indian salt**, **Lapis Lazuli**, and others. The dose ranges from 1.5 drams <note>original: *ʒj ß.*</note> to 2 drams, taken with **whey** <note>original: *aqua casei*; literally "cheese water"</note> in which dodder, raisins, and rock salt have been infused. 

He also adds a **decoction of dodder** containing **turbith** <term>turbith: the root of a plant in the morning glory family, used as a purgative</term>, **black hellebore**, **rock salt**, **senna**, etc. Likewise, he includes the **Infusion of Hamech** <note>a famous complex electuary used for melancholic diseases</note>, the **Pills of Alexander made of Armenian stone** <note>original: *lapide armeno*; a blue mineral related to azurite, used to purge "black bile"</note>, and so on. Regarding these medicines of his—which are certainly quite powerful and even contain minerals—he sets a rule: they should be administered in such a way that the purging does not occur all at once in a single rush.

Note indeed that this decoction and infusion are proposed by a man who said that these operations **separate the form from the matter** <note>original: *separare speciem à materia*</note>, which is the work of the **Great Mastery** <term>magisterii: the highest level of alchemical skill or the preparation of a "master" medicine</term>. If he had judged chemical extracts to be useless for melancholic patients on the grounds that they are "fiery," he would not have prescribed these infusions and decoctions. 

It is clear, therefore, that *Mesue* instructs on behalf of the chemists and is by no means opposed to their study. This makes the malice of *Riolan* <note>Jean Riolan the Younger, a fierce defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical therapies</note> all the more execrable, as he spares no slander in order to heap disgrace upon chemical matters. Furthermore, our extracts are not so fiery that they must [be rejected]...

...that melancholy is avoided [by these chemical medicines] is false. Experience itself testifies concerning the essence of **senna**, **hellebore**, **lapis lazuli**, **Armenian stone**, **vitriol**, **antimony** <note>original: *stibii*</note>, **mercury**, **copper**, **iron**, and the like: if prudence and skill are not lacking in their use, they may be successfully employed in cases of **mania** and **melancholy**. Therefore, we dismiss Riolan along with his censorious school to those same conditions. For if the mania be "cold" (as it sometimes is; for his own reasons often freeze so much that you would think they had turned plainly into ice), it will be warmed by fiery essences, and the malignant matter, having been thinned out, will easily follow [be expelled]. But if the mania be "hot" (as his accusations sometimes rise to fury and madness), then—because "like attracts like," and as Riolan himself argues that thin bile and serous humor are drawn out by fiery chemistry—it will happen that they are delivered from that most pestilential sink-hole <note>original: *camarina*; a reference to a stagnant Sicilian marsh. Let them therefore be left as incurable and desperate.

As for the medications, Riolan cited to us a far different opinion from **Hippocrates** and **Galen** than he did from **Mesue** (on page *mania 97*). For according to Hippocrates *in his book on the Nature of Man*, when a drug enters the body, it first draws that which, among all things existing in the body, is most naturally familiar to itself; then indeed it also draws and purges other things. For example, drugs for **phlegm** <term>pituita: phlegm, one of the four humors, traditionally considered cold and moist</term> first draw the most pure phlegm, and afterwards that which is mixed, etc. Likewise, Galen writes *in book 3 on Simple Medicines, chapter 26*: "If a drug is naturally suited to purge **black bile** <term>atra bilis: the humor associated with melancholy</term>, it will indeed draw that out first, and after—"

## CHAPTER LXXI.

### *The arguments of Riolan concerning the "third qualities," which he claims the Dogmatists <note>The "Dogmatists" were traditional physicians who followed the established theories of Galen and Hippocrates, as opposed to the new "Chemical" physicians.</note> employ better; from his manuscript pages 102 and 103.*

**W**e shall discuss these matters in the examination of *page* 44. There, we taught that the <term>chemists</term> <note>original: *chymicos*; followers of the new Paracelsian medicine who used distillation to find the "essence" of drugs</note>—whose pursuit since ancient times has been not to scrutinize the primary and elementary qualities <note>The basic qualities of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> existing merely in the "husk" or outward appearance of things (for these are obvious)—excel in bringing forth what is hidden within substances. As <term>Mesue</term> and likewise <term>Sylvius</term> <note>Jacques Dubois (Sylvius), a famous anatomist and teacher of Vesalius who remained a staunch Galenist</note> say, the chemists are superior in this regard. He writes that the "occult <note>Hidden or unexplained by the four basic elements</note> qualities" include the power of purging, poisons, and medicines specifically suited to certain organs. He also lists those suited to specific diseases, such as "epileptic," "nephritic" (for kidneys), "arthritic" (for gout), and "synanchic" (for sore throat/quinsy). First, he argues concerning purgatives:

> *He who purges more specifically, purges better.*
> *The Dogmatists purge more specifically than the chemical physicians.*
> *Therefore, they purge better.*

The minor premise is "proved" by the claim that they do not purge just any humor indiscriminately. Rather, they first purge the offending humor, and the others follow either by consequence or by the **DREAD OF A VACUUM** <note>original: *F V G A  V A C V I*; the ancient physical theory that "Nature abhors a vacuum," used here to explain why one fluid moves to fill the space left by another</note>. (For this is true only of strong medicines, not of those which do not go beyond the first or second region <note>In early modern medicine, the body was often divided into three "regions" or "venters": the abdomen (digestive), the chest (vital), and the head (animal). For nature, when excessively provoked, exceeds its bounds, just as <term>Riolan’s</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657) was a prominent French physician and a fierce defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories.</note> mania is agitated with a more powerful paroxysm <note>original: *paroxysmo*; a sudden attack or increase in the intensity of a disease.</note>.

Some are pleased to believe that an impression of the acting agent is left in the prepared patient, such that the altered nature afterwards acts just like the medicine. For the thing altered follows the nature of the thing that altered it. If, therefore, a strong change has been made even after the medicine is expelled, nature will nevertheless continue to move until the force wears out, or is wiped out by an opposing stronger motion, or is itself bound and numbed—just as <term>excessive purging</term> <note>original: *hypercatharses*; a dangerous condition where a laxative causes uncontrollable bowel movements.</note> sometimes ceases on its own, sometimes is stopped by sleep, and sometimes by foods and <term>theriac</term> <note>original: *theriaca*; a famous ancient medical compound consisting of dozens of ingredients, used as an antidote and universal cure.</note>, etc. But let these matters be dismissed. We deny the minor premise, and prove the contrary with this argument:

> *He who possesses various and sometimes contrary faculties within one mixture can purge less "definitely" than he who possesses a selected and certain faculty, chosen according to nature against the definite cause of the disease.*

> *Galenic "simples" <note>Medicines made from a single unadulterated herb or plant, rather than a chemical extract.</note>, who are opposed to the Galenic chemical physicians, have various faculties in one mixture; but the chemical physicians <note>original: *chymiatri*; doctors who used alchemy and chemistry to extract the "pure" essence of a medicine.</note> have a definite faculty according to nature against the cause of the illness.*

<page-num>702</page-num>

*Chemical physicians, therefore, purge more definitively than Galenic simples.* <note>original: "simplicibus"; "simples" are individual medicinal herbs used in their natural state, as opposed to complex chemical extractions.</note>

The major premise is manifest. For "determination" <note>In this context, the specific focus or targeted action of a medicine.</note> exists among things that are singularly disposed. Where there are many and contrary faculties <note>properties or powers</note>, but only one thing in the patient to which the appropriate agent should be directed, the action is so far from being "defined" that it is even hindered by the faculty of the contrary property. When one property conquers, the other resists; it is necessary that force be brought upon nature. The minor premise is clear from the nature of things, as Galen admits, and as <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional medicine.</note> posits regarding his **rhubarb** when it is given in powder, or otherwise in its whole state: it possesses an astringent <note>binding or tongue-drying</note> quality alongside a laxative one, which are opposites.

That the chemists separate property from property, and the specific essence from the raw matter, <term>Mesuë</term> <note>Mesuë the Younger, a name attached to influential medieval pharmaceutical texts that bridged the gap between herbalism and early chemistry.</note> taught long ago, and experience confirms. Riolan himself admits this, as he attempts the same through the chemical rudiment of infusion <note>The process of soaking a plant to extract its properties.</note>. What occurs in the case of rhubarb is also carried out in other medicines according to the nature of each. Such is the argument regarding purging medicines. Regarding the rest, the following general reasoning applies:

> *Those things which act by the property of their "whole substance" do so better when all substantial parts are united than when they are separated.*

*The Dogmatic <note>Referring to the "Dogmatists," the traditional medical school following Galen and Hippocrates.</note> remedies of Riolan act by the property of the whole substance, as has been proven regarding poisons, remedies appropriated to specific limbs, and specifics for diseases. Therefore, they act better with all parts of the substance united than separated. And as a consequence, chemical remedies are forced to yield to the Dogmatic ones.*

The major premise is proved; because whoever separates the matter takes away a substantial part; when this is removed, the whole substance ceases to be "whole," and the **specific** <note>original: "specificum"; the unique, identifying power or "blueprint" of a medicine</note> is destroyed. The consequence is limited by the exception of poisons, which are the more harmful the more **spiritual** <note>meaning refined, vaporous, or concentrated into an "essence"</note> they are—a prerogative that <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger, the conservative defender of traditional medicine mentioned on the previous page.</note> easily grants to the chemists. But this is the refuse <note>original: "excrementum"; used here as a biting insult for a poor argument</note> of a maniacal fit. For if even poisons act by the force of their "whole substance," which, once the matter is removed, is no longer whole and loses its specific property, they cannot be exempted from this rule; or, if these poisons do not lose their specific property when the elementary matter is separated, then neither will the other medicines.

Therefore, by this very example, Riolan's reasoning goes up in smoke, the major premise having been denied. If the specific property of the whole substance does not perish when the poison is extracted, then it does not perish in other cases either, such as with <term>alexipharmics</term> <note>medicines intended to neutralize or ward off poison</note> and appropriate remedies; but according to Riolan, it does not perish. Therefore, it does not perish in the others. Consequently, a logical fallacy of "non-cause as cause" <note>treating something as a cause that is not actually the cause</note> is committed. For it is manifest that the matter which is separated does not belong to the completion of the "whole substance," or if it does belong, then the "occult power" is falsely attributed to the whole substance.

Behold, Riolan, we slit your throat with your own weapons! You turn your horns against yourself. Furthermore, there are various opinions regarding the term "whole substance." If it is to be retained, it can signify nothing other than the internal subject in which the **substantial crasis** <note>original: "crasis"; the fundamental mixture or temperament of a substance</note> resides along with its properties; and thus it is the **chemical essence** which is sometimes divided into its integrating parts, which are the principles, each of which [contributes] to the power of the whole...

## THE TRIUMPH OF GALENIC MEDICINE

Just as it is common to be struck from both sides and to yield now to these waves and now to those, so too am I forced to feel the fury of both sides, positioned between the pure, unadulterated **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who championed chemical medicine and often rejected ancient authorities</note> and the spurious **Galenists** <note>Adherents to the traditional medical system of Galen, which emphasized the balance of "humors" and herbal remedies</note>, and to cautiously turn away wherever their force rushes in. My fellow <term>iatrochemists: physicians who apply chemistry to medicine</term> and lovers of **Arabic medicine** <note>The medical traditions of scholars like Avicenna and Rhazes, which synthesized Greek knowledge with new pharmacology</note> experience the same thing. When the storms of <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a famous botanist and physician who sought to "purify" medicine by removing medieval Arabic influences in favor of original Greek texts</note> **Fuchs** break over them, they are tossed nearly to the most distant **Garamantes** <note>original: "Garamantes"; an ancient Saharan tribe used here as a metaphor for the ends of the earth</note>; but again, when the Arabic waves grow strong, they are pushed back. Thus, sailing between the Greeks and the Arabs, they are forced to endure much hardship.

**Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Elder, a staunch defender of traditional medicine in Paris</note> exults in his "Galenic simplicity." When he reads my writings disputing the absurdities of the Paracelsians—whether they were produced by **Paracelsus** himself or by those who use the mask of Paracelsus as a deceptive front—he believes me to be entirely one of his own. However, when I demonstrate that I do not oppose the truth of **Hippocratic** and **Galenic** medicine, and do not stray from it by even a hair’s breadth, yet nonetheless admit the science of **Alchemy**, and take up arms against its enemies for the sake of its dignity, antiquity, utility, and necessity for the art of healing, he then accuses me of defecting to **Paracelsianism** and "**Neo-Paracelsianism**."

I bear this with a calm mind, well aware that not even **Jove** <note>The Roman king of the gods, Jupiter</note> satisfies everyone, whether he brings rain or withholds it. There was room for bitterness and a justified defense against this accusatory argument. But I shall restrain myself, so that students may see what truth or falsehood is being charged, by [listing] in distinct... <meta>catchword: stin- (likely "distinctis" or "distinct numbers")</meta>

<margin>Chemical principles are physical <note>meaning they belong to the study of nature/physics</note> rather than medical. I did not attack the chemical principles; I denied that they were *medical* principles. Chemistry is one thing, medicine is another, even if the former adapts itself to the latter in some part. <header>ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS</header>

*...he solemnly promises and swears that he will never depart even a hair’s breadth* <note>original: "ne latum quidem unguem," literally "not even a fingernail’s width"</note> *from the principles of ancient medicine.*

These are my words: I grant much to the knowledge and right use of minerals; I grant much to **chemistry**; and would that everyone would experiment with me with equal opinion and effort; **soon** we would have a more refined preparation of medicines. A lie.

-> ## Alchemy: On the Falsehoods of Paris ## <-

...with their qualities. We leave those things in their own category. By the act of creating, God produced **mixed bodies** <note>original: *mixta*; in early modern science, these are complex substances formed by the combination of the four basic elements</note> from the elements, and through the process of generation, He propagated them. These mixed bodies become the subject of <term>Alchemy</term>. Within their inner parts, Alchemy discovers an essence distinguished by a **threefold form** <note>This likely refers to the "Tria Prima" (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury), which Paracelsian and chemical thinkers argued were the true building blocks of matter</note>, which is of such a nature that nothing more pure or noble can be found in any mixture. 

Therefore, and because it transcends the elements, they have called it the <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: *quinta essentia*; literally the "fifth essence," a refined substance thought to be superior to the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water)</note> and a specific type or form. These are the roots and foundations of powers, which have nothing prior to them of the same kind. For while the elements are indeed prior by reason of their physical and perceptible simplicity, they are not prior in terms of their essential faculties. By the right of their own discipline, the chemists have called these "principles," a fact which <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*</note> seems not to have been ignorant of when he calls **Salt** a necessary element. 

From this it is clear: just because Aristotle’s logical causes and **privations** <note>original: *privantia*; the absence of a quality that ought to be present</note> are true principles adapted from metaphysics to physics, it does not mean that the principles of chemistry are false. Just because <term>Peripatetic physics</term> <note>the school of philosophy following Aristotle</note> posits the elements as the first of perceptible things, it does not follow that the principles of chemistry are mere fictions. 

The one does not overrule the other, just as the <term>Hippocratic humors</term> <note>the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) used in ancient medicine to explain health and temperament</note> are not banished by our chemical principles—except when they also become the subject of our art. For then they are **derived products** <note>original: *principiata*; things produced from principles</note> and not principles; just as, in respect to the natural elements, they are **composed of elements** <note>original: *elementata*</note> rather than being the elements themselves. Nevertheless, the principles and elements of Hippocratic medicine arise from a different starting point; these were rejected neither by Aristotle, nor Plato, nor the <term>Arab chemists</term> <note>referring to medieval Islamic scholars like Geber or Rhazes, who laid the groundwork for European alchemy</note>, even though those men held different principles for their own sciences...

It is obvious from Book 12 of the *Metaphysics*, text 22 and following, that the use of these terms varies, and it is no crime to adapt names in different ways depending on what one is looking at. In that work, three elements are called "principles" by analogy, which elsewhere are not; and the four causes and principles are elsewhere called "Elements." **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian or Arab physician known in the West as Mesue the Elder.</note> calls the extract of Rhubarb, of Myrobalans <note>A fruit used in medieval and Renaissance medicine as a purgative.</note>, etc., the "species" and "form." He does the same for oils, waters, and whatever things are produced from the hidden and separated from their bulk matter. 

For **Aristotle**, "form" is more truly a principle than "matter" is. Thus, the word "principle" has been adapted to describe chemical essences. Riolan thinks that if this is true, then every compound becomes a principle of an even greater compound. He is raving. It is one thing to have no existence in act, and another in potency. That things exist in potency before they exist in act is a dogma of the Natural Philosophers: [he denies] that nature generates from two [acts]...

actually existing, but coming together into a new essence which was in them potentially, as the ancients taught by "mother and father," "active and passive," and entirely by mixture, etc. That petty lawyer <note>original: "Rabula." A derogatory term for a loud, unlearned speaker, used here to insult Riolan.</note>, with his canine eloquence—which resides in the tongue without the mind—rashly blathers whatever blind hatred dictates. These things are refuted at length in the *Examination*. Now at least let us run through the eloquence of his "Madness" <note>original: "maniae." This is the author's mocking nickname for Riolan’s book, *Adversus Paracelsistas*.</note>.

He asks whether chemical essences are made through transmutation by art, or whether they are inherent in nature so that they may be extracted. If he has shown that they are made by us through transmutation, he thinks it is immediately concluded that they are not "principles," which he believes must be present in actuality <note>original: "actu." In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" is the finished, realized state, while "potency" is the potential state.</note> so that they can be separated and drawn out—just as if someone had hidden pearls in a dung heap <note>original: "sterquilinio."</note>, and later picked them out and cleaned them up when brought into view; in the same way Hercules is imagined to have brought Cerberus from the underworld into the light of day. 

But I say, whether they are in the thing actually, or potentially—like elements in a mixture, salt in brine, silver in a solution of caustic water <note>original: "aquae causticae." Likely a reference to nitric acid (aqua fortis), used to dissolve silver.</note>, etc.—it does not prevent chemists from calling them "principles" with respect to material elements and impurities, for in them is the root, foundation, and origin of the powers <note>original: "facultatum."</note> in things. Why do they care for that storyteller, whose talkative tongue has been made bold and rash by ignorance? Argue thus:

> *Things arise by the conjunction of matter and form,*
> *and perish by their separation. (Therefore, he says)*
> *principles likewise must be joined with matter;*
> *And thus pre-exist.*
> *But they do not pre-exist.*
> *Therefore, they are made.*

-> # THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM <note>original: "GALENIA TRIVMPHVS." This title likely refers to a specific chapter or a mocking header in this polemical work against the Galenic physician Jean Riolan.</note> <-

<meta>catchword: This</meta>

This force must be contained in the general statement, unless that trifler poured out reckless words. The thesis is that principles are not extracted, but are made through transmutation. For if they were extracted, they would have existed through a meeting with matter and coalesced into one. The foolish man composes natural things as children do dollhouses. But **form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is, as opposed to "matter," which is the raw substance.</note> is a certain perfection, and it does not come to the composition as if it were a part of the matter; rather, it is born within. Therefore, if our essences are formal, when a thing is born and perfected through the "forms of imperfection" <note>This likely refers to the developmental stages of a substance before it reaches its final, perfected state.</note>, they are simultaneously made and drawn out from the **potency** <note>original: "potentia." The capacity for a thing to become something else.</note> of matter. 

In this matter, they exist either in **actuality** <note>original: "actu." The state of being fully realized or physically present.</note> or in "proximate potency": in actuality, as when oil and water are spread through a mixture, which we see in many things from which they emerge by a simple pressing; in potency, as when they are actualized, having previously neither appeared to the senses nor existed separately. Nature also actualizes certain things, as we see in balsamic tears <note>original: "lachrymis balſameis." These are natural resins or saps that exude from plants.</note>, while some require art. Some are in a more "remote potency," others in a "closer" one. All things exist within, whether in act or potency, to a greater or lesser degree. 

The premise of <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a conservative French physician and fierce opponent of Paracelsian chemical medicine.</note> is foolish; a wise conclusion cannot be born from it. He seeks another argument from the elements. Elements that are in mixtures have come together. <term>Salt</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, and <term>mercury</term> <note>These are the *Tria Prima*, the three fundamental chemical principles of Paracelsus, which he believed composed all material things.</note> did not "come together" <note>i.e., they were not combined like ingredients in a recipe at the start.</note>. Therefore, they are not in the mixtures, and consequently, when they are drawn out, they are made by transmutation and are not extracted. We deny that this follows, because the logic of elements and principles is not the same. The former [elements] are imagined to come together separately; the latter [principles] come forth through generation by the movement of the generating nature. And therefore, they are not elements.

<summary>The author refutes Jean Riolan's claim that chemical principles are artificial creations, arguing instead that they exist "potentially" within matter and are brought into "actuality" through nature or art. He distinguishes between traditional elements, which combine to form mixtures, and Paracelsian principles, which are innate to the generation of a substance.</summary>

-> ### ON THE PURITY OF ALCHEMY <note>original: "ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS." This header likely refers to a discussion on the purity of alchemical principles or is part of a running title for the section.</note> <-

Furthermore, there is also an ambiguity in the word **Extraction**. That foolish man <note>Referring to Jean Riolan the Elder, a prominent Galenic physician who opposed the use of chemical medicines.</note> thinks that nothing can be extracted unless it is hidden like a sword in a scabbard, or a viper in the grass: and is already present in **actuality** <note>original: "actu." In Aristotelian philosophy, "actuality" refers to something fully realized and physically present, as opposed to "potentiality."</note> within things. But we also extract that which was present in **potency** <note>original: "potentia." The inherent capacity of a substance to become something else or reveal a specific quality.</note> and has been drawn out from the center to the surface.

Therefore, our method of extraction in some cases consists of a double movement: the **actuation** <note>The process of bringing a potential quality into an actual, manifest state.</note> and the separation of what has been actuated. In other cases, where the essence is more exposed and pushed forward by nature itself, there is no need for actuation; this is clearly seen in oily substances. However, the earthy matter of these same substances has **salt** <note>One of the three "Primes" or fundamental principles in Paracelsian chemistry (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury).</note> more tightly enclosed, which must therefore be drawn out by a more remote path.

We say nothing of **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the controversial founder of iatrochemistry (chemical medicine).</note> for now. We defend our own views. He, however, wished to place principles in things just like **vitriol** <note>A term for metal sulfates, often used as a primary example in alchemical reactions.</note> in its own solution. He mocked **Peripatetic potency** <note>The Aristotelian concept of "potentiality" taught by the "Peripatetics" (Aristotle's followers).</note>; we, however, allow him to enjoy his own dreams.

The third argument of Riolan—that **sulphur** is produced by the dissolution of a mixture, etc.—is utterly false. He claims it is therefore not extracted, but produced by a change. We will prove the falsity of this premise below through the study of natural solution. Just because Riolan’s eyes do not see a thing, it does not mean no one sees it. An **artificial solution** <note>A chemical process using heat or solvents to break down a substance.</note> which imitates nature in closed vessels places the truth before one's eyes. In some things, however, those principles lie hidden more deeply and are more firmly locked away. Therefore, more than one "unlocking" is required.

Nothing, however, prevents you from saying here that an **act** <note>The manifest reality of a thing.</note> is led forth from a more remote potency. For a manner of speaking does not overturn the truth of nature, just as it is not usually denied that **fire** is within a thing simply because it must be provoked from a more remote source <note>Likely referring to striking a flint to produce a spark; the "fire" is considered present in the stone potentially even if it is not currently burning.</note>. Furthermore, the fact that a thing is not resolved by natural corruption does not stand in the way of the logic of its <unclear>constituent principle.</unclear>

For by the same argument, one must deny that the **Humors** of Hippocrates <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that Galenic medicine believed governed health.</note> and the **seed** and **blood** of Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a prominent French physician and critic of chemical medicine.</note> are "principles" <note>fundamental building blocks of nature.</note>, because none of these emerge through natural corruption. From these points, he [Riolan] draws a general conclusion: "What is left then," he asks, "except that they are present only in **potency** <note>The inherent capacity for a thing to exist, as opposed to its actual physical existence.</note> or materially?"

He understands this **sophistically** <note>Using clever but fallacious reasoning.</note> indeed; as if they were present in potentiality on account of matter, which is changeable into every "miracle of things." However, we [the chemists] prove by the property of their **virtues** <note>The specific medicinal power or "hidden strength" of a substance.</note> that they are present **formally and definitely**. For if they were present only by reason of **transmutation** <note>The process of changing one substance into another, as in alchemy.</note>, our principles or essences would not possess the same specific power that we perceive nature has implanted in mixtures with definite qualities and effects.

But in most cases, we demonstrate that this power is retained determinately, as in the case of **extracted purgatives**, etc. Some substances are produced from a more remote source. But these likewise have a power that primarily agrees with their own kinds. For if they did not, then from different individuals, affected differently in themselves, the same results would emerge through the same transmutatory operation.

But that is not what happens. For **salt** produced from all sources is definitely salty; **glass of antimony** <note>original: "vitrum stibii." A substance made by roasting and melting antimony ore, used as a powerful emetic.</note> emerges from every antimony with the same virtue; the **Regulus** <note>The metallic part of a mineral that settles at the bottom during smelting.</note> and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum." Literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note> likewise, along with the others, according to the method of processing.

Therefore, once vague generality and that "all-seeding" potentiality are removed, our adversary is forced to concede a **determined potentiality** to us, and to say: that they are present by a determined potentiality and a definite disposition of matter—just as that which is ripened from the raw, perfected from the imperfect, or separated with a different form from the variously affected members of an entire essence, and from...

The power of life in wine is certainly not wandering, but ordered, although here we also perceive the actual state through the senses and the effect. Likewise on page 113 regarding *Madness* <note>original: "Maniae"; likely a reference to a specific medical text or chapter on the condition.</note>, where elements existing in **potency** <note>The inherent capacity for something to exist or act, even if not currently visible.</note> are said to **TRULY** be within, etc. Now we take up and conclude concerning the principles, and we declare our premise in the same manner. Therefore, we finish off our antagonist with his own weapons, and we make his foul ignorance—joined with malice—known to everyone, "even to the bleary-eyed and the barbers." <note>A Latin idiom meaning "everyone knows it," as barbershops and clinics were centers for local gossip.</note>

He sets against us the example of bread and chyle <note>The milky fluid formed in the stomach during digestion.</note>. From this arises such a logic: If chyle is not **TRULY** in bread, then neither are chemical principles in compound bodies. But it is not [truly there]: because it exists [only] in potency or materially. Therefore [they are not there]. We deny this connection because of the <term>fallacy of the qualified statement</term>. <note>original: "Elenchum secundum quid"; a logical error where a general rule is applied to a specific case that has qualifying circumstances.</note> For it does not follow that if chyle is not in bread in the same way that salt is in brine, then our principles are not present at all. For one must distinguish between the nature and the **perfection** <note>The fully realized or completed state of a substance.</note> of things. In some things, the principles have reached maturity to such an extent that they even blossom forth to the senses; in others, not yet; and yet in both cases they are truly present. Unless perhaps there is no truth in potency, and no Being or thing exists that is in a state of potency. Thus in the blood of *Riolan* <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a prominent conservative physician in Paris.</note> the four **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that Galenic medicine believed governed health.</note> exist in potency; are they therefore not truly present? We deny that chyle is in bread in its **actual state** <note>original: "actu"; the state of being fully formed or functional.</note>; but to say it is therefore not "truly" there is false. For it is truly present according to its potency. The purgative juice of *Rhubarb* is a chemical species, form, and essence...

-> ## GALENIC TRIUMPH ## <-

oil of caraway, cinnamon water, water of fresh and still succulent **Rhubarb** <note>original: "Rhabarbari"</note>, juice of roses, **tincture of violets**, **extract of Hellebore**, **oil of myrrh**, etc. **Vulcan** <note>The Roman god of fire, here representing the chemist’s furnace or the transformative power of heat.</note> has an indeterminate power unless it is governed by art; but the principles [of a substance] are determinate and consistent with their own nature. The ultimate end of **Vulcan** is fire; therefore, he ought not to make diverse things but rather one single thing out of everything. Often we also use a faint heat which is by no means transformative, but rather dissolutive, as in putrefaction through a **bath** <note>original: "balneū"; likely a *balneum Mariae* or water bath used for gentle heating.</note> or **dung** <note>original: "fimum"; horse dung was frequently used in early chemistry to provide a slow, steady, fermenting heat.</note>. Sometimes we express juices and allow the expressed juices to be separated by themselves. Sometimes we use cold, as in the **quintessence** <note>original: "qnta essentia"; the "fifth essence," or the most purified and potent form of a substance.</note> of wine and the ice of crystals. Sometimes we use dissolving solvents without any flame. **Vulcan** can be the instrument of the art, but the work of the principles is not his when he acts by himself; rather, he separates those things which nature has mixed together—which exist in act or in potency—once these have first been brought into act. An example is **metallurgy**, in which he gathers together homogeneous things once the heterogeneous things have been separated; he removes the dross and refuse from the essential metals by means of vapor, flux, sediment, swimming, and so on. But we say again: if **transmutation** is the bringing into act and the separation of those things whose principles were lying hidden in the matter, the term does not offend us. Our **Vulcan** separates the Elements along with the principles. Do you also declare concerning these that they were not truly in the mixture? Is the reasoning not the same in both cases? But even **Riolanus** <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a conservative French physician who often opposed the new chemical medicines of the Paracelsians.</note> contradicts himself when he writes that our **Vulcan** [acts] in imitation of nature

...in some substances [this happens] immediately, namely in those where the essence is already prepared and in readiness, so much so that it can even be separated by a press. The author is mocking Riolan for using a vague philosophical term instead of specific chemical reality.</note>. This follows the nature of each thing toward its own essential perfection, separated from the rest through its own specific act and form.

...in the works of nature or of art. In your Peripatetic <note>The "Peripato" refers to the followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the colonnades (peripatoi) of the Lyceum in Athens. They believe that the extracted essence lay hidden within, unseen, and could not come forth unless the gates or bonds were loosened, either by putrefaction <note>In alchemy, a process of breaking down a substance's structure through gentle heat or moisture to release its inner spirit.</note>, or by resolution through solvents, or by the force of fire, or by maceration <note>Soaking a substance to soften it and extract its properties.</note>, according to the different ways things are locked away. As an example, we often cite the smelting of metals. Galen <note>The famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated European medicine for over a millennium.</note> thought that quicksilver <note>mercury</note> was a work of art, not of nature, because he saw it smelted from stones, in which he judged it lay hidden in potentiality, and could not be extracted otherwise than through transmutation. Yet none of these things appear [initially]. They are said by the Peripatetic school to be present in potentiality, and to emerge through reciprocal transmutation. Those things truly were present in potentiality. Thus we accommodate ourselves to the phrasing of Aristotle and Galen. ## CHAPTER 77.

->*Whether Riolan wrote that chemical essences exist or do not exist. Regarding page 113 of the manuscript. Also, whether these are "forms."*<-

**I**n the fourth argument against the principles, the words of the <term>censor</term> <note>Referring to Jean Riolan, a prominent critic of chemical medicine who acted as a reviewer or "censor" of these ideas.</note> were: "You seek in vain for what does not exist; your essences are nothing; otherwise, things would exist before they were made." From this, a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> follows:

> *If chemical essences were something (or some type of Being), things would exist before they were made.*
> *But things do not exist before they are made.*
> *Therefore, chemical essences do not exist. (They are not something; they are not any type of Beings, such as forms, etc.)*

The argument was not taken up to address the question of whether our essences do not exist, or are nothing. Riolan denies that he remembers writing "if they were something." But whoever wrote what is equivalent in meaning has written the same thing in reality. However, that he wrote that chemical essences do not exist, that they are nothing, and that they are a fiction and madness, is clear from his *Brief Excursion, page 4*, where he wants to demonstrate with "invincible arguments" that our <term>pyrotechnia</term> <note>original: "Pyrotechniam"; literally "fire-art," a common term for chemistry or the use of fire in laboratory work.</note>—that is, the chemistry of essences which use fire—is nothing other than a fiction of empty imagination. If the art is what he says it is, why wouldn't the work of that art also be a fiction? Then, on page 93, the following is read: "Away with <term>forms</term> <note>original: "formas"; in Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or soul of a substance that makes it what it is.</note> and spiritual essences, formal and active principles, mercury, salt, and sulfur!"

Perfection from the imperfect is pleasing, as is maturation from the immature, and manifestation from the most hidden recesses, and so on. The Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> schools dispute these things in one way, and the chemical schools in another; yet the reality of the matter does not change, only the manner of speaking. If an Aristotelian form can be a form and a principle at the same time—and yet the thing does not exist before it is made, because the form is the final state of the thing—then our principles can also be forms. Furthermore, while the mixture exists, our principles are not yet forms in <term>act</term> <note>original: "actu"; actually existing in a finished, distinct state.</note>, but in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; existing as a possibility or latent power within the matter.</note>. <header>ON THE SPURIOUS PARTS OF ALCHEMY.</header>

->*If principles were in form and in act in mixtures,*<-
->*nothing new would be made.*<-

->*But this is absurd to you. And therefore, so is that.*<-

You prove your logical connection because a thing becomes "new" by the addition of a new form. You demonstrate this through the elements <note>The four Aristotelian elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, which are established as being present *in reality*, though in an indefinite way. If these were the form of the mixture, then since the thing is made from them, it would already exist, and nothing "new" would be made. Here, the chemists will purge your brain for you; and afterward, they will command you to see more sharply. For if the principles did not all exist together in any other way, and there were no process of generation, then wherever they were in <term>act</term> <note>original: "actu"; meaning actually and fully realized.</note>, there a mixture ought to be; and there would be as little need for something to be generated as there is in the heavens <note>Aristotelians believed the celestial spheres were perfect and unchanging, thus no "generation" or "corruption" occurred there.</note>. 

But since they are in the seeds and elements in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to become something else.</note>; and also when a mixture is naturally corrupted, they return to their own kind, or constitute something else, the generation of new things is not abolished. Thus, when they are in "act" within the mixtures, their form is a state of being, not a process of generation. But when they come forth from the seeds of things together with the elements and strive toward the essential perfection of the thing, then the thing is made according to its species, and another individual thing is generated. 

The contrary is concluded for you by the example of the elements. For they are the matter of mixtures, and by their coalition they bring forth a <term>crasis</term> <note>original: "crasin"; from the Greek 'krasis,' meaning a temperament or specific blending of qualities.</note>, which two causes are prior in reason to the thing caused; yet it is not necessary for the thing to exist before it is made. Place the elements in the position of our principles. These are for you in the mixture both in reality and in potentiality. They are also, before your mixing, impure and in no way unmixed—just like our principles—even though with respect to what follows they are called "simple."

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM</header>
<sig>Bbb 2</sig>

...and potentiality <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity for a thing to become something else, as opposed to what it currently is.</note> are this or that. Why should our principles <note>The chemical principles: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> not also be such? If the elements are present, and the chemical principles are within the elements like form within matter; then insofar as they already exist, the mixture must necessarily *be* already, rather than *becoming*. 

However, insofar as both the elements and the principles are moved by generation from a seed toward the <term>determined act</term> <note>original: "actum determinatum"; the final, specific state of a finished object.</note> of a thing—in the presence of which, although they are within it, they are nevertheless hidden by the singular "act" of the whole—just as the form of gold makes it gold, or the form of a jacinth <note>A precious gemstone, likely a variety of zircon or garnet.</note> makes it a jacinth; then in that state the thing is *made*, and it does not exist except in potentiality until the motion ceases when the <term>Entelechy</term> <note>original: "Entelechia"; a term from Aristotle meaning the full realization or "perfection" of a potentiality.</note> is present. 

But when they are called "forms" and "acts," they are named in a different way than "generated acts," such as the acts of a rose, a violet, a dog, etc. But setting the chemists aside, imagine yourself dealing with Severinus <note>Petrus Severinus (1540–1602), a Danish physician who synthesized Paracelsian chemistry with traditional philosophy.</note> or some other Paracelsian. Let the hypothesis be: *Principles are the forms and acts of mixtures.* 

If this is true while they are mixtures, and if the principles of existing things possess their "act" in the heavens and the elements, then it must be that the heavens and the elements are already mixed; or that the thing exists before it is made. For if the form of a mixture is what makes it a mixture, then the mixture must necessarily exist if the form exists, especially since "act" [actuality] is posited as being present at the same time. 

But if Severinus did not wish to answer you by means of potentiality—by which the principles hidden in the heavens and elements can become the form of a mixture once a coalition or mixing is established—he would at least answer by means of <term>disjoined acts</term>. For just as the elements, when divided, are elements in act, and yet are simultaneously the matter of mixtures: so too the principles can exist as separate in act; they are what they are when they are separate acts; but by their coming together, they complete the essential act of the whole mixture. For the nature of a mixture is thus twofold...

He specifically addresses the theories of the Paracelsian philosopher Petrus Severinus regarding how substances are generated.</summary>

### *Regarding the fifth argument against chemical principles.*
### *Referring to manuscript page 115.*

**T**he fifth argument was that whoever establishes chemical principles undermines all the principles of the art of Physics. ### CHAPTER 80.

#### Regarding the seventh argument against the principles.
#### To page 116 of the *Madness* <note>original: "Maniæ." A reference to Riolan's polemical writings, which the author characterizes as insane.</note>.

# ALCHEMY AGAINST THE PARISIAN DEFILERS
<meta>The Latin "SPVR. PARIS." likely refers to "Spurcitias Parisiensis" (Parisian filth/defilements), a derogatory reference to the medical faculty of Paris who opposed chemical medicine.</meta>

...will appear in their true likeness. Lay aside your fantasies and preconceived opinions, and learn the nature and function of the principles held by the chemists; then you will gain sharp insight. Indeed, you previously wrote more soundly when you said that the chemist works by imitating nature. Since this stands, it is necessary that nature does not shrink from chemical principles, but rather yields them from its innermost shrines. However, we have long known that you act like Vertumnus <note>A Roman god of the seasons and change, here used to accuse the opponent of being fickle or "flip-flopping" in his arguments.</note>. Your jokes about the "foolish fire" <note>original: *ignis fatuus*. Let us examine your "wisdom" once again.

Nature, you say, eventually breaks things down into the very materials from which it first composed them, and vice versa. Yet, [you claim] it does not eventually resolve things into chemical principles, but into the four elements <note>The traditional Aristotelian elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. Therefore, [you conclude] it did not compose its things from chemical principles. You attempt to prove your secondary point by arguing that nature cannot resolve things into principles that are themselves composite. Then you bring up the observation of decayed corpses, in which you claim no "chimerical" principles <note>The critic likely used the word "chymerica" as a pun, linking "chemical" to the "Chimera"—a mythical monster—to imply the principles are imaginary.</note> can be found. This is your "prize-winning" argument; but nothing proves your childishness in the study of Physics more. For the denial of the first composition and the final resolution does not destroy the nature of a **principle**, but only the nature of the **elements**. 

A **principle** <term>principle: in alchemy, the "Tria Prima" (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury) which act as the internal "seeds" or spiritual forces of matter</term> is that which is present first, and by whose primary existence a thing is made. An **element** <term>element: the material substrate or physical "shell" of a substance</term>, however, is a body into which other bodies are divided, and which exists within them potentially. These are the decrees of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, whose philosophy dominated the universities of the time.</note>. The chemists agree that it is not an element if God, in establishing nature, [did not use it] as the basis of a corporeal constitution...

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM
<note>The title is likely ironic, as the author is currently dismantling Galenic arguments.</note>

...nature did not create the mixture from that part, nor is the final resolution into that part achieved through the ultimate stage of rot. According to Aristotle, it is not necessary for principles to be physical bodies themselves, nor must they combine in a simple mixture; therefore, they do not necessarily resolve back into those same mixtures at the end. Principles of a specific kind behave in the same way.

<margin>Short Excursion, page 157: We are formed from moist things alone.</margin>
For when Riolan’s own corpse <note>A provocative and typical "ad hominem" attack common in Renaissance polemics.</note> eventually decays, it will not resolve back into the semen and blood—or similar substances—from which he was formed; rather, it will turn into earth. Nevertheless, those substances, along with the humors, are still called "principles."

<margin>Apology, page 54: Menstruum and semen are the principles of animals. Page 71: The two principles of minerals.</margin>
Therefore, even if a natural breakdown into salt, an oily part, and a liquid <note>original: *salem, oleosam partem, & liquorem*. These correspond to the three chemical principles: Salt, Sulfur (the oil), and Mercury (the liquid).</note> did not occur, the logic of them being "principles" would still hold firm. Furthermore, there is one kind of resolution achieved by Art <term>Art: In this context, "Art" refers to the laboratory practice of chemistry or alchemy, as opposed to natural processes.</term> and another achieved by Nature. If these three are the final components found through the resolution of Art, nothing prevents them from being the same in Nature.

But tell the truth, Riolan: the chemists recognize a double composition and resolution. One is **elemental**, and the other is **essential**. You confuse the former with the latter, and you wrongly try to use the one to overturn the other. Recognize your own foolishness, therefore, and submit your hand to discipline, however old you may be. This is how the premise of the argument stands. The parts of your false reasoning <note>original: *paralogismi*. A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note> are no wiser.

Nature does not compose things in the way your opinion has persuaded you. Instead, it ordinarily generates things from composite concepts, both **univocally** and **equivocally** <note>Aristotelian terms: "univocal" refers to things of the same species (like a human producing a human), "equivocal" refers to generation from different materials.</note>. Indeed, we gather the "prior" from the "posterior"; from the senses and what is better known to us, we arrive at what is more fundamental to nature. You might have seen mud made from dust and water, and from that a stone or a tile; but you have never seen nature composing things in such a way, since both the dust and the water were already composite substances themselves. The same applies to nutrition. You have borrowed a major premise from elsewhere, but you have never understood it. The minor premise...

[The argument] is false regarding essential resolution, but true regarding elementary resolution. I still demonstrate to the senses the **fatty oil** <note>original: *pinguedinem*. In Paracelsian chemistry, this refers to Sulfur, the principle of combustibility.</note> from corpses; I demonstrate the **salt**, and I demonstrate the **liquid** <note>original: *liquorem*. This refers to Mercury, the principle of fluidity and volatility.</note>. Why do we not go to marble tombs before the spiritual essence, resolved into a breath, vanishes? Why do we not consider the worms born from heat and the moist spirit held within, or re-cook the ashes from the urns of the ancients? 

But what happens in nature in a dispersed and indeterminate way, happens determinately and conclusively in the vessels of **Art** <term>Art: The standard Renaissance term for Alchemy or chemistry, implying the human ability to perfect or accelerate natural processes.</term> through the power of that same nature. Here, certainly, we show the elements and principles so evidently that whoever does not recognize them lacks both sense and reason. In **essential resolution** <note>The process of breaking a substance down into its three chemical "prime" components: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>, our principles are the ultimate stage, because they cannot be reduced into simpler essences of power. 

I would not deny they can be reduced into [the four] elements, since many things are consumed by fire. Therefore, we do not deny that they consist of elements to which the **fifth nature** <note>original: *quinta natura*. The Quintessence or ether, believed to be the purest, most celestial part of a substance.</note> from the ethereal substance is bound. Thus, your first **syllogism** <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> perishes. For although the chemical principles are composite—just like the humors of **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated European medicine for 1,500 years.</note> or the semen and blood of **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), a conservative French physician and fierce critic of chemical medicine.</note>—they do not lose their status as "principles." And since they are the component parts of the essence, they also deserve the name of "element," although for the sake of distinction, that term is not in common use among chemists when discussing principles. 

Your other syllogism **begs the question**. Unless you had the eyes of a nocturnal animal, you would certainly see this essential resolution. You would see the principles dwelling in those things you call "elements" before they expire; you would see the liquid and the fatty oil being squeezed out; and in what remains, you would see the salt staying more tightly locked away, such that its locks must be opened with stronger instruments.

...miracles to extract the oil of cloves, the laxative water of rhubarb, and the theriacal salt <note>A medicinal salt derived from Theriac, a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical "cure-all" containing dozens of ingredients.</note>. But you can do neither.

Chemists deny that they can make "anything from anything." <term>Riolanus</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent French physician who staunchly defended traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories.</note> himself confessed above that we make a specific thing from a specific thing. But listen to this most beautiful reasoning: Our principles are not *actually* <note>original: *actu*; a state of being fully realized or present.</note> in the **mixtures** <term>mistis</term> <note>The Aristotelian term for a compound where the ingredients have combined into a new, single substance.</note>, but in that most vague *potentiality* <note>original: *potentia*; the capacity or power to become something else.</note> of <term>Anaxagoras</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that "everything is in everything," and that all things contain the "seeds" of all other things.</note>. Truly amazing! Where did Aristotle ever say—concerning that whole Anaxagorean nursery which is transmutable into every face of nature and relates equally to all things, not unlike your **prime matter** <term>materia prima</term> <note>The formless, fundamental substance that is the basis of all physical reality in Aristotelian philosophy.</note> and the "common receptacle" of <term>Plato</term>—that **similar parts**, such as flesh, bone, and so on, were present in "proximate potentiality"? 

How do the most general and common matter and "proximate potentiality" (by which a change most easily happens into a final and unique act) ever agree? Who was that **Riolanian** sophist who introduced nearly infinite preparations, so that the "final potentiality" could not be in that fictional seed-mixture, but in matter that is already defined? It is no longer "prime matter" if it possesses a proximate potentiality toward action. But perhaps that school has an Aristotle different from ours, unless that most learned school is raving. "Blood," you say, "is flesh in proximate potentiality." Imagine this. Is blood then the **seed-mixture** of Anaxagoras? What could you have written more insanely...

...be? If you compare these things, no longer with Anaxagoras's views, but with Riolan's...

# CHAPTER XXII.

## *Concerning the ninth argument against the principles. Manuscript pages 118, 119.*

**T**he chemical principles were also being rejected on the grounds that through secretion <note>The chemical process of separating components from a mixture.</note>, the form, power, and property of natural mixtures would be destroyed. This foolish, judgmental school presses no point as much as this one, and yet that same school—by cooking, infusing, and separating the whole of a particular body and merely "transferring its power" (as Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent French physician who staunchly defended traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories.</note> dreams), and likewise by squeezing, calcining <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder or ash.</note>, turning to ash, mixing, and performing other actions—is far more cruel toward the things of nature than any chemist could be. The chemist's aim from ancient times has been not to destroy, but to separate the form <note>original: *speciem*; the essential nature or "blueprint" of a substance.</note> from the matter, and to make manifest what is hidden within things. While he attempts to perform this through art and science, proven by the practice of many centuries and the consensus of the wise, surely the external and rug- <note>The text cuts off here. a stable mixture must necessarily perish. You might say it does not remain, and therefore a change is instituted so that something nobler is made from the ignoble; from the inconvenient material of a drug, a most suitable medicine is made. ### OF THE SPURIOUS PARTS OF ALCHEMY

But let us nevertheless listen to Riolan, who plays and tosses nuts as if among children <note>A classical idiom (nuces relinquere) meaning to engage in trivial or childish arguments</note>.

->*If the temperament of the whole is one thing, and that of the parts another, the same <term>crasis</term> <note>original: *crasis*; the specific "blend" or mixture of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry)</note> does not remain in the divided parts as was in the joined ones. The former is true. Therefore the latter follows: and consequently, the <term>chemists</term> <note>original: *chymici*; here referring to those who use chemical distillation and extraction to prepare medicines</note> do not retain the mixture of the compound.*<-

The response is clear from what was said before: that the <term>temperament</term> of the whole composite is different from the temperament of the essence. The latter is preserved in extracts, while the former is neglected. This is because the practical use of things requires it, just as a cook kills a whole chicken so that he may prepare a good broth for Riolan; and the <term>pharmacist</term> <note>original: *Pharmacopola*; a seller of drugs or an apothecary</note> buys <term>rhubarb</term> <note>original: *Rheum*</note> which is not, however, the whole rhubarb plant, but its root, which has lost the temperament of its parent plant.

The chemist has fulfilled his duty if the parts that lay hidden in the whole—whatever essential <term>crasis</term> they possessed in and of themselves—exhibit that same pure mixture once they are released. For example, if the flesh of a bull, which was contained under the common form of the bull, retains its own quality when it is separated after the bull is slaughtered; and so it is in plants: whether flower, seed, leaf, bark, root, fruit, or wood, each retains its own specific nature. If Riolan seeks that original mixture of the whole and wishes it to be preserved, let him not build a house from felled trees, but let him live in the woods among the dens of wild beasts. If, however, he destroys that mixture and form for the purpose of producing an action suited to the work at hand, why does he quarrel with the chemists? Galen himself longed for this **separation** <note>original: *διάκρισιν* (diakrisin); the act of separating or distinguishing components</note>, so that he might have pure medicinal powers for use, just as in milk and almost every kind of expressed juices—

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM <note>original: *GALENIA TRIVMPHVS*; likely a satirical title or the name of a section in a debate against the Galenic school, which favored the ancient Greek theory of humors over new chemical medicine.</note>

The <term>Galenic school</term> <note>the followers of the ancient Greek physician Galen</note> pursues its goals with terrible curses, acting as a spurious offspring rather than the genuine child of Galen. But let us slay this school with its own sword:

> *If individual parts separated from the whole have their own proper being—as cheese, whey, and butter are parts of milk—then chemical principles also have their own being.*
>
> *The first part of the statement is true. Therefore, the second part follows.*

Whatever has its own proper being also possesses its own <term>crasis</term> <note>original: *crasin*; the specific "blend" or mixture of qualities that gives a substance its unique character</note>, and with this comes its own power and the specific property by which it can be used. Therefore, <term>chemical principles</term> <note>original: *chymica principia*; the primary substances—usually salt, sulfur, and mercury—that chemists believed were the building blocks of matter</note> will not be useless. Furthermore, if they possess their own blend, they receive it either from art or from nature. It is not from art. For art cannot provide innate dispositions. Indeed, if they received it from art, they would no longer be the works of nature, nor would they be in reality what they previously were in potential according to nature. 

Just as whey, cheese, and butter separated from milk—although they were separated by art—do not receive the action and power of their own nature from art; and as it is with honey, wine, and countless other foods and medicines, so it is also with the <term>essences</term> <note>original: *essentiæ*; the concentrated, purest part of a substance</note> collected by <term>chemists</term> from an elementary body through the art of separation. 

<margin>Riolan</margin> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent French physician and critic of chemical medicine.</note> brings forward the example of a magnet, and he denies that its essence retains the power of the whole. What does it matter? I ask. When you prepare an infusion of <term>rhubarb</term> <note>original: *Rhei*</note>, it does not act as both a binder and a purge like the whole root does; instead, it only purges. But that power which it possessed through nature, it gives off freely when treated by art. When we have achieved this, we have reached our goal.

> *If your essences, you say, acted by themselves without the assistance of matter, they would be able to retain outside of the mixture that same power of acting which they possessed when joined to matter. But they do not so act. Therefore [they are powerless].*

You bring up as an example the human intellect, which is quite unlike our essences—as if it could see without eyes, and walk without feet, or as if the stunned Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent French anatomist and defender of traditional Galenic medicine against the new "chemical" physicians.</note> could understand whispers in his ear. But let us fix upon you the **ornament of Midas** <note>original: *Mydae ornamentum*; a reference to the donkey ears given to King Midas in Greek mythology as a mark of his foolishness and poor judgment.</note> so that you may hear better. Our essences are not freed from *all* matter, but only from the **elementary dross** <note>original: *fece elementari*; the heavy, inactive material "impurities" that chemists believed masked the active power of a medicine.</note>. Indeed, they are the soul, just as you used to name the juice of plants. This soul is said to be more active without its prison than when bound within it. For this reason, our essences are the more praiseworthy because they are **more formal** <note>original: *formaliores*; in the philosophy of the time, the "form" was the active, life-giving principle of a thing, while "matter" was passive and heavy.</note>; yet they do not acquire foreign powers by their departure from matter, but perform their own actions by the force of their innate nature.

> *Just as the visual and auditory spirit, separated from its sense organ, cannot see or hear; so an essence separated from a mixture can no longer perform the function it held within the mixture.*

Oh, what a clever argument! Let it be so. But would that spirit then be useless, and would it possess no other power, if indeed it could be separated like an **extract of rhubarb**? Do you throw away the bark of cinnamon because it no longer possesses that power it held while it was in the tree? A rose flower cannot fulfill the duty it performed for its plant while it was attached to it; does it follow that it can perform no others? The blood of turtledoves does not perform the duty it did in the turtledove, after [it has been separated—]

*What of it, I say? If they require instruments, they are organic* <note>In this context, "organic" means "acting as a tool or instrument" (from the Greek *organon*).</note>. *But our discussion concerns homogeneous mixtures.* A homogeneous substance, insofar as it is homogeneous, acts by the force of its own nature without an instrument. *The separated spirits of sight and hearing are, for you, examples of physical forms. Fool. Each of these is an instrument of the soul perceiving external things through its sense organs. Blood, too, is in a certain way an organ. Let it be the same for the juice extracted from plants. That juice was, in one sense, an organ; in another, an essential member. While the plant lived, it used that juice as an organ. Once extracted from the dead plant, having lost its organic function, it acts by the force of its own homogeneous nature—which is exactly what we seek for medicine. If your madness so pleases you, you should devour live herbs, so that you might also enjoy their organic status!*

# THE ALCHEMY OF SPURIOUS PARISIANS
<note>original: *ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS.*; This refers to a polemical defense of chemistry against the conservative medical faculty in Paris.</note>

->...by its power.<-

The **quintessence** <term>quintessence</term> <note>Literally the "fifth essence," the most purified and potent form of a substance, separated from its raw, material "dregs."</note> of the liver extracted by the chemist is no longer "blood-making" in the biological sense. But neither is the liver of a wolf blood-making while it sits in your shop. Wretched you are if you must seek a blood-making power for yourself from such a source! The same judgment applies to the **essence of amber** <note>original: *eſſentia ſuccini*; Succinum is fossilized resin (amber). In early medicine, it was used for nervous disorders.</note>. It is not necessary for us to attract bits of straw with oil of amber <note>The author is distinguishing between the physical property of static electricity (amber attracting straw) and its internal medicinal power.</note>. It is only required that it disperses the fuel of **epilepsy**, aids women suffering from **hysterical conditions** <note>original: *hyſtericas*; in this era, this referred to "suffocation of the womb," a common diagnosis for various physical and emotional distress in women.</note>, corrects putrid air, and performs other actions by the power of its own nature. Hence, if we prepare an effective medicine, we have performed our duty. Let a thief or a greedy man worry about pulling straws and gold; what does that matter to a physician?

You also snatch an argument from your counter-writings: "I attribute to whole things a certain **temperament** <term>crasis</term> <note>original: *craſin*; from the Greek for "mixture," referring to the specific balance of qualities or humors that gives a substance its unique character.</note> and composition that cannot exist in separated parts." You are correct: a whole frog can live, and a live frog can even be tied [to a patient] to fight a fever. While alive, it croaks. A dead frog does not croak, nor does a severed foot. If we desire *those* specific powers of the living animal, we must use the whole. 

But does it therefore follow that the **extracts of mixtures** <note>original: *extracta miſtorum*; substances chemically separated from a compound or raw material.</note> do not possess that temperament of essence which they had when they were joined to the elements in the whole? Not at all. According as the essences are refined, so must we judge them. A simple extract of **monkshood** <note>original: *napelli*; a highly poisonous plant, also known as aconite.</note> kills just as the raw monkshood does. An extract of **hellebore** <note>original: *ellebori*; a plant used as a powerful, often dangerous, purgative.</note> purges with the same force as the whole hellebore plant. **Tincture of saffron** <note>original: *Tinctura croci*</note> strengthens and colors just as the whole saffron does. **Oil of citrus** <note>original: *Oleum citri*</note> reflects the citrus in both its scent and its medicinal faculty (understand this refers to the peel and seed from which it is extracted). 

In some cases, however, the task of the [chemical] art is to destroy malignant qualities so that the benign ones may operate safely. In others, the exterior is wiped away, and that which was hidden within as a potential power is brought forth. Therefore...

Chemistry is both an art and a science because it is able to correct materials and make them suitable for medicine—something that the Galenic practitioners of "simples" <note>Medicinal plants or substances used in their natural, unmixed state.</note> also attempt in their own fashion. However, a <term>crasis</term> <note>original: *crasis*; the specific "mixture" or balance of qualities and humors that gives a substance its unique character.</note> exists entirely through nature, whether in actuality or in potentiality. For it is certain that no art can produce almond oil unless nature has first generated it. The immediate potential is proven by a ready-made force; and in some things, the action of the virtues is even the same, such as the scent of a rose found in rose water. Stop throwing <term>Libavius</term> <note>Andreas Libavius (1550–1616), a German chemist who tried to bridge the gap between traditional medicine and Paracelsian chemistry.</note> in my face, whose counter-arguments you have never understood. But if he is an author worthy enough of your trust, why do you not accept the test? You write that I am most estranged from philosophy; surely this is due to your own foolishness. For that saying of Saint Paul is most true regarding you: *Claiming to be wise, they became fools* <note>original: "σοφοὶ εἶναι φάσκοντες ἐμωράνθησαν"; from Romans 1:22.</note>. If the philosophy of <term>Libavius</term> had not existed, you would not have been able to say even a "mu" <note>original: "ne my quidem"; referring to the Greek letter 'mu,' meaning not even the slightest sound or word.</note> against <term>Quercetanus</term> <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and advocate of chemical medicine.</note>, except for foolish insults—the kind of "philosophizing" in which I easily allow you to excel.
