...with the heart and others. Maniographus <note>Likely a disparaging nickname for a critic, meaning "the scribe" or "hand-writer."</note> produces a notable specimen of his philosophy, and proves by clear arguments that it is nothing but foolishness. 
Aristotle says that the elements in mixtures <note>original: *mistis*; substances formed by the combination of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note> exist in potentiality, and when a resolution <note>The chemical breakdown or analysis of a substance into its components.</note> is performed, they are separated <note>original: *ἐκκρίνεσθαι*.</note>. Therefore, it is not only those things which are present in act <note>original: *actu*; actually or manifest in their own form.</note> that are separated, but also those in potentiality. Riolanus <note>Jean Riolan (1539–1606), an influential and conservative French physician who opposed modern chemical medicines.</note> says they are present IN TRUTH. This is not denied, although he will struggle if he must demonstrate his own fire, for which there is a place neither in heaven nor on earth. But what does this "IN TRUTH" mean? It hides a festering wound <note>original: *ὕπουλόν τι* [something concealed under a scar] and *vomicam* [an abscess or ulcer].</note> and a sophisticated trick.

For Plato, to exist "in truth" would be to exist essentially. For what truth is to faith, essence is to generation. What truly exists for the logician, exists *really* <note>original: *ὄντως*.</note> for the physicist. But that which exists in this way is not always present in act, since there is "being in act" and "being in potentiality." So that the sophist may hide his cancer <note>original: *carcinoma*; used here metaphorically for a logical flaw or a "malignant" argument.</note>, he says it is present "in truth" instead of "in act." But this is as false as anything can be. To what end do we seek elements even in the elements themselves around us if they are present "in act" within mixtures? There would be no homogeneity in the mixture if the elements existed in act; indeed, there would not even be a mixing <note>original: *mistio*.</note>. Of no similar part <note>original: *parte similari*; a term for substances like flesh or bone where every part is identical to the whole, as opposed to "organic" parts like a hand or eye.</note> can you say: "this is earth," "this is water, fire, or air." Even the smallest parts are mixed, as is apparent in bone, flesh, skin, blood, phlegm, etc. Where is the earth "in act" here, or the air, fire, and water "in act"? He is forced to admit they are present in potentiality. But by what reasoning? Because, he says, they are present with broken powers <note>original: *refractis viribus*; the idea that the primary qualities of the elements are tempered or weakened when they combine.</note>; they are said to be present in potentiality, or to exist indefinitely: for example, fire is not present in its hottest state, but temperately. ...[philoso]phical critic <note>Completing the word from the previous page.</note> gone so wretchedly insane? How can things that are present through a determined motion of nature be present "indefinitely"? Earth, air, water, and fire are in bone according to the defined ratio of bone; they are in flesh according to the nature of flesh, and so too in all other things. This is one particular madness of that censorious school. The other is their claim that an element is present in potentiality <term>potentia; the Aristotelian concept of a thing's capacity to exist or act, as opposed to its actual manifest state</term>, existing with its powers broken and tempered. But I say that such a thing, if it exists, exists in act <term>actu; actually present in its own form</term>, not in potentiality. For it is merely altered; it retains its own proper form and matter in act, so that it can be recognized, and one might say "this portion is fire, this is water, this is earth, and that is air," even if their qualities are diminished. But no one can ever demonstrate these things in skin, hair, eggs, and so on. That which is not perceptible to the senses in a natural thing does not exist in act, especially when it is exposed on all sides to the senses. 

Physicians conclude that "fire" excels in spurge <note>original: *euphorbio*; a plant with highly caustic, "fiery" sap used in early medicine.</note> based on the resulting effect it has. They cannot, however, show it sensibly in its own actual state. You might call the oil drawn from it "fiery," but you cannot call it "fire" itself. You have written nothing more true, Riolan <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories.</note>, than that I am most estranged from your philosophy. I hate it as much as I hate delusions. But what do you say against chemical principles?

*Salt, sulfur, and mercury <note>The "Tria Prima" or three primary principles of Paracelsian chemistry.</note> are present in mixtures neither definitely nor indefinitely.*

*Therefore, they are present in no way—neither in act nor in potentiality—and consequently, they cannot be separated out.*

Zeno <note>Zeno of Elea, a philosopher famous for paradoxes denying the possibility of motion.</note> once, in his school and in the presence of Diogenes, wished to prove with the most acute arguments that motion does not exist. Diogenes, rising, began to walk about. To Zeno, who asked what he was doing, he replied: "I am [con]futing..." <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "futo," completing the Latin *confuto* (I confute/I disprove). The anecdote refers to Diogenes the Cynic disproving Zeno’s logic simply by moving.</note>

### ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS

...[I con]fute your arguments. In the same way, the salt-makers can confute the follies of **Riolan**; likewise those who prepare oil, water, and lime (from which salt comes) from an egg, and place them before the eyes. Those things which emerge from resolved <note>resolved: broken down into its base components through chemical or heat processes.</note> mixtures, having been hidden before and unable to be recognized by their own form and act <term>actu; actually present in its own manifest form</term>, must necessarily have been in them. The principles emerge: but are they present in a definite way? Indeed, definitely. They are present either in potentiality <term>potentia; the capacity to exist, though not currently manifest</term> or in act. In both ways, they are present definitely.

For everything is not found in everything, nor is just anything resolved into just anything, but into a determined thing; this is so true that not even that most vain sophist *Riolan*, who makes "everything out of everything," could deny that *chemists* produce determined things from determined things. How deplorable and ruined, therefore, is the malice of *Riolan* in denying that they are present <gloss>is it definite or indefinite?</gloss> definitely? 

But he cannot deny that they are present at all. What mode, then, I ask, remains besides the "definite" and the "indefinite"? There is no logician who can find a third option between contradictions. One thing is contrary to one other thing. *Riolan* has devised a new logic in which a third option is given. *What is that?* "The principles," he says, "are in mixtures in the same way that the four humors are in the chyle <note>chyle: the milky fluid formed from digested food in the stomach; in Galenic medicine, it was believed to be the precursor to blood.</note>." 

Truly a wonder. Do the Parisian physicians then teach that the four humors (which are the principles of **Hippocrates**) are in the chyle neither definitely nor indefinitely, neither in act nor in potentiality? The supreme dictator of the college <note>referring to Jean Riolan the Younger, a powerful and conservative leader of the Paris Faculty of Medicine who famously opposed the use of chemical medicines.</note> teaches thus in public. His fellow Doctors are erecting a monument to him before all Europe—certainly a monument of folly and disgrace. For those are the fables of madmen.

But who was that Riolan who, on page 118 of his "Madness" <note>original: *maniae*; likely a sarcastic pun on Riolan's *Encheiridion*, implying the work is a product of insanity</note>, wrote that chyle passes into blood, which then, by proximate potentiality <term>potentia; the state of being "almost" something else, lacking only a final trigger</term> and the slightest alteration, becomes flesh? As blood differs from flesh, so chyle differs from blood. In both cases, there is proximate potentiality. The distance between chyle and the other humors <note>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> is the same. It is necessary, therefore, that chyle be blood, phlegm, and yellow and black bile in proximate potentiality. If it is proximate, it is also moveable into act <term>actu; the state of being fully realized or manifest</term> by the slightest alteration. Now, therefore, from Riolan’s own quiver, this weapon is turned against Riolan:

*That which is present in another thing—just as those four Galenic principles, the humors, are in the chyle—is present in proximate potentiality, and by the slightest alteration can emerge in act.*

*Chemical principles are in mixtures just as the four humors, or Galenic principles, are in chyle. Therefore, they are present in proximate potentiality and can come forth by the slightest alteration.*

This is well said for those chemical principles which were hidden in secret and have need of manifestation. But by this battering ram, Riolan’s panspermia <term>panspermia; the theory that every substance contains the "seeds" or components of all other things</term> is overturned; the accusation that the chemical art merely "creates" its results <note>Riolan argued that chemists don't find salt or sulfur, but create them through the heat of the furnace</note> is overturned; and nature is established as the producer of the principles. A constitution <term>crasis; the specific temperamental mixture of humors or elements</term> is given which nature has perfected so nearly that there is no need for any transmutation <note>a fundamental change from one substance to another</note>, but the slightest alteration suffices. To what end, then, did Riolan resist the chemists? Only to waste paper and time, oil and labor <note>a classical idiom for wasting effort</note>, and to prove by evident proof that he, along with his condemning school, is raving. The juice of roses, the water, and the tincture extracted from roses possess the same faculty, taste, and smell—even being numerically the same <term>numero eadem; a philosophical term meaning the exact same individual thing, not just a similar type</term>—as the essential faculty, taste, and smell of the whole rose, with the sole exception of those parts which remain in the elementary dregs <term>crassamento; the solid, coarse residue or "dead earth" left behind after distillation or extraction</term>. Why then should we not say that certain principles are present not only in defined potentiality, but some even in act?

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM # <note>original: GALENIA TRIVMPHVS. This title suggests the author is defending Galenic medicine, or perhaps using the term ironically while promoting chemical pharmacy.</note>

...did not leave it as something undefined, but placed within each thing the capacity to produce a likeness in its substance.

That which is generated by the determined motion of nature, our art <note>The "art" refers to the work of the pharmacist or chemist.</note> draws forth. It is present either in **act** <note>fully realized and active</note> or by a **determined potential** from which that act emerges—the very thing toward which the substance was naturally disposed—and it responds differently according to the various motions of the art. For the dispositions themselves are different, and nature, following along, takes on various forms. This is how an extract of rhubarb is made, or a tincture, a water, and the rest; some substances are capable of taking on many forms, others fewer, just as the art of the pharmacists extracts, powders, and prepares electuaries <term>medicinal pastes made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term>, pills, and thickened or diluted juices, and so on. But back to Riolan. He writes contradictory things in barely four lines.

<margin>What "indefinitely" means to Riolan.</margin>

For he says that fire exists in a mixture **potentially** or **INDEFINITELY**. And so that you may know what it means to be present "indefinitely," he adds that it is "actually present" but tempered by its opposite, rather than being at its hottest. Then he admits that the principles are in the mixtures **POTENTIALLY**, just as the four humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Galenic medicine believed governed health.</note> are in the chyle <term>the milky fluid of digested food before it becomes blood</term>. From this, we argue as follows:

> *That which is present potentially, is present indefinitely.*
> *The chemical principles in mixtures are present potentially.*
> *Therefore, they are present indefinitely; and consequently, Riolan is talking nonsense when he says they are present neither definitely nor indefinitely.*

<margin>Riolan’s contradiction.</margin>

Behold this "mirror of wisdom" and this example of the censorious philosophy of the Parisian doctors. If being "indefinitely present" means being **ACTUALLY** present (albeit potentially), just as fire is in a mixture; and if the chemical principles are present potentially, why shouldn't they be present indefinitely and—

IN TRUTH? That which is truly within is truly separated. Chemical principles are truly within; therefore, they are truly separated. And if "truly" is the same as "in act" <note>meaning fully realized or active</note>, who refutes Riolan more than Riolan himself? In what philosophy does "to be present indefinitely" mean "to be present potentially," while "to be present definitely" means "to be present in act"? The metaphysics of Riolan manufactures such subtleties. For to define is to state the **quiddity** <term>the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> of a thing, the existence of which is an existence in act and in form. Hence, to be present "definitely" is to be present by its very definition. 

Yet even a "potentiality" is something defined. We are listening to the rubbish and dung-heaps of a most learned school—or rather, the spit of a mad dictator <note>A derogatory reference to Riolan as a tyrant of medical doctrine</note> among the benches of the Parisian College, leaping forward to sit in judgment of chemistry. For why should we not be allowed to define even a "being in potential"? That which is present by a certain reason, or is able to be present determinately, is likewise present "definitely," or as they say, "limitedly." 

Even children know what is logically and grammatically "indeterminate" or "undefined." For who did that? "Someone," or "something"—or phrases without a specific subject, such as: "arrogance is the companion of opinion" or "the end of folly is evil." In this way, fire is not [indefinitely] in bile, since it is present there by a certain and determined reason. I was teaching from Aristotle that, in a certain way, 

<margin>How the heart is separated.</margin>

the heart is also separated. The "mad-writer" <note>original: Maniographus. A Greek-derived pun likely aimed at Riolan, combining 'mania' (madness) and 'graphos' (writer).</note> explains this in terms of maternal blood, as if Aristotle intended **NOT THE HEART** but the *matter* of the heart to be separated from the maternal blood; as if "to be separated" simply meant to divide and distribute to each part its own share from a common nourishment or matter. But Aristotle’s actual words are: "the heart is separated in actuality" <note>original: ἡ καρδία ἀποκρίνεται ἐνεργείᾳ</note>. He does not say "the matter of the heart" <note>original: ὕλη τῆς καρδίας</note>, but "the heart in actuality" <note>original: καρδία ἐνεργείᾳ</note>, which refers to its secretion <note>In this context, 'secretion' or 'separation' refers to the biological differentiation of an organ during development.</note>.

Only an artificial secretion <note>the act of separating or setting apart</note> is required, so that what lies among the dross of the elements may be segregated once the bonds are loosened by actual fire, potential fire, or other instruments. ## CHAPTER XXIV.

->On the argument of the chemists regarding the separation of<-
->principles, up to the page concerning the madman<-
->121.<-

**T**he twelfth argument against the principles was that our principles exist neither in the elements nor in mixtures. This has been extensively examined and refuted. The Madman <note>Referring to Jean Riolan the Younger, the author's opponent</note> repeats his same stale, warmed-over arguments <note>original: *pridianam suam cramben*; literally "yesterday's cabbage," a Latin idiom for a boring, repeated story</note> and defends himself only with rehashed material, though it is now even filthier and more corrupt. He attributes to the chemists the claim that they wish to demonstrate their principles are present in mixtures **ACTUALLY** <note>original: *actu*; existing as a distinct, completed reality</note>; his reasoning is that they are extracted from there so that they are visible to the eyes. Indeed, some are accustomed to speak this way, especially those following Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine</note>, who regard Riolan’s trifles as dung-heaps and mock even the bombastic boastings and haughty expressions of the Aristotelians. For they maintain their own right, being impatient at having the rules of their art prescribed to them by the incompetent.

Let those men bicker in their circles in their own way. Let them leave the chemists to their own customs. But we, to whom the <term>Peripatetic doctrine</term> <note>the philosophy of Aristotle, so named because he taught while walking (peripatētikos) in the colonnades of his school</note> is more familiar, when we deal with those who think themselves clever in it, we adapt our speech to their understanding. We say, according to Aristotelian judgment, that the principles are present either **actually** or **potentially** <note>original: *potentia*; having the capacity to exist but requiring a process to bring them out</note>, from which state they must be brought into actual reality by the chemist's art. Riolan attacks both modes, as was clear in the preceding sections.

Now, as to what he brings forward—though it is troublesome to exchange words with such a <term>quibbler</term> <note>original: *vitilitigatore*; a person who starts lawsuits or arguments over petty faults</note>—

Thus the chemists argue: That which is separated from the elementary body of a mixture must necessarily have been inside it. Chemical principles are separated from the elementary body of a mixture. -> # THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS <-
<note>original: *ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS.* The author is likely referring to the "spurious" or false doctrines of the Paris Medical Faculty, who opposed chemical medicine.</note>

The very **smelting of metal**, unless it is managed by a skilled man, does not bring forth all the metal, of which sometimes a not insignificant part is still found among the **dross** <note>original: *recrementa*, the waste matter or slag left over from smelting</note>. Therefore, the opposite must be asserted against the **Unlearned One** <note>original: *Amusus*, the author's derogatory nickname for his opponent Riolan</note>: that a substance is present within a mixture all the more certainly when it is extracted through greater skill. For that which is separated sluggishly and unskillfully cannot be judged so well. 

When something is dissolved by **nature** alone, because the parts are scattered and evaporate, or are absorbed by the earth, or are tainted and disrupted by the entry of foreign substances—and since there are many violent causes by which matter is variously changed or altered—these natural processes cannot produce a definite **scientific knowledge** <note>original: *scientificam*; here meaning a rigorous, provable understanding</note>. The Unlearned One is so foolish, or rather malicious, that he would rather place his scientific judgment in the uncertainty of nature than in the experience of the craftsman who scrutinizes the interior secrets of nature. 

It is as if a human being did not receive the **beginnings of the body** <note>original: *primordia corporis*</note> from the four humors, the seed, the blood, and the similar parts <note>original: *similaribus*, a Galenic term for tissues like bone or fiber that are uniform throughout</note>, simply because nature does not resolve corpses back into these components—but the **anatomist** does. 

"We see," says the Unlearned One, "that all things naturally perish into the **elements**." 

You are merely boasting of the sharpness of your own eyes. We have not yet been able to see what you and your faction claim to see. If "all things" perish thus, do you mean even **Jupiter** <note>the alchemical name for Tin</note>, and the **Sun** <note>the alchemical name for Gold</note>, and fire, and water? The speech of a foolish mind cannot be wise. As the mind wanders, so does the tongue. Show us your "fire"; show us your "air." But we have spoken of this before. 

The **Chemists** separate **symbolic elements** <note>The author distinguishes between the visible substances produced in a lab and the abstract "elements" of the philosophers</note> and are able to demonstrate them. They can also demonstrate the **principles** <note>referring to Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>. Perhaps you will not deny that our elements are truly natu-

-> # THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM <-
<note>original: GALENIA TRIVMPHVS. This title likely refers to the debate over the "triumph" of chemical medicine over the traditional Galenic school, or it is the specific title of the section within the larger work.</note>

...natural things, although they are reduced by a skillful solution. Why do you deny that the same **principles** <note>In the chemical philosophy of this era, "principles" usually refers to Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which the chemists believed were the true building blocks of matter, as opposed to the Aristotelian "Elements" of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> are drawn out by that very art? But if you see this, what is it that you do not see? We see nothing in nature being dissolved into your "principles." To be sure, you have eyes with which you might see **dung** <note>original: *stercora*; the author is using a crude metaphor to suggest Riolan only sees the waste products of nature, not the inner spiritual or chemical essence.</note>; but for the **essence**, you have none. Nature strives for its own conservation. It does not resolve itself; rather, it suffers a kind of violence in natural **putrefaction** <note>original: *putredine*; the natural breakdown of organic matter.</note> caused by the heat of the surrounding environment. 

According to the judgment of **Aristotle**, this heat does not draw out air, fire, or water, but rather the **inborn heat** <note>original: *insitum calorem*; a vitalistic concept in ancient biology referring to the internal warmth that sustains life.</note> along with the spirit and innate moisture. You, seeing these things incorrectly, think they are the "elements," and thus you are deceived by a false judgment. This is because those things which are drawn out in nature do not present themselves to your "tribunal of investigation," but are poured out and flee into the breezes. 

The **eyes of the Art** <note>The "Art" here refers to Alchemy or Chemistry. The author argues that the laboratory provides better evidence than the naked eye.</note>, however, contemplate those things which exit quite exactly, because—once captured, included, and collected—they are forced to undergo a true judgment regarding themselves. The same thing happens when something is destroyed by "Aristotelian force" by **corrosive waters**, spirits, or fires. If you should see the **ashes of Etna** <note>original: *aethnaeos cineres*; a reference to the volcanic ash of Mount Etna, used here as a metaphor for a substance reduced to such a state that its original nature is hidden from the ignorant observer.</note>, and you did not see the mixture that went into them, this is the first cause of your ignorance; the second comes from the agent that acts and transforms without limit; the third comes from the "husk" <note>original: *cortice*; meaning the outward appearance or shell of a thing.</note> from which you judge, thinking that which is actually still a mixed body to be an "elemental earth." 

In the same way, if you see **smoke**, you think it is "air" or "fire." But if you were able to catch it in an **alembic** <note>original: *alembicum*; a chemical vessel used for distillation, consisting of a gourd-like container and a cap with a downward-pointing tube.</note> or a chimney, and thoroughly scrutinize its nature, you would be forced to judge quite differently. Your vision is **blindness** <term>ablepsia: from the Greek ἀβλεψία, meaning a lack of sight or spiritual blindness</term> rather than vision. Let us, however, turn this weapon back against you, and speak thus: **Riolan's** <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a famous physician of the Paris Faculty and a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against the new chemical theories.</note> decoctions, infusions, and extracts...

# ON THE ALCHEMICAL CONTROVERSIES OF PARIS
<note>original: ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARÍS. This likely refers to the "spurious" or "counterfeit" arguments raised by the Parisian medical establishment against alchemical medicine.</note>

<meta>catchword: nature</meta>

...[things] are extracted, they are things made through a violent transmutation from the Anaxagorean **panspermia** <note>original: *panspermia Anaxagorica*; the theory of the Greek philosopher Anaxagoras that every substance contains the "seeds" of every other substance. Here, the author uses it to describe a chaotic mixture of all possibilities.</note>. We see, to be sure, that mixtures decay into their **elements** <note>The four traditional Aristotelian elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>; but we do not see them decay into thickened or liquid juices, nor into oils, decoctions, or infusions. How shall we please you? If the addition of our art does not prevent your preferred elements from being present in mixtures by nature, then it certainly does not prevent our principles from being present. Indeed, our craftsmen strive much more precisely to preserve the gifts of nature than your **pharmacists** <note>original: *pharmacopœ*; here used dismissively to refer to traditional Galenic apothecaries.</note> do, who often lose or weaken the **essence** <note>The concentrated "spirit" or "virtue" of a substance, which chemists sought to isolate.</note> by over-boiling. 

The miner does not see a vein of silver resolved into pure silver and dross by natural **putrefaction** <note>Natural decay or breakdown over time.</note>; yet he sees it through the work of art, when, once the filth is wiped away, he contemplates each thing with its own genuine face. Remove the cloud from your eyes, and shake the malice from your spiteful heart; you will see and judge more rightly. It is a wonder, moreover, that the **censors of the Parisians** <note>The Faculty of Medicine at the University of Paris, which famously banned the use of chemical medicines like antimony in the late 16th century.</note> are so unskilled in these matters that they have never seen what is known even to the common people. 

For just as in mines pure metal sometimes comes into view, and at other times is recognized by other signs; so too do the chemical essences and principles manifest themselves not rarely. The essence of **cinnamon** is revealed by the juice which, during chewing, communicates itself to the salivary moisture of the tongue; once this is separated, the empty body of the bark is spat out, with the exception of the **salt** <note>In alchemical theory, "Salt" is the solid, non-combustible principle that remains after distillation or combustion, representing the physical body of a substance.</note> hiding deeper within. There also emerges a fragrant spirit <note>original: *spiritus halituosus*; literally a "breath-like spirit," referring to the volatile aromatic oils.</note> which moves the organ of smell. These two senses—taste and smell—are valid for other substances as well. If you consult your sight, look at resin-bearing trees and plants sweating their own juice, whether...

-> # GALENISM TRIUMPHANT <-

A moderate amount of it is even necessary for generations so that a certain limit might be established. It is evident, surely, that nature itself, without any art, also yields our principles by its own power.

What exhales from there is neither simple fire nor air, but something fragrant, though darkened by the force of the flame. That is the **essential part** <note>original: *essentiale*; the author argues that the smoke we smell is the actual "essence" of the wood being released.</note>. Around the hearth, **soot** <term>fuligo: the black carbon deposit from smoke, which chemists analyzed for its salt and oil content</term> collects—sharp, bitter, and salty. From fatty materials, the soot is fatty, although the oiliness is less because most of it serves as fuel for the fire. The ash that remains...

-> ### THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIAN ### <-
<note>original: ALCHYMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS. This refers to the author's rebuttal of Jean Riolan the Younger, a famous Parisian physician who attacked the "new" chemical medicine.</note>

...hides the salt. Wateriness also often slides back or exudes from the chimneys <note>Referring to the flues of a furnace or still.</note> of the furnace, as also happens in **distillation by descent** <term>distillation by descent: a technique where vapors are forced downwards into a receiver, used for extracting heavy oils or essences.</term>. Open your eyes, Riolan, and admit the evidence of nature. You will see without a doubt what you deny seeing. But you demand from us that, if we wish to be believed, we should show **by sense, or by reason, how mixed bodies depart into elements, and thus into our principles, and how sulfur is returned to sulfur, salt to salt, and mercury to mercury.** But why should you believe us, you who have neither senses fit for knowing, nor reason? We taught this long ago, and we have presented natural and artificial experiments to all the senses. When, at last, will you be wise?

Indeed, I laugh at your simplicity. If I were to show you something earthy resulting from a natural or violent resolution <note>resolution: the breaking down of a substance into its component parts.</note>, you would immediately believe it to be something of the element of earth, and likewise for the others. For that which I would show as being produced would be **calx** <term>calx: the powdery residue left after a mineral or metal has been burned or calcined.</term> or ash. Neither is the "element of earth"; rather, both are an earthy body. I would soak this in water and prepare a **lye** <term>lixivium: a solution created by leaching ashes to extract soluble salts.</term>, from which I would collect salt, which I would call a principle.

You would not believe it to be a principle, but you are plainly persuaded that it emerged from the **panspermia** <term>panspermia: the theory that seeds or potentials for all things are scattered throughout matter; Riolan argued that chemists were merely transforming these "seeds" rather than finding fundamental principles.</term> through a violent transmutation. <note>original: GALENIA TRIVMPHVS. This title likely carries a heavy satirical tone, as the author is systematically dismantling the Galenic/Aristotelian worldview.</note>

...because it has been drawn back from a mixed substance, why is **salt** not a principle in the earth? Smell and taste prove this. Thus, incenses <note>original: "suffimenta"; materials burned for their scent.</note> resolved by a smaller flame do not breathe out "air," but a sweet essence made volatile from what was fixed.

Behold, Riolan, you unlearned man! <note>original: "Amuse"; literally "one without the Muses," a common scholarly insult for someone lacking refinement or true knowledge.</note> The things you imagine to be certain are uncertain; those you think uncertain are the most certain of all. <meta>This page continues the author's argument against Jean Riolan the Elder. Having previously described the visible separation of substances in a workshop, the author now challenges Riolan’s logic. He argues that if chemical principles (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury) are rejected because they do not visibly return to a universal "whole," then Riolan must also reject Aristotelian principles like "form" and "matter," which are even less visible.</meta>

<page-num>807</page-num>

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM.</header>

If you cannot believe these things, you have lost the capacity for faith. Do you not believe that which daily exhausts the smelters, who see the **sulfurous part** collect around the chimneys; the **mercurial part** flow down and coalesce in the basins; the **earthy dregs** settle at the bottom; and the stone and dross float? Argue thus:

> *If it is necessary for elements to be reunited with their wholes, it is also necessary for chemical principles to be reunited with their wholes, or they are not principles.*

That is the point, then. The connection holds by parity <note>The author is using a logical "argument from parity," suggesting that what is true for one set of principles must be true for the other.</note>. The <term>minor premise</term> <note>original: "minor"; the second proposition in a logical syllogism.</note> is proven: because since every finite thing is eventually consumed by the subtraction of the finite, the elements would have been exhausted long ago and the birth of new things would have ceased, unless a restoration occurred through the resolution of mixtures. But since [according to Riolan] a similar return to principles does not happen, it follows that chemical principles are not principles. 

Who would deny that Riolan is here playing the fool and joking rather than arguing? For by the same argument we could remove from the nature of things the metallic principles and the dual principles of animals—namely, the **humors**, and the **seed** with the **blood**—as well as the <term>Aristotelian principles</term> <note>original: "principia Aristotelica"; refers to Matter, Form, and Privation.</note> and those of the other arts. For since in <term>sublunary</term> <note>original: "sublunaribus"; the region below the moon, which in ancient science meant the Earthly realm subject to change and decay.</note> things generation and corruption do not cease, if <term>matter, form, and privation</term> <note>The three basic principles of Aristotelian physics used to explain change.</note>, seed, blood, the four humors, and their contrarieties did not return to their own kinds upon the dissolution of mixtures, generations would have ceased long ago. 

Therefore, one must imagine with Socrates that <term>ideal forms</term> <note>original: "formas ideales"; the Platonic theory that perfect versions of all things exist in a spiritual realm.</note> exist somewhere, namely on the "back of heaven," from whence they flow down and where they return; and that there is another place for "privation," as if in a <term>pandochaeum</term> <note>original: "pandochæo"; a Greek-derived term for an inn or a place that receives all guests.</note>.

<header>ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN SPAGYRICISTS</header>
<meta>catchword: mercury</meta>

...or underground in the region of the departed, or in **Utopia**, you would eventually have to find matter somewhere—perhaps in that place God found when He wished to fashion the world, where all things were driven up and down in the greatest confusion <note>The author is referring to primeval Chaos, arguing that Riolan's logic requires a physical place for "abstract" matter to exist.</note>. If you do not grant me these points, Riolan, I shall deny that you can ever become a wise man from a fool or an idiot; for otherwise, there would be no source from which you could seek the **form of wisdom**, or else wisdom must not be the starting principle of a wise man. Are we not playing the fool beautifully? 

But if I were to conclude rashly against your principles, and since your condition and mine are equal, it is necessary that you also use sophistry and confuse the truth of things with a crowd of dreams. The things you chatter about regarding the restoration of elements are wretched fictions. The elements do not fail because generation and corruption are circular, even arising from one another. Their analogues are also found around the place of generation. 

However, in your school, "elementary fire" has been consumed. Therefore, you seek heat from the sun, which rubs against the air as if struck against a flint, and from there awakens the heat. But I have dealt with these things above. Our principles <note>The "chemical" principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> also do not fail because they are reborn from <term>seminaries</term> <note>original: "seminariis"; the vital "seeds" or spiritual blueprints within matter that allow substances to regenerate their form.</note>. What prevents them from being restored in the same way you claim to repair your elements?

I say, what is more probable than that the spirit of a rose is the spirit of a rose? "I mean something else," you will say. Why then, you fool, do you not speak differently? Let the question be whether that essence extracted from wine, which the <term>chemists</term> <note>original: "chymici"; in this period, the term referred to both alchemists and practitioners of chemical medicine.</note> call the **spirit of wine**, is the same spirit that exists within the whole wine, by which drinkers become inebriated, grow warm, and suffer other effects; and likewise for <term>perry</term> <note>original: "pyratio"; a fermented pear drink.</note>, <term>cider</term> <note>original: "pomatio"; a fermented apple drink.</note>, and similar things. An argument is brought forward from a threefold identity and difference. Let us drive it into the form of a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>.

*If it were the same, it would be the same in its threefold genus, species, or number, or in its accident, essence, or property. It is none of these. Therefore, it is not the same.*

The <term>major premise</term> is proved because things are commonly the same or different from one another in just so many ways. The <term>minor premise</term> is proved: 1. It departs into another genus. Therefore, it is not the same in genus. The reason is: because all **distilled waters** are artificial, not natural, inasmuch as they do not arise spontaneously. Nature gives them their matter; art gives them their form. 2. Not in species, because wine is one species of liquid, and spirit of wine is another. Concerning number, more later.

The assumption is denied: although in the major premise, the distinction of "number" is not sufficiently philosophical, but by its own foolishness it proves the author to be <term>uninspired</term> <note>original: "amusum"; literally "one without the Muses," implying someone lacking in learning or artistic grace.</note>. The "property" is already contained within the term "accident." One ought to have said that to differ in number is, first and foremost, to differ in the individuality of the substance. From that depend the proper and common <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities (like color or temperature) that do not change what a thing fundamentally is.</note>, some of which are immutably attached. But let those things pass. The first proof concerning genus fails by the <term>fallacy of the qualified statement</term> <note>original: "elencho secundum quid." A logical error where a general rule is applied to a specific case that has an accidental or unique quality.</note>. For the role of art is only in separation,

Also to be noted is the <term>solecism</term> <note>A grammatical mistake or, in this context, a logical blunder.</note> of the **Unlearned One** <note>original: "Amusi"; a derogatory term for someone who lacks the education of the Muses.</note> who reckons the spirit of wine among "distilled waters," when spirit is one thing and water another. "Arising spontaneously" is the opposite of <term>univocal generation</term> <note>A biological theory where offspring are exactly like their parents; the author is arguing that "artificial" extraction doesn't change the substance's natural identity.</note>, not the opposite of artificial production. That "matter" of yours is an old woman's tale. What would become of it? The reasoning is based on parity.

### CHAPTER 86.

->Whence comes the heat in wine and blood. Page 24.<-
->of the *Antigramania*.<-

**L**est Riolanus seem insufficiently **unlearned, ignorant, or childish** <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἄμουσος, καὶ ἀμαθὴς ἢ νήπιος"</note>, he presents another specimen of his thinking. He asks regarding wine: whence comes the heat in a substance that is watery in its consistency? He could have answered from Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his theories on humors and "crasis" dominated medicine for 1,500 years.</note> that there are diverse parts underlying mixed bodies—some hot, others cold—according to each one's particular <term>crasis</term> <note>The "crasis" or temperament refers to the specific blend of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) that defines a substance's nature.</note>. This can be seen in roses, milk, unfermented wine, and the rest. Nature has produced these parts just as it has produced the whole, and this occurs through a certain maturation and purification. This is visible in stored juices—wine, oil, honey—which with age (if they are treated correctly and possess a principle of motion toward perfection from nature that is sufficiently strong, for raw grape juice never becomes a strong wine) turn out hotter, and indeed almost "fiery" as we commonly say, and sharp, even when kept in underground cellars surrounded by cold. This was also the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle; they believed that heat was an internal "form" or quality of certain substances.</note>, and the chemical separators and refiners <note>A reference to alchemists or "spagyrists" who used heat to separate and "exalt" the hidden properties of matter.</note> cannot disagree. But Riolanus has his own <term>amusia</term> <note>original: "amusia," meaning a lack of harmony or culture, a pun on his nickname "Amusus."</note>, or Parisian philosophy. Whence comes the heat in wine? From the heavens and the Sun, he says. Therefore, it does not come from nature—that indwelling principle which has its root in the seed of the vine, and from there...

...in the vine itself, the grape, and the must <note>unfermented grape juice</note>, from which it is transferred into the wine. If this heat does not come from nature, but from an external cause—which is nevertheless not the art of the chemist—how is it that certain Alsatian and Greek wines are said to be perfected by the boiling of the must? Or how are they "awakened" by the addition of lime, as was once done in Egypt? Is it not necessary for this to be hot through a violent mutation or alteration? It is truly a wonder how our wines could derive their heat from the sun, since we keep them far removed from the sun, and we do not leave even the must in the sunlight. Indeed, if anyone wishes to turn wine into vinegar, he usually exposes it to the sun, or moves it near a furnace, or boils it slightly. For once the hot spirits have exhaled <note>evaporated or breathed out</note>, what remains turns into vinegar; and although it may have different <term>crases</term> <note>mixtures of the four qualities: hot, cold, wet, and dry</note> in its various parts, it is nevertheless judged to be entirely cold.

<margin>Hippocrates in his book *On the Nature of the Child*: Whatever humor <note>fluid or essence</note> the earth has within itself, such also have the things growing from it. According to Aristotle, the earth serves as a stomach and liver for plants, and it supplies digested food to the roots without any waste.</margin>

In Egypt and Ethiopia, and even indeed in America and other burning regions, good wine is not produced. Therefore, it is considered cold in comparison to others. If the heat came from the sun, the best wine ought to be produced there. As for the earth, it is cold on the inside when the sun burns on the outside—unless perhaps one must take into account the ash of Mount Etna, and the sulfurous spirits of the Campania region <note>Areas known for volcanic activity and fertile, "fiery" soil</note>. But in other places it is quite different, and so that the roots of the vines may be better ventilated, the soil is often turned. A different nature lies beneath the soil, as our **Virgil** <note>The Roman poet Virgil, whose *Georgics* provided a philosophical and practical guide to agriculture</note> philosophizes better than **Riolan**. According to **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, **Mesuë** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian or Assyrian physician influential in the medieval West</note>, and their followers, every plant draws from the earth a humor familiar to itself; one draws sweet juices, another nitrous, another bitter, and other similar juices.

...juices. Where vines find nutrients suitable for themselves, they produce better wine than where they do not. Yet it was fitting for <term>Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a prominent Paris physician known for his traditionalist views and opposition to many new medical discoveries</note> to rave in such a way, as he is ignorant of elementary fire and derives heat and forms from the sun. By this logic, blood could have been beautifully set on fire—so much so that it would be necessary for Ethiopians to have the most boiling blood, were it not altered by the cold of the night.

Blood is not hot in only one way, although it varies among different men, as well as in different ages and dispositions. It is sometimes hotter and sometimes colder, as indicated by the differences of the <term>choleric</term> <note>related to yellow bile, associated with a hot and dry temperament</note>, <term>melancholic</term> <note>related to black bile, associated with a cold and dry temperament</note>, <term>pituitous</term> <note>phlegmatic; relating to phlegm or mucus, associated with a cold and moist temperament</note>, <term>serous</term> <note>watery or thin parts of the blood</note>, <term>ichorous</term> <note>referring to thin, watery, or blood-stained discharge</note>, etc. Taken purely by itself, blood is compared to the element of air. It possesses heat primarily from the matter of both its generation and its nutrition. For there is an innate heat within it from its birth...

...larger <note>The word begins on the previous page as "major."</note>. Afterwards, the spirit is a perpetual companion if it is of a single nature <note>original: "univocus"—meaning the spirit and the body it inhabits share a consistent essence</note>, as is the case in living beings. Once the spirit is separated, the matter congeals and is deprived of its spiritual heat, though it is not deprived of that other heat which follows the form within the matter.

**Truly**, regarding the temperament of the blood, one may read <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher whose biological works were central to medical education in the 17th century</note> in Book 2 of *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 2, where he discusses blood that is hotter, thicker, colder, or thinner. <margin>Book 2 of *On the Parts of Animals*, chapters 2 and 1.</margin> The <term>Hippocratic Philosopher</term> <note>A reference to a follower of Hippocrates, or perhaps Galen, who synthesized Hippocratic ideas</note> established the principles of the elements as the hot, the moist, the cold, and the dry. He declares that elements exist for the sake of "similar parts" <note>original: "similarium partium"—uniform tissues like bone, fat, or fiber, which were thought to be made directly from the elements</note>. Better explanations are sought from these primary principles than from an overriding coction. Therefore, you might even say that the state of the blood is due to its primary constitution. For **God** entrusted life to the blood, which therefore exists in a proper proportion of the hot and the moist. Our blood is hot for this reason: because the blood of our ancestors was hot, from whose seed and blood we were born.

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM

->Fff 5<-

...shakes <note>original: "quat," likely a continuation of "quatiat" (let him shake) from the previous page</note> the blood, let Riolan boil it, let him roast it; and let him see afterward whether it ought to be pronounced hot or cold. This is also evidence of Riolan’s <term>ignorance</term> <note>original: "amusia"—literally a lack of the Muses; a lack of culture or scholarly refinement</note>, in that he preferred to bring forth collected filth from Empedocles, Athenaeus, and others, rather than the pure philosophy of the Master of the Peripatetics <note>Aristotle</note>, and wished to engage in idle rhetoric. What is wine? Water that has putrefied in the vine—that is, it has been <term>cooked</term> <note>original: "cocta"—referring to the process of "concoction," the internal heat that matures substances</note>. It suits a rhetorician to play with figures of speech. Otherwise, nothing is created by the fact that it putrefies, but by the fact that it is <term>concocted</term> <note>The vital process of maturing or digesting nutrients</note>. **Putrefaction** is the leading out of the innate heat along with its accompanying moisture. It is the loosening or removal of boundaries and the departure into the elements, as the common Aristotelians maintain.

That which putrefies becomes colder. It is not fitting for one disputing the causes of heat to seek an argument from putrefaction. But our "Uncultured One" <note>Referring to Riolan</note> maintains a double putrefaction: one that is corruptive, and another that is perfecting. But there is no reason why we should listen to a fool rather than the wise Aristotle, who admits no putrefaction among the processes of generation, but teaches instead that <term>concoction</term> within putrefaction is the cause by which animals and plants are made from rotting things. Away to the rhetoricians with this "perfecting putrefaction."

You say that the <term>lientery</term> <note>A form of diarrhea where food passes through the body undigested</note> of Hippocrates is said to occur when things pass through you without being putrefied—which is to say, they are raw and <term>unconcocted</term>. Therefore [you argue], what is putrefied is "cooked." I deny that this follows for you. The denial of putrefaction can imply natural concoction just as much as it can imply the putrefactive kind, by which "concocted pus" is produced—which is the end-point of such putrefaction. Indeed, by itself, the denial of putridity establishes integrity, just as the denial of <term>privation</term> <note>The absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</note> in a thing...

# CHAPTER 89.

## *Regarding the 14th Argument against the principles of chemistry. A comparison of the principles of Hippocrates with those of the Chemists.*

### To page 127 of the Manual.

**A**musus <note>original: "Amusus." A Greek-derived pun meaning "without the Muses" or "unlearned," used here as a derogatory nickname for Jean Riolan.</note> has a truly slippery memory: just a little while ago, he said that his cause and that of his censoring school was Anti-Paracelsian, not Anti-Chemical. Scarcely a few lines have been finished, and yet weapons are taken up again against the principles of Chemistry. You say that you demonstrate by sense and reason that the four principles of Hippocrates <note>The four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> concur in the generation of **ALL** mixtures. Here you commit at least four outrages. You demonstrate this neither by sense nor by reason, as was said above; rather, you are driven by a deceptive opinion. 

Furthermore, it is false that all mixtures consist of the four Hippocratic principles, if fire is nowhere to be found, nor can it be shown to exist in any mixture. For to you, flames are not elementary fire; rather, you believe heat comes from the sun and is produced—according to a certain lying opinion—through the friction of the heavens against the element of air. Moreover, you use the name "Principles" falsely in this comparison with chemical principles. The elements that Hippocrates posits are the same as those the chemists use. How then can they disagree? 

*Aristotle, in Book 2 of On the Parts of Animals, Chapter 1,* calls the elements "primordia" <note>first things or origins</note>; but he soon corrects himself, and makes the "beginnings" of the elements the powers or qualities of the elements by which the common matter is distinguished. These are <term>humidity</term> <note>original: "humiditas"</note>, <term>heat</term> <note>original: "caliditas"</note>, <term>dryness</term> <note>original: "siccitas"</note>, and <term>coldness</term> <note>original: "frigiditas"</note>. These are said to be the matter of composite bodies; which matter otherwise is only water and earth, given for the sake of "similar parts" <note>In Aristotelian biology, "similar parts" (like bone or flesh) are those that can be divided into parts identical to the whole, as opposed to "organic" parts like a hand or eye.</note>.

In chapter 2 of the same book, the first beginnings of the elements are said to be the hot, the cold, the dry, and the moist. Therefore, when these are posited as principles for Aristotle, they are forms assigned the names of qualities: and thus they are the first beginnings not only of mixtures but also of the elements themselves. Let us also look at Hippocrates, since you so boldly oppose his opinions to us, trusting in your own sense and reason. 

<margin>The Hippocratic creation of the world from which Plato constructed his own.</margin>
In his book *On Fleshes* <note>original: "In lib. de carnibus." A treatise in the Hippocratic Corpus that discusses the origin of the universe and the human body.</note> he writes thus: "Now I myself set forth my opinions. It truly seems to me that what we call the 'hot' <note>The element of fire or heat as a primary force.</note> is immortal, and understands all things, and sees, hears, and knows all things, both present and future. Therefore, the greatest part of this, when all things were in turmoil, withdrew into the upper circumference. And it seems to me that the ancients called this the Ether. Another part, the lower, is called earth—something cold and dry and subject to many motions—and in this, indeed, much of the 'hot' is present. A third part occupied the middle place of the air, being something hot and moist. A fourth part took the place closest to the earth, something very moist and very thick <note>This refers to the element of water.</note>." 

Read the rest as well, especially concerning the generation of bone, flesh, and similar things, where this is also found: "When these things were in turmoil and revolving in a circle, a large part of the hot was enclosed in the earth—in some places more, in others less, in some very little, in others a great abundance—and with the passage of time, the earth was dried out by the heat," etc. 

You see here the first principles of Platonic and Peripatetic <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle.</note> philosophy, and almost the very *Timaeus* <note>Plato's famous dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world.</note> of Plato; these are the very elements of Aristotle, except for fire.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Things that live, especially plants, draw and pull into themselves a moisture or nourishment familiar to them, without waste in the genus of plants, as Aristotle wrote. <margin>The Ignorant One refutes the Ignorant One.</margin>

For this "familiar attraction" relates to a similarity in substance <note>The author is using the ancient principle that "like attracts like." The chemists **KNOW** that salt is hidden in the earthly body. It is plainly delirious to say that nature strips away salt by a triple digestion; since it is certain that the more something is "cooked," the thicker and saltier it becomes, as roasting testifies, and finally incineration, <term>calcination</term><gloss>the reduction of a mineral or metal to powder through intense heat</gloss>, and scorching.

Thus, a glutinous humidity is the cause of evident concretion in external changes; I do not think Quercetanus denies this, any more than he denies the Aristotelian concretion where moist things are bounded by dry things—the heat moderating the moisture and, as if by roasting, causing the superfluities to evaporate, while the cold comes upon it and closes it. <note>The header "ALCHIMIÆ DE SPVR. PARIS" likely refers to the "Spurious Parisians," a jab at the conservative medical faculty of the University of Paris who famously opposed Paracelsian chemical medicine in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.</note>

...of salt. **Nitre** <note>original: "Nitrum," referring to saltpeter or a similar mineral salt</note> also solidifies into stone by itself. Those who have not seen experiments of this kind, nor have ever been occupied with the skillful investigations, <term>resolutions</term><gloss>the chemical breaking down of substances into their parts</gloss>, and compositions of nature, believe nothing except what they read behind their **pulpits** and **stoves** <note>The author is mocking academic doctors who stay in their lecture halls or by their kitchen hearths rather than working in a laboratory furnace.</note> among those whom they magnify with blind love. Their Philosophy is concerned more with the **bark** <note>original: "corticem." Yet, he who knows how to manifest that essence has from of old been called a **Philosopher** by excellence, as one who scrutinizes internal wisdom, and is such in deed, not in words. 

But let no one think, when we discourse on more hidden causes, that we repudiate the "sticky humor" of the Physicians, or heat, cold, fibers, and the other things which are said to **bound** <note>original: "terminare," the process of giving a fixed physical shape or limit to a substance.</note> matter. We acknowledge these things too, but we deny that they suffice for a deeper knowledge, which is truly Philosophical, seeking demonstration from first and unchanging principles, not only from supervening or secondary ones. 

Though it is permitted to **Aristotle** to render the evident causes of external qualities from the powers of the elements; let it also be permitted to the **chemists** <note>original: "chymicis"</note> to likewise produce those things which lie hidden among the mixed elements. Let it be permitted to seek that "reason" or "forming principle"—of which is spoken in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*, text 40, and elsewhere—not only in the **seminal motion** <note>The "seminal" power was believed to be the blueprint or life-force that directed the growth and shape of an organism.</note> outside the elements (for these elements cannot shape anything in a certain and determined way, nor give a defined species to generated things), but also in the principles of certain "seeds," especially in **salt**, as nature itself demonstrates. The question regarding the use of **primordial salt** is not resolved even if you say the blood is thickened by the benefit of fibers or a sticky humor. ### ON THE SPURIOUS ALCHEMY OF PARIS ###

The argument before this is truly that of an unlearned man and the most ignorant of all doctors. Where, I pray, do you forge <note>original: *cudis*; a metaphorical use of "striking" or "minting" an argument</note> the origin of kidney and bladder stones if you do not acknowledge the existence of **salty phlegm**? <term>Salty phlegm: in early modern medicine, a specific type of "cold and moist" humor that has become corrupted by salt or minerals, leading to the formation of solid deposits in the body.</term> Sometimes the fluid of an arthritic patient has been tasted; it appeared saltier than nitre <note>Saltpeter</note>. This fluid, together with phlegm, gathers around the joints to form **tophi** <note>Gouty deposits of urate crystals that look like chalky stones</note>. In those suffering from the itch <note>likely scabies or psoriasis</note>, it produces crusts and scales. 

Those suffering from stones sometimes discharge a mucus clearly similar to that which is excreted and released through the nostrils, or even that which is expelled when pure phlegm is purged—looking much like the white of an egg. This mucus, if caught in a cloth, hardens into a stone; it is sharp and so salty that it even causes erosion. Such mucus often hardens within the intestines as well.

<margin>(y) Add his impiety from chapters 1 and 16 of the commentary on Fernel’s *On Hidden Causes*; there he writes that the Egyptians were undeservedly accused of idolatry and compares Moses to Apollonius the mage <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Christ or Moses in controversial texts</note>. At times he even judges that the very beginnings of the Christian religion flowed from the Egyptians.</margin>

And is Riolanus <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against the new "chemical" physicians</note> ignorant of all these things? What an unrefined man you have admired until now, O School of Paris! Is this that Riolanus, your dictator and censor, than whom there is no greater or sharper Aristotelian? **(y)** Is this the Riolanus who even cast Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a massive authority in French medicine whom Riolan apparently criticized for being too theoretical</note> beneath himself, and threw others, better and older than him, "off the bridge"? <note>A Latin idiom, *de ponte præcipitauit*, meaning to declare someone obsolete or stripped of their right to speak or vote.</note> Why do you not strip the lion’s skin from this donkey of Cumae? <note>A reference to Aesop’s fable of the donkey who wears a lion’s skin to scare others until his long ears or braying give him away.</note>

He dares to ask what I might answer on behalf of Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent Paracelsian physician</note> regarding salt. Why do you ask, unless to show that madness has blinded your eyes? I deny that I agree with those Paracelsians <note>Followers of Paracelsus who believed the "Three Principles" of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury were the fundamental building blocks of all matter</note> who say our limbs, when they are generated, are composed of the elements and, at the same time, of **salt, mercury, and sulfur**. I show another account of our origin, according to which each thing is procreated from a seed already mixed, and at the same time those things which the chemists call the "principles of powers," or **essences**, are generated within it.

Would I have produced the "deliriums of madmen" then too? Perhaps you should be forgiven for this, because in opposition to Scaliger, Curaeus, **Rondelet** <note>Guillaume Rondelet (1507–1566), a famous anatomist and naturalist</note>, and others, you love only your own whims and pursue their settled opinions with hatred. Yet those were wise men.

<header>On the Falsehoods of Alchemy</header>

There was also this point in the argument: those **Three Principles** <note>original: *Tria illa principia*; referring to Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which the Swiss physician Paracelsus argued were the fundamental building blocks of all matter</note> are unsuitable for biological faculties. I respond that they are not unsuitable when they are in their proper moderation and mixture, both among themselves and with the four elements, according to the natural mode of each thing. **Secretion** <note>The process of separating the pure essence of a substance from its raw form</note> reveals these principles in nature: a separation that occurs sometimes through human art, and sometimes spontaneously by nature, such as when salt exudes from a willow tree, resin from a pitch-pine, balsam from a balsam shrub, and so on. If these principles exist in nature, and the vital faculties flourish as long as they are present—for the entire life of a pitch-pine perishes when its **sulfur** <note>In this context, sulfur represents the "oily" or flammable principle that sustains the tree's life-force</note> is totally exhausted, and the same is true for balsam and others—then they cannot be "unsuitable" for biological faculties. Nutrition itself demonstrates the same thing.

This uncultured boor <note>original: *Amusus*; literally "one without the Muses," implying someone ignorant of the arts and sciences</note>, because he sees himself abandoned by all the Muses and finds no way to escape, flees to the **devil’s Delphic oracle** <note>An ironic reference to the famous Greek oracle; the author implies his opponent is receiving "prophecies" or arguments that are actually demonic lies</note>, and from there he seeks out horrible lies and insults. For he most mendaciously attributes this line of reasoning to me:

> ->*In the dregs we find salt.*<-
> ->*Therefore, salt is the constituent and preservative of all living things.*<-

Be gone to your dregs with your foul mask! I propose instead the **seed**; such as that of almond, or anise, cumin, caraway, fennel, citrus, and so on. Having crushed this, we cause it to rot in the vessels of our art, with heat working naturally as it does in the **greater world** <note>original: *in maiore mundo*; the Macrocosm or the universe at large, which alchemists believed was mirrored in their laboratory experiments</note>, following the **putrefaction of Aristotle** <note>Aristotle viewed putrefaction (decay) as a necessary stage where the old form of a substance breaks down so a new, higher form can be generated</note>, but not in an indefinite way, since our art circumscribes everything within certain limits. By that maceration or putrefaction...

-># THE TRIUMPH OF GALENIC MEDICINE<-

<meta>catchword: property</meta>

The enclosures of coarse elementary solidification are opened: and often no other labor is required than **pressing** <note>original: *expressione*; the physical act of squeezing a substance to extract its juices or oils</note>, from which is collected the **essence** in which there are three parts besides the added **solvent** <term>solvent: original *menstruum*; a liquid used to dissolve or extract active ingredients, often alcohol or water</term>, which however is sometimes the herb's own water. The essence thus extracted is separated into its component parts by **distillation**, **digestion** <note>the process of softening or breaking down a substance using gentle heat over time</note>, or by other methods as the principles reveal themselves. 

If oil floats on top, it is removed. The remainder is distilled until it is dry. The water drawn forth by distillation is purified in a **water bath** <note>original: *balneo*; referring to the *bain-marie*, a vessel of hot water used to ensure gentle, even heating</note>, where the **mercurial spirit** <note>original: *spiritus mercurialis*; in early chemistry, this represents the volatile, spirit-like principle of a substance</note> exits, while the watery element remains. What remained at the bottom of the still, as well as the dregs from the pressing (because they hold the **salt** more tightly enclosed), are reduced to ashes. From these, the salt is collected by means of an elementary **phlegm** <term>phlegm: original *phlegma*; in this context, a tasteless, watery distillate used as a medium for extraction</term>. The phlegm and the useless earth are then thrown away. 

Thus we see it is true what **Aristotle** wrote: that water and earth, in their elementary solidification, are the matter of bodies; and it is true what **Hippocrates** said: that much of the ethereal nature has remained in the earth. For those essential principles are of a celestial nature—though not exclusively so—but are bound to the elements, so that the **oil** has fiery spirits associated with it, the **liquor** <note>here referring to the "mercurial" or spirituous liquid</note> has airy ones, and the **salt** has earthy ones. The watery parts are also distributed among all the parts. These principles of ours have not taken on any power other than that which they exerted while in the mixture—as far as the **medical temperament** <note>original: *crasin*; the specific balance of qualities that gives a medicine its healing power</note> is concerned—and they manifest themselves through odors, tastes, and effects, although one principle may be perceived more clearly in one substance than in another. **Oil of anise** smells and tastes of anise and provides that effect. So does the liquor. The salt possesses less of it, but nevertheless its own property <note>The text cuts off at *proprie-* with the catchword *tatem*, completing the word *proprietatem* or "property/characteristic"</note>...

<page-num>360</page-num>

->### THE ALCHEMY OF THE PARISIAN SLANDERER<- <note>original: *Alchymiæ de Spur. Paris.*; likely a reference to a specific critique of the Paris Medical Faculty</note>

<meta>catchword: nea. <note>likely referring to the start of "homogenea" on the next page</note></meta>

We prove by the experience of their effects that a specific property exists in this [part] as well as in the whole. I conclude that if these parts do not hinder the medicinal powers even now [when separated], they hindered them much less when in the mixture. **Pure substances** <note>original: *syncera*; refers to the chemically isolated principles</note> retain their powers, and regarding medicine, they possess them more evidently; therefore they were not useless in their first generation. But *Riolan* <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine who opposed chemical innovations</note> understands the faculties of life only insofar as life is present. I say that we do not care for that [definition], just as the **Apothecary-shops** <note>original: *Pharmacopolia*</note> do not. If one must deny that something was in the mixture for that reason, then deny that rue <note>a bitter herb common in traditional medicine</note> has leaves, flowers, roots, or bark, simply because these parts are useless for "life" once they are dried. There is one logic for lone and pure salt, oil, or liquid, and another for mixtures. So that they might be born and ripen by the benefit of life, they had to be joined together and grow into one with the elements. But for medicine, they are more rightly used when separated. This is the reasoning of my opinion opposed to the censor. It is remarkable malice to deny so stubbornly and shamelessly that the oily, liquid, and salty parts are unfit for medicinal powers, when it is well known that life consists of the airy fat, the moderate liquid, and the salt. Such is the blood; such is the marrow, milk, and fat—all of which are excellent nourishments. But there is no need for words to declare the stupidity of that school of censors. Amusus <note>Likely a derogatory pseudonym for an opponent, literally meaning "one without the Muses" or unlearned.</note> confused this argument with the preceding one. Since enough has already been said there regarding salt, we shall spare our words here. I was overturning argument with argument by the same principle, and thus I was demonstrating the vanity of the refutation <term>elenchus</term> <note>A logical tool for refuting a proposition by proving the opposite of its conclusion.</note>. For if something is not a principle or an element simply because we are not nourished by it in its solitary state, it follows, by the logic of the elements, that we do not consist of fire; that earth is not an element of our bodies; nor water nor air, because none of us is nourished by these things in isolation. By the same logic of principles, seed <note>original: *semen*; in this context, it refers to the generative "first principle" of life.</note> could not be a principle because no one is nourished by it (I speak in the sense of **Riolanus** <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a famous French physician and staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against new chemical theories.</note> regarding the seed of the male and female in our own kind, from which an analogy is drawn to all others). It would also follow that **Aristotle's** <term>matter</term>, <term>form</term>, and <term>privation</term> <note>Aristotle’s three principles of natural change: the substance (matter), the quality it takes (form), and the lack of that quality (privation).</note> cannot be principles, because we are nourished by none of them; indeed, in Riolanus’s judgment, matter and privation are harmful, and form is something metaphysical. For that reason, he claims, they nourish. What wretched ignorance in a man! If this is so, he admits that things nourish when joined together, not when separated. Our chemical principles <note>Referring to the "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>, when taken together, truly provide nourishment. Yet, let those be principles of knowledge adapted from Logic to Physics. No less authority belongs to our chemical principles than to the Aristotelian ones; indeed, ours possess far greater authority because they are more evident in sensible nature <note>The physical world that can be seen, felt, and tasted.</note>. It is not citing "this person" or "that person" that wins authority for a physical doctrine, but rather the power of nature and sensible demonstration. Thus, we argue against the unlearned school:

> *If elements taken separately are not disqualified as elements simply because they do not nourish alone, then principles taken separately are not disqualified as principles just because they do not nourish alone.*
> *But the former statement is true <note>original: "Verum autem illud"; referring to the fact that Aristotelians accept that pure Fire or Earth does not nourish.</note>.*
> *Therefore, the latter is also true. The connection proceeds from an equal consequence <note>original: "A pari"; a logical term for an argument from analogy or equal standing.</note>.*

...denying the chemical principles. This cannot happen except through similarity and familiarity <note>The principle of "like cures like" or "like sustains like," suggesting that these chemical principles are fundamentally the same as those in the human body.</note>, which is the root of conservation and the primary basis of sustenance.

Indeed, nutritive mercury, nutritive sulfur, and salt of the same kind—without any external element <note>The Aristotelian elements: Earth, Air, Fire, Water.</note> whether separated by art or by nature—procure nutrition primarily and by their own power. 

Let Riolanus live on his "air" among the ghosts, let him eat "earth," let him be satisfied by "fire," and let him fill his belly with "waters." We will throw up our hands in surrender if he can demonstrate that he can live on these alone—or even on those elements collected from the greater world <note>The "macrocosm" or the universe at large.</note> where they are said to exist separately—just as we sustain both the healthy and the sick with extracted principles and other chemical essences prepared for nourishment.
