# ALCHEMICAL DISPUTATIONS: PART.

These things are common themes among the followers of Paracelsus; namely, that salt is cured by salt in diseases caused by salt, <term>mercury</term> <note>In alchemical medicine, mercury represents the principle of fluidity, volatility, and spirit.</note> by mercury, and <term>sulfur</term> <note>The principle of inflammability, oiliness, and heat.</note> by sulfur—a phrasing that, in its very wording, sounds absurd <note>To the traditional Galenic doctors, who believed in curing by contraries, e.g., treating a "hot" fever with "cold" herbs.</note>.

This is indeed a bit of a detour. However, so that this too may be explained, one must understand that there is more than one way to interpret this saying. Regarding the consideration of "similarity" in healing, we have already mentioned the views of *Hippocrates* and *Mesue* <note>Mesue the Younger, an influential but likely pseudonymous Arabic medical authority whose works were foundational in medieval and Renaissance pharmacy.</note> above. Nature delights in and is strengthened by things similar to itself. Nature then removes the disease with the help of its own "instruments," which act on its behalf against the cause of the disease, or the disease itself.

If the powers of the "faculties" <note>In early medicine, "faculties" were the inherent abilities of the body to perform functions like digestion, growth, or sensation.</note> in mixed bodies do not reside in the elementary dross, but in the essential nature—which is called the "extract," and is broken down through the <term>magisterium</term> <note>A technical alchemical process for preparing or "mastering" a substance to reach its highest medicinal state.</note> into the <term>three principles</term> <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the three substances Paracelsians believed made up all matter.</note>—and if these principles through processing become essences (whether simple essences or a "quintessence"), then it is clear that we must defend the foundation of how these powers act against diseases. If anyone were so "lynx-eyed" <note>original: "lynceus." A reference to Lynceus, the Argonaut famous for sight so sharp he could see through stone and trees; used here to mean someone with extraordinary scientific insight.</note> that he could see whether the <term>salt</term> <note>The principle of solidity, structure, and consistency in the body.</note> of the bone or the mercury was weakened, or if the sulfur had fallen from a healthy state, he would—following the axioms of the traditional medical school—rightly assist salt with salt and like things with like things. This is not absurd even according to common medical teaching. For even by the testimony of *Riolan* <note>Jean Riolan (1577–1657), a conservative physician and leading critic of the alchemical movement.</note> himself, essential deficiencies of the spirits are restored by spirits, solids by solids, and moist things by moist things. So it is with qualities: sluggish spirits are, as it were, animated by vigorous ones, impure by pure, and weak by strong; this is a type of restorative medicine <note>original: "medicina analeptica"</note> and dietary [regimen]...

He judges it best to cure the sick parts through those very things which cause the diseases. For in this way, one will best heal the origin of the patient's illness. 

This is indeed usually explained as healing the "commanding" member first, so that the flow or transfer from it ceases. Once the <term>primary disease</term> <note>The root cause or the first organ affected.</note> is healed, the secondary condition—which depends on it like a symptom—is easily driven away (so long as it hasn't developed its own deep-seated habit, which would require its own special treatment, or unless its severity forces the Physician to soothe the onset of the secondary ailment first). 

But some interpret this in another way: Medication happens through a medicinal agent. Since, therefore, a part of the body is healed by another part, a member of the body ought to be cured by a "medicinal member." For example, the head, when essentially affected, should be treated by things corresponding to the head, such as **betony**, **nutmeg**, **marjoram**, **rosemary**, and similar plants. 

From this arises again the axiom: **A cure must be established through familiar and similar things, acting on behalf of nature against the disease.** 

With this in mind, I judge that **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a famous French physician who sought to reconcile Paracelsian chemistry with the traditional teachings of Galen and Hippocrates.</note>—who is clearly a follower of **Hippocrates** and also a symbolic <term>chemical physician</term>—writes that "likes" are a remedy for "likes": salt for salt, sulfur for sulfur, and so on. This holds true if only the Physician, by his <term>conjectures</term> <note>original: "stochasmis." From the Greek for "aiming" or "guessing," referring to the physician's skill in intuiting the hidden, specific cause of an individual's illness.</note>, can singularly reach such specific, indeed individual, defects. This is surely so difficult that it is even impossible. For mixtures are clearly <term>homogeneous</term> <note>In early chemistry, this meant the substances were so thoroughly blended that their individual elements could not be seen separately.</note>, and you cannot show an element without...

...to govern the whole mixture, if that is the argument. Go on. It would more truly be called "concretion" <note>original: *concretio*; a growing together or solidifying</note> than "mixture." Both, I say, are natural. For those things which are mixed together grow together and are integrated, both by the motion of nature and by the power of opposites. He claims that "synthesis" <term>synthesis: the act of putting things together, often associated with human art</term> and "genesis" <term>genesis: natural generation or coming-into-being</term> differ as art and nature. This is false. For synthesis belongs not only to an external principle <note>meaning human agency or art</note>, but also to an internal one, which is nature. Indeed, the same word is sometimes attributed to art, as in Book 6 of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Chapter 4: "All art is concerned with generation" <note>original Greek: πᾶσα τέχνη ἐστὶ περὶ γένεσιν</note>. There is a famous passage comparing art and nature in the first book of the *Physics*, Text 63. "Things that come into being simply," says the philosopher <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the primary authority on natural philosophy in this period</note>, "do so in various ways: some by transfiguration, like a statue from bronze; others by addition, like things that grow; others by subtraction, like a statue of Hermes <note>original: *mercurius*</note> carved from stone; others by composition, like a house; and others by alteration, like things that change according to their matter." And in Text 64, he says, "it is manifest that everything which comes into being is always composed," etc.

<margin>It is well enough known that nature also possesses accidental forms <term>accidental forms: qualities like color, shape, or size that are not part of an object's essential nature</term>. If a natural form is a substance, then qualities are rightly called the "essential forms of the elements" under the benches of the Parisians <note>A sarcastic jab at the professors of the University of Paris faculty, suggesting their logic is backwards</note>.</margin>

He explains nature through art, and shows that the same thing happens in both, since art is a certain imitation of nature. How great a scandal then is that of Amusus <note>A pseudonym for a detractor of alchemy, likely meaning "one without the Muses" or unlearned</note>, who denies that our chemical principles come from nature because they are "composed," claiming that composition belongs only to art? In paragraph delta, he even ascribes an "accidental form" to them, because art creates an accidental form by composing, while nature creates a "substantial form" <term>substantial form: the essence that makes a thing what it is (e.g., what makes a human a human)</term> by generating. He is utterly raving. Nature also creates substance through its own compositions, such as "dissimilar organs" <note>original: *membra dissimilaria*; complex body parts like the hand or head made of various tissues</note>—unless perhaps Riolan's <note>Jean Riolan, a leading conservative physician in Paris</note> head is artificial rather than natural, accidental rather than substantial, simply because it is composed of many parts!

# THE SPURIOUS PARTS OF ALCHEMY
<page-num>890</page-num>

It has long been accepted in the chemical schools, although not clearly enough explained in the writings of the ancients—as happens with all arts that grow from small beginnings and eventually receive light from obscure principles. **Sulphur** and **mercury** are established in metallic bodies; in others, their counterparts are placed together with **salt**, which Paracelsus wrongly writes was omitted by the ancients. <margin>Paracelsus presented the discoveries of the ancients as his own.</margin> He was not ashamed to claim these discoveries for himself with a certain reckless arrogance. Our "Amuser" <note>A mocking nickname for Jean Riolan the Younger</note> refers back to the fiction of Petrus Severinus the Dane <note>Petrus Severinus (1541–1602) was a major proponent of Paracelsian medicine</note>; but he is mistaken. Since the time of metallic or fusible alchemy, chemical principles have been immediately recognized and propagated through consistent teaching, as is clear enough from the art described by Geber <term>Geber: Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century figure whose writings formed the foundation of medieval alchemy</term>. This art could not be the work of a single man or a single age, since nothing is invented and perfected at the same time.

And as Aristotle writes in the first book of the *Meteorology* (Chapter 3), we say that the same opinions return to men not once, or twice, or rarely, but an infinite number of times; and according to the wisdom of Solomon, there is **nothing new under the sun**.

But what, finally, of Riolan—now *our* Riolan? That fiction of his regarding principles having their roots in the **seeds of things** <term>seeds of things: "semina rerum," a concept suggesting that matter contains formative "seeds" or spiritual blueprints that direct its growth</term> carries some appearance of truth. Well done, my dear Riolan! If this is so, we have reached the realm of probability, and as Aristotle judges, we are "good philosophers" who do not despise even small certainties. Indeed, there was a reason for everyone to doubt, so that they might philosophize (Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, Book 2, Text 78). We are worthy of respect, not hatred, because—as it says in Chapter 12 of the second book of *On the Heavens*—because of a thirst for philosophy, we love even small certainties...

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM
<page-num>891</page-num>

...we [reason] in those matters about which we have the greatest doubts. Thus, we have finally moved from mere probability to a **sensible and natural demonstration**, not merely an artificial one. (As the Philosopher <note>Aristotle is traditionally referred to as "the Philosopher" in scholastic texts.</note> says in the <term>third book of *On the Heavens*, text 61</term>: "the goal of a productive science is the work [the result], but in natural science, it is that which always properly appears according to the senses.")

We draw these things out by our art; for this reason, the principles are our "work." And we show to the senses that these principles are present in every "perfect mixture." For if they were not present within it, as the Philosopher says again regarding the elements in <term>book 3 of *On the Heavens*, text 33</term>, they could not be separated from it.

What is the nature of our truth? That <term>chemical principles</term> <note>Original: *principia chymica*. Specifically Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> are fundamentally present in the "seeds," which gradually grow along with the plants—and understand this to apply to all mixtures, whether they possess a <term>univocal seed</term> <note>A seed that produces an offspring of the same species, like a grain of wheat.</note> or an <term>equivocal seed</term> <note>A term used in older biology for life thought to arise from different sources, such as spontaneous generation.</note>—and these principles acquire their power little by little along with the substance itself. Indeed, they are an interior part of the substance, even more so than the separable elements.

If these views have the appearance of truth, then by your own judgment you have lost your case, because our "essences" and "principles" will not be nothing, and our art will not be an empty name. Likewise, it is nature that generated our principles; art did not merely compose them. We do not "make" them; nature does, even though we may have produced them through our art.

Altogether, whatever arguments you have brought against us all become mere <term>sophistry</term>, since it is necessary that if our views have the appearance of truth, yours must have the appearance of falsehood. But so that we may move from the appearance of truth and falsehood to a clearly demonstrated truth and falsehood, let us offer the following in addition to what has been said so far.

->*If that juice by which the seed is nourished, and which the plant draws from the earth for its sustenance and growth, consists of earth, spirit, fire, and water, which gradually mature; then chemical principles are nothing other than elementary portions—just as oil is of the air, spirit is of fire, distilled water is of water, and salt is of the earth.*<-

->*The former is true. Therefore, the latter follows.*<-

Consequently, the principles of Hippocrates and Aristotle ought not to have been excluded simply so that chemical principles could be substituted in their place. In your <term>major premise</term> <note>The first part of a logical argument (syllogism).</note>, when you say the **SEED** is nourished, see how you might reconcile this with our Savior, who affirms that the seed of wheat must die in the earth so that it may grow into a fruit-bearing plant. Therefore, it is not strictly proper to say the seed is "nourished." 

However, you seem to be speaking alongside Hippocrates, who says: 
<note>original Greek: "τὰ φυόμενα καὶ σπειρόμενα ὁκόταν εἰς τὴν γῆν ἔλθῃ, ἕλκει ἕκαστον τὸ κατὰ φύσιν ἑωυτῷ ἐνεὸν ἐν τῇ γῇ. ἔνι δὲ καὶ ὀξὺ, καὶ πικρὸν, καὶ γλυκὺ, καὶ ἁλμυρὸν, καὶ παντοῖον. πρῶτον μὲν οὖν πλεῖστον τούτων εἵλκυσεν εἰς ἑωυτὸ ὅ τι ἂν ᾖ ἑωυτέῳ κατὰ φύσιν. ἔπειτα δὲ ἕλκει καὶ τ' ἄλλα."</note> 
"When things that grow and are sown enter the earth, each draws to itself the substance naturally present in the earth that suits it. For there is acidic, bitter, sweet, salty, and every kind of humor within it. First, then, it draws the greatest amount of that which is natural to itself, and afterward, it draws the rest." 

These are the words of Hippocrates, which Galen, Mesue, and others embrace and repeat, so that it is the common opinion of the Greeks and Arabs, of the <term>Galenic herbalists</term> <note>Original: *simplicium Galenicorum*, those who used "simples" or unmixed medicinal herbs.</note> and the <term>chemical physicians</term> <note>Original: *chymiatrorum*, doctors who combined alchemy and medicine.</note>. Regarding the seed, you first needed to be warned of this.

"I demonstrate to you," you say, "the four elements in the generative and nutritive juice of a plant. Now, demonstrate your <term>radical principles</term> <note>In Paracelsian thought, these are the three prime substances—Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—that make up all things, rather than the four Aristotelian elements of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> to me." 

I say I have already shown them! I wish your school had eyes with which it could see those juices in the earth, in plants, and in animals—juices that can arise from no element. Just like the soul, there is a **virtue** <note>An active power or life-force.</note> that participates in a body more divine than any of the elements. From what elementary combination can the **noble essence of a skull**, **hartshorn** <note>powdered antler of a male deer, used for ammonia and other medicinal properties</note>, **wolf's liver**, **wolf's skin**, **cinnamon**, and so on, be constituted? These are available in the chemical workshops and even in those of the **Galenic chymiatrists** <note>Physicians who attempted to blend traditional Galenic medicine with the new chemical methods.</note>. 

But your school is so blind it cannot see; and whatever it does see, its foul **sophistry** <note>The use of clever but false arguments.</note> ensures it does not truly perceive, as if your school were born for stage-tricks and illusions.

Proceed. You say: "The principles of your dissolution are composite. Therefore, the radical principles must also be composite." What of it? The juices drawn from the earth—bitter, sweet, and the rest—are indeed composite. Therefore, so too is that which was inherent in the seeds, and that which is extracted from them. 

Let your school know that our principles are **simple** in terms of their powers, and also in respect to the whole mixture of elements and principles. But if you compare them with the bare and simplest elements, they are "mixed" or "composite," just like **seed**, **blood**, and the other **Galenic humors** <note>The four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Galenists believed governed health.</note>. If you were to likewise compare those humors with our principles...

<center># ON SPURIOUS ALCHEMY IN PARIS</center>

...it is clear, because they are mixed and possess elements prior to them. This **sophism** <term>sophism: a clever but false argument intended to deceive</term> is easily dismissed by demonstrating the **homonymy** <term>homonymy: when the same word is used to describe different concepts</term> of the word "principle." Aristotle possesses principles that are absolute and first in all logic; he also possesses "firsts" of a specific kind. Such things are the Galenic principles, like semen, blood, and so on. **Chemical** principles are not the absolute "firsts" of bodies; rather, they are the "firsts" of powers credited to spiritual essences. In this context, they are the first of all things, because powers have no body prior to them. Elemental qualities certainly possess elements; but these are not the powers of mixtures *insofar as they are mixtures*. When elements are dissolved through putrefaction, the elemental **crasis** <term>crasis: the specific blending or "temperament" of the four qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry—that defines a substance</term> vanishes, and the opposing forces return to their original simplicity. But Aristotle demonstrates in his *Analytics* that principles must be "first," because if they had something prior to them, they would not be principles, but rather conclusions.

Learn, foolish school, that the principle of a specific science—which may be subordinate or subject to a higher science—is one thing; the principle of **syllogistic** <term>syllogistic: a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given premises</term> demonstration is another; and the principle of a natural mixed body is yet another. An analytical principle is a universal axiom <note>original Greek: καθ' ὅλου πρῶτον, meaning "first according to the whole" or "primarily universal"</note>; it is not a singular physical thing, whether Hippocratic or Galenic, within a mixture. We, on the contrary, say: That which is first, is a principle. Our essences or **magisteries** <term>magistery: a concentrated "master" substance or extract representing the purest form of a medicine</term>—**salt**, **sulfur**, and **mercury**—are first: because they are the first of the essential powers in mixtures. This is demonstrated not only by the evidence of the senses, but also by the Hippocratic [theory of] generation and the nutrition of plants. Therefore, our essences are principles.

## CHAPTER 99.

->Argument 22 against Chemical principles, page 138 of the manuscript.<-

**P**rinciples do not appear to the senses, but are known through reason. Chemical principles are perceptible. Therefore, they are not [true] principles. This is overturned by Argument 14, where a sensible demonstration was demanded, since according to the judgment of Aristotle, the principles of perceptible things are themselves perceptible. Whether you bring forth the senses as a witness or not, for that foolish School <note>The "School" refers to the traditional medical establishment at the University of Paris, which strictly followed the ancient teachings of Galen and Aristotle.</note>, our principles cannot be [true] principles. Why waste many words? They are simply condemned. Arguments are brought forth recklessly. For whether you prove them or not, they are rejected—just like the man who denied he could believe in the **transmutation** into gold even if he saw everything with his own eyes. So powerful is opinion among fools that whatever is not clearly seen is held as nothing at all. Let us therefore give like for like, and whatever the School says, let it be condemned as madness. Let others be valued only as much as they are able to prove.

He denies that our principles can be shown because they are not present in reality, but only as a "remote potential" <term>remote potential: a philosophical state where something could eventually become another thing, but lacks the immediate power to do so</term>: as if that insane School could show blood, phlegm, and both types of bile <note>Referring to the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> inside a solid bone, or resolve the bone back into these things. When, at last, will you show **Platonic matter** <term>Platonic matter: the "Receptacle," an underlying, formless substrate described in Plato’s Timaeus</term> and **prime form** along with **privation**? <term>privation: in Aristotelian logic, the absence or lack of a specific quality that a substance should naturally possess.</term> A principle is better known to Nature than to us, for whom the individual compound is more familiar. Why do you ask, vain School, for it to be shown to you? That we produce extracts while the capable matter in them...

## *Argument 23 against the principles, page of madness, 138.*

**I**t used to be said that the defining property of a "principle" is that it is not created from the mutual exchange of other things. But chemical principles are created from such mutual exchanges; therefore, they are not [true] principles. If this were actually the case, then phlegm and yellow bile could not be Hippocratic principles <note>In the traditional medicine of Hippocrates and Galen, the body was governed by four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, because phlegm passes into the blood, and yellow bile into black bile. Amusus denies that the elements are principles because they are not "primary substances." This is false. Perceptible substances are primary substances. Or must that School be taught even the basics of Aristotelian logic? <term>primary substances: in Aristotelian logic, "substantia prima" refers to individual, existing things (like "this specific water"), while "secondary substances" refer to general categories or species</term>. Primary substances are singular and individual, such as *this* specific element. Secondary substances are the species and genera, which cannot exist if the individuals do not exist. But where are this form, this matter, and this privation found separately? <note>Matter, form, and privation were Aristotle’s three theoretical principles of change; the author argues they are abstract concepts rather than real, physical things.</note> These logical concepts are mental entities, not primary substances; and thus, by the judgment of Amusus himself, they cannot be principles.

This calumny is easily recognized. As far as elementary qualities are concerned, they follow their own elements, although the primary goal of chemistry is to investigate the hidden things <note>the "occult" or internal properties</note> of nature, not the manifest ones, and this is especially true regarding the subject of the powers which mixtures <note>substances composed of multiple elements</note> possess.

Through magisteries <term>magisteria</term> <note>refining processes used to "master" or exalt a substance to its highest potency</note>, even manifest powers can be exalted; and if any elementary powers were hindered or in retreat, these are also drawn forth as use demands. Riolan wittily writes that I am "coming to my senses," as if I had ever denied that. He adds that I admit we do not extract essences, but rather that matter is transmuted into those forms—namely, through **Riolanian panspermia** <note>original: *panspermiam Riolaneam*; a theory that "seeds" or potentials for all things are latent within matter and only need a trigger to appear</note>. But he is mistaken. There is a case where a simple secretion <note>separation</note> occurs; and there is a case where it happens with "actuation" (as the Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note> call it) or, as Mesue <note>an influential medieval pharmaceutical authority</note> says, with the "manifestation of the hidden," the veil having been removed. Under different words, the same meaning lies. On page 145, he ridiculously asks whether in another re- <note>Catchword: *feram*—refer</note>

Indeed, Paracelsus denies in certain places that it is useful to work without corrosives. But we propose far different methods, as Paracelsus himself does in his manual. It is a sign of ignorance to call the concept of essences a "mastery" <term>magisterium</term> <note>a technical term in alchemy for a substance that has been perfected or transformed into a superior state</note>, unless the word is used figuratively.

Furthermore, what is better known than the fact that <term>Mesuë</term> was a distinguished chemist? It is true that in his practical works he did not use chemical terminology. But when the whole substances are named, their extracts are named at the same time. It is enough that he gave universal instructions for their preparation and illustrated them with several specific examples. 

On page 153, there is a strange statement regarding the Baker: that he supposedly retains the "mixture" <term>crasis</term> <note>from the Greek word for "mixture," referring to the specific temperament or healthy balance of qualities in a substance</note> and the powers of wheat even after it has been cooked three times into bread made from wheat flour, water, and leaven. It is likewise claimed he retains them after the separation of the bran, which is itself a basic chemical process. If wheat were to retain its original mixture and form in bread, then let us plant loaves of bread in the ground so that they might grow into wheat plants! <note>The author uses this humorous image to show that cooking and preparation—like alchemy—permanently change the nature of a substance.</note> If the baker is said to retain the mixture and powers of the original grain, what madness is it to deny this same ability to the chemists, who do not always mix substances, nor do they always transmute them?

# ON THE HONOR OF TRUE CHEMISTRY *

## A Letter to Cosmas Pegandrus, 
## physician of Stade, etc.

The title of the previous letter, which **Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a Parisian physician and fierce defender of traditional Galenic medicine against the new chemical theories</note> replaced in a truncated form, was: **On the reproaches of Paracelsian chemistry**, (namely, the kind practiced everywhere by impostors, many of whom return to Germany having barely glanced once at Spain, France, Italy, England, etc., and profess themselves to be finished chemists—despite having been barbers, goldsmiths, and the like—and boast of their knowledge of the most secret medicines; while others, fugitives from other workshops, suddenly emerge as experts in <term>chemical medicine</term> <note>original: *chymiatrices*; the practice of using chemical preparations for healing, as opposed to purely herbal Galenic remedies</note> after merely reading a few Paracelsian pamphlets) and the arguments of its opponents (namely, those who oppose the true art as well, such as the many "lizards and scorpions," <note>metaphorical terms for treacherous and stinging detractors</note> slanderers, and haters who are found in great numbers). 

**Riolan** omitted this title, undoubtedly realizing that if it were included, it would be manifest that he is among those who slander and disparage this most wise art, since he uses the same arguments. He also removed the beginning of that letter, in which, among other things, are these words: "I would contend that in chemistry, <term>nothing in excess</term> <note>original Greek: *meden agan*; the famous Delphic maxim advising moderation in all things</note> ought to be done, and I would advise—as Cato <note>Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman famous for his cautious and often suspicious view of Greek philosophy and medicine</note> suggested—that chemical literature should indeed be inspected and tasted, but not thoroughly mastered to the point that you trust yourself to any master, follow them without sharpness of judgment, or believe just anything they say."

### THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM

...it lay hidden in the laboratories of kings and sages, until by some accident or error it fell into the hands of the idle. These people, being unable to imitate the true good, manufactured a certain **parachemical** <term>parachymicum</term> <note>A derogatory term used here to describe a corrupted or "side" version of chemistry that deviates from ancient truths</note> and **falsehood** <note>original Greek: ψεῦσμα (pseusma), meaning a lie or a deceptive fabrication</note> which they substituted in place of the former. What majesty or holiness has ever existed in the world that was so safe from the attempts of wicked men as to remain unviolated? And since [true chemistry] is so unlike wickedness, is it not attacked by that very wickedness with the most extreme hatred? Only the evil and impious hold in hatred that which is good and holy. The crop of the wicked is always more fertile. If, therefore, the best of arts has suffered this treatment, its splendor is all the more commendable among the good. Wherefore, it is rightly compared in equal measure to that most holy thing, the **Gospel**, in the context of pure **chemistry** <term>chymia</term>. Both have their place among the holy and the good. Both suffer the same treatment from the profane. That [critical] voice is plebeian; it belongs to the common crowd, and is noted in common records according to the custom of men, by which that which is more loud-mouthed and more frequently boasted in public is usually marked.

<margin>
What is despised by the common people is usually excellent in its hidden depth. For the common crowd lacks the eyes of the mind, with which internal things are seen.
</margin>

Therefore, the fact that common descriptions everywhere proclaim its contempt actually holds a certain dignity in secret. For the more divine and noble something is, the viler and more abject it is to the common folk, because it is further from their comprehension. The common crowd celebrates nothing except what is common-place <note>original Latin: "ad salinam," literally "at the salt-works," an idiom for something basic, salty, or unrefined</note>, and it throws itself with thick smoke into their eyes—so infused and boiled down in the workshops of a thick and heavy **Minerva** <term>Mineruæ</term> <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom; the phrase "crassa Minerva" refers to a plain, unrefined intellect or "rough-and-ready" common sense as opposed to high learning</note>...

(Riolan is more pleased by the external luster of gold than by its internal tincture, or by **potable gold** <term>aurum potabile</term> <note>A legendary liquid medicine made from gold, believed by alchemists to have miraculous healing powers</note>, etc.) Usually, that which shines on the outside is a **counterfeit** <term>fucatum</term> <note>Literally "painted" or "dyed," referring to something that has a deceptive, superficial beauty</note>. But just as this outward show is customary and pleasing to the common folk, yet suspect and contemptible to the wise; so let it be granted that true chemistry has always excelled and abounded in all honor and majesty among the wise (contrary to what Riolan has written). 

<margin>*Antisthenes, when someone told him that "most people praise you," replied: "What evil have I done?" Menander once said to Philemon, who was winning favor with the people: "I ask you, Philemon, with all due respect, tell me: when you defeat me, do you not blush?"* <note>These anecdotes illustrate that popularity with the masses is often a sign of mediocrity or error rather than truth.</note></margin>

It has not, however, found such favor among the common people, whose judgment has been infamous in every record of wisdom—so much so that the wisest of the Greeks did not hesitate to write that one must not judge by the multitude (referring to the School of Paris), which should be judged well, but rather by **knowledge** <note>original Greek: ἐπιστήμη (episteme)</note> (which Riolan clearly lacks in chemical matters). This knowledge arises from the very sanctuary of essential causes and exists only in the possession of the wise. 

But I pass over that. What was the second reproach? It was said that chemistry stands in the way of the goal we owe to God and society, using the argument that it involves hiding away among **the pots of Vulcan** <note>original: "Vulcanicas ollas." An allusion to the alchemist's furnace and laboratory equipment, implying that chemists waste their lives in isolation.</note>. This very claim is surely a twin to that corrupt ignorance. It is so foreign to the true art that nothing could be more alien. If any...

**The glory of God lies hidden within nature; the chemical searcher and true contemplator brings it forth and shows it openly. (In the judgment of the Parisians <note>A reference to the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Paris, which famously banned chemical medicines in the late 16th century</note>, we ought to remain on the surface <note>original: "in cortice," literally "in the bark" or "on the shell"</note> and not scrutinize internal principles.) How could it be possible that he does not reach the goal of divinity?**

It is said that Archimedes <note>The famous Greek mathematician and inventor</note> took such great joy from a certain almost common discovery that he burst out of the bath naked into public, shouting his **"I have found it!"** <term>eureka</term> <note>original: εὕρηκα</note>. He wished, of course, that what had been found by him alone should be common to his companions. The zeal of the true chemist is far more fervent. He works in his **workshop** <term>officina</term> <note>A laboratory or "office" of nature where chemical operations are performed</note>, which is most well-supplied with a storehouse of natural things. When the work is finished, he does not hide it, but brings it forth for public use; he explains the reason for the wonders, and arranges them so that human society may consider itself satisfied. 

It is ingrained in good minds to seek faithful witnesses and approvers of their works, just as the Savior said that they loved the light. Therefore, the professor of chemistry communicates his goods out of duty without shame, and can endure expert judges (though many at this time oppose chemists with every effort, and are accustomed not to judge, but to condemn noble works). Those who act as **counterfeiters** <term>falsarios</term> and brew chemical adulterations do not indeed hide like dormice or moles in underground rooms; for they do not blush to burst even into the marketplace with their impostures. However, they hide the reasons for their works so much that even a single little word costs a great deal. For adulterations cannot bear the light, nor thefts—

# THE ALCHEMY OF THE SPURIOUS PARISIANS

...and by fear of punishment and refutation. The **true chemist** must enter the workshop, but not in such a way that he becomes useless for the other duties of life. Human duties are varied, but to all things their own times and hours. (Even the directors and judges of works perform many tasks through their assistants.) He cultivates the art in such a way that he does not neglect **duty toward the divine** <note>original: τὸ περὶ τὸ θεῖον</note>; he does not cast aside the state, nor desert his home. Everywhere, in his own time, he appears faithful at his post—something you will not find among the **Paracelsians** <term>Paracelsici</term> <note>Followers of the controversial physician Paracelsus, often accused by traditionalists of being secretive, nomadic, and religiously heterodox</note>, who withdraw from these duties, intent on a single small profit and deception. Once they have seized their prize, they retreat to their caves, and it is not rare for them to never appear in the same place more than once.

Indeed, some are accustomed to claim all knowledge for themselves in words; but you cannot trust them with any matter, unless you wish to ruin everything and mix divine things with human. These people keep visitors away from their hiding places, and with a thousand evasions and barriers they remove the **laboratory**—or "work-house" <term>ergastulum</term> <note>original: ergastulum; historically a Roman private prison for slaves, used here to imply a dark, forced, or secretive place of labor</note>, as they call it—from the access of men and even of friends. I remember once asking to see the little furnace of the **Philosophers** <term>Philosophorum</term> <note>Likely referring to the "chemical philosophers" or the search for the Philosopher's Stone</note> and the tripod of secrets from one who pretended to be my closest friend. But I was pushed back. **Assyluanus** <note>Possibly a contemporary figure or a specific nickname for a secretive alchemist</note> is said to have a little furnace for cooking cinnabar in the most secret places. 

The true **chemist** <term>chymicus</term> does not drive away the wise and the good, but bids them enter in the manner of **Heraclitus** <term>Heraclitus</term> <note>Referring to an anecdote where the Greek philosopher Heraclitus invited guests into his humble kitchen, saying "Here too are gods," suggesting divinity is found in everyday work</note>; for in the **Resolution** <term>Resolutione</term> <note>The chemical process of breaking a substance down into its constituent parts to reveal its internal nature</note> of natural things, that wonderful power of God appears most clearly. The Author [God] himself commands us to observe it from that vantage point and to pursue it with the highest glory. To play with those seeking wisdom using empty words is not...

<page-num>919</page-num>

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM
<note>original: GALENIA TRIVMPHVS. This title suggests a defense of traditional Galenic medicine against the perceived radicalism of Paracelsus.</note>

...is nothing but the work of shamefully scurrilous men. Just as it is far removed from the practice of **true chemistry**, so it closely approaches the **Paracelsian** <term>Paracelsica</term> <note>The medical and alchemical system of Paracelsus, which many traditionalists viewed as heretical or fraudulent</note> method, which is spurious and counterfeit. This group even dares to write commentaries and name-lists <term>onomastica</term> <note>technical lexicons or dictionaries of specialized terms</note>, but these are even more obscure than obscurity itself, so that you cannot carry away anything certain from them, either here or there. 

(See the "Serianum" of **Gerard Dorn** <note>Gerard Dorn (c. 1530–1584) was a prominent editor and defender of Paracelsus; the author here cites him as an example of confusing terminology</note> and others. Because Paracelsianism has departed from **true chemistry** in most matters, it has also invented new words <term>vocabula confinxit nova</term> that none of the ancients would have understood, nor almost any of the moderns, since even the followers of the sect argue among themselves about their meanings.) 

Therefore, turn away from the speech of these fools, and call them "dogs," because they foully pollute the sanctuary of God, bark shamefully, and bite rabidly—those whom the seekers of **true wisdom** <term>sapientia</term> happen upon. Call these same men "pigs" on account of their filthy vileness and their grunting, which is more ignorant than all ignorance itself. For when they are questioned about the wonders of nature, they grunt with porcine rudeness, and like **Homer’s Gryllus** <note>In Greek mythology, Gryllus was a companion of Odysseus who was turned into a pig by Circe and famously refused to be changed back, preferring the mud to human reason</note>, they value their own mud more than any noble balsam found in the secrets of true wisdom. 

**True chemistry** <term>chymia</term> <note>The author uses "chemistry" here to refer to a legitimate, transparent science of nature, distinct from the "spurious" alchemy of his rivals</note> cultivates **humanity**, hates morose harshness, is affable and gentle, and does nothing with a haughty brow or under the pretext of feigned religion. It honors every work of nature and art with its proper name and dignity, and does not offer dung in place of pearls. 

Therefore, such a chemist neither casts off his humanity, nor does he allow himself to be transformed into swine or wolves. But if there is any glory to be had from this—when you treat and practice true and proper things while remaining within the boundaries of a civilized profession—then the chemist shall not be without his own praise.

<margin>
Here begin the objections of Riolan.
<note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605) was a conservative French physician and a staunch defender of traditional Galenic medicine against the rising tide of chemical medicine.</note>
</margin>

But does the chemist destroy nature, and declare himself its enemy? Certainly, if this effort stems from a spirit opposed to divine things, or from a desire to undo or detest whatever God has made, I cannot help but condemn such an attempt. Likewise, if it is done out of contempt for whole substances, or through that depraved malice used by the **Paracelsians** <term>Paracelsitæ</term> <note>Followers of the radical Swiss physician Paracelsus</note>—who deny that there is any aid for human health in whole substances, and indeed accuse everything of that kind of being poisonous, simply so they can push their own "little broths" <note>original: iuscula</note> more plausibly and sell them more dearly—I would reject and rightly detest that as well. 

But the purpose of the **true chemist** is holy; it is useful and beneficial to the human race. So far from opposing the divine creation, he reverently seeks the material for his work from the vast field of the world. In this material, he investigates the secrets of God's majesty and comes to know the miracles of nature—not only on the surface, but deep within. (Though to Riolan, these are like cataracts in the eye <note>original: vngues in oculo; literally "nails in the eye," a reference to medical obstructions of vision</note> and "invisible stars"—referring to the **three principles** <term>tria principia</term> <note>The alchemical triad of Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt, which Riolan rejected</note> which are changed into pure **essences** <term>essentias</term> through laboratory labor). 

He is not ignorant of the course of the world. He knows that pure essences—because of the various injuries and hardships of heaven and earth—could not be born without assistance. (Pay attention, Riolan, and consider at the same time that because of sin—see **Genesis 3:17, Genesis 4:12, Romans 8**, etc.—the earth was cursed so that it could no longer produce such healthy fruits; and consider that **medicine** <term>medicina</term> is the relief for our miseries, which repairs the defects of nature as much as it can, separates the good from the evil, and employs them for our health). These essences could not have been born without help, just as in the animal kingdom many aids are summoned from outside for the...

# THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM #

<margin>If certain individual items are consumed in chemical works, the entire genera and species are not destroyed.</margin>
...to drive away noxious qualities. Not only chemistry, but also cooking, sculpture, and the whole range of manual arts remove these things for convenient and healthy use. The Creator does not at all disapprove of these purifications of nature for human and divine use; indeed, He Himself showed and commanded that the refuse be set aside. (In Exodus 30, when the **sacred oil** <note>The holy anointing oil described in the Bible, made from a blend of liquid myrrh, cinnamon, cane, and cassia</note> is made, the ingredients cannot be kept whole.) Generations and nourishments do not come from whole, unaltered substances. Therefore, although the integrity of a singular, individual thing is destroyed by this work, the **universal** <note>original: τὸ καθόλου</note> and the **form** <note>original: εἶδος</note> are not.

Each thing has its own perfection, which commends and adorns the integrity of nature for outward contemplation. However, to the art looking toward practical use, that natural state is an "imperfection." (Nature gives the material for wine, but not the wine itself. For wine to be made, the grape must be destroyed, and from the imperfect, the perfect is made.) Nature is left with its own glory, but let nothing be taken away from art, which is no less a gift from God than nature is His own invention. However, the operation of a true chemist is a far cry from the deceptions of the **Paracelsians** <term>Paracelsitæ</term> <note>Radical followers of Paracelsus who often claimed supernatural results</note>.

A **painted face** <note>original: cerussata facies; white-lead makeup used to hide blemishes, here a metaphor for intellectual dishonesty</note> belongs to them, not to the chemist. They are accustomed to sell any of their works as **quintessences** <term>essentiæ quintæ</term> <note>The "fifth element" or purest extract of a substance</note> which they claim have been freed from all "contagion of the elements." This—to present a pure, heavenly essence without any element of this **middle world** <note>The physical, earthly realm below the heavens</note>—is impossible for any human art. Therefore, it is inevitable that they offer lies instead of the truth. A true chemist shows each effect of his art in its true likeness, and does not overstep the truth, just like an honest sculptor...

...he does not propose a wooden <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "mercurio"; mercury was considered a fundamental principle of metals and medicine</note> instead of a golden one. There is no reason, therefore, why the <term>chemist</term> <note>original: "chymicus"</note> should expect any disgrace for himself from this, etc.

The native mixture does not perish in every operation. The <term>extract</term> <note>original: "Extractus"</note> of <term>rhubarb</term> <note>original: "Rhabarbaræ"; a common medicinal root used as a laxative</note> agrees with the whole plant in its <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "crasis"; the specific balance of qualities or humors in a substance</note> and its (purging) effect. Where indeed a substance must be destroyed, it is not done without a certain plan and aim (<term>constitution</term> passes from one determined state into another. Although one may be destroyed because it was going to be troublesome, it is destroyed; but another succeeding it is conducive to healing and other uses). 

We are not ignorant that the <term>juices</term> <note>original: "χυμὸς" (chymos)</note> in any (mixed) thing are diverse, and that they are not equipped with just one faculty. It is also established that anything is not corrupted into just anything else, but into that which still smells of its prior substance. If, therefore, we seek and draw out that which rightly serves the present necessity—even if the <term>mixture</term> <note>original: "mistura"; the philosophical union of elements</note> of the whole has perished—it is not an illegitimate work of the art, nor is it so discordant with nature, etc. He speaks falsely who declares that the true <term>chemist</term> destroys things to the very end. This was not the way of the art. There are limits to individual preparations in...

<meta>This page continues the defense of the chemical art (alchemy) as a legitimate handmaid to medicine. Having previously distinguished the true chemist from the reckless "Paracelsian," the author now explains the technical philosophy of chemical processes—specifically the use of heat to unlock nature's secrets without destroying her essence.</meta>

<page-num>923</page-num>

# ->THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM<-

...with which the art ceases. For this reason, instructions are so carefully given regarding the governing of fire and the administration of heat. From this, the stages of change and the signs of progress are so faithfully emphasized. Some substances are pressed with more severe fires, by which more fleeting matter would be reduced to ashes and basic elements.

<margin>Fixed essences are separated from volatile impurities by the force of fire, just as with asbestos cloths <note>original: "asbestina lintea"; asbestos was famously "cleaned" by fire rather than water in antiquity, serving as a common metaphor for purification</note>; where the essence is volatile and the impurities are fixed, the opposite process is performed, etc.</margin>

But the <term>tenacity of the composition</term> <note>original: "concretionis tenacitas"; the physical bonding or "hardness" of a substance</note> is observed at the same time, which in some things cannot be overcome except by great heat. Hence, let it be established that the <term>chemist’s</term> <note>original: "chymico"</note> goal is for the most part not to dissolve the mixture entirely, but, while preserving it, to dissipate the locks and bonds of the materialized composition. This is done so that there may be an opening to the innermost substance, which nature has enclosed in the tightest embrace lest it be easily exposed to external harms. For the sake of this, fires are sometimes employed—be they large, medium, or small according to the firmness of each substance—and sometimes other instruments are used, etc.

It is plain to see what forms the chemist bestows by the benefit of natural and artificial instruments. He moves nature through nature; just as the farmer and gardener produce <term>pears</term> <note>original: "pyra"; a reference to the art of grafting, where a gardener assists nature to produce fruit the tree could not produce alone</note> from an apple tree. This form of creation does not oppose the Creator. There is another form belonging to bare art. This looks to the potential of matter and comes forth through deliberate design. Nor can the Creator regret this, as He is the one who gifted men with arts and equipped them with a free will for acting, etc. Man does not produce new species of nature; but to effect new species of art through his labor holds nothing absurd. A certain <term>transmutation</term> <note>original: "transmutatio"</note> through the aids of nature must also be granted to him, etc.

Lest we waste too much time by transcribing too many things and become a burden to the reader, we omit the rest, and bid the reader seek it from the epistolary work if—

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF GALENISM <note>original: "Galenia Triumphus"; likely the title of the larger work or section, perhaps used ironically here given the defense of chemistry that follows.</note></header>

## *The Censure of the Society of Chemists opposed to the spurious Parisian censure issued against Alchemy.*

The action of the censors in the medical college of the Parisian school against **Alchemy**—concerning its principles and essences, gold-making <term>chrysopeia</term> <note>The art of transmuting base metals into gold</note>, and other masterful works <term>magisteries</term>—having been diligently examined and carefully weighed on a just scale, is found to be an unjust condemnation. At the same time, it is clearly perceived that this censure was instituted and concocted out of a certain spite <note>original: "livore"; literally 'blueness' or 'bruise', used here to mean envy or malice</note> and malevolence by those who do not understand the precepts of true Alchemy. They have never learned nor experienced the preparations of chemical remedies for healthy use; they are ignorant of what is true, what is fraudulent, what is chemical medicine <term>chymiatria</term> <note>The application of chemistry to medical theory and treatment, as opposed to traditional herbal Galenism</note>, and what is Paracelsianism <term>Paracelsia</term> <note>The medical system of Paracelsus, which emphasized mineral cures and the "tria prima" (salt, sulfur, and mercury)</note>. 

While they wish to appear to have foolishly condemned some "fourth sect" of their own invention, they now proscribe the whole of Alchemy, the good along with the bad. Shortly thereafter, they send only mineral medicines into exile, even though they nevertheless—through a certain bold and shameless pettifogger <note>original: "rabula"; a term for a loud, unprincipled advocate or brawling speaker</note>—stubbornly attack the quintessence <term>essence fifth</term>, the principles, and all other things. They even seek to have the users of chemical remedies punished by death and desire that legal action be taken against those who publish books on gold-making. It is also seen that they rage with insults, slurs, calumnies, and lies to a miraculous degree—so furiously that this most excellent art is attributed to the Devil. Both the most ancient and the most recent chemists, who "separate the species from the matter," as Mesue <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), known as Mesue the Elder, an influential Persian physician whose works on pharmacy and simple medicines remained standard in Europe for centuries</note> says, [they] prepare...

<meta>Catchword: prepare,</meta>

<summary>This page contains a formal rebuttal by a group of chemists against the Medical Faculty of Paris, accusing the traditionalist doctors of condemning chemical medicine out of ignorance, malice, and professional jealousy. The text highlights the intense legal and religious stakes of the debate, including threats of capital punishment for those practicing "chrysopeia" or chemical medicine.</summary>

<header>ALCHEMY: CONCERNING THE SPURIOUS PARISIAN GALENIC TRIUMPH</header>
<meta>Catchword: lum</meta>

...they prepare, let them be called enemies of nature, insulting toward God and nature; and let students of medicine, along with physicians wherever they may be among the nations, be forewarned that they should not wish to initiate medical consultations with <term>chymiatrists</term> <note>Physicians who used chemical and mineral-based remedies, often following the school of Paracelsus</note>, nor use any medicines other than the ordinary ones that are congruent with <term>Galenic</term> <note>Referring to the traditional herbal and humoral medical system based on the teachings of the 2nd-century Greek physician Galen</note> prescription. No example of such madness <note>original: "rabiei"; literally 'rabies' or 'fury'</note> can be found in any age.

By unanimous consent and with one voice, the chemists and chymiatrists living among all nations decree that this censure is of no moment and of no authority; it is to be abolished, and—to the shame of its authors—affixed to the gallows of the condemned, or rooted out by the funeral flames. They also decree that the pamphlets written for this shameful censure by the pen of <term>Jean Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657), a staunch defender of Galenism and a fierce opponent of chemical medicine in Paris</note> should be deleted from human memory along with the name of their author. Finally, the monument which they have most stupidly erected to this most demented madness <note>original: "Maniæ dementissimæ"</note> ought to be cast headlong into the sewers and dung-heaps, and trampled underfoot, as is fair and just. 

Let the most just King of France see whether these censors are henceforth worthy of any authority to judge—always preserving the honor and dignity both of the Royal Academy and of those professors who were not partners in this most corrupt judgment. 

Furthermore, they ask all members of the clergy, politicians, physicians, natural philosophers, and all good men that they grant nothing to these anti-chemical censors. In no disease should they even expect, desire, or even ask for advice from these "adulterous" Galenists of deplorable ignorance and stubbornness; rather, being content with this, they should seek the method of proper healing from experienced chymiatrists. For thus, at last, the work of justice will be done, by which

->to each is given his own, and to the one thinking evil,<-
->evil happens.<-

<summary>A fierce counter-attack by the "Society of Chemists" against the Paris Medical Faculty and Jean Riolan, calling for the public shaming and destruction of the Faculty's anti-chemical decrees.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Riolan, Galenism, Chymiatria, Paris Medical Faculty, medical conflict, alchemy defense, King of France</keywords>

### ALCHEMY: CONCERNING THE SPURIOUS PARISIAN GALENIC TRIUMPH

...they prepare, let them be called enemies of nature, insulting toward God and nature; and let students of medicine, along with physicians wherever they may be among the nations, be forewarned that they should not wish to initiate medical consultations with <term>chymiatrists</term> <note>These were physicians who championed the use of chemical and mineral-based remedies, often inspired by the controversial Swiss doctor Paracelsus, rather than relying solely on traditional plant-based cures.</note>, nor use any medicines other than the ordinary ones that are congruent with <term>Galenic</term> <note>Referring to the traditional medical system based on the teachings of the 2nd-century Greek physician Galen, which focused on balancing the four bodily "humors."</note> prescription. No example of such madness <note>original: "rabiei"; this term implies not just insanity, but a frantic, aggressive rage or "fury."</note> can be found in any age.

By unanimous consent and with one voice, the chemists and chymiatrists living among all nations decree that this censure is of no moment and of no authority; it is to be abolished, and—to the shame of its authors—affixed to the gallows of the condemned, or rooted out by the funeral flames. They also decree that the pamphlets written for this shameful censure by the pen of <term>Jean Riolan</term> <note>Jean Riolan the Younger (1577–1657) was a prominent and highly conservative professor at the University of Paris who famously opposed both the circulation of the blood and the use of chemical medicines.</note> should be deleted from human memory along with the name of their author. Finally, the monument wh... <note>The text breaks off here. According to the page's metadata, the final word likely completed the phrase "evil monument" or "harmful monument," reflecting the chemists' view of the Parisian decree.</note>

<summary>This page captures a peak moment of the "Antimony War" in 17th-century medicine, recording a fierce counter-declaration by chemical physicians who reject the Parisian Faculty's attempt to ban their practices and call for the erasure of Jean Riolan's works.</summary>

<keywords>Chymiatry, Galenism, Jean Riolan, Paris Faculty of Medicine, medical controversy, chemical medicine, Paracelsianism</keywords>
